en: The Nyāya Darśana with the Bhāṣya of Vātsyāyana.

When there is comprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that means of valid cognition is effective because it possesses the capacity for successful purposeful action (*pravṛttisāmarthya*).
Without a means of valid cognition, there is no comprehension of an object; and without the comprehension of an object, there is no capacity for successful purposeful action.

Indeed, by means of a valid cognition (pramāṇa), this knower desires to acquire or desires to avoid an object. The effort of one thus impelled by the desire to acquire or avoid is called "activity" (pravṛtti). Furthermore, its efficacy consists in its connection with the result.
One who exerts effort, desiring to attain that object or wishing to abandon it, either attains that object or abandons it.
An object, moreover, consists of pleasure and the cause of pleasure,
as well as pain and the cause of pain.
Thus, this object of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is incalculable,
because the variety of living beings is incalculable.
And when the means of valid cognition possesses its object, then the knower, the object of knowledge, and the act of knowing likewise become purposeful.
Why? Because if any one of these were absent, the apprehension of the object would be impossible.

In this context, he who, impelled by the desire to acquire or the desire to avoid, engages in activity is the knower (*pramātṛ*); that by which he correctly cognizes the object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
That object which is cognized is the *prameya* (the object of knowledge); that cognition of the object is the *pramiti* (the result of knowledge);
and within these four, the true nature of reality (*arthatattva*) is fully encompassed.
What, then, is reality?
It is the existence of what exists and the non-existence of what does not exist.
That which is existent, being apprehended as "existent," is reality insofar as it is according to fact and non-erroneous.
Reality is that which is as it truly is and non-erroneous.
When the non-existent is apprehended as "non-existent," it becomes reality as it truly is and non-erroneous.
How, then, is the subsequent [object] apprehended by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
Because it is not perceived when that which is perceptible is being perceived, like a lamp.
Just as when an object visible by means of a lamp is grasped, that which is not grasped like it does not exist;
if it had existed, it would have been cognized just like this.
Because of the absence of cognition, it does not exist.

Thus, when something exists and is apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that which is not apprehended in the same manner as it does not exist. If it were to exist, it would be cognized just like this [thing].
Because consciousness does not exist, it is said that [the object] does not exist.
Thus, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while being a manifester of what exists, manifests even that which does not exist.
Furthermore, that which exists will indeed be taught as arranged in sixteenfold form.

Indeed, from the knowledge of the true nature of these sixteen categories— namely, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), tenet (*siddhānta*), members of a syllogism (*avayava*), reasoning (*tarka*), ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), discussion (*vāda*), wrangling (*jalpa*), cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), quibble (*chala*), futile rejoinder (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)— there arises the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
In the exposition, the analysis [of the compound] follows the literal wording.
The *dvandva* compound is used in the sense of "and.
In the phrase "the reality (tattva) of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth," the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation (*śaiṣikī*).
"The knowledge of reality is the attainment of the supreme good"— here the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
These are all the existing categories for the sake of which instruction is given here so that their knowledge may be non-erroneous.
[...vidyamānārthā... /p/32 This summary of the meaning of the system (tantrārtha) should be understood as presented without omission:

namely, that from the knowledge of the reality (tattvajñāna) of the objects of valid cognition (prameya), such as the self (ātman) and so forth, the attainment of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) occurs.
And this very point is restated by the subsequent sūtra:

"That which is to be abandoned, that which brings it about, abandonment itself as absolute, and the means thereto— having correctly understood these four categories of objects, one attains the supreme good."

In that regard, the separate mention of doubt and the other categories is purposeless—since doubt and the rest are included within the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) as the case may be, and do not exist apart from them.
This is true;
however, these four sciences (*vidyā*) are taught with distinct systems for the benefit of living beings.
Of those [sciences], this fourth is Ānvīkṣikī, the science of logic (*nyāyavidyā*). Its distinct categories (*pṛthakprasthāna*) are the topics (*padārtha*) beginning with doubt (*saṃśaya*).
If these were not stated separately, this [treatise] would be merely the inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*),
like the Upaniṣads.
Therefore, it is established as a distinct system by means of categories such as doubt and the rest.
In that regard, reasoning (*nyāya*) does not operate upon an object that is either unperceived or already determined; rather, it operates upon an object that is doubted.

As it has been said: "Determination (*nirṇaya*) is the ascertainment of the truth after having deliberated by means of the proponent's position (*pakṣa*) and the opponent's counter-position (*pratipakṣa*)."
Vimarśa is doubt.
The proponent's position and the opponent's counter-position constitute the operation of logic (*nyāya*).
The ascertainment of the object is the conclusion (*nirṇaya*), which is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
And that—namely, a non-ascertaining cognition consisting merely of an inquiry into the nature of an object, such as "What might this be?"—is doubt (*saṃśaya*).
While it is included within the category of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), it is mentioned separately for this purpose.
Now, as for the motive (*prayojana*): it is that by which one is impelled to act.
That is the purpose: that object which one desires to obtain or desires to avoid when one undertakes an action.
By this [Self], all living beings, all actions, and all sciences are pervaded,
and it is upon this that reasoning proceeds.
But what, then, is this reasoning?
Nyāya is the examination of objects by means of the instruments of valid cognition (pramāṇas).
Inference based upon perception and scripture is *anvīkṣā*;
it is the subsequent investigation (*anvīkṣaṇa*) of that which has been perceived through both perception and scripture.
That which proceeds by means of that [reasoning] is *ānvīkṣikī*—the science of logic (*nyāyavidyā*), the treatise on logic (*nyāyaśāstra*).
Furthermore, that inference which contradicts perception and scripture is a fallacy of logic (*nyāyābhāsa*).
Among these, debate (*vāda*) and sophistry (*jalpa*) are purposeful.
Now, cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) is examined. One who proceeds by means of cavil is a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*).
If, when questioned about his purpose, he admits [one], then that is his position (*pakṣa*), and that is his tenet (*siddhānta*).
He abandons his status as a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*).
Alternatively, if he does not establish [his own position], he falls into the state of being neither a worldly person nor an investigator.
Furthermore, even if he states that the purpose [of his argument] is to make known the refutation of the opponent's position, [he still fails].
This too is exactly the same:
if one accepts that there is one who makes known, one who knows, that by which something is made known, that which is made known, and that which is understood,
then one abandons the status of a mere caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*).
If, however, one does not proceed [to establish a position], then the statement that "the purpose is to make known the refutation of the opponent's side" becomes meaningless for him;
and a collection of such statements devoid of a formal proof-thesis (*sthāpanā*) is *vitaṇḍā*.
If he accepts its denotation, that becomes his thesis to be established;
but if he does not accept it, [it cannot be].
It becomes mere idle chatter and devoid of meaning; thus, the character of cavil (vitaṇḍā) is excluded.
Now, an example is an object that is within the scope of direct perception (pratyakṣa).

That in which the views of worldly investigators are not contradicted is also an object of cognition (*prameya*). Its separate mention is for the sake of [establishing] inference and scripture, which have that as their basis.

If that exists, inference and scripture would exist; if it does not exist, they would not exist. Furthermore, the operation of logic is dependent upon it, and the refutation of the opponent's position must be stated by means of a contradiction with their illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta).
Furthermore, one's own position is to be established by means of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
If a nihilist accepts an illustrative example, he abandons his nihilism;
if he does not accept it, what proof would he have with which to reproach his opponent?

And by means of etymological derivation and illustration, it is possible to state: "An example is an instance which, through similarity with the probandum, possesses the properties of that [probandum]" and "the opposite is the reverse. An object that is accepted as existing is a tenet (*siddhānta*), and that is an object of valid cognition (*prameya*).

The separate mention of these [three] is because debates— namely *vāda*, *jalpa*, and *vitaṇḍā*— proceed only when there exist distinct philosophical systems (*siddhāntabheda*), and not otherwise. The collection of words within which the establishment of the matter to be proven is completed consists of five members, beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*).
The parts are spoken of in relation to the whole;
among these, the convergence of the means of valid cognition is the scripture, which is the proposition (*pratijñā*).
The reason (*hetu*) is inference (*anumāna*);
the example (*udāharaṇa*) is perception (*pratyakṣa*);
the application (*upanayana*) is analogy (*upamāna*).
The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the demonstration of the capacity [of the proof] when all [the members] converge upon a single object.
This is the supreme method (*nyāya*).
It is by means of this that formal debate (*vāda*), sophistry (*jalpa*), and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) proceed, and not otherwise.
And the establishment of reality (tattvavyavasthā) is based upon that.
Furthermore, these members (avayava), being specific types of verbal expressions, are indeed included within the objects of knowledge (prameya); they are mentioned separately for this purpose.
Reasoning (tarka) is not subsumed under the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
It is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*);
rather, as an auxiliary to the means of valid cognition, it serves for the sake of knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
An example of this is: "Is this birth produced by a created cause?"
Or is it unconditioned, or is it accidental?
[It is] accidental.

When the matter is thus unknown, reasoning proceeds by means of the application of causes: "If it is produced by a caused factor, then this cessation of birth is logically established through the destruction of its cause;
but if it were produced by an uncaused factor,"
Therefore, because the severance of the cause is impossible, the severance of birth is untenable.
Alternatively, if it were accidental, then that which is produced by chance would not cease again; thus, a cause for its cessation is not established.
Thus, there is no cessation of birth.
Regarding this domain of reasoning, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that operate on the principle that "birth has karma as its cause" are supported by reasoning;
for reasoning serves the attainment of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) by way of distinguishing the objects of such knowledge.

This *tarka* (reasoning), being of such a nature and accompanied by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), serves for the establishment or the refutation of a matter in debate; it is for this reason that it is mentioned separately, even though it is included within the objects of knowledge (*prameya*).
Ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is the knowledge of reality, which is the fruit of the means of valid cognition;
debate culminates in that.
For the sake of its protection, these two— casuistry (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*)— carry on the course of worldly affairs;
this very determination (*nirṇaya*), being included within the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), has been separately mentioned for this purpose.

Debate (*vāda*) is indeed a collection of sentences involving various speakers, which establishes a proof for each respective point and concludes with the determination of one of those points. It has been mentioned separately for the sake of illustration.
Conventional discourse characterized by these [fallacies] serves the purpose of attaining knowledge of reality;
thus it is said: "The two specific types of this—disputation (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*)—are for the sake of protecting the determination of reality.
Furthermore, since fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) have been enumerated separately from the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), they will be subject to censure in formal debate (*vāda*).
Regarding the statement that "wrangling and cavilling consist of points of defeat":
the separate teaching of quibbles, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat is for the purpose of illustration;
once they have been illustrated, they are to be avoided in one's own discourse.

The interrogation of the opponent's statement regarding the fallacies (chala), the futile rejoinders (jāti), and the points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) is easy to manage when a *jāti* is employed by the opponent, as its refutation is readily available and its own application is easy to perform.

This very Ānvīkṣikī, being analyzed through categories such as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and so forth, is proclaimed in the enumeration of sciences as follows: "It is the lamp of all sciences, the means for all actions,
and the foundation of all duties."
This knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) should be understood according to its respective branches for the sake of attaining the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).

Here, however, in this science of the self (adhyātmavidyā), the knowledge of the self and so forth is the knowledge of reality; the attainment of the supreme good is the achievement of liberation (apavarga). //1//
Is that supreme good (niḥśreyasa) indeed something that occurs immediately after the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna)?
No, it is said.
What then? It arises from the knowledge of reality—
NyS 1.1.2: Upon the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, there follows the removal of each preceding member; from this, liberation results.
In that regard, false cognition of many kinds exists concerning the objects of knowledge beginning with the self and ending with liberation.
First, regarding the self, [there is the notion] "it does not exist";

regarding what is not the self, [the notion] "it is the self"; regarding suffering, [the notion] "it is pleasure"; regarding the impermanent, [the notion] "it is permanent"; and regarding what is not a refuge, [the notion] "it is a refuge."
In that which is without refuge, it is a refuge; in that which is full of fear, it is fearless; in that which is loathsome, it is desirable.
"Regarding that which is to be abandoned, one should not be obstructed;
in [the cycle of] active involvement, there is no karma,
and there is no fruit of karma."
Regarding the defects, it is not that this saṃsāra is caused by defects;
regarding rebirth, there is no creature, no living being, no sentient being, nor any self that could pass away.
And that there may be existence after death; thus,
birth is without cause,
and the cessation of birth is without cause— such is the beginningless state of existence after death.
And [the claim that] it is infinite:
[this refers to the view that] rebirth, though having a cause, is not caused by karma;
and [the view that] rebirth is soulless, occurring through the cessation of the continuum of body, sense-faculties, intellect, and sensation, followed by their reconnection.
In liberation, this indeed is the cessation of all activity and the dissociation from everything;
since much that is auspicious is lost in such a liberation, how could a wise person find pleasure in this liberation, which is the annihilation of all happiness and a state of insentience?
From this false knowledge arises attachment toward things that are favorable.
Hatred arises toward disagreeable things.
Due to the predominance of passion and hatred, defects such as falsehood, envy, deceit, and greed come into being.
Impelled by these defects, one who acts through the body commits violence, theft, and prohibited sexual intercourse.
Falsehood, harshness, calumny, and incoherent speech by way of speech;
malice toward others, the desire for another's property, and atheism by way of the mind—
this activity, being evil in nature, leads to unrighteousness (*adharma*).
Now, as for the auspicious [actions]: with the body, giving, protection, and service;
with speech, truthfulness, what is beneficial, what is pleasant, and the study of sacred texts; and with the mind, compassion, lack of greed, and faith.
This is for the sake of dharma.

Here, dharma and adharma, which are the means for engaging in activity, are expressed by the word "activity" (pravṛtti), just as life-breaths whose means are food are referred to as "food," according to the saying: "Food indeed is the life-breaths of living beings."
This very process of activity (pravṛtti) is the cause of birth, whether it be contemptible or honored.
Birth, moreover, is the manifestation of a specific aggregation of body, sense-faculties, and intellect;
when that exists, there is suffering.
Furthermore, that which is to be experienced as adverse consists of affliction, pain, and distress.
These factors, beginning with false knowledge and ending with suffering, proceeding without interruption, constitute *saṃsāra*.
However, when false knowledge departs due to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), [the cycle ceases].
Then, with the disappearance of false knowledge, the defects disappear; with the disappearance of the defects, activity disappears. (p. 80)
Upon the cessation of activity, birth ceases; upon the cessation of birth, suffering ceases;
and upon the cessation of suffering, there is absolute liberation, which is the supreme good.
True knowledge, indeed, is explained as the opposite of false knowledge:
namely, that there is a self where there is a self, and that there is no-self where there is no-self.
In this way, it should be understood according to their respective objects that [the world] is suffering, impermanent, unprotected, fearful, loathsome, and to be abandoned;
and regarding active involvement: "there is action, there is the fruit of action."
Regarding the defects: "This saṃsāra is caused by defects.
Regarding rebirth after death: "Indeed, there exists a creature, a living being, a sentient entity, or a self, which continues to exist after passing away."
Birth has a cause, and the cessation of birth has a cause; thus, transmigration (pretyabhāva) is beginningless and ends with liberation (apavarga).
Being caused, transmigration is the cause of [further] activity.
Being endowed with a self, it proceeds through the cessation and reconnection of the continuum of body, senses, intellect, and feelings;
indeed, liberation is peaceful, for liberation is the dissociation from everything and the cessation of everything.
Since much that is painful, terrible, and evil is abolished, how could a wise person not find pleasure in liberation—the destruction of all suffering and the non-experience of all suffering?
"One should not find pleasure in that which is devoid of liberation"— just as food mixed with honey and poison is not to be consumed,
so too pleasure that is followed by suffering is not to be accepted. //2//
The operation of this treatise is threefold:
namely, enumeration (uddeśa), definition (lakṇa), and critical examination (parīkṣā).
Among these, enumeration is the naming of categories by their mere designations.
[The definition: "By name... [is] the enunciation (*uddeśa*).
Among these, the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is the property that distinguishes the reality of what has been enunciated.
Investigation (*parīkṣā*) is the determination by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) as to whether that which has been characterized conforms to its characteristic or not.

Therein, the definition of that which has been mentioned and divided is stated—namely, [the definition] of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of valid cognition (*prameya*). As follows: p.85.

The statement of the classification of that which has been mentioned and that which has been defined, as for example: regarding *chala*, "Chala is the subversion of speech through the fabrication of alternative meanings," and "It is of three kinds."
Now, the statement regarding the division of what was previously mentioned:
*Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.3: Perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇas*).
Perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the operation (*vṛtti*) of each sense-organ (*akṣa*) with respect to its respective object.
This operation, however, is either contact (*sannikarṣa*) or cognition (*jñāna*).
When it is contact, then cognition is the resulting valid knowledge (*pramiti*).
When there is knowledge, then the cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, and indifference are the result.
Inference (*anumāna*) is the subsequent measurement (*māna*) of the object possessing the mark (*liṅgin*) by means of a measured mark (*liṅga*).
Comparison (*upamāna*)—which is the cognition of similarity—is, for example, "as is a cow, so is a gavaya. Similarity, moreover, is the connection with a common universal (*sāmānya*).
Verbal testimony (*śabda*)—that by which an object is expressed (*śabdyate*), that is, it is named or made known.

The means of apprehension are the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this should be understood from the force of the etymological definition of the term. For the word *pramāṇa* denotes an instrument in the sense that "by means of this, something is correctly cognized" (*pramīyate*).
The same explanation applies to the specific designations for its particular types as well.
Furthermore, do the means of valid cognition converge upon a single object of cognition, or do they remain distinct for each respective object of cognition?
Both views are observed.

The existence of the self (*ātman*) is understood from the instruction of a reliable authority (*āpta*), namely: "The self exists. Regarding this, there is inference: "Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks (*liṅga*) of the self.

And there is perception: for one who is practicing yoga, the self becomes perceptible through a specific conjunction of the self and the mind arising from yogic concentration (*samādhi*). Thus: "The self is perceived [directly] due to a particular contact between the self and the mind."
Fire is understood through the instruction of a reliable person as "there is fire here";
it is inferred by one approaching [the site] upon seeing smoke; and it is perceived directly by one who has reached its vicinity.
Furthermore, the formal injunction is: "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra";
regarding the worldly [notion of] heaven, there is neither observation of an indicative mark (liṅga) nor direct perception (pratyakṣa).
When the sound of thunder is heard, there is an inference of its cause; in that case, there is neither perception nor scripture.
When the hand is perceived through direct observation, there is neither inference nor scripture.
And this valid cognition culminates in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
One who understands an object of inquiry through the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*) still desires to know it even by means of observing a logical mark (*liṅga*). (p. 93)
And what is inferred through the observation of a mark one desires to see directly;
once the object has been apprehended, the desire to know ceases.
The previously mentioned example is "fire."
The occurrence of multiple means of valid cognition for a single cognizer is "convergence" (abhisaṃplava); their non-occurrence is "distinction" (vyavasthā). //3//

Thus ends the commentary on the three aphorisms. Now follows the definition of the [means of knowledge] as they have been distinguished: NyS 1.1.4: Perception is cognition produced by the contact of a sense organ with its object, which is non-verbal, non-erroneous, and of a determinate nature.
The knowledge that arises from the contact of a sense faculty with its object is perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In that case, this [following statement] would not now be possible:
"the self (*ātman*) is conjoined with the mind (*manas*)."
Is it that [the object is grasped] by means of the mental faculty (*manas*), or the faculty by means of the object?
This is not a restrictive determination of the cause— namely, that "this much alone is the cause of perception."
However, it is a statement regarding the specific cause;
that which is the specific cause of perceptual knowledge is stated here,
whereas that which is common to inferential and other types of knowledge is not.
"It does not cease.
Well then, should the conjunction of the mind with the sense organ be mentioned?
It is not mentioned because it is the same; for this [conjunction] does not differ when perceptual knowledge differs.
To whatever extent names and words correspond to objects, by means of them there is a comprehension of the object; and from the comprehension of the object, linguistic usage arises.
In this regard, the cognition of an object produced from the contact of a sense-organ with its object is "form," or—
Or it occurs as "taste" (*rasa*); and since the words "form" (*rūpa*) and "taste" (*rasa*) are designations for objects,
cognition is designated by them— one cognizes [it] as "form."
One cognizes it as "taste.
Since that which is designated by a name-word would result in being verbal (śābda), he says: "not expressible" (avyapadeśyam).
That cognition of an object which occurs when the relationship between word and meaning has not yet been employed is not designated by a name-word;
for even when the relationship between word and meaning has been grasped, one understands that "this word is the name of this object."
But when that object is apprehended, it is not distinguished from the prior cognition of the object.
That cognition of the object is exactly like that [cognition of the word]; however,
for that cognition of the object, there is no other denotative word by which it, being cognized, could be employed in linguistic usage.
Furthermore, there can be no linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) with respect to that which is not being cognized.

Therefore, the object to be known is indicated by means of a nominal word accompanied by the particle *iti*— for instance, "the cognition [that it is] form" (*rūpam iti jñānam*), or "the cognition [that it is] taste" (*rasa iti jñānam*).
Thus, at the time of the cognition of the object, that denotative word does not function;
however, it functions at the time of linguistic usage.
Therefore, the cognition of the object produced from the contact of the sense-organ with the object is non-verbal (aśābda).

In summer, rays of light mixed with terrestrial heat, flickering and brought into proximity by the eye of one standing at a distance, give rise to the cognition "this is water" due to the contact between the sense organ and the object; since this would result in [the definition] over-extending to such a case as being perception, he says: "non-deviating" (*avyabhicārī*).
"That which [perceives] something as being what it is not is a deviant perception.
For when one sees an object from a distance with the eye, one does not determine whether it is smoke or dust.

Consequently, it would follow that this indeterminate cognition produced by the contact of the sense-organ and the object is also perception; therefore, he says: "it consists of determination" (*vyavasāyātmakam*).
And it should not be thought that non-determinative cognition (*anavadhāraṇa-jñāna*) arises solely from the contact between the self and the mind;
for one perceives this object with the eye and yet does not determine it. (p. 122)
Just as one perceives an object with the mind that has been perceived by a sense organ,
so too, one does not determine with the mind what has not been determined by the sense organ.
And that non-determination by the mind which is preceded by non-determination by the sense organ— being a mere deliberation dependent upon specific qualities— is doubt (*saṃśaya*).
"Not previously" means that in every case regarding an object of perception, there is first an ascertainment by the knower through the sense faculty.
Subsequently, there is reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) by means of the mind, because those whose sense organs are impaired lack such reflective awareness.
Furthermore, the definition of perception must be stated with respect to the self and so forth, as well as pleasure and so forth.
For that [cognition] is not produced from the contact of a sense-organ with its object.
Indeed, although the mind is a sense-organ, it is taught separately from the other sense-organs because of a difference in its nature:
the sense-organs are composed of material elements and have restricted objects.
The sense-faculties have restricted objects,
and they possess the nature of sense-faculties only when endowed with their respective qualities;
the mind, however, is non-material and has all things as its object.
"The state of being a sense-organ does not belong to this [self] when it possesses qualities (*saguṇa*).

And when there is contact between a sense-organ and its object, we shall explain that its simultaneous presence and absence is the cause for the non-arising of simultaneous cognitions. [We shall explain its presence and absence... we shall explain. p. 129
And since the mind is of the nature of a sense faculty, no other definition need be stated;
this is to be understood from the established practice of other systems,
for it is a principle of system-building that what is not explicitly refuted is accepted as consented to.
Direct perception has been explained. //4//
Now, inference, which is preceded by that [perception], is of three kinds: that which has a prior [cause], that which has a remainder, and that which is observed through general correlation.

By the phrase "preceded by that" (*tatpūrvakam*), both the perception of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) and the perception of the mark itself are connected.
Through the perception of the related mark and the bearer of the mark, the recollection of the mark is connected.
By means of that recollection and the perception of the mark, the unperceived object is inferred.

"Like the former" (pūrvavat) refers to that case where an effect is inferred from a cause, such as when it is said, "there will be rain because of the rising of clouds. "The remainder-like" (śeṣavat) is that— where a cause is inferred from an effect.
Having observed that the water of a river has changed from its former state, and seeing its fullness and rapid flow, one infers from the current that rain has occurred;
this is *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation)—namely, the perception elsewhere of what was previously seen elsewhere [in another instance]. p.149
And likewise in the case of the sun;
therefore, there exists a motion of the sun even though it is imperceptible.
Alternatively, "as in the previous case" refers to those instances where, as before, upon seeing one of two things that were previously perceptible, there is an inference of the other.
Inference from perception is,
for example, [the inference of] fire by means of smoke.
That which is called *śeṣavat* is the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).

And when there is a negation of what has been proposed, since it does not apply elsewhere, there is a comprehension of that which remains; for example, when sound— having been distinguished from generality, particularity, and inherence by such [statements] as "it exists" and "it is impermanent"— is without distinction among substances, qualities, and actions,
and there arises a doubt regarding whether it is a substance, an action, or a quality.
It is not a substance,
because it consists of a single substance;
nor is it an action.
Because it is the cause of another sound, that which remains is this [sound]; thus there is the cognition of sound as a quality. (p. 156)

Inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is that wherein the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) is not perceived; rather, the unperceived bearer of the mark is known through the generality of the mark's connection with some other object, as for example, the self [is inferred] by means of desire and so forth,
since desire and the like are qualities (*guṇa*).
The qualities (guṇas) reside in substances;
that which is their locus is their self (ātman).

Since it is already established that [the treatise] is threefold by the very mention of its divisions, the explicit statement "threefold" is intended to show that the author—considering the extreme brevity of the aphorism through which this great system with its vast scope is taught—has no regard for any other kind of verbal economy.

Thus, he proceeded with such a variation in phrasing; indeed, the extensive practice in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), regarding quibbles (*chala*), words, and so forth, constitutes the nature of this treatise.
Perception has for its object that which exists, whereas inference has for its object both that which exists and that which does not exist.
Why?
Because it grasps all three periods of time.
Objects associated with the three times are apprehended through inference;
it is inferred that "it will be," and "it is."
And it was so; moreover, the past and the future are indeed non-existent. //5//
Now, as for analogy (upamāna):
NyS 1.1.6: Analogy is the means of establishing the object to be established through its well-known similarity [to another object].
Analogy (*upamāna*) is the making known of that which is to be made known through its similarity to something already known;
for example, "as is a cow, so is a gavaya.
But what, then, is accomplished here by analogy?
When one indeed apprehends the common property with a cow, one then apprehends that object through direct perception;
thus he says that the apprehension of the relationship between a name and its referent is the purpose of analogy (*upamāna*).

When the analogy "As is a cow, so is a *gavaya*" is employed, one perceives the object possessing properties in common with a cow through the contact of the sense organ with the object, and [thereby understands] "the word *gavaya* is the name for this"—thus [one grasps] the relationship between the name and the named.
"It is understood thus:
just as a cow is, so is a gavaya... it is understood.
As the mung bean is, so is the mudgaparṇī.

Just as when the comparison "māṣaparṇī is like a bean (māṣa)" is employed, one who understands the relationship between the name and the named through that comparison fetches that medicinal herb for the purpose of medicine;
in this way, other instances of the scope of comparison in the world should also be understood. //6//
Now, as for verbal testimony (śabda): Nyāyasūtra 1.1.7: Verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person (āpta).
An authoritative person (*āpta*) is indeed one who has directly realized the Dharma; being motivated by the desire to communicate an object exactly as it was perceived, he acts as a teacher.
Direct realization of an object is "attainment" (*āpti*); because he proceeds by means of that, he is called "authoritative" (*āpta*).
The characteristic [of speech] is the same for sages, Aryans, and Mlecchas;
likewise, the linguistic conventions of all people proceed in this same way.
Thus, by means of these instruments of knowledge, the linguistic conventions of gods, humans, and animals are established;
it is not otherwise than this. //7//
It is of two kinds, because its objects are either perceived or unperceived.
That whose purpose is perceived here in this world is one with visible purpose; that whose purpose is understood there in the next world is one with invisible purpose.
Such is the distinction between the words of sages and those of worldly people.
But for what purpose is this stated?
It is so that he should not think: "The instruction of a reliable person is a means of valid cognition only when its object is already perceived, because the object has been ascertained."
Even that which has an unseen object is a means of valid cognition, because the object is inferred from it. //8//
But what, then, is the collection of objects to be known by this means of valid cognition?
— NS 1.1.9: The objects of knowledge (prameya), however, are the self, the body, the sense organs, the objects, intellect, mind, activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation.
In this system, the self (ātman) is the seer of all, the enjoyer of all, omniscient, and the experiencer of all.
Its locus of experience is the body;
its instruments of experience are the sense organs.

The objects of the senses are to be experienced; experience is the intellect (*buddhi*). Since the sense organs are not capable of perceiving all objects, the internal organ that encompasses all objects is the mind (*manas*).
The cause of the cessation of the body, the senses, objects, intellect, pleasure, and pain is activity (*pravṛtti*) and the defects (*doṣas*).
This body of his is neither unprecedented nor final;
there is no beginning to previous bodies.
The end of liberation for those who follow the higher path is "pretyabhāva" (rebirth after death).
Its fruit is the experience of pleasure and pain along with their causes.
By the term "suffering," this is not a rejection of pleasure as something experienced as agreeable; rather, it is [a statement] regarding [the nature of existence].

What then? It is taught that this very birth, together with its means of pleasure, is suffering because it is accompanied by suffering, because there is no separation from suffering, and because it is joined with manifold afflictions; thus, the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is instructed. One who is concentrated cultivates [this].
By contemplating [this], one becomes weary;
for one who is weary, there is dispassion;
for one who is dispassionate, there is liberation.
The severance of the continuity of birth and death and the abandonment of all suffering is liberation (*apavarga*).
Furthermore, there is another object of valid cognition (*prameya*), namely substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence;
and through its subdivisions, it is incalculable.
However, since liberation results from the knowledge of reality while worldly existence results from false knowledge, this has been taught specifically for that purpose. //9//
In this regard, the self is not apprehended through direct perception.
Is it then understood solely on the basis of authoritative instruction?
No, it is said.
And it is to be understood through inference. How so?
Nyāyasūtra 1.1.10: Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks (liṅga) of the self.
When one has experienced pleasure through contact with an object of a certain kind,

upon seeing an object of that very same kind, one desires to acquire it; this desire to acquire arises from the synthesis of perceptions belonging to one who perceives multiple objects, and it is the mark (liṅga) of the self.
For a mere difference in cognition regarding a fixed object is not possible [for a single entity] as it is in the case of different bodies;
thus, for one who perceives multiple objects, aversion toward the cause of suffering arises from the synthesis of those perceptions.

[...hatred toward one who perceives multiple objects: When a person perceives an object of a certain kind that is well-known to be a cause of pleasure for him, he exerts himself to acquire another object of that same kind.
This would not be possible without a single perceiver who observes multiple objects and connects those observations.
This is not possible in the case of mere cognition regarding a restricted object,
as in the case of another body;
by this, effort directed toward a cause of suffering is also explained.
Furthermore, through mindfulness of pleasure and pain, this person, while undertaking the means for those [experiences], experiences pleasure, experiences pain,
and feels pleasure and pain;
the reason is exactly as previously stated.
Indeed, one who desires to know reflects, "What might this be?"; and while reflecting, he knows, "This is it.
Thus, this knowledge—being perceived as having the same agent as both the desire to know and the reflection—is the inferential mark (liṅga) of the self.
The reason is precisely that which was stated previously.

In this regard, the phrase "like [cognitions] in another body" is analyzed as follows: just as for one who maintains the doctrine of non-self (*anātmavādin*), distinct cognitions restricted to specific objects in different bodies are not synthesized, so too cognitions restricted to a single body would not be synthesized, because there is no distinction between the two cases.
Such is the conduct of this single being: it is the recollection of what was seen by oneself,
not of what was seen by another, nor of what was not seen at all.

Thus, indeed, the conduct of various beings is such that one who has seen something does not remember it as another; therefore, both of these [facts] cannot be established by one who maintains the doctrine of no-self (*anātmavādin*). Consequently, it is logically established that the self exists. //10//
Its locus for experience (bhoga) is as follows:
NS 1.1.11: The body is the substratum of movement, the sense organs, and their objects.

And how is it the substratum of effort (*ceṣṭā*)? With reference to an object that is desired to be obtained or avoided, the exertion (*samīhā*) characterized by the performance of the means thereto—belonging to one impelled by the desire to obtain or avoid—is "effort" (*ceṣṭā*); that body in which this [effort] resides is the substratum of effort.
That body is characterized by the practice of the means for that [attainment].
How is it the support of the sense faculties?
That body is their support because, through its favor they are favored and through its injury they are injured, and thus they operate upon their respective objects—whether good or bad.
How is it that they have the object as their basis?
That [object] is their basis; that is their body.
How is it that they have the object as their basis? p.195

That locus in which the experience of pleasure and pain, produced from the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects, occurs—that is their substratum; that body is the substratum in which the experience of pleasure and pain occurs. //11//
Furthermore, the instruments for the enjoyment of objects—Nyāyasūtra 1.1.12: the sense organs, namely the olfactory, gustatory, visual, tactile, and auditory, [are produced] from the elements.
The nose (*ghrāṇa*) is so called because one smells by means of it; it perceives odor.
The tongue (*rasana*) is so called because one tastes by means of it; it perceives flavor. The eye (*cakṣus*) is so called because one sees by means of it; it perceives form.
The sense faculty whose location is the skin is the skin itself. Its metaphorical designation [as "the sense of touch"] is based on its location. p.198
It is called "ear" (*śrotra*) because one hears by means of it; it grasps sound.
Thus, by the force of this etymological definition, it should be understood that the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are characterized by the apprehension of their own respective objects.
[The phrase] "from the elements" (*bhūtebhyaḥ*)...
For these [senses] which possess diverse constituent natures (*prakṛti*), there is a restriction of their respective objects, but not for those with a single constituent nature.
And when there is such a restriction of objects, they possess the characteristic of grasping their own specific objects. //12//
What, then, are the causes of the sense organs?
NS 1.1.13: Earth, water, fire, air, and ether are the elements.
The separate teaching of the elements as distinct from their designations and words will be easy to express and will serve its purpose. //13//
Now, indeed—NyS 1.1.14: odor, taste, color, touch, and sound are the qualities of earth and the other elements; they are the objects of those [senses].
The qualities of earth and the other elements correspond to their respective functions; the objects of the sense organs, in their proper order, are the [corresponding] sense-objects. //14//

As if rejecting the meaning that contradicts reason—namely, that the function of the insentient instrument, the intellect (*buddhi*), is "cognition" (*jñāna*), while the perception of the sentient non-agent is "apprehension" (*upalabdhi*)—he says this:
"Intellect, apprehension, and cognition are not different in meaning" (NyS 1.1.15).
Knowledge cannot belong to the insentient instrument, the intellect;
for that [intellect] would have to be sentient,
and this sentient being is one, distinct from the aggregate of the body and the senses.

[The phrase] "distinct from the aggregate of the body and the senses" is the manifestation of another meaning for the sentence whose purpose is to define the object of cognition (*prameya*), by virtue of the power of logical justification. //15//
Memory, inference, verbal testimony, doubt, intuition, dream-cognition, deliberation, the direct perception of pleasure and so forth, and desire and the like are the marks of the mind.
When these exist, this too—namely, the non-arising of cognition when [the senses] are in contact [with their objects]—is a mark of the mind. (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.16)
Memory and the other [mental functions] must have causes other than the sense organs, since they are not themselves sense organs.
Furthermore, when the contacts between the nose and the other [senses] with their respective objects, such as odors, occur simultaneously, cognitions do not arise all at once.
Indeed, even though the contacts of the nose and the others with odors and so forth are simultaneous, cognitions do not arise simultaneously.

From this it is inferred that there exists another non-pervasive auxiliary cause conjoined with that sense organ, due to the absence of which cognition does not arise, and due to the presence of which it does arise.
[The opponent argues: "Cognition arises from proximity [alone].
For if the contact between the sense organ and the object were the cause of cognition without depending on the conjunction with the mind (*manas*), cognitions would arise simultaneously. //16//
Now, that which follows in order—NyS 1.1.17: Activity (pravṛtti) is the initiation of speech, intellect, and body.
In this context, "mind" (manas) is intended to mean "intellect" (buddhi),
for intellect is that by which one understands.
This undertaking— whether meritorious or sinful— is tenfold, consisting of actions performed with the body, speech, and mind.
This constitutes the commentary on the second sūtra. //17//
The defects (doṣas) are characterized by incitement to activity.
*Pravartanā* is the state of being a cause for engagement;
for it is passion and the like that impel the knower toward merit or demerit,
since where there is false cognition, there is passion and aversion.
Why are these faults, which are to be personally realized within oneself, described by way of their characteristics?
Indeed, those who are lustful, hateful, and deluded are characterized by their actions;
for one who is lustful performs that action by which, through that very action, one obtains pleasure or pain.
"Likewise the hateful, likewise the deluded"—when one speaks of passion, hatred, and delusion, much has been said. //18//
NyS 1.1.19: Rebirth after death is pretyabhāva.

Rebirth after death (*pretyabhāva*) is the renewed arising, after having died, within some class of sentient beings of one who has already arisen— that is, one who is bound. This "bondage," however, consists in connection with the body, the sense faculties, the mind, the intellect, and feelings.
Rebirth—this refers to the connection with a body and so forth once again.
The word "again" denotes repetition.
Wherever one exists within the class of living beings, one abandons the body and other factors previously acquired; that is what is meant by "departing."

One abandons the body and other aggregates previously acquired and departs from them; that which there or elsewhere one takes up as other bodies and so forth is "existence after death" (*pretyabhāva*)— that is, birth again after having died.
Thus, this practice of the continuous succession of birth and death, which is beginningless and terminates in liberation, is to be understood as *pretyabhāva* (rebirth). //19//
NyS 1.1.20: The object produced by activity and defects is the result.
The experience of pleasure and pain is the fruit;
it consists of karma that ripens as pleasure and karma that ripens as pain.
Furthermore, since this occurs when the body, sense faculties, objects, and cognitions exist, the fruit is intended here as being together with the body and the other factors.
For in this way, all this result arises as an object produced by activity and defects;
that very result, once acquired, must be abandoned again and again.
Thinking "what is abandoned is to be taken up again," there is for him no finality or conclusion regarding abandonment and acquisition;
indeed, this world is carried away by the currents of abandoning and acquiring the fruits [of action]. //20//
Now, this very [point]:
NyS 1.1.21: Suffering is characterized by affliction.
"Affliction," "torment," and "fever"—
that which is permeated by these, followed by them, and existing inseparably from them is called "suffering" because of its connection with suffering.
Thus, seeing that all this is permeated by suffering, one who desires to abandon suffering becomes disenchanted with birth upon seeing it as suffering.
Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; being dispassionate, one is liberated. //21//
But that wherein there is finality, that wherein there is the ultimate goal—this is it: "Apavarga is the absolute liberation from that [pain]. (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.22)
By that birth characterized by suffering, there is absolute liberation, which is *apavarga*.
How so? Through the relinquishing of the birth already acquired and the non-acquisition of another.
Those who know liberation describe this state as infinite liberation;
it is the fearless, undecaying, immortal station of Brahman, the attainment of security.
Eternal bliss, like the greatness of the Self, is manifested in liberation.
Some believe that when [the self] is manifested, it appears as one who is utterly liberated and happy;
however, their position is untenable due to a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*).
There exists neither perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor inference (*anumāna*), nor scripture (*āgama*) to establish that eternal happiness manifests in liberation for the self, just as its greatness does.
The manifestation of the eternal is its perception;
this is the statement of its cause.
Manifestation of the eternal is perception, which is to say, knowledge.
Its cause must be stated, from which it arises.
If it is argued that it is eternal like pleasure, then there would be no distinction between one abiding in saṃsāra and one who is liberated.

Just as one who is liberated would necessarily be endowed with pleasure and its perception as something eternal, so too would one remaining in saṃsāra be so endowed; for both [states] would be eternal.
And if this were admitted, then the concomitance of the fruit of dharma and adharma with the self would have to be perceived as simultaneous.
If this fruit of merit and demerit— namely pleasure or pain— is experienced alternately in its various places of origin,
then that experience and the permanent consciousness would be perceived as coexistent and simultaneous;
there would be neither an absence of pleasure nor a lack of manifestation.
Because both [liberation and the experience] would be eternal;
if it were non-eternal, there would be a need for a statement of its cause.
Now, is the perception of the eternal bliss in liberation itself non-eternal?
That from which [an effect] arises must be stated as its cause.
Is it the conjunction of the self and the mind, accompanied by other instrumental factors, that possesses causality?
If you say that the conjunction of the self and the mind is the cause?
Even so, another auxiliary cause for that must be stated;
this is the statement of the cause of dharma. If dharma is [itself] another cause?
The cause from which it arises must be stated.
Since there is a contradiction with the determination of the effect for that which is born of yoga and meditative concentration (*yoga-samādhi*), consciousness ceases upon its exhaustion.
[Objection: If the dharma born of yoga and meditative concentration is the cause?
[The dharma born of samādhi is the cause:
because it is incompatible with the determination of an effect, consciousness ceases entirely upon its exhaustion;
and in the absence of consciousness, there is no distinction from that which does not exist.
If it is argued that because of the cessation of sensation due to the exhaustion of phenomena, eternal happiness is not experienced— then is it that which exists which is not experienced,
or that which does not exist? There is no such inference regarding a specific case.
Furthermore, there is no inference for the non-destruction of dharma, because it possesses the property of arising.
There is no inference to support the claim that "dharma born of yoga and meditative concentration does not perish";
rather, there is an inference for the opposite, namely, that "whatever possesses the property of arising is impermanent."
However, for one for whom there is no cessation of cognition, it must be inferred that the cause of cognition is eternal;
and it has been stated that if [the cause] were eternal, there would be no distinction between those in liberation and those remaining in saṃsāra—
just as, for example, the liberated one possesses eternal bliss and its cause of cognition.
However, there is no cessation of consciousness because its cause is eternal;
likewise, this is also the case for one who remains in saṃsāra.
And this being the case, there would be perceived a concomitance with the experience of pleasure and pain, which is the fruit of merit and demerit.

If it is argued that the connection with a body and so forth is the cause of this restriction, we say no; for bodies and the like exist for the purpose of experience, and the contrary cannot be inferred.
[And because there is no inference for the contrary.
It might be thought: "The connection with the body and so forth belonging to one in the state of saṃsāra is an obstacle to the cause of the perception of eternal bliss;
therefore, there is no lack of distinction [between the two states]."
And this is incorrect:
it is untenable that the body and so forth, which exist for the sake of experience, would bring about an obstruction to that experience;
nor is there any inference that a bodiless self possesses any experience whatsoever.
If it is argued that activity is for the sake of attaining what is desired, we say no, because its purpose is the cessation of the undesired.
This is the inference: the instruction on liberation and the activity of those seeking liberation have as their object the attainment of what is desired.
"Neither [of these] is purposeless"—
this too is incorrect, because the teaching on liberation has as its ultimate goal the cessation of what is undesirable, and yet there is the engagement of those seeking liberation.
Since it is not possible for the desired to occur without being interwoven with the undesired, even the desired turns into the undesired;
and while striving to eliminate the undesired, one also loses the desired, because it is impossible to abandon [the two] through discrimination.
Furthermore, the transcendence of what is observed is the same in the case of the body and so forth.
Just as one abandons observed impermanent pleasure and desires permanent pleasure,
so too, having transcended the impermanent body, senses, and intellects that are observed, one must postulate permanent body, senses, and intellects for the liberated one.
Furthermore, in this way, the imagined identity of the liberated one with [the body] becomes even more consistent.
If it is argued that this contradicts logical reasoning, then the same applies [to your position]:
it is impossible to postulate the eternality of the body and so forth, as it contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

It is impossible to postulate that the permanence of happiness is the same [as that of suffering], for such a claim contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, even if there were a scriptural statement (*āgama*) asserting happiness, there would be no contradiction, provided it refers to the absolute absence of the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
Even if some scripture were to state that the liberated one possesses absolute happiness, [there would still be no conflict].
[Is there some scripture that states] "the liberated one has ultimate happiness"?
It is thus established that the word "happiness" (sukha) is employed for the absolute absence of suffering;
for indeed, the use of the word "happiness" in the sense of the absence of suffering is frequently observed in the world.
If passion for eternal bliss is not abandoned, there can be no attainment of liberation,
because passion is known to be a bond.
If it is argued that this liberation is simply the manifestation of eternal bliss, [the response follows].
One who strives for liberation through attachment to eternal pleasure would not attain liberation;
indeed, he is not fit to attain it. For passion is designated as bondage.
And it is not tenable that anyone is liberated while bondage still exists;
for there is no lack of aversion toward one who has not abandoned attachment to eternal bliss.
Now, if his attachment to eternal bliss is abandoned, [then liberation is possible].
When that [craving] has been abandoned, does his attachment to eternal happiness not become adverse?
If this is so, then for one who is liberated, there is either eternal happiness,
or else it does not exist.
For him, the attainment of liberation is not conceptualized in terms of either of these two positions. //22//
In that case, the definition of doubt, which possesses a specific locus, must be stated; thus it is said:

NyS 1.1.23: Doubt is a deliberation requiring further investigation [of the particulars], arising from the perception of common or multiple properties, from conflicting testimony, and from the lack of determination regarding perception and non-perception.
"Doubt is a deliberation that depends on a particularity, arising from the perception of common properties.

Seeing the common properties of height and girth in both a post and a person, and desiring to know the previously observed particularity of those two, one does not determine either one, thinking "what could it be?
This lack of determination is the cognition known as doubt.
The cognition that "I perceive the common property of these two, but I do not perceive the distinguishing property of either one" is *apekṣā* (expectancy);
this expectancy exists as the precursor to the arising of doubt.
Therefore, doubt is a deliberation that depends upon a distinguishing feature,
[as stated in the definition] "because of the occurrence of multiple properties. Here,
"multiple" refers to both that which is of the same class and that which is of a different class.
Because that manifold [entity] possesses various properties— [that is,
because of the occurrence of properties]—
and because its specific characteristics are observed in both ways.
Objects are distinguished from those of the same class as well as from those of different classes;

for example, earth is distinguished from water and fire by its possession of odor, and it is distinguished from qualities and actions as well. Furthermore, sound possesses the specific characteristic of being produced by disjunction.
Regarding that [object], there arises a doubt as to whether it is a substance, a quality, or an action,
because the specific characteristic is observed in both ways.
Is it a distinction of a substance that exists [as such] from qualities and actions, or rather of a quality that exists [as such], or of an action that exists [as such]?
"Dependence on a distinction" means the cognition that one does not perceive a defining property (*dharma*) for any one [of the two].
"Disagreement" (*vipratipatti*) means a contradictory perception of a single object.
Contradiction (vyāghāta) means opposition or non-coexistence.
"The self exists" is one view; "the self does not exist" is another.
Furthermore, existence and non-existence cannot coexist in one and the same place,
nor is a reason found that establishes either one; therefore, the lack of determination regarding the true nature of the object is doubt.
Furthermore, because perception occurs in dependence upon parts, water is perceived in ponds and the like where it exists,
yet water is also perceived in mirages where it does not exist.

Therefore, when something is being perceived, since the means of valid cognition that determines its true nature has not been apprehended, a doubt arises as to whether what is perceived is real or unreal.
Because of the lack of a fixed rule regarding non-apprehension:
that which exists, such as a tree-root, a stake, or water, is not apprehended;
and that which does not exist, such as what is unarisen or ceased, is likewise not apprehended.
Or, when something obstructed [is not perceived], then, since it is not being perceived in some place, a doubt arises:
"Is it that what exists is not perceived, or is it that what does not exist [is not perceived]? Thus there is doubt.
The requirement for a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣāpekṣā*) is as before.
The preceding [characteristics]—the common and the manifold properties—reside in the object of knowledge (*jñeya*);
however, apprehension (*upalabdhi*) and non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) reside in the knower (*jñātṛ*).

This repetition is for the sake of specifying the distinction: [p.255] "Doubt is a state of hesitation dependent upon the recollection of a specific difference, arising from the perception of common properties and the occurrence of common properties. //23//
The definition of those things that possess a locus is the same [as before].
NyS 1.1.24: That object with reference to which one acts is the purpose (*prayojana*).
That object which one undertakes to attain or abandon after having determined the means for its attainment or abandonment— that should be known as the *prayojana* (purpose),
because it is the cause of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).
The "exercise of authority" (adhikāra) over an object is the determination that "I shall attain this object" or "I shall abandon it";
thus, an object being so determined is said to be "exercised" (adhikriyate). //24//
NyS 1.1.25: That object regarding which there is a consensus of understanding among ordinary people and experts is an example (dṛṣṭānta).

Those who have not transcended worldly commonality are the worldly; they have not attained either innate or acquired excellence of intellect. Those who are the opposite of them are the investigators (*parīkṣaka*);
they are capable of investigating an object through reasoning and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Just as worldly people understand a certain object, so too do investigators;
that object which worldly people [understand] is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

For it is by means of a contradiction with an example that opposing positions are to be refuted, and by means of the resolution through an example that one's own position is to be established; thus, it serves as the illustration among the members [of the syllogism]. //25//
Now, as for the *siddhānta*:
the collection of objects that is accepted as being "thus" and "of such a nature" is established (*siddha*);
the formal establishment of what is established is the *siddhānta*.

Establishment (*saṃsthiti*) is the determination of a state of being, the fixed rule of things (*dharmaniyama*). Indeed, this is as follows: *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.26: "A tenet (*siddhānta*) is the establishment of a system, a topic, or an admission."
The establishment of the meaning of the tantra (*tantrārthasaṃsthiti*) is the establishment of the tantra (*tantrasaṃsthiti*);
a tantra is a treatise (*śāstra*) that is an instruction on a collection of meanings mutually interconnected.
The establishment of the meanings connected to the topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) is the establishment of the topical sections (*adhikaraṇasaṃsthiti*).

The establishment of a formal admission (*abhyupagama-saṃsthiti*) is the acceptance of a matter that has not yet been definitively determined; it is the "admitted tenet" (*abhyupagama-siddhānta*) for the purpose of examining its specific details.
However, due to the division of systems (*tantra-bheda*), indeed...
And that [acknowledgment] is of four kinds, because of its existence as the object of the entire treatise, of a specific treatise, of a context, and of a provisional admission.
In this regard, these four established positions constitute the meaning of the subject matter. //27//
Among these—NyS 1.1.28: An object that is not contradicted by any system and is authorized within a system is a tenet common to all systems (*sarvatantrasiddhānta*).

Just as the sense organs such as the nose, the objects appropriate for those organs such as odor, and the primary elements such as earth, [are established] by means of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too is the apprehension of an object [established]. //28//
NyS 1.1.29: A tenet established in one's own school but not established in other schools is a tenet specific to that school (pratitantrasiddhānta).
Just as there is no acquisition of self-nature for that which is non-existent, nor the loss of self-nature for that which is existent,
and as consciousnesses are without distinction— despite the differences found in the body, senses, mind, objects, and their respective causes— such is the view of the Sāṅkhyas.
The creation of the elements has its cause in the karma of persons and so forth;
the defects and worldly activity have karma as their cause;
and conscious beings are distinguished by their own specific qualities.
"That which is non-existent arises, and that which has arisen ceases"—this is the view of the Yogas. //29//
NyS 1.1.30: That, upon the establishment of which there is the establishment of another matter, is the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion based on a foundational premise).
When, upon the establishment of a certain matter, other matters follow as necessary consequences—
such that without them that matter cannot be established— and those matters have that [original matter] as their basis, that is an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a tenet established by the context).

Just as the cognizer is established as distinct from the body and the senses by the principle "because of the apprehension of a single object through both seeing and touching," so too, in this context, the following corollary points are established:
the plurality of the senses; that the senses have restricted objects and are the instruments of the cognizer's knowledge, as indicated by their respective apprehensions of their own objects;

that substance is distinct from qualities such as odor and is the substratum of qualities; and that consciousnesses have unrestricted objects. These are established upon the proof of the preceding point, for that primary point could not be possible without them. //30//
NyS 1.1.31: The examination of the specific characteristics of that which has been accepted without prior investigation is the tenet of acceptance (abhyupagama-siddhānta).
Where some category of object is accepted without prior investigation—
such as, "Let sound be a substance; but is it eternal or non-eternal?"—
it is the specific quality of that which exists as a substance, namely its eternality or non-eternality, that is being investigated.
This is the *abhyupagamasiddhānta* (presumptive tenet); it proceeds from a desire to proclaim one's own superior intellect and from a disregard for the intellect of others. //31//
Now, the members [of a syllogism]:
Nyāyasūtra 1.1.32: The thesis (pratijñā), the reason (hetu), the example (udāharaṇa), the application (upanaya), and the conclusion (nigamana) are the members.
Some Naiyāyikas enumerate ten members in a formal argument:
inquiry, doubt, possibility of attainment, purpose, and the removal of doubt; why are these not mentioned?
In that regard, when an object is not yet cognized, there arises a desire to know (jijñāsā) which impels one toward the object of cognition.
Why does one desire to know an unapprehended object?
Because one thinks: "Once it is known in its true nature, I shall either abandon it, or accept it, or remain indifferent toward it."
These cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, and indifference are the purpose of the knowledge of reality; for that purpose,
one desires to know it.
Indeed, this [inquiry] is not a means for the object itself;
rather, doubt, which is the locus of the desire to know, is proximate to the knowledge of reality because it involves a collection of contradictory properties,
for between two contradictory properties, one must necessarily be the truth.
Even though it is taught separately, it is not a means for the realization of the object;
for the instruments of knowledge (pramāṇas) belong to the knower and serve the purpose of apprehending the objects of knowledge (prameya).
That "attainability" is not logically connected with a constituent part of the statement that establishes [the thesis], such as the proposition (pratijñā) and so forth.
The purpose is the ascertainment of reality; it is the fruit of a statement that establishes a point, not merely a part thereof.

The refutation of doubt and the description of opposing views are for the sake of permitting the knowledge of reality by means of their negation, but they are not themselves parts of the statement that establishes the point.

In this context, however, [the elements] such as the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) are capable [of being considered members], because they assist in the determination of the object to be established. On the other hand, because they bring about the realization of the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha*), the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth are the parts, portions, or members (*avayava*) of the argumentative statement that establishes it. (32)
Of those [members], as they have been divided:
NyS 1.1.33: The statement of that which is to be proven is the proposition (*pratijñā*).

A thesis (*pratijñā*) is the statement that apprehends a qualified subject (*dharmin*) by means of a property (*dharma*) to be made known; it is the indication of what is to be proven (*sādhya*), as in: "Sound is impermanent. (33)
NyS 1.1.34: The reason (hetu) is the means of proving the probandum through its similarity to the example.
The reason (*hetu*) is the proof or demonstration of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) by means of its similarity with the example (*udāharaṇa*).

Having connected the property to the subject to be proven and having connected it to the example, the statement of its being the means of proof is the reason; for instance, "because of the quality of having the nature of arising" (*utpattidharmakatvāt*).
[Regarding the phrase] "because it has the nature of arising": that which has the nature of arising is seen to be impermanent. // 34 //
Is this the complete definition of a reason (*hetu*)?
No, it is said. What then?
Nyāyasūtra 1.1.35: Likewise [it is established] through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
And because of dissimilarity with the example, the reason is that which establishes the probandum.
How so? "Sound is impermanent because it possesses the property of being produced;
that which does not possess the property of being produced is permanent, as for instance the substance of the self and so forth. //35//
NS 1.1.36: An example is an instance which, by virtue of its similarity to the subject of proof, possesses the property of that [subject].
Similarity with the probandum (sādhya) is the state of possessing a common property.
Because of this similarity with the probandum, the example is that which possesses the properties of that [probandum]. [Example. p. 308
"His property" (*taddharma*) means the property of that [subject];
"of that" refers to the probandum (*sādhya*).
And the probandum is of two kinds: either a property qualified by the subject, such as "the impermanence of sound," or...
Or, [the example] "sound, which possesses the property, is impermanent" is qualified by the property (*dharma*).
Here, the answer is that it is included by the mention of "that" (*tat*);
why? Because the property is stated separately.

The property of that is "its property" (*taddharma*); the state of being that property is "the state of having that property" (*taddharmabhāva*). That example in which this state exists is the illustrative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*). Because of its similarity to the probandum (*sādhyasādharmya*), that which possesses the state of having that property—namely, the quality of having the nature of arising (*utpattidharmakatva*)—is intended as the "example" (*udāharaṇa*). In this context, whatever arises is "that which has the nature of arising."
And that which, having come into being, does not remain, but abandons its own nature and ceases, is impermanent.
Thus, the property of having the characteristic of arising is the probans (*sādhana*), and impermanence is the probandum (*sādhya*).
This relationship between two properties—one as the probandum and the other as the probans—is established and perceived through similarity (*sādharmya*).
Perceiving that example, one infers with respect to sound as well: "Sound is also impermanent because it possesses the property of being produced, like a cooking pot and so forth.
This is called an *udāharaṇa* (example) because by means of it the relationship of probandum and probans between two properties is illustrated. //36//
Or, by the reversal of that, it is the opposite.
The subject under discussion is that "the example is the illustration.
An example that, by virtue of its dissimilarity to the probandum, does not possess the property of that [probandum] is the illustration.
For instance: "Sound is impermanent because it has the property of being produced; that which has the property of not being produced is permanent, such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth."

This instance, such as the self (*ātman*), possesses a property dissimilar to that which is to be proven (*sādhyavaidharmya*); because it lacks the property of being produced (*anutpattidharmakatva*), it does not possess that property [of the probandum]. That is to say, the property of impermanence (*anityatva*) which belongs to the subject to be proven does not exist in that [self]. Here, observing that impermanence does not exist in the instance of the self and so forth due to the absence of the property of being produced, one infers the opposite in the case of sound, because the property of being produced exists there.
"Sound is impermanent. An example (udāharaṇa) is an instance that possesses the property of the probandum because of its similarity to it, in the case of a reason stated through similarity;
an example is an instance that does not possess that property because of its dissimilarity to it, in the case of a reason stated through dissimilarity.

In the first example, one observes that those two properties stand in the relation of the probandum and the probans; one then infers that they likewise stand in the relation of the probandum and the probans with respect to the subject of inference (*sādhya*).

In the second example, one observes the absence of the one property due to the absence of the other property, and infers the presence of the one property due to the presence of the other property with respect to the subject of inference.
Since this [logical structure] is not possible in the cases of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), these are non-reasons (*ahetu*) despite being called "fallacious reasons."
[Those which do not occur are non-reasons (ahetu), i.e., fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa).
This capacity of the reason and the example is extremely subtle, difficult to comprehend, and to be understood only by those who possess the character of a scholar. //37//
The application (upanaya) is the subsumption of the probandum (sādhya) as "so it is" or "not so it is," depending upon the example (udāharaṇa).
"Dependent on the example" means being governed by the example and subject to the example;
"subject to" (vaśa) means capacity (sāmarthya).
In an example that possesses similarity with the probandum (*sādhyasādharmya*), such as a pot or other substance, it is observed that things possessing the property of arising are impermanent.
Likewise, in the statement "sound has the property of arising," the fact that sound, which is the subject of the thesis, possesses the property of arising is being applied [to the example].

Furthermore, in an example characterized by dissimilarity to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyavaidharmya*), it is said: "Substances such as the self (*ātman*) are seen to be eternal and not subject to arising."
And since sound is not like that,
by the negation of the application of the property of being non-originated, the property of being originated is applied.
This twofold nature of application arises from the twofold nature of the examples.
And it should be understood that "synthesis" (upasaṃhāra) is that by means of which [something] is synthesized. //38//
Furthermore, regarding the two kinds of reasons, the two kinds of examples, and the duality of the conclusion, it is the same:
"The conclusion (nigamana) is the restatement of the proposition (pratijñā) following the presentation of the reason (hetvapadeśa). (NyS 1.1.39)
