Whether the conclusion is drawn through the statement of similarity (*sādharmya*) or the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), as in the example, the final step is:

"Therefore, because it has the property of being produced, sound is impermanent"—this is the *nigamana* (conclusion). It is called *nigamana* because by means of it the proposition (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*udāharaṇa*), and application (*upanaya*) are brought together (*nigamyante*) into one. They are brought together—that is, they are supported and connected.

In that regard, concerning first the reason stated by way of similarity (sādharmya), the statement "sound is impermanent" is the proposition (pratijñā); "because it possesses the property of arising" is the reason (hetu);
and "a substance such as a cooking pot, which possesses the property of arising, is impermanent" is the example (udāharaṇa).
And likewise, "sound has the property of being produced" is the application (*upanaya*).
Therefore, "because sound has the property of being produced, it is impermanent" is the conclusion (*nigamana*).
Even when stated by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*): "Sound is impermanent because it has the property of being produced."
Because it possesses the property of arising:
substances such as the self (*ātman*) are seen to be eternal because they do not possess the property of arising;
however, sound does not likewise possess the property of non-arising. Therefore, because it possesses the property of arising, sound is impermanent.
And in a sentence, which is a collection of constituent parts (*avayava*), the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establish the objects by coming together through mutual connection.
First, the thesis (*pratijñā*) has sound as its object,
because the teaching of a reliable person (*āpta*) is a synthesis of perception and inference, and because independence is impossible for one who is not a seer (*ṛṣi*).
Inference is the logical reason (*hetu*),
because through the example (*udāharaṇa*) there is the comprehension of similarity;
and that has been explained in the commentary on the example.

The example has perception as its object, because the unperceived is established by means of the perceived. The application is analogy (*upamāna*), because it is a conclusion [stating] "so it is," or "and not so it is," whereby, upon the negation of the properties of the analogous object, the establishment of the opposite properties follows.
The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the demonstration of the capacity of all [the members of the syllogism] to bring about the comprehension of a single object.
Furthermore, there is a mutual interconnection: if the proposition (*pratijñā*) were absent, the reason (*hetu*) and the other members would not function, as they would lack a basis;
and if the reason were absent, for what would the status of being a means of proof (*sādhanabhāva*) be demonstrated?
If there were no example, of what would there be a conclusion (upasaṃhāra), and by what indication (apadeśa) would the restatement of the proposition (pratijñā) constitute the conclusion (nigamana)?

In the absence of an example, by means of what similarity (sādharmya) or dissimilarity (vaidharmya) could the proof of the probandum (sādhyasādhana) be undertaken, or on the basis of whose similarity would the conclusion proceed?
Without the application (*upanaya*), the proving property (*sādhaka-dharma*), not being applied to the subject to be proven (*sādhya*), would not establish the point.

And in the absence of the conclusion (*nigamana*), for whom would there be the demonstration—by means of a single purpose—that the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the other members proceed with a connected relationship as previously stated?
Now, the meaning of the individual members: the statement of the connection between the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) and the locus (*dharmin*) is the meaning of the proposition.
The meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is the statement that a property similar to, or contrary to, the example possesses the status of being the prover of the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
The meaning of the example (*udāharaṇa*) is the demonstration of the relationship between the two properties as prover and proven within a single instance.
The meaning of the application (*upanaya*) is the establishment of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the property serving as the prover with the property to be proven.

The conclusion (*nigamana*) serves to refute the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that would arise from the opposite of the probandum, once the relationship of probandum and probans has been established between the two properties residing in the example.

Furthermore, when this purity of the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*udāharaṇa*) is present, the proliferation of futile rejoinders (*jāti*) and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)—which result from the various ways of opposing [the argument] through similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—does not occur.

For indeed, it is only after the relationship of probandum and probans between the two properties has been established in the example that the proponent of the futile rejoinder (*jātivādī*) opposes [the argument].

Indeed, when the relationship of probandum and probans between two properties has been established and the instance is being apprehended, it is the property functioning as the probans that is taken up as the reason (*hetu*), and not mere similarity alone, nor mere dissimilarity alone. // 39 //

Since reasoning (*tarka*) must be defined after [the means of valid cognition] that serves as the instrument for proof, the following is stated: *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.40: Reasoning is the deliberation (*ūha*) concerning an object whose true nature is unknown, for the purpose of attaining knowledge of its true nature, based on the logical possibility of a cause.

When the reality of an object is not yet known, first of all a desire to know arises, [in the form]: "May I come to know this object. Then, one reflects by way of distinction upon the two mutually exclusive properties (*dharma*) of the object that has been desired to be known—[namely, its being so or otherwise]. (p. 321)
"Is it thus, or is it not thus?"—when two doctrines are being deliberated in this manner, one accepts the other through the logical consistency of its cause, thinking:
"In this case, a cause, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and a reason (*hetu*) are possible; therefore, by the logical consistency of the cause, it must be thus, and not otherwise."

In this regard, there is an illustration: when one desires to know the knower who knows the object to be known, the inquiry is, "Does he know that [object] in accordance with reality? The deliberation is, "Is he of the nature of arising, or is he of the nature of non-arising?
When the object whose true nature is unknown is being deliberated upon, one accepts that property for which a valid reason for its admission is established.
If this [self] is of a nature that does not arise,
then it is the knower who experiences the fruit of its own performed karma;
furthermore, among suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, each subsequent one is the cause of each preceding one.
Liberation would consist in the cessation of each subsequent [state] following the cessation of the one immediately preceding it; thus would saṃsāra and liberation exist.
However, if the knower were subject to the property of arising, these two could not exist.
Indeed, once the knower has arisen, he becomes connected with the body, sense-faculties, cognitions, and feelings; thus, this is not the fruit of his own previously performed action.
Furthermore, having arisen, he does not continue to exist; therefore, for one who is non-existent or who has ceased, there can be no experience of the fruit of his own performed action.

Thus, when one perceives that a certain cause is untenable—such as the notion that a single [self] could not possibly have connection with multiple bodies nor be separated from them—one does not accept that [cause].
This process, characterized in this way, is called *ūha* (consideration) or *tarka* (reasoning).
But why is this for the sake of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and not the knowledge of reality itself?
Because of non-determination:
he allows one or another phenomenon through the occurrence of a reason, but he does not determine, resolve, or decide that "this is exactly thus."
In what sense is it "for the sake of the knowledge of reality"?

Because from a mind that has become serene through being cultivated by the favor characterized by the authorization of the objects of the knowledge of reality, the knowledge of reality arises by the power of the subsequent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus it is "for the sake of the knowledge of reality.

This very *tarka*, connecting the means of valid cognition and because it authorizes the means of valid cognition, is taught in debate as being accompanied by the means of valid cognition; it thus authorizes one whose reality is not yet known.
In debate, that which is designated as such—its being in that manner is its reality (*tattva*);
it is non-perversion, its being according to fact (*yāthātathya*). //40//
And regarding this domain of reasoning:
*Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.41: "Ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is the determination of the truth after deliberation by means of the thesis and the counter-thesis."
Establishment is proof (*sādhana*),
and negation is refutation (*upālambha*).
These two— proof and refutation— relying upon a thesis and its counter-thesis, being intertwined and proceeding in continuous succession, are called "thesis and counter-thesis" (*pakṣapratipakṣa*).
The cessation of one of these two and the persistence of the other is inevitable;
the determination of the object belonging to that which persists is the final conclusion (*nirṇaya*).

It is not possible for the determination of the object to occur through both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*), because one person establishes the proposed object by means of a reason and removes what has been refuted by the second.

By the second [reason], the reason for establishing [the opponent's position] is refuted; the reason for refuting that very [position] is then raised, and it is set aside. When that is set aside, that which remains serves as the determination of the object; this is *nirṇaya* (ascertainment).
He says that the determination of the meaning is indeed by means of both.
By what reasoning? The possibility of one and the impossibility of the second.

These two—possibility and impossibility—jointly bring about the cessation of doubt: for doubt does not cease when both are possible, nor when both are impossible. "Having deliberated" (*vimṛśya*) means having performed the act of deliberation (*vimarśa*).
This deliberation, having illuminated the thesis and the counter-thesis, sets the process of reasoning (*nyāya*) in motion; thus it is employed.
And this [contradiction] is to be understood as applying to two contradictory properties residing in a single locus (*dharmī*).
However, where two contradictory properties are possible through a reason (*hetu*) regarding a common locus (*dharmisāmānya*), there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*),
because the existence of the object in that manner is established by the reason.

For example, in the statement of a definition such as "substance possesses action," that substance for which a connection with action is possible due to a cause is "possessing action," while that for which it is not possible is "actionless.
Furthermore, regarding two contradictory properties residing in a single substratum that do not exist simultaneously, there is a temporal alternation.

For example— that very same substance, when conjoined with action, is "possessing action," whereas when its action has not yet arisen or has ceased, it is "actionless. Furthermore, this is not a fixed rule regarding determination (*nirṇaya*), namely that determination is the ascertainment of an object through the examination of a thesis and its counter-thesis.
However, in the case of perception produced by the contact of a sense-organ with its object, the determination of the object is *nirṇaya* (ascertainment);

but regarding the subject matter of investigation, *nirṇaya* is the determination of the object after deliberation (*vimṛśya*) through the presentation of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*).
In debate (*vāda*) and in the treatise (*śāstra*), [the determination occurs] excluding deliberation. 41.
Thus ends the first section of the first chapter in the Nyāyabhāṣya of Vātsyāyana. The second section:
There are three types of discourse—vāda (discussion), jalpa (wrangling), and vitaṇḍā (cavil). Of these—

NyS 1.2.1: Debate (vāda) is the taking up of a position and its counter-position, employing means of valid cognition and reasoning for proof and refutation, not contradicting established tenets, and consisting of the five members [of a syllogism].
Two contradictory properties residing in a single substratum constitute the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*), due to their state of mutual opposition,
such as "the self exists" and "the self does not exist."
Thesis and counter-thesis do not exist when they reside in different substrata or are contradictory,
such as "the self is eternal" and "consciousness is impermanent.
Acceptance (parigraha) is the formal determination of what is admitted.

This debate consists of the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis. Its qualification is "establishment and refutation by means of valid cognition and reasoning," meaning that within this [debate], establishment and refutation are carried out by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*).

The proof (*sādhana*) is the establishment (*sthāpanā*), and the objection (*upālambha*) is the refutation (*pratiṣedha*). These two—proof and objection—are intertwined and connected in both positions until one has ceased and the other remains established; for the one that has ceased, there is the objection against the one that remains established.
Regarding the term "proof" (*sādhana*):
since both [of these] are proofs,
[it is said that] because points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) are employed in debate (*jalpa*), they are prohibited in formal discussion (*vāda*).

The statement "not contradictory to the tenet" (*siddhāntāviruddha*) is for the purpose of permitting certain [reasons] while prohibiting others. Regarding the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) which is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), defined as "that which, having accepted a tenet, contradicts it," its permission is granted in formal debate (*vāda*).

The phrase "endowed with five members" is intended to permit those two [definitions]: that "it is deficient if it lacks even one member," and that "it is redundant if it has more than the reason and the example.

Since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*) are already included within the members, their separate mention is for the purpose of making known the interconnection between proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*upālambha*).
Otherwise, both positions, when engaged in establishing [a thesis], would constitute a formal debate (*vāda*). Furthermore,
it is observed that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establish an object even without a connection between the members of a syllogism (*avayava*).
By this [separate mention], he indicates that both proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*upālambha*) occur in debate (*vāda*).

According to the statement, "A disputation (*jalpa*) is the proof and refutation by means of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)," one should not understand that disputation is merely characterized by defeat; nor should one understand that disputation consists solely of proof and refutation by means of quibbles, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat, while debate consists solely of proof and refutation by means of valid instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*). It is for this purpose that *pramāṇa* and *tarka* are mentioned separately.

NyS 1.2.2: *Jalpa* (wrangling) is a debate consisting of the establishment of one's own position and the refutation of the opponent's, employing the previously mentioned [fallacies], as well as quibbles, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat.

"Endowed with what has been stated" means: the undertaking of a position and its counter-position, which employs means of valid cognition and reasoning for proof and refutation, is not contrary to established tenets, and is endowed with the five members [of a syllogism].
"Employing means of proof and refutation through quibbles, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat" means...

Jalpa (disputatious debate) is characterized by the fact that within it, both proof and refutation are carried out by means of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Indeed, it is not possible for the proof of any object whatsoever to be accomplished by means of quibbles, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat;
rather, their purpose is solely for the sake of refutation, as is heard in both their general and specific definitions: "The obstruction of speech... [and so forth].

"Quibble (*chala*) is [the opposition] through the fabrication of a different meaning"; "A futile rejoinder (*jāti*) is an opposition based on similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*);
and "Points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) are misconception (*vipratipatti*) and non-comprehension (*apratipatti*). [End of citation. p. 359.

Regarding the specific characteristics as well, [the term] "according to their respective [definitions]" is used so that one would not think that these [defeats] establish their meaning solely by way of negation; for even when it is stated that "disputation (*jalpa*) is the censuring of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*"), this very point is understood.

The status of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) as subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) and the refutation [of an opponent's position] is due to their purpose of protecting one’s own position; they do not possess the status of independent means of proof. That which is the proving of an object by means of the *pramāṇas*—in that regard, quibbles, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat function as subordinate members because they serve the purpose of protection.
For when these are employed, they protect one’s own position by means of the destruction of the opponent’s position.
[They protect their own position by warding off obstacles.

And so it has been said: "Wrangling (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) are for the purpose of protecting the determination of reality, just as the covering of thorny branches is for the purpose of protecting the growth of seeds.

Furthermore, these [fallacies], when employed, become auxiliaries to that refutation of the opposing position by means of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because they obstruct its negation.
Thus, in debate (*jalpa*), there is the employment of quibbles (*chala*) and the like as subordinate members (*aṅga*), but they do not possess the status of independent means of proof (*sādhana*);
however, in refutation (*upālambha*), they also possess independence. // 2 //
That same [kind of debate], when it lacks the establishment of a counter-position, is vitanda (cavil).
That speech becomes vitandā (cavil).
With what qualification?
It is devoid of the establishment of a counter-position.

It has been stated that there are two contradictory properties in a common substratum which constitute the two "sides" (*pakṣa*); of these two, the caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*) does not establish either one, but proceeds solely by negating the opponent's position.

Well then, let that [negation] be the *vitaṇḍā*, being devoid of a counter-position (*pratipakṣa*). Indeed, that speech characterized by the negation of another's position is the "position" (*pakṣa*) of the caviller.
But since he does not establish any object to be proven after having proposed it as a thesis, let it remain exactly as it was originally stated. // 3 //
Because they lack the defining characteristics of a reason, these are non-reasons (*ahetu*); yet, due to their similarity to a reason, they appear as if they were reasons.

These are the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*): the deviant (*savyabhicāra*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the one whose presence is equal to the context (*prakaraṇasama*), the one whose presence is equal to the probandum (*sādhyasama*), and the mistimed (*kālātīta*). NyS 1.2.4.
Among these—NyS 1.2.5:
The inconclusive [reason] is that which deviates.
Inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*) is non-occurrence in one [place]. That which exists together with inconstancy is "inconstant" (*svayabhicāra*).
[Note: *cāraḥ*] p.374

The illustration (*nidarśana*) is as follows: "Sound is eternal because it is intangible; a jar, which possesses tangibility, is seen to be non-eternal; and sound does not possess tangibility in that manner; therefore, because it is intangible, sound is eternal.
[Likewise, that which possesses tangibility... p.375

In the example, the two properties—possessing tangibility and impermanence—are not apprehended as being in the relationship of the probandum and the probans, for it is held that "the atom possesses tangibility and is eternal.
And likewise in the example of the self (*ātman*) and so forth... [p. 376]

"The reason (*hetu*) is that which establishes the probandum (*sādhya*) through similarity with the example (*udāharaṇa-sādharmya*). In this regard, the reason "because of being intangible" (*asparśatvāt*) deviates from permanence (*nityatva*), for thought (*buddhi*) is intangible yet non-eternal.

Thus, because there is deviation in both types of examples, the relationship of probandum and probans does not exist; therefore, due to the absence of the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), it is not a valid reason.

Eternality is one extreme, and non-eternality is another extreme; because it exists within one extreme, it is "exclusive" (*aikāntika*). By contrast, that which pervades both extremes is "non-exclusive" (*anaikāntika*) due to its opposite nature. // 5 //
NS 1.2.6: Having accepted a tenet, that which contradicts it is the "contradictory" (viruddha) [reason].
"It contradicts that" means it subverts the accepted tenet (siddhānta) that has been admitted;
for example: "This modification departs from its manifestation, because of the negation of permanence"—[p. 378].
A modification that is eternal is not tenable; furthermore, even when a modification has departed, it still exists because its destruction is denied.
This [argument]—namely, "because of the denial of eternality"—contradicts one's own established tenet, which holds that "even when a modification has departed from manifestation, it still exists."
How so? Manifestation (*vyakti*) is the acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*);
passing away (*apāya*) is falling away (*pracyuti*).
If there were a modification that had fallen away from the acquisition of self-nature, the negation of permanence would not be tenable.
That which is the existence of a modification even after it has departed from its manifestation is indeed permanence.
The negation of permanence is the demonstration that a modification has fallen away from the acquisition of its own nature.
That which falls away from its acquisition of self-nature is observed to be impermanent; that which exists does not fall away from its acquisition of self-nature.
Furthermore, existence and falling away from the acquisition of self-nature are two contradictory properties that cannot coexist simultaneously.
Thus, this very reason, by relying upon a certain tenet, contradicts that very same tenet. // 6 //
NyS 1.2.7: That [reason] for which there is deliberation regarding the subject (prakaraṇa) and which is put forward for the sake of a definitive conclusion is "equal to the subject" (prakaraṇasama).
A *prakaraṇa* (investigation) consists of both the thesis and the counter-thesis, which are based on deliberation and remain undecided;
the *cintā* (inquiry) regarding it is the examination [of them] starting from deliberation up until the final determination.
[The examination prior to determination. p. 381

That inquiry which has been raised, when employed for the sake of a definitive conclusion, does not lead to a decision because it fails to transcend the *prakaraṇa* (the state of indecision) due to the equality of both sides; this is the *prakaraṇasama* (the counter-argument that leaves the matter in suspense). For instance, in the demonstration "Sound is non-eternal because its eternal properties are not perceived," one observes that things like a cooking pot, which do not possess the perceived properties [of sound], are indeed eternal.
"Sound is eternal because the properties of the non-eternal are not perceived; that which does not possess perceived non-eternal properties is seen to be eternal, such as space and so forth.

Where a common property is employed as a reason for doubt, that is the "equal-to-doubt" (saṃśayasama) fallacy, which is indeed a case of the "inconclusive" (savyabhicāra). However, when there is a requirement for further investigation regarding the doubt and a failure to perceive any distinguishing feature between the two sides, that initiates the "equivalence of the point at issue" (prakaraṇasama).
Just as the property of permanence is not perceived in sound, so too is the property of impermanence.
This non-perception of a distinction between both positions gives rise to an inquiry into the matter (*prakaraṇacintā*). [It gives rise to an inquiry into the matter. p.383

How so? Because the context ceases upon the contrary: if a property of the eternal were perceived in sound, the context would cease; and if a property of the non-eternal were perceived, the context would likewise cease.
Thus, this reason, while setting forth both positions, is not capable of establishing a definitive conclusion for either one. // 7 //
NyS 1.2.8: That which is not distinct from the probandum, because it is itself yet to be proven, is "equal to the probandum" (sādhyasama).
"Shadow is a substance" is the thesis (*sādhya*);
"because it possesses motion" is the reason (*hetu*). Since this reason is not distinct from the thesis—because it itself remains to be proven—it is "equal to the thesis" (*sādhyasama*).
This [reason] also must be demonstrated like the probandum, because it is unestablished.

First, this is the point to be proven: does the shadow move just like the person, or is it that when the obscuring substance moves, this absence-series of light is perceived due to the series of obstructions? [p.386]
Indeed, as a substance moves, whatever portion of light is obstructed by it, the non-presence of that very portion is perceived as continuous;
thus, obscuration is the negation of reaching [the object]. //8//
NyS 1.2.9: That which is stated when the time [for its application] has passed is the "mistimed" (kālātīta) fallacy.
That whose portion of the meaning is stated after the [proper] time has passed is "stated at a time that has elapsed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), and is called "one whose time has lapsed" (kālātīta).
An illustration: "Sound is eternal because it is manifested by conjunction, like color.
Color, which exists prior to and after its manifestation, is manifested by the conjunction of a lamp and a jar.
And likewise, sound, though already existing, is manifested by the conjunction of a drum and a stick, or by the conjunction of wood and an axe;
therefore, because it is manifested by conjunction, sound is eternal.
This is not a valid reason, because it is stated at a time when its application has passed (kālātyayāpadeśāt).
The manifestation of the manifested color does not transcend the time of its manifestor, which is conjunction;
when there is conjunction with a lamp, the perception of color occurs, but when the conjunction has ceased, the color is no longer perceived.
When the conjunction of the axe and the wood has ceased, the sound is heard at a distance at the time of disjunction;
thus, this manifestation of the sound transcends the time of conjunction and therefore is not produced by that conjunction.
Why? Because, as the principle holds, "in the absence of the cause, there is an absence of the effect."
Thus, because it lacks similarity with the example (*udāharaṇasādharmya*), this reason is not a valid proof but a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
However, the statement that reverses the order of the members (*avayava*) is not the meaning of the Sūtra. Why? Because:
"Whatever has a semantic connection with something, that [connection] belongs to it even if it is situated far away."
For from this statement— "In reality, for those [reasons] that are incapable [of proving the conclusion], immediate succession is not a cause"—

it follows that a reason stated even by way of inversion does not abandon the definition of a reason (*hetu*), namely, the proof of the probandum through similarity to the example (*udāharaṇasādharmya*) or, likewise, through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). And since it does not abandon the definition of a reason, it does not become a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
"The statement of the members [of a syllogism] in reverse order is a 'mistimed' [defeat]"—this was stated as a point of defeat;
since this very same thing is being stated again, it is therefore not the meaning of the Sūtra. // 9 //
Now, regarding quibble (chala):
"Quibble is the subversion of a statement by means of the fabrication of an alternative meaning. (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.10)
Quibble cannot be illustrated with respect to the general definition;
however, examples are provided for its specific divisions. //10//

And the classification [is as follows]: NS 1.2.11: That [quibble] is of three kinds—quibble regarding speech (*vākchala*), quibble regarding a general term (*sāmānyacchala*), and quibble regarding metaphorical usage (*upacāracchala*).
Among these—NyS 1.2.12: *Vākchala* (quibble regarding speech) is the imagining of a different meaning from what was intended by the speaker when the meaning expressed was non-specific.
The usage "This young brahmin is *navakambala*" (one who has a new blanket) is as follows:
here, the speaker's intention is "he whose blanket is new.
However, there is a distinction in the analytical statement (*vigraha*), but not in the compound (*samāsa*).

In this regard, this quibbler (chalavādī), disregarding the speaker’s intention, imagines another meaning not intended by him—namely, that "he has nine blankets" (*nava kambalā asya*) was what was stated—and having so imagined it, he refutes it on the grounds of impossibility: "He has only one blanket; how could he have nine?"
This is "verbal quibble" (*vākchala*), which occurs when a general term is used.
The rebuttal to this is as follows: when a general term has multiple meanings, the statement of a specific qualification is intended to establish one particular meaning among them.
In the expression "new blanket" (*navakambala*), there is an expression with multiple meanings.
Regarding the two expressions "navaḥ kambalo 'sya" (he has a new blanket) and "nava kambalā asya" (he has nine blankets):

when this [latter] formulation is employed, the conceptualization that "he has nine blankets" which you have stated is not possible; therefore, a distinction must be stated regarding this alternative conceptualization of the expression.
Because a distinction is recognized among specific objects such that "this object is expressed by this [word]," yet that distinction does not exist;
therefore, this is merely a false accusation.

Furthermore, the relationship between word and meaning is well-established in the world as a fixed application of the designator and the designated; namely, that "this meaning is the designated of this designator. This is common to general terms, while it is specific to particular terms.
These words are employed with respect to their meanings only when they have been used previously, not when they have never been used before.
And usage is for the purpose of conveying meaning;
and from the comprehension of meaning, linguistic communication arises.

Thus, in that case, when words are employed for the purpose of conveying a meaning, there is a restriction on the use of general terms by virtue of their inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*). For instance,

in the expressions "Lead the goat to the village," "Bring the ghee," and "Feed the Brahmin," these general terms are employed with respect to specific portions of the referent by virtue of their capacity.

Where a mandate for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is possible, there people act; they do not act with respect to a mere generic property (*sāmānya*), because an instruction regarding an action is impossible therein.
Thus, this word "navakambala" (nine-wool), which is a term for a generic property, applies to that object for which the meaning "he has nine woolen blankets" is possible.

But that which does not occur—namely, "nine blankets do not belong to him"—does not apply in that case; thus, this censure of another's statement based on the postulation of an impossible meaning is not tenable. //12//
NyS 1.2.13: Quibble concerning a genus (*sāmānyacchala*) is the imagining of an impossible meaning due to the application of an overly broad commonality to a possible object.

When it is said, "Aha! This brahmin is indeed endowed with both knowledge and conduct," someone says, "The perfection of knowledge and conduct is possible in a brahmin. Against this statement, a refutation is made by means of a conceptualization of an impossible meaning through a shift in the sense of the words: "If the perfection of knowledge and conduct is possible in a brahmin, it would also be possible in a *vrātya* (an outcaste brahmin)."
Even a *vrātya* is a Brahmin; let him also be one endowed with learning and conduct.
That which reaches and even exceeds the intended meaning is "overly general" (*atisāmānya*).

Just as the state of being a Brahmin is sometimes attained and sometimes transcended through the perfection of knowledge and conduct, so too is "quibble based on a general property" (*sāmānyacchalam*) a quibble that takes a general property as its basis.

And the rebuttal to this is as follows: it is a restatement of the subject matter of a statement whose specific cause was not intended to be expressed, because the sentence is for the purpose of praise.
Therefore, in this case, the postulation of an impossible object is untenable.
Just as in the statement, "Rice grows in this field," the production of the seed is neither denied nor intended to be expressed;
rather, the field is praised as the locus of activity.

Thus, this is a reference to the field (*kṣetra-anuvāda*), meaning that rice is not being enjoined here; rather, the production of rice from the seed, though it exists, is not intended to be expressed.

Similarly, in the case of the statement "the perfection of learning and conduct is possible in a Brāhmaṇa," the status of being a Brāhmaṇa is the object of the perfection, not the cause of the perfection.
Nor is a logical reason intended here; rather,
this is a restatement of the subject for the sake of praise,
meaning that when Brahminhood exists, it is a capable cause for prosperity.
And by praising the object of perception with words, the production of a result from its cause is not denied.
This being so, it is not tenable to refute the statement by means of a conceptualization of an unreal object.
NyS 1.2.14: When there is an instruction based on a distinction of properties, the denial of the actual existence of the object is quibble regarding metaphorical usage (*upacāra-chala*).
The property of a designation is its application according to the actual object;
the differentiation of properties is the application elsewhere of what was seen elsewhere;
in the instruction on that, it is "the instruction on the differentiation of properties."
Just as in the expression "the beds are crying," there is a negation based on the actual state of things: it is the persons situated on the beds who are crying, not the beds themselves.
What, then, is the logical justification for this figurative interpretation of the meaning?
*Upacāracchala* (the quibble of metaphorical usage) is the misrepresentation of the meaning of something employed in one way by imagining it to have another meaning;

it concerns the domain of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), where there is a figurative application (*bhakti*) rather than a primary sense, and involves an intentional interpretation based on causes such as association (*sahacaraṇa*).
Metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) is a derivative meaning (*nītārtha*) [derived] through such causes as association.
"Metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is the application of a term to something that does not possess its actual nature.

To this, the resolution is as follows: when usage is well-established, the speaker may either authorize or prohibit the meaning of words according to his intention, but not according to his own arbitrary whim.
The employment of both primary terms and secondary (metaphorical) terms is established by worldly convention.
When the application [of a word] is established, the meaning of the word should be accepted or rejected according to the speaker’s intention, and not according to one's own whim.
If the speaker employs a term denoting the primary [cause], then acceptance or rejection must accord with the thing as it actually is,
and not according to whim.
If, however, it is subordinate,
then [the prohibition applies] to that which is subordinate.
But where a speaker employs a word as subordinate while intending it to be primary, another person objects to it.
This is a refutation based on one's own reasoning; it is not a criticism of another.
NyS 1.2.15: Figurative quibble is merely verbal quibble, because there is no difference between them.

Quibble concerning metaphorical usage (*upacāracchala*) does not differ from quibble concerning verbal expression (*vākchalā*), because there is no distinction in both cases regarding the postulation of a different meaning.
Here too, having postulated that the word for a quality refers to its locus and the word for the primary refers to the locus, it is then refuted.
NyS 1.2.16: No, because that is a different thing.

Quibble with regard to usage (*upacāracchala*) is not the same as quibble with regard to speech (*vākchala*), because the negation of the existence of the object [in the latter] is distinct from [the negation of] the object [in the former].
Why? Because it involves the postulation of a different meaning.
For the postulation of another object is one thing,
while the negation of the existence of an object is another.
Or, if there were no distinction, it would follow that because of some similarity, all would be one kind of quibble (chala).
Having permitted the duality of the fallacy (*chala*), its triplicity is denied on account of some commonality.
Just as this reason denies triplicity, so too does it deny the duality that was previously permitted;
for indeed, there exists some commonality between both.
If duality does not cease because of some commonality, then triplicity likewise will not cease.
After the definition of the *chalas*:
NyS 1.2.18: *Jāti* (futile rejoinder) is the opposition [to an argument] by means of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
For when a reason has been employed, the consequence that arises is a *jāti* (futile rejoinder).
And that consequence consists of an objection (*pratyavasthāna*), a censure (*upālambha*), or a refutation (*pratiṣedha*) by means of similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
The counter-argument against the statement "the reason is that which establishes the probandum through similarity with the example" is by means of dissimilarity with the example;

and the counter-argument against the statement "the reason is that which establishes the probandum through dissimilarity with the example" is by means of similarity with the example, because they exist as opposites.
The meaning "that which is being born" is *jāti*.
NyS 1.2.19: Misconception and lack of comprehension are points of defeat.
Misconduct (*vipratipatti*) is either erroneous or contemptible practice. One who practices misconduct incurs defeat;
indeed, a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is the attainment of defeat.
Non-engagement (*apratipatti*), however, is the failure to initiate action regarding a subject that ought to be initiated;
it consists in either not refuting what has been established by another, or not rescuing one's own refutation.
Furthermore, because they are not mentioned in the compound [of the *nigrahasthāna* list], these two alone do not constitute points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
But is there non-difference between *jāti* and *nigrahasthāna*, as in the case of examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), or is there difference, as in the case of established tenets (*siddhānta*)? To this he says:
"Due to their various subdivisions, there is a multiplicity of *jāti*s and *nigrahasthāna*s. (NyS 1.2.20)

The multiplicity of *jātis* arises from the various ways of opposing [an argument] through similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*); and the multiplicity of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) arises from the various ways of misapprehension (*vipratipatti*) and non-apprehension (*apratipatti*). "Vikalpa" means a manifold conceptualization.
Or, "conceptualization" (*kalpa*) is manifold conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Among these, non-reproduction, ignorance, lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), distraction, admission of the opponent's position (*matānujñā*), and neglecting what ought to be questioned constitute "non-comprehension" (*apratipatti*), which is a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*);
the remainder, however, constitutes "miscomprehension" (*vipratipatti*).
These categories, beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), have been enumerated;
they have been defined according to their enumeration, and they will be examined according to their definitions. Thus, it should be understood that the operation of this treatise is threefold.
Thus ends the second daily lesson of the first chapter in the Nyāyabhāṣya of Vātsyāyana;
and this first chapter is completed.
From this point forward follows the examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth.

And that [examination] begins with the examination of doubt (*vimarṣa*) itself, as stated later: "Determination of an object through the consideration of the thesis and the counter-thesis is ascertainment" (NS 1.1.41).
[Objection: There can be no doubt based on the apprehension of common or multiple properties, nor from the apprehension of one of the two properties.
Doubt arises from the ascertainment of a common property (*dharma*), not from the mere presence of that property.
Alternatively, [if one were to think], "I perceive a common property of these two," then since both the property and the property-bearer (*dharmin*) have been apprehended, there would be no doubt.
Alternatively, doubt regarding a subject (*dharmin*) that is a distinct entity is untenable based on the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of a common property (*sāmānyadharma*),

for there is never a case where doubt arises regarding touch— which is a distinct entity— based on the determination of color, which is a distinct entity. Or rather, doubt, which is a non-determinative cognition (*anavadhāraṇajñāna*), cannot arise from determination, which is the ascertainment of an object, because there is no similarity between cause and effect.
By this, the [objection] that "doubt arises from the determination of multiple properties" is explained. Furthermore, doubt does not arise from the determination of only one of the two properties,
because in that case there is simply a definitive ascertainment of one side.
And because of the determination [of truth] despite conflicting views and the lack of a settled rule.
Doubt does not arise merely from conflicting opinions or merely from a lack of consensus;
rather, doubt arises for one who perceives a conflict of opinions,
and likewise in the case of a lack of consensus.
Alternatively, one might argue: "Since some think 'the self exists' and others think 'the self does not exist,' how can there be doubt based on such perception?

To this we reply: since perception is itself unsettled and non-perception is likewise unsettled, once these have been determined through their respective distinctions, the occurrence of doubt is not tenable.
And because there is agreement even in the face of disagreement.

And that which you consider to be a cause of doubt, namely disagreement (*vipratipatti*), is actually agreement (*sampratipatti*); for it concerns the presence of contradictory properties in two [objects].
In that case, if doubt arises from disagreement, [it is because]...
Doubt arises precisely from the fact of conflicting interpretations.
And because non-determination itself is determined within that which is not determined.
There is no doubt.
If this indeterminacy were itself established within the self, then because it would be established, it could not be indeterminate; thus, the doubt is untenable.
Now, if non-determination does not reside in a self that is undetermined, then, because of this lack of identity, non-determination cannot occur; thus, there is an absence of doubt.
Likewise, there would be perpetual doubt, because of the constant occurrence of those [doubtful] properties.
By that same reasoning by which you consider doubt to arise from the occurrence of common properties,
an absolute doubt would necessarily follow;
for as long as the occurrence of common properties is not terminated, the doubt will not be terminated.
For this subject, when being examined, is not perceived as lacking that property;
rather, it is always possessed of that property.

The brief rebuttal of this elaborate refutation is as follows (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.6): From the aforementioned determination itself, which takes into account its non-distinction [from other objects], there arises doubt; thus, there is neither the absence of doubt nor absolute doubt.
It would follow that neither the non-arising nor the non-cessation of doubt occurs.

How so? First, as for the claim that it is the ascertainment of a common property (*samānadharmādhyavasāya*) that is the cause of doubt, and not the mere common property itself—that is indeed correct.
Why, then, is it not stated in this way?
Because it is established by the statement "dependent upon a particularity" (*viśeṣāpekṣa*): "dependence upon a particularity" means a desire for it;
and that [desire] is capable [only] when a particularity is not being perceived.
Furthermore, it was not stated that [the doubt] is dependent upon a common property (*samānadharmāpekṣa*).
And since the property is common [to both], how could there not be a desire [to know] if this were perceptible?
By this implication, it is understood that [inference proceeds] from the determination of a common property (*samānadharmādhyavasāyāt*).

Or, because of the statement regarding its logical possibility—namely, "from the possibility of a common property" (*samānadharmopapatteḥ*)—there is no possibility of a common property other than the perception of its actual existence.
For a common property whose existence is not perceived becomes, as it were, non-existent.

Alternatively, the word "object" (viṣaya) may be used to denote the cognition (pratyaya) which possesses that object—as when it is said in common parlance, "fire is inferred by smoke," it is understood to mean "fire is inferred by the perception of smoke.
How so? For one infers fire after having seen the smoke, not without having seen it.
Furthermore, the word "perception" (darśana) is not heard in the sentence [of the opponent],
yet he acknowledges that the sentence conveys its meaning;
therefore, we consider that the cognizer permits the use of the word for the object (viṣaya) as a designation for the cognition (pratyaya), which is the subject (viṣayin).
Likewise here too, by the term "common property" (*samānadharmā*), [the author] expresses the apprehension of a common property (*samānadharmādhyavasāya*).

Just as it was stated that "having apprehended a property common to these two, there is an absence of doubt in the grasping of the property and the property-possessor," this refers to an object previously perceived.
"As long as I have previously perceived two objects and perceive their common property while not perceiving their difference,
how indeed might I see a difference by which I could determine one or the other?
And this [doubt] does not cease merely through the apprehension of the property-possessor when there is the perception of a common property."
As for what was said— that there is no doubt regarding one thing based on the determination of another—
this would indeed have to be asserted by anyone who would maintain that the mere determination of another object is the cause of doubt.
Furthermore, as for the argument that there is an absence of similarity between the effect and its cause:
The presence and absence of the effect following the presence and absence of the cause is the similarity between cause and effect.
That which arises from the arising of something, and which does not arise from the non-arising of something—that is the cause; the other is the effect. This is their similarity.
And this [definition] applies both to the cause of doubt and to the doubt itself.
By this, the refutation based on the "ascertainment of multiple properties" (*anekadharmādhyavasāya*) is answered.
As for what was further stated—that "doubt does not arise from the ascertainment of conflicting opinions (*vipratipatti*) or from the lack of a fixed rule (*avyavasthā*)"—[that too is addressed].
I perceive contradictory meanings in two opposing disputants, yet I do not know nor perceive any distinction by which I might determine one or the other.
[I perceive contradictory meanings...
What could be the distinction here by which I might determine one or the other? This doubt, produced by the disagreement, cannot be dispelled merely by the agreement on the disagreement.
Thus, it should be understood that doubt arises when there is no fixed determination between apprehension and non-apprehension.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "and because of the convergence of conflicting opinions," the meaning of the term *vipratipatti* (conflicting opinion) is the ascertainment [of contradictory attributes]; when that ascertainment requires further specific details, it becomes a cause of doubt. And its status as a cause of doubt is not removed simply by changing its designation.

The meaning of the term *vipratipatti* (disagreement) is two statements whose objects are contradictory while referring to the same locus; and the determination of those [statements], which requires further specification, is the cause of doubt.
Nor does its status as a cause of doubt cease when it is applied under a different designation, such as the term *sampratipatti* (agreement).
Therefore, this [objection] is merely a delusion of the unrefined intellect.

Furthermore, as for the argument that "non-determination [is established] because it is established within non-determination," since the object that serves as the cause of doubt has not been refuted and non-determination is thereby admitted, the postulation of another term based on a different reason is redundant.
Indeed, the non-determination consisting in the postulation of another term is not itself non-determination, because it is established within non-determination.
Indeed, the determination through conceptual construction [is as follows]:

it is denied that the fact that these two—perception and non-perception—have existence and non-existence as their respective objects does not become a cause for doubt when a specific distinction is required; and as long as this lack of determination remains established within itself, it does not thereby abandon its own nature.
For by that much alone is the established rule of authorization [maintained].
Thus, even though this hypothesis of a different word is being formulated, it does not establish a different object.
As for the further point, "Likewise, there would be perpetual doubt because of the occurrence of the continuity of its properties," [it is as follows]:
This doubt does not arise from the common properties and so forth alone;
rather, it arises from the ascertainment of those objects accompanied by the recollection of their specific differences. Therefore, there is no perpetual doubt.
Alternatively, because there is an ascertainment of one of the two properties, there is no doubt.
That is not correct;
for it is stated that doubt is a deliberation dependent upon a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣa*).
And since a distinguishing feature is a property of one of the two [alternatives], when that [object] is being determined, dependence upon a distinguishing feature is not possible.
NyS 2.1.7: Where there is doubt, there follows this same sequence of successive implications.

Wherever there is an investigation preceded by doubt, whether in a treatise or in debate, in each such case, when the doubt has been refuted by the opponent, a resolution must be stated. Therefore, because it pervades all investigations, doubt is examined first.

Now, the examination of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇaparīkṣā): NyS 2.1.8: Perception and the other means of cognition are not valid, because they cannot be established in relation to the three periods of time.

The meaning is that perception and the other means of valid cognition lack the status of being valid cognitions because they are not established across the three times, due to the impossibility of their existence as prior, posterior, or simultaneous.
The analysis of the meaning of this general statement is as follows:
*Nyāyasūtra* 2.1.9: For, previously, when the means of valid cognition have been established, perception does not arise from the contact of the sense organs with their objects.
Cognition whose object is odor and so forth is perception;
if that [cognition] were prior, then the establishment of the odor and so forth would be subsequent.
This [cognition] does not arise from the contact with odor and so forth.
If [the means of knowledge] are established subsequently, there is no establishment of the objects of knowledge from the means of knowledge.

In the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), by what could an object being cognized be an object of cognition (prameya)? Indeed, it is established that an object is an object of cognition only when it is being cognized by a means of valid cognition.
NyS 2.1.11: If [the senses] were established as functioning simultaneously, there would be an absence of sequential occurrence for cognitions, because they are restricted to their respective objects.

If the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) exist simultaneously, then even so, cognitions restricted to their respective objects would arise simultaneously regarding sensory objects such as odors and the like; thus, because cognitions are restricted to direct perception, there would be an absence of sequential occurrence. Consequently, it would be impossible for these cognitions that operate upon objects sequentially to possess such sequential operation.
And there is a contradiction with the [Nyāya] definition: "The non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark of the mind.
Furthermore, this much—which concerns the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*)—is untenable.
Therefore, the status of perception and the other [means] as valid cognitions is not possible.

The summary of this [section] is as follows: Since there is no fixed rule regarding the prior, posterior, or simultaneous occurrence of the cause of apprehension and the object that is apprehended, their distinction is stated according to how they are observed.
In some cases, the cause of apprehension [is mentioned first].
In some cases, it is first the object of cognition and subsequently the cause of cognition,
as for example, the light of the sun is for those things that are arising.
In other cases, it is first the object of cognition and subsequently the cause of cognition.
A lamp is [an example] of things existing as they are.
In some cases, the cause of perception and the object of perception occur simultaneously,
as in the apprehension of fire by means of smoke.

The means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the cause of apprehension, while the object of cognition (*prameya*) is the domain of apprehension. Thus, since the temporal relation between the means and the object of cognition—whether prior, posterior, or simultaneous—is not fixed, one must speak by making a distinction according to how the matter is observed; therefore, an absolute negation [of their relationship] is untenable, for the negation was stated as a general rule after having made such a distinction.
Because the designation is applicable across the three times, the designation is established accordingly.

Furthermore, regarding this [objection]: "If the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not established first, the object of valid cognition (prameya) is not established; for it is understood that an object being measured by a means of valid cognition is an *prameya*."
The cause for the designation "pramāṇa" is its being the cause of apprehension;
[the cause for the designation] "māna" is its connection with the three times.

Because it has apprehended, it is apprehending, and it will apprehend—due to this connection with the three times based on the cause of its designation—the designation is likewise established: "the object has been measured by this, is being measured, and will be measured," thus it is a *pramāṇa* (means of valid cognition); [and] that which has been measured (*pramita*).
That which is being cognized and that which will be cognized is the object of cognition (*prameya*).
This being so, there will be a perception of this [object] by means of a cause.

"This object will be cognized" and "this is the object of cognition"—all such [conceptions] would be impossible. Furthermore, if the existence of the three times is not admitted, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) becomes untenable.
For one who does not admit this, such transactions as "bring the cook, he will cook" or "bring the reaper, he will reap" would be impossible.

"The invalidity of perception and the other means of knowledge [follows] from their non-establishment in the three times"—such statements as these constitute the negation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In this regard, one must ask:
what, then, is being done by you through this negation?
Is it that possibility is being negated, or is impossibility being made known? [It is the latter.
If possibility were being negated, then while possibility exists, the refutation of perception and the other means of knowledge would be untenable.
If, on the other hand, non-existence is being made known,
then the negation itself must possess the characteristics of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because it is the cause for the apprehension of the non-existence of a means of valid cognition.
And what follows from this?
Since [the reason] is not established in the three times, the negation is untenable. (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.12)
However, its analysis is as follows:

if the negation were established prior [to the object of negation], then since the object of negation does not exist, what would be negated by it? If it were established later, there would be no establishment of the object of negation because the negation itself would be absent.
If they were established simultaneously, the negation would be purposeless because it would imply the admission of the existence of the object of negation.
Since a sentence characterized by negation is impossible [without presupposing other means of knowledge], it follows that the validity of perception and the other means of knowledge is established.
How so?
Because the negation itself is untenable due to the negation of all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

If an example is adduced for this reason— "because [the object] is not established across the three times"— then the capacity of the meaning of the reason to prove [its conclusion] must be demonstrated in the example;
and in that case, the invalidity of perception and the other means of knowledge would not [follow].

Now, if perception and the other means of valid cognition are invalid, then even an example being employed will not establish the point; thus, this reason, which contradicts all means of valid cognition, is no reason at all.
As it is said: "That which, having accepted a tenet, contradicts it, is the contradictory [reason]."
For the meaning of this [sūtra] is its established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

And that meaning of the sentence is: "Perception and the other means of knowledge do not establish the object"; and the employment of the members [of the syllogism] is for the purpose of establishing that object.

Now, if they were not employed, then since the capacity of the reason (*hetu*) to prove the object has not been demonstrated by the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the refutation would not be tenable, because the status of being a reason would remain unestablished.
Or, if that [scripture] is authoritative, there is no sublation of all means of valid cognition.

If, in your own statement characterized by negation, you were to admit the validity of those means of knowledge such as perception that depend on the [syllogistic] members, then it would follow that the validity of those depending on the members in the opponent's statement would also result, because there is no distinction. And thus, not all means of knowledge would be negated.

Regarding the term *vipratiṣedha*, the prefix *vi-* is used in the sense of "agreement" (*sampratipatti*), not in the sense of "contradiction," because [in that case] the meaning would be non-existent.
And there is no prohibition against [the existence of the cause] in the three times, because its establishment is like the establishment of a drum from its sound.
For what purpose, then, is this stated?
It is for the sake of the previously mentioned justification.

Namely, that which was stated before: "Because there is no fixed rule regarding the prior, posterior, or simultaneous existence of the cause of apprehension and the object of apprehension, the distinction [between them] is stated according to how they are observed."
This is stated so that its origin may be understood:
this seer, seeing impermanence, indeed rejects the prohibition [of sound] as a rule, on the grounds that "a prohibition regarding the three times is illogical.
In that regard, he provides one illustration: "like the establishment of the musical instrument from the sound."
as it is said: just as a previously established musical instrument is inferred by means of a subsequently established sound,
where the musical instrument is the object to be proven (*sādhya*) and the sound is the means of proof (*sādhana*).

For when a musical instrument has disappeared, there is an inference from its sound, such that one understands the specific instrument through the specific sound, thinking, "The lute is being played" or "the flute is being blown.
Likewise, an object of perception already established is subsequently understood through a cause of perception that is established later.
And because this is intended as an illustration, the examples for the remaining two modes of proof should be understood as stated.
But why is that not stated here? Because it is to establish what was previously mentioned;
in any case, this matter must be elucidated.
Whether it is manifested here or there,
there is no difference whatsoever.

The designations "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) and "object of valid cognition" (*prameya*) function through mutual inclusion by virtue of their respective grounds for designation. The ground for designation is as follows: that which is the instrument of apprehension is the means of valid cognition, and that which is the object of apprehension is the object of valid cognition.

However, when the object of apprehension in some instances becomes the instrument of apprehension, then the single entity is designated by both terms, "means of valid cognition" and "object of valid cognition."
To illuminate this point, it is said:
"And the object of cognition [is both], like the validity of a scale" (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.16).

The balance (*tulā*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), being the instrument for the knowledge of weight and measure; the heavy substance such as gold, which is the object of that knowledge, is the object of cognition (*prameya*).

Just as when another balance is calibrated by means of gold and the like, then in the apprehension of that other balance, the gold and so forth are the means of valid cognition and the other balance is the object of cognition.
Thus, the meaning of the system (tantra) should be understood as indicated without omission:
first, the self (ātman), because it is the object of apprehension, is listed among the objects of knowledge (prameya);
yet, because of its independence with respect to apprehension, it is the knower (pramātṛ).
The intellect (*buddhi*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is the instrument for apprehension;
it is an object of valid cognition (*prameya*) because it is the objective domain of apprehension; but valid cognition itself (*pramiti*) consists in the absence of both [instrument and object].
In this way, the co-occurrence of designations should be applied according to specific meanings.
Thus, words denoting grammatical relations (*kāraka*) function through co-occurrence by virtue of their underlying causes. [They function through co-occurrence. p. 434
In the expression "the tree stands," the tree is the agent (*kartṛ*) because of its independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to its own state of being.
In the expression "he sees the tree," the tree is the object (*karman*) because it is that which is most desired to be reached through the act of seeing.
[He sees... through the act of seeing... p.437.

In the expression "he makes the moon known by means of the tree," the tree is the *karaṇa* (instrument) because the instrument is that which is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) of cognition. In the expression "he pours water for the tree," the tree is the *sampradāna* (recipient), because he intends the tree by means of the water being poured.

In the expression "the leaf falls from the tree," the tree is the *apādāna* (ablative case) according to the rule "that which is fixed [as the point of departure] in a separation is the *apādāna*. In the expression "birds are in the tree," the tree is the *adhikaraṇa* (locative case) according to the rule "the substratum is the *adhikaraṇa*.
This being the case, a *kāraka* (grammatical participant in action) is not merely a substance (*dravya*).
It is not merely action;
what then? An agent (*kāraka*) is that which accomplishes an action and is connected with a specific action.
That which is independent in accomplishing an action is the agent (*kartṛ*).
It is neither substance alone nor action alone;
rather, the object (*karman*) is that which is most desired to be pervaded by the action.
It is the object most intensely desired [to be reached]. (p. 439)
It is neither substance alone nor action alone;
the same applies to the "most effective instrument" (*sādhakatama*) and so forth.
Thus, the grammatical description of the *kārakas* is established both through logical justification and through formal definition.
The designation of a *kāraka* (participant in action) applies neither to the substance alone nor to the action alone;
rather, it applies to that which accomplishes the action and is connected with a specific action.
This term *kāraka* is used, for instance, in such expressions as "the means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*) and "the object of knowledge" (*prameya*).
And he ought not to abandon the nature of an agent. //16//
Indeed, sir, there is a co-inclusion of action-denoting terms by virtue of their causal basis:

the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas), such as perception and the rest, are so called because they are the causes of apprehension, and the object of cognition (prameya) is so called because it is the objective domain of apprehension.
Furthermore, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas), such as direct perception and the rest, are themselves objects of experience;

for one apprehends specific distinctions by thinking, "I perceive this through direct perception," "I perceive this through inference," "I perceive this through comparison," or "I perceive this through scripture," and likewise, "My knowledge is perceptual," "My knowledge is inferential," "My knowledge is comparative," or "My knowledge is scriptural."

And when these [objects] are made known by means of their defining characteristics—such as "knowledge produced from the contact of a sense-organ with its object" and so forth—they are specifically cognized.

Now, regarding this apprehension which has perception and the other means of knowledge as its objects: does it arise from another means of knowledge, or is it without a means of proof, being independent of any other means of knowledge?
And what is the distinction in this regard?

NyS 2.1.17: Since the establishment of means of valid cognition occurs through a means of valid cognition, it follows that there must be the establishment of those means of valid cognition by yet other means of valid cognition.

If perception and the other means of valid cognition are apprehended by a means of valid cognition, then there exists yet another means of valid cognition by which they are apprehended; thus, the existence of an infinite regress of further means of valid cognition follows, as he says: "of that too by another, and of that too by another."
And an infinite regress cannot be admitted, because it is untenable.
"Then let it be that [the proof of the means of knowledge] is without a means of proof, being independent of another means of knowledge?"—[The answer is:
"Or rather, from the cessation of that [means], there is the establishment of the objects of knowledge, just as there is the establishment of the means of knowledge. (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.18)

If another means of valid cognition is required for the apprehension of perception and so forth in order to negate it, then another means of valid cognition will likewise be required for the apprehension of the self and so forth, since there is no distinction between the two cases.
And thus, there would be the abolition of all means of valid cognition; therefore, he says:
"Not so, because its establishment is like the establishment of the illumination of a lamp" (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.19).

Just as the light of a lamp is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the perception of visible objects because it is an auxiliary factor of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and that light is itself apprehended by another direct perception through the contact (*sannikarṣa*) of the eye;
so too, because the occurrence of seeing depends upon the presence or absence of the lamp, the cause of that seeing is inferred.
One understands even through the instruction of a trustworthy person that "one should take up a lamp in the darkness";
likewise, the apprehension of perception and the other means of knowledge occurs through perception and the others themselves, according to their respective modes of appearance.
To begin with, the sense organs are inferred solely by the grasping of their own objects.
Objects are apprehended through direct perception;
however, the contacts between the sense organs and their objects are inferred by means of the mark (liṅga) that is the obstruction [of the object].

Knowledge produced from the contact of the sense organ and the object is apprehended—due to a specific conjunction of the self and the mind, and due to its inherence in the self—just like pleasure and other such qualities.
In this way, the specific distinction of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is to be explained by way of division.

Just as the light of a lamp, being itself visible, serves as the cause for the perception of other visible objects and thus acquires the status of "visible perception," so too some class of objects (*arthajāta*), being themselves objects of knowledge (*prameya*), acquires the status of "means of valid cognition" and "object of valid cognition" because they serve as the cause for their own apprehension.

If it is argued that this apprehension of perception and the other means of knowledge by perception and the others themselves occurs exactly as they are observed, and not through another means of knowledge, and that there is no proof without a means of knowledge—therefore, a thing cannot be grasped by that very same thing; [The response follows: ... [as per the source text] ... [the opponent's position is thus stated].

No; because the objects differ despite the similarity of their definitions—it is incorrect to say that perception and the other means of knowledge are apprehended by perception and the others themselves, for it is observed that one thing is apprehended by another.

No, because although the objects differ, there is a commonality of definition: many objects are subsumed under the single definition of "perception," and thus it is not a fault that some [means of knowledge] apprehends another within that category.
The same applies to inference and other means of knowledge as well;
for instance, by means of water drawn up from it, one perceives that which remains in the reservoir.
Furthermore, because both the knower and the mind are perceived—through the very cognition "I am happy" and "I am suffering"—it is observed that the object is apprehended by that same knower.
And by that very same [sūtra], "The non-simultaneity of cognitions is the mark of the mind," an inference of that very [mind] is observed;
for there is no difference between the knower and the object known, nor any difference between the act of grasping and the object grasped.
If it is argued that there is a difference of instrumental causes (*nimitta*) here, the same applies: the knower does not know himself without another instrumental cause.
And since the mind cannot be apprehended by the mind without another sign (nimitta), this case is the same:
[it is like] the claim that "the perception of perceptions and so forth occurs through direct perception," wherein no distinct object is apprehended.

Furthermore, because it is impossible for there to be anything that is not an object of perception and so forth—if there were some class of objects that was not an object of perception and so forth, such that it could not be grasped by perception and the rest—[then the claim would hold]. But since that is not the case, [the argument fails].
To apprehend that [non-existence], another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) would have to be employed, but it is impossible for anyone to establish such a thing.
For perception and the other [means of knowledge] have as their objects everything— both existent and non-existent— exactly as it is observed.
Because cessation is observed in some cases and non-cessation is observed in others, there is an inconclusiveness [of the reason].
Some, however, employ an unestablished example as a means to prove their thesis without a supporting reason (*hetu*) or a specific reason (*viśeṣahetu*); for instance:

"Just as the light of a lamp is perceived without the light of another lamp, so too are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) perceived without another means of valid cognition. And this [example]—just as this reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) is employed to establish the means of valid cognition because the cessation [of the need for further means] is observed—[is likewise used].

In this way, it should also be accepted for the sake of establishing the object of cognition (*prameya*), because there is no distinguishing reason [to exclude it]. Just as the light of a lamp is employed for the sake of establishing the object of cognition when perceiving the form of a pot or the like,
so too should it be employed for the sake of establishing the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since there is no specific reason [not to do so].
Thus, this example, without being embraced by a specific reason (*viśeṣahetu*), is to be accepted for one side but not for the opposing side; therefore, it is inconclusive (*anekānta*).
Furthermore, because it is an example for only one side, it is inconclusive due to the absence of a specific reason.

When there is the embrace of a specific reason, there is no refutation because the application (*upasaṃhāra*) is permitted; however, an example embraced by a specific reason cannot be permitted when it is being applied to only one side.
And this being so, the objection that there is "indefiniteness" (anekānta) does not hold.

If it is argued that there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if perception and the other means of knowledge were themselves apprehended by perception and the others, we say no; for practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is established through the apprehension of consciousness, its objects, and their causes—such as, "I perceive an object through perception."
"I perceive an object through inference; I perceive an object through comparison; I perceive an object through scripture."
My knowledge is perceptual; my knowledge is inferential;
my knowledge is analogical.

For one who perceives both the object of cognition and the cause of cognition in the form "my knowledge is derived from scripture," worldly activity (*vyavahāra*)— which has as its purpose the attainment of dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, as well as the avoidance of their opposites— is possible;
yet this very activity ceases once that [perception] alone has occurred.

It ceases at that very point; nor is there any other linguistic usage to be established by means of an infinite regress (anavasthā) such that one would have to resort to an infinite regress already refuted. //20//
Having examined the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in general, they are now examined in detail. In this regard:
NyS 2.1.21: "The definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) is untenable because it is stated incompletely."
For the contact between the self and the mind has not been stated as a separate cause. //21//

Furthermore, since a quality produced by conjunction cannot arise in a substance that is not conjoined, the contact between the self and the mind (*ātma-manaḥ-saṃnikarṣa*) is the cause, as this is observed in the arising of cognition. Moreover, if the contact between the sense organ and its object were the cause of cognition independently of the contact with the mind, cognitions would arise simultaneously; therefore, the contact with the mind is also a necessary cause.
This sutra has already been commented upon above.
