NyS 2.1.22: Perception does not arise in the absence of contact between the self and the mind.
In the absence of contact between the self and the mind, perception does not arise, just as it does not arise in the absence of contact between the sense organ and its object. //22//

For one who asserts that [the sense-organ] is the cause because the arising of cognition is observed when there is contact between the sense-organ and its object—[it follows that] this same consequence applies to direction, location, time, and space as well. (NyS 2.1.23)
Is it because knowledge exists when space and the other [factors] exist that they too are causes?

Even if they are not causes, the arising of knowledge cannot be avoided due to the unavoidable proximity of space and the others; for even when space and the others are not causes for the arising of knowledge, knowledge must still occur when space and the others are present.
[In these cases,] there must be cognition [of the directions and so forth],
for it is not possible to avoid the presence of the directions and such;
in that regard, the statement of the reason concerns their status as causes.
For this reason, direction and the other factors are causes of cognition. //23//
"In that case, the contact between the self and the mind must be added [to the list of causes of perception].
To this, it is said:
"Because the self has cognition as its mark, there is no failure to include it. (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.24)
Knowledge is the inferential mark of the self because it is its quality;
and the production of a quality born of conjunction does not occur in a substance that is not conjoined [with another]. //24//
And because their non-simultaneity serves as a mark, [it follows that] the mind [is not eternal].
The term "non-inclusion" (anavarodha) carries over [from the previous sūtra].

When it is stated that "the non-simultaneous production of cognitions is the mark of the mind," it is thereby established that the contact between the sense organ and its object depends upon the contact with the mind as the cause of cognition. //25//
And because the contact between the sense organ and the object is the instrumental cause of perception, it is mentioned by its own specific term.
The cause for perception, inference, analogy, and verbal testimony is the contact between the self and the mind;
however, for perception alone, it is the contact between the sense organ and the object.
Because these are not the same, that [specific contact] is mentioned. //26//
And [it is not so] because for those who are asleep or whose minds are preoccupied, [the cognition] has as its cause the contact between the sense organ and the object.
The apprehension [of objects] belongs to the contact between the sense organ and its object, not to the contact between the self and the mind.
Indeed, at one time this person, having directed his attention toward the time of awakening while asleep, awakens by virtue of that mental resolve (*praṇidhāna*).
But when loud sound and touch become the causes of awakening, then for the one who is fast asleep, the knowledge of awakening arises due to the cause of contact with the sense organs.
In that case, the predominance belongs neither to the knower nor to the contact of the mind;
rather, it belongs to the contact between the sense organ and the object.
For the self, desiring to know, does not then impel the mind with effort.

At one time, indeed, when this person’s mind is attached to another object and, by the force of a volition (*saṅkalpa*), desires to know yet another object, he joins the sense organ with that other object by means of a mind impelled by effort; however, when knowledge arises for him— whose volition and desire to know have ceased, and whose mind is distracted— due to the encounter with an external object, then the predominance belongs to the contact between the sense organ and the object.
For in this case, one who desires to know does not intentionally direct the mind [toward it];

rather, because of its predominance, the contact between the sense organ and the object must be mentioned as the cause of perception, whereas the contact between the self and the mind is not, due to its subordinate status. //27//
And there is another reason for their primacy: "By means of them, there is the designation of specific cognitions" (NyS 2.1.28).
The specific types of cognition are designated by means of those sense faculties and their objects.
How so? One smells with the nose;
one sees with the eye.
It is called "tasting" because it tastes with the tongue;
thus there are the olfactory consciousness, visual consciousness, gustatory consciousness, olfactory cognition, visual cognition, and gustatory cognition.
Furthermore, cognition becomes fivefold due to the distinctions among the sense faculties and their objects.
Therefore, the contact between the sense organ and its object is the primary cause. //28//

As for what was stated—that the mention of the contact between the sense organ and its object should be included [in the definition of perception], but not the contact between the self and the mind—why is that?
Because for those who are asleep or whose minds are distracted, the contact between the sense organ and its object is the cause of cognition. This is as follows:
NyS 2.1.29: It is not a valid reason because it is contradictory.

If, first of all, the contact between the self and the mind is not accepted as a cause of cognition in any instance, then the principle that "the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark of the mind" would be contradicted;
for in that case, the contact of the sense organ with its object would no longer require the contact of the mind.

[If it were so,] it would not depend upon the contact with the object. Furthermore, if there were no dependence on the conjunction of the mind (*manas*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the simultaneous arising of all cognitions.
Now, lest there be such a contradiction, if it is maintained that the contact between the self (*ātman*) and the mind is the cause of all cognitions, [then...]
This [perception] remains in that very state;
since the contact between the self and the mind is the cause of knowledge, the apprehension must be brought about. //29//
NyS 2.1.30: Not so, because of the intensity of a particular object.
There is no contradiction, for the fact that the contact between the self and the mind is a cause of knowledge is not subject to deviation; rather,
the primacy of the contact between the sense organ and its object is what is being asserted.
For, due to the intensity of a particular object, the arising of cognition occurs at times even for those whose minds are asleep or distracted.
A "particular object" is a certain sense-object;
its "intensity" consists in its sharpness and clarity.
And that intensity of the specific object pertains to the contact between the sense organ and the object, not to the contact between the self and the mind;
therefore, the contact between the sense organ and the object is primary.

This is because even when there is no focused attention (*praṇidhāna*) or volitional intent (*saṅkalpa*), knowledge arises from the contact between the sense organ and the object for those who are asleep or whose minds are distracted.
In that case, since the conjunction with the mind (*manaḥsaṃyoga*) is also a cause, the cause of action within the mind must be stated.
Just as this effort (*prayatna*), produced by desire, is a quality of the self (*ātman*) that impels the mind,
so too there exists in the self another quality, productive of everything, which is generated by activity and defects (*pravṛttidoṣa*).
By that [quality] the mind is impelled and becomes connected with a sense organ;

for if the mind were not impelled by it, there would be no conjunction [between the mind and the organ], and consequently, due to the non-arising of cognition, its capacity to apprehend all objects would cease.
Furthermore, this other quality must be admitted to be the cause of substances, qualities, and actions.

Otherwise, since there would be no cause for action other than those four kinds of atoms—the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), minds (*manas*), and [the self]—it would follow that bodies, sense organs, and objects could never arise. //30//
NyS 2.1.31: Perception [is not the means of knowing dharma], because inference [is required] for the apprehension [of an object] based on the perception of a single part.
That cognition which arises from the contact of a sense faculty with its object, such as "this is a tree," is indeed claimed to be perception;
however, that is actually nothing but inference.
Why? Because a tree is perceived through the apprehension of one part;
having grasped its front portion, one perceives the tree.
And yet, a single part is not the tree.
In this regard, it is exactly as when one perceives smoke and thereby infers fire; that [inference] is of such a nature.
But do you consider the object of inference (*anumeya*) to be something other than the part being perceived?

In the view that [the whole] is a collection of parts, it would be the other parts; in the view that a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) arises [from the parts], it would be both those [parts] and the whole (*avayavin*).

First, regarding the position that [the whole] is a collection of parts: there would be no cognition of a tree from the perception of only one part, because a part not being perceived cannot be grasped as a tree in the same way as the part currently being perceived.
Alternatively, if the cognition of a tree arises there through the synthesis of the whole by means of inferring other unperceived parts from the perception of one part?
In that case, it would follow that the cognition of a tree cannot be an inference.
[Cognition of a tree can indeed be an inference when this is the case.
Under the view that a distinct substance arises, the composite whole (*avayavin*) is not to be inferred.
Because that which is connected to only one part [of the object] is not apprehended, and because there would be no distinction if it were apprehended, there is an absence of inferability.
Therefore, the cognition of a tree is not an inference. //31//

The status of perception as inference is established by relying on the apprehension of a single part; and that [is not so], because whatever [of the object] is present is perceived through perception. (NyS 2.1.32)
Inference is not perception; why?
Because it is apprehended by perception itself.
That which is relied upon as the grasping of a single part is an apprehension by means of perception.
Furthermore, there is no perception that lacks an object;
and as long as a class of objects constitutes its object, it is accepted as being that which establishes [the status of] direct perception.
What, then, is this other class of objects?
Is it the whole (avayavin) or the collection (samudāya)?

Nor can the apprehension of a single part be established as inference due to the absence of a logical reason (hetu). Furthermore, there is no consequence of perception being [classified as] inference; for inference is preceded by that—that is, inference is preceded by perception.
For one who has perceived through direct perception that fire and smoke are connected, an inference regarding fire arises from the direct perception of smoke.
This consists of both the direct perception of the connection between the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*),
and the apprehension of the direct perception of the mark alone.
Without this [perception], there is no occurrence of inference;
yet this [inference] is not itself perception because it arises from the contact of the sense organ with its object.
Furthermore, inference does not occur through the contact of the sense organ with the object of inference.
Therefore, this great distinction between the definitions of perception and inference must be maintained.
Furthermore, the apprehension of one part [of an object] does not constitute the apprehension of the whole, because the whole exists as a distinct entity;
nor is there merely the apprehension of one part.
What then? It is the perception of one part and the perception of the whole (*avayavin*) which coexists with it. Why? Because of the actual existence of the whole.
For this whole exists as distinct from its parts; since it has reached the conditions for perception at the location of its parts, its non-perception when one part is perceived is untenable.
If it is argued that [the whole] is not grasped in its entirety, we say no;
for there is no "part" other than the cause itself. Furthermore, the parts are not grasped in their entirety because the parts themselves are obstructed by other parts. [p. 471]
"The whole is not perceived," meaning that it is not fully completed within the parts being perceived; thus, this perception of only a single part remains unrefuted.
"Whole" (*kṛtsna*) indeed occurs when there is no remainder (*aśeṣatā*), whereas "not whole" (*akṛtsna*) occurs when a remainder exists;
and this [distinction] applies to many parts because they are perceived when there is no interval [between them], but not perceived when there is an interval.
Now, my friend, being asked, please explain: when a whole object (*avayavin*) is being perceived, what do you consider to be unperceived, such that there would be a perception of only one part?
[Being asked by you... what do you consider to be unperceived? (p.
472) By means of which [unperceived part] there might be a perception of only a single portion?
For its parts do not exist as something other than the causes [of the whole]; thus, the occurrence [of the whole] in the parts is not tenable.
This is its mode of occurrence: it is perceived together with those parts whose perception arises from sense-contact.
That which is not perceived due to the intervention of certain parts is not grasped along with them;
nor does this constitute a distinction [between the whole and its parts]. Alternatively, the tree would be either the remainder of the aggregate, or the aggregate itself, or the attainment thereof.
There is an absence of apprehension in either case.
Whether the tree is defined as the entirety of the roots, trunk, branches, leaves, and so forth, or as the collection of those parts,
in both ways the apprehension of the tree— which is the composite whole— is not possible.
First of all, because one part is obstructed by another part, the perception of the whole is not possible.
Furthermore, perception through contact is also not possible, since those things that possess contact [the parts] are not themselves perceived.

Thus, this cognition of a "tree," which is accompanied by the perception of only a single part, is accounted for by the production of a distinct substance (dravyāntara), and not by a mere collection [of parts]. //32//
Nyāyasūtra 2.1.33: Because it is that which is to be proven, there is doubt regarding the whole.
As for what was stated—that [the whole] does not exist because of the non-existence of the composite—this is not a valid reason, because it is itself yet to be proven.
Indeed, this remains to be proven: that a substance distinct from its causes is produced.
This has not been established;
and this being so, there is merely a misconception, and from that misconception arises doubt regarding the whole (avayavin). //33//
NyS 2.1.34: There would be no perception of anything at all, because the whole (avayavin) is not established.
If the whole (avayavin) does not exist, the apprehension of everything is not possible.
What is that "everything"?
It consists of substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence.

How so? First of all, the state of atoms in aggregation does not become an object of vision because atoms are beyond the senses; nor does there exist any other distinct substance consisting of a composite whole that could serve as an object of vision.
These [qualities] such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth, which reside within the range of perception, are apprehended; they would not be apprehended if they lacked a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Yet, they are indeed apprehended: "This is a jar, dark-colored, singular, large, conjoined, moving, and made of clay," and "these qualities (*guṇa*) and other attributes (*dharma*) exist."
Because it apprehends everything, we see that there exists a whole (avayavin) which is a distinct substance. //34//
And because holding and drawing [objects] are possible.
"The whole (avayavin) is a distinct entity.
Holding and pulling are indeed caused by cohesion (saṅgraha).
Cohesion is a distinct quality (guṇāntara) that accompanies conjunction (saṃyoga) and is produced by moisture and fluidity.
Due to contact with water, [the qualities] exist in an unbaked jar,
and due to contact with fire, in a baked one;
for if these two were modifications of the whole (avayavin), they would be perceived even in things such as a heap of dust.

Furthermore, if no distinct substance were produced, then even grass, stones, wood, and so forth, when held together by lac, would not become objects of cognition. Now, one who rejects the whole (avayavin) might argue that the collection of atoms (aṇusañcaya) is the object of perception, so as not to contradict direct perception; such a person should be questioned as follows: "This is one substance"—is this object of the unitary cognition (*ekabuddhi*) one whose referent is non-different, or is its referent different? Regarding the first alternative: if the unitary cognition has a non-different referent, then since the atoms are many and distinct, how can they be the object of a single cognition? If, on the other hand, the cognition has a different referent for each atom, then the cognition would be manifold, like the cognitions of various individual trees. Moreover, if the atoms themselves were the object of the unitary cognition, then because the atoms are imperceptible, the cognition would be of something imperceptible, which contradicts the claim that it is a perceptual cognition. Therefore, the unitary cognition must have a single, undivided substance as its object. Thus, the existence of the whole is established.
If it is argued that [the reason] has as its object a non-different thing,
then because another thing is admitted, there is a failure of the constituent parts.

If it is argued that [the universal] has various objects as its domain—[we reply: the perception of a single [universal] in distinct [particulars] is untenable; a cognition that conceives of "one" in what is "many" is seen to be contradictory. //35//
If it is argued that the perception [of atoms] is like that of an army or a forest, we say no, because atoms are beyond the reach of the senses.

Just as in the case of the components of an army or the components of a forest, where their distinctness is not perceived from a distance, the cognition "this is one" arises; so too, when atoms are accumulated and their distinctness is not perceived, the cognition "this is one" arises.
Just as in the case of the components of an army or a forest, whose distinctness is being perceived, there is a non-perception of their distinctness from afar due to another cause.
Just as there is no immediate apprehension of the genus when [objects] such as the *palāśa* or the *khadira* are being perceived,
and just as there is no immediate apprehension of motion when moving things are being perceived; so too,
when a class of objects is being perceived, because their distinctness is not apprehended, the cognition "it is one" arises figuratively (*bhākta*).
However, since the distinctness of atoms—which possess a perceived distinctness—is not perceived as a cause [of the whole], the cognition of oneness is merely figurative;
for atoms are beyond the reach of the senses. And this very point is being examined: whether the cognition of oneness has the collection of atoms as its object, or whether it does not.
An army, a forest, and so forth are merely collections of atoms;
and it is not logical to say that the example is not subject to investigation because it is yet to be proven,
for if you argue that it is "observed," we reply no, since the object of that observation is itself subject to investigation.
Furthermore, one might think that this perception of an army or a forest as a single entity without distinction arises because the individual parts are not perceived separately;
and that what is perceived cannot be denied.
But that is not so.

Because the examination of its object is logically possible: it is precisely this object of perception that is examined—namely, this cognition "one" which is observed—and it is examined whether its object is a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) or an aggregation of atoms (*aṇusañcaya*).
In this regard, perception does not establish either one.

Since atoms exist in a state of diversity, their distinctness is not perceived; consequently, there arises the apprehension of them as one through non-differentiation, which is a cognition of something as what it is not (*atasmiṃs tad iti pratyaya*), such as [the cognition] "a man" with respect to a post. What follows from this? Why?
Because the cognition "that" with respect to what is not that depends upon a primary [object], there must be the establishment of that primary object.
In the case of the cognition "a man" with respect to a post, what is the primary object?
It is that very cognition of a man which occurs with respect to an actual man.
Since that [pradhāna] exists, there would have to be a perception of a universal, such as "this is a man" in the case of a post, because of the apprehension of a commonality among diverse things;
thus, the notion of "one" in what is manifold could only exist if a pradhāna existed.
However, it is not tenable [to claim] that a pradhāna exists, because nothing at all is perceived.
Therefore, this cognition of non-difference, "one," is indeed non-distinct [from the object].

If it is argued that the cognition of non-difference regarding the objects of other sense-faculties is primary, we say no; for there is no specific reason [to distinguish them], and thus the application of the example remains unsettled—the cognition of one in respect to sounds and so forth, which are non-distinct objects of the ear and other faculties, is the cognition of one in respect to what is manifold.

This being the case, the employment of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is not established, because there is no specific reason (*viśeṣahetu*) [to determine its application]. When atoms are perceived as a unity, is this a cognition of "that" in what is not "that," like the cognition of a man in a post? Or is it a cognition of "that" in that very thing, because the object exists in such a way, like the cognition "the sound is one" due to the oneness of the sound? Without grasping a specific reason, these two examples lead to doubt.

Since odors and so forth are also merely accumulations like a jar, "odors and so forth" is not a valid example. In this same manner, one should also interrogate [the opponent] regarding the cognitions of dimension, conjunction, motion, and specific universals.
And in their case, there would be this same undesirable consequence:

the notion of unity [would apply] to that [object], because the cognition "that" is a specific cause [of the cognition] through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the cognition "great"—namely, "this one thing is great. Thus, two cognitions having a single object become coreferential; by this, it is understood.

If it is argued that "that which is large is one," and that the cognition of "large" is merely the apprehension of a superior aggregation of atoms, then this cognition of "large" regarding atoms that are not large is a cognition of something as being what it is not (*atasmiṃs tat*).

What follows from this? Since a cognition of something as being what it is not depends upon a primary reality (*pradhāna*), there must be the establishment of a primary reality; thus, the cognition of "large" must occur only with respect to something that is actually large.

If it is argued that the existence of *pradhāna* (the primal cause) is established because of the determinations "the sound is minute" and "the sound is great," [we reply: no, for there is only the perception of dullness and intensity, not the determination of magnitude. Just as in the case of a substance, there is the perception that "the sound is minute, small, or dull," and the perception that "the sound is great, clear, or intense. Why? Because there is no determination of magnitude (*iyattā*).
For one who determines that "this is a great sound" does not ascertain its magnitude as being "this much," in the way that one ascertains the size of jujube, myrobalan, or bilva fruits.

Furthermore, the apprehension of conjunction in the form "these two are conjoined" involves the grasping of a magnitude that has a common substratum for duality— if you say that the substratum of the conjunction is two aggregates, then what is this "aggregate"?

If it is argued that the acquisition (*prāpti*) of many things is multiple, or that the acquisition of a single thing is a collection (*samudāya*), then there would be no perception of acquisition because it is dependent upon [the acquired objects].
In the case of "these two things are conjoined," two acquisitions conjoined are not perceived here.
If it is argued that a collection is a multitude of many things, [then the same fault follows].
Because there is no apprehension of that which is in a common locus with duality;
for when there is the apprehension "these two objects are conjoined," the conjunction is not apprehended as residing in a collection of many [atoms],
nor is there any apprehension of two atoms.
Therefore, conjunction has its locus in the substance that serves as the substratum for duality.
If it is argued that conjunction is not a distinct entity, but rather proximity (pratyāsatti) which terminates in resistance (pratighāta),
we say no, because conjunction is the cause of a distinct entity.
Conjunction is the cause of sound, form, and so forth, as well as motion.
Furthermore, the causality of two substances with respect to sound, form, and the like, or with respect to motion, is not perceived except through the production of another quality;
therefore, it is a distinct quality.
Furthermore, the object of a cognition [of conjunction] must be either a distinct entity or the negation of that [entity],
as in the cases "the teacher is wearing earrings" (*kuṇḍalī*) and "the student is not wearing earrings" (*akuṇḍalaḥ*).
And if a distinct entity is not the object of the cognition of conjunction, then the negation of a distinct entity must be its object.
In this regard, the statement of what is being negated is as follows: that which is seen elsewhere in the case of "substances in conjunction" and is here negated must be stated.
Because there is the perception of two large [substances] as a substratum, it does not have atoms as its substratum.
Furthermore, there is no denial of the specific universal (jāti-viśeṣa), which is characterized by the persistence of the corresponding cognition.
Alternatively, if [the universal] is denied [to reside in the atoms], the establishment of the cognition [of it] would be untenable.
Since that which resides in a different locus is not manifested, there must be a statement regarding its locus.

If it is argued that the "state of the atoms" (*aṇusamavasthāna*) is the object [of perception], this amounts to a statement concerning the capacity of what is reached versus what is not reached: is the specific universal apprehended when the state of the atoms has not been reached, or when it has been reached?
If it is argued that perception occurs without contact, then there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving even a collection of atoms that is spatially obstructed;
for in that case, the specific universal residing in those obstructed atoms would be perceived.
If, on the other hand, it is argued that perception occurs only upon contact, [then...]
If it is argued that there is no manifestation because the middle and the far parts have not been reached,
and that manifestation occurs only to the extent that [the object] has been reached; then:
The status of being a substratum belongs to the arrangement of atoms to that extent;
it follows that its substratum is as much as is reached when a particular universal (jāti) is perceived.
In that case, when a single aggregate is being cognized, there is a distinction of objects.

This being the case, when this collection of atoms is perceived as "a tree," a multiplicity of trees would have to be perceived therein, for wherever a portion of the collection of atoms is grasped as being a tree, that too would be a tree.

Therefore, because the distinct state of the aggregated atoms is the object for the manifestation of a specific universal (*jāti*), the whole (*avayavin*) is an entity distinct [from its parts]. //39//
Perception has been examined. Now inference is being examined:
"Inference is not a valid means of knowledge because it is subject to error due to obstruction, destruction, and similarity. (NyS 2.1.37)
"Invalid" means that it does not establish the object even once.
For example, when a river is full due to being dammed,
one might conclude, "It has rained upstream," which is a false inference.
Even from the destruction of a nest, there occurs the movement of ants with their eggs;
at that time, the inference that "it will rain" is a false inference.
Furthermore, when a person also imitates the cry of a peacock, even then, due to the similarity of the sound, it becomes a false inference. //37//
NyS 2.1.38: [The fallacy of] "partial apprehension" does not apply, because [the object of inference] is a distinct entity from the fear of a part and from similarity.
This is not a case of deviation in inference;
rather, this is merely a misconception regarding inference where there is no actual inference.
How so? That which is undistinguished cannot serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*).

Indeed, perceiving that the rainwater is distinguished from the previous water by its greater rapidity and by its carrying away more foam, fruit, leaves, wood, and so forth, one infers, "It has rained upstream on the river," and not merely from the increase in the volume of water. Similarly, when there is a migration of eggs by a swarm of ants, it is inferred that "rain will fall," and not merely because of some individual ants.

"This is not the cry of a peacock; this sound is similar to it"—such is a false inference because of the failure to discern the distinction. However, for one who perceives the specific peacock's cry as distinct from a merely similar sound, the specific object being perceived serves as the inferential mark (*liṅga*), just as in the case of [inferring] snakes and the like.

This is a fault of the inferrer, not of inference, that he seeks to understand the object to be inferred through the observation of an unqualified object when there is a specific object [to be known]. //38//
It has been stated that inference has the three times as its object because it apprehends the three times. And therefore:
NyS 2.1.39: There is no present [action], because for something falling, there is the occurrence of the time already fallen and the time yet to fall.
When a fruit has fallen from its stalk and is approaching the ground, that which is above it is the path already traversed; the time conjoined with that is the "time already fallen" (*patitakāla*).
That which is below it is the path yet to be traversed; the time conjoined with that is the "time yet to fall" (*patitavyakāla*).
Now, there exists no third time-path where it could fall such that the present time might be apprehended;
therefore, the present time does not exist. //39//
NyS 2.1.40: These two also do not exist, because they depend upon the present, which itself does not exist.
Time is not manifested by the [three] paths;
rather, it is manifested by action, as in "he falls.
When the action of falling has ceased, that time is called the "time of having fallen."
When that time of falling is about to arise, it is the future time;
when the action existing in the substance is perceived, that is the present time.
And if one does not perceive the falling as existing in the substance, toward what would it attain the state of being about to arise or the state of cessation?
The action that has already occurred is expressed as "the time has fallen" (*patitaḥ kālaḥ*), while the action yet to arise is expressed as "the time is to fall" (*patitavyaḥ kālaḥ*);
in both of these temporal states, the substance is devoid of action.
"It falls downward" is connected with an action;
this [word] grasps the relationship between the action and the substance, and thus it is the present tense.
If that were not the case, the other two tenses, which depend upon it, would not exist. //40//
Moreover:
"The establishment of the past and the future is not through mutual dependence. (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.41)

If the past and the future were established through mutual dependence, we might accept the annihilation of the present. However, the establishment of the future does not depend on the past, nor does the establishment of the past depend on the future.
By what reasoning?

By what definition is the past established? How is the future established in dependence upon the past? And by what definition is there a future? This cannot be definitively stated; it is undeclared (*avyākaraṇīya*) because it would entail the negation of the present.
Furthermore, one might think that just as short and long, high ground and low ground, and shadow and sunlight are established through mutual dependence, so too are the past and the future.
That is not tenable, because there is no specific reason [for such a distinction].
Just as the example [of form and touch] applies, so too does the counter-example:

just as color (rūpa) and touch (sparśa), or smell (gandha) and taste (rasa), are established without depending on one another, so it is with the past and the future; thus, nothing is established through mutual dependence.
[The proof is established thus: ...

"proof" [is so called] because in the absence of one, there is the absence of the other, and consequently the absence of both. For if the establishment of one depends upon the other, then what does the other depend upon now?
And if the establishment of the other depends upon the one, then what does the one depend upon now?
Thus, in the absence of one, the other is not established; consequently, the non-existence of both follows as a logical consequence. //41//
And this present time is manifested by the actual existence of an object, as in the expressions: "substance exists," "quality exists," and "action exists.
For one for whom this [present time] does not exist—
NyS 2.1.42: If the present does not exist, there would be no apprehension of anything at all, because perception would be impossible.
Perception arises from the contact of a sense faculty with its object;
that which is non-existent or unreal cannot come into contact with a sense faculty,
nor does this [perception] authorize the existence of anything already existing.
The cause of perception, the object of perception, and perceptual knowledge—all of these are untenable.
Since perception is untenable, inference and verbal testimony are also untenable because they are preceded by it.
When all means of valid cognition are abolished, there can be no apprehension of anything at all. //42//
And time, existing in both ways, is apprehended in some cases as manifested by the existence of an object, as in "the substance exists";
in other cases it is manifested by a series of actions, as in "he cooks" or "he cuts.
A series of actions (*kriyāsantāna*) and the repetition of an action (*kriyābhyāsa*) consist of various kinds of actions directed toward a single purpose.

And various actions having a single purpose are expressed by the word "cooks" (*pacati*): placing the pot on the fire, pouring water, adding rice, adding fuel, stirring the fire, moving the ladle, draining the scum, and taking it down from the heat.
Similarly, the repetition of an action is expressed by "he cuts" (*chinatti*); that is, repeatedly raising the axe and bringing it down upon the wood, one says "he cuts."

And that which is being cooked and being cut is "being made" (*kriyamāṇa*); regarding that which is being made—NyS 2.1.43: "But because the states of having been done and of being to be done are possible, there is apprehension in both ways."
The sequence of action (*kriyāsantāna*) that has not yet begun but is intended to be performed is expressed as "the time has come; it will cook" (*āgataḥ kālaḥ pakṣyatīti*).
The cessation of the sequence of action, which has reached its purposeful completion, is expressed as "the time has passed; it has cooked" (*atītaḥ kālaḥ apākṣīd iti*).
[The cessation of the sequence of action is the past time: "it has cooked. (p. 526)
The present time is the continuum of an action that has begun, expressed as "he cooks. In this context, that which has ceased is "the state of having been done" (kṛtatā);
that which is intended to be done is "the state of being to be done" (kartavyatā).
That which exists is the state of being acted upon (*kriyamāṇatā*).

Thus, for one situated within a continuum of action (*kriyāsantāna*), the synthesis of the three times (*traikālyasamāhāra*)—expressed as "he cooks" or "it is cooked"—is grasped by the designation of the present;
for here it is the non-interruption of the continuum of action that is denoted, not its commencement nor its cessation.
Thus, existing in both ways, it is perceived as both separated and not separated from the past and the future;
it is manifested by its duration, as in "the substance exists";
and it is associated with the three times, expressing the non-interruption of the continuum of action, as in "he cooks" or "he cuts."
Furthermore, when there is a desire to express meanings such as proximity and so forth, one should observe that many types of words denoting those meanings are employed in common usage.
Therefore, the present tense exists. //43//
The establishment of analogy [is possible] through absolute, general, or partial similarity.
Comparison is not established because of absolute similarity;
for it is not the case that "as is a cow, so is a cow. (p. 528)
Comparison is not established through general similarity;
for it is not the case that "just as an ox, so is a buffalo.
Comparison is not established through partial similarity either.
For nothing whatsoever can be compared with everything. //44//
Since the establishment of analogy (*upamāna*) occurs through a well-known similarity, the aforementioned fault does not apply.

Comparison does not function by relying on the entirety, the majority, or the smallness of a common property; rather, it functions by relying on the relationship between the probandum and the probans based on a well-known similarity. And where this [relationship] exists, comparison cannot be denied.
Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not arise. //45//
Let it be, then, that analogy is inference—because the unperceived is established by means of the perceived. (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.46)

Just as the apprehension of the imperceptible fire by means of the perceptible smoke is inference, so too is the apprehension of the imperceptible gavaya by means of the perceptible cow; thus, this does not differ from inference. //46//
He says that it is distinguished.
By what reasoning?
*Nyāyasūtra* 2.1.47: "We do not see the purpose of comparison as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when the gayal is not perceived."

For when one who has already employed the analogy sees an object similar to a cow, he then understands the application of the name-word "this is a gavaya. And analogy is not inference, nor is it for the sake of another—[for it might be argued: "If analogy is not established for someone, it is performed for his sake by means of two well-known things; thus, analogy is for the sake of another. [We reply: No, because it is a determination made by oneself. Indeed, there is a determination made by oneself, such as: "As is a cow, so is a gavaya."

It is not the act of determination (*adhyavasāya*) that is being negated; rather, it is that [cognition] which does not constitute analogy (*upamāna*). For analogy is "the means of establishing what is to be established through a well-known similarity.
And for one to whom both [the object and its similarity] are already well-known, the relationship of "that which is to be established" and "the means of establishment" does not exist. //47//
Moreover:
"Because comparison is established through the application [of the word] 'so' (tathā), there is no lack of distinction. (NyS 2.1.48)
Thus, through the application of common properties (*samānadharmopasaṃhāra*), analogy (*upamāna*) is established, not inference (*anumāna*);
and this is the distinction between the two. //48//
NyS 2.1.49: Verbal testimony is inference, because an object is inferable from the non-perception [of it].
Verbal testimony is inference, not a separate means of valid cognition.
Why? Because the object of verbal testimony is something to be inferred.
How is it that [the object] is inferable?
Because it is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Just as the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), being unperceived, is subsequently measured by means of the measured mark (*liṅga*), it is therefore called inference (*anumāna*).
Thus, when an object that is not being perceived is subsequently measured by means of a measured word, verbal testimony is inference.
For this reason as well, sound is an inference:
because perception does not function in two ways.

When there is another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), perception (*upalabdhi*) functions in two ways; for it has been explained that in inference it functions in one way and in comparison (*upamāna*) in another.
However, the perception of both verbal testimony (*śabda*) and inference functions in a non-dual way; as it is in inference, so it is in verbal testimony as well.
Because there is no distinction [between them], inference is verbal testimony.
And because of the connection.
The term "inference" carries over [from the previous context].

When the relationship between a word and its object is established, the apprehension of the object occurs upon the perception of the word; just as, when the relationship between a mark (liṅga) and the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) is recognized, the apprehension of the possessor of the mark occurs upon the perception of the mark.
As for the claim that [the object] is an object of inference because it is an object (*artha*), that is not so—NyS 2.1.52:
Through the power of the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*), there arises a correct cognition of the object from the word.
Regarding such non-perceptible objects as heaven, the Apsarases, the Northern Kurus, the seven continents, the ocean, and the structure of the world, cognition arises not from the mere word alone;
rather, cognition arises because [one knows] "this word was spoken by trustworthy persons," for in the absence of such [trustworthiness], there is no cognition.
However, this is not the case with inference.
As for the argument that "because perception functions in two ways," this is precisely the difference in the operation of perception regarding verbal testimony and inference;
since there is a distinction there, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is not a valid reason because it lacks a specific distinction.
Furthermore, as for the phrase "and because of the relationship," there is indeed a relationship between word and meaning that is accepted,
and there is also one that is rejected.
A specific meaning for the sentence qualified by the genitive case "this belongs to that" has been admitted;
however, the relationship between word and meaning characterized as "attainment" (prāpti) is rejected.

Why? Because it is not perceived through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). First of all, attainment of word and meaning is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is beyond the reach of the senses.
An object that has transcended the state of being the domain of the sense-organ by which sound is perceived is not perceived;
yet there exists an object that has become a supersensible (atīndriya) domain, and between two things being perceived by the same sense-organ, contact is perceived.
And because filling, burning, and splitting are not perceived, there is an absence of connection.
Furthermore, if a connection characterized by attainment (*prāpti*) between word and meaning were accepted, then either the meaning would be located near the word,
or the word would be located near the meaning, or both would be located in both places.
Furthermore, is it not rather both?
The meaning is that this is because of the absence of place and articulatory effort (*sthāna-karaṇa*).
Moreover, this [word] is not perceived even through inference as being in proximity to the object.

Even on this view, the word is to be pronounced with its mouth, place of articulation, and manner of production, while the object is in proximity to it; thus, upon the pronunciation of the words "fire," "sword," and so forth, filling, cutting, and splitting would be grasped [as the actual effects], yet they are not so grasped.
Because they are not grasped, the relationship characterized by "attainment" (prāpti) cannot be inferred.

Regarding the statement "the word [is] near the object," there is no utterance because of the impossibility of the place and the instrument: the *sthāna* (place) refers to the throat and so forth, while the *karaṇa* (instrument) refers to a specific effort;
since these are not applicable when the object is at a distance, [the word cannot be uttered].
And because both are negated, it is neither;
therefore, the object is not reached by means of the word.
NyS 2.1.54: There is no refutation [of our position], because the determination of word-meanings is established.
Since we observe the determination of the cognition of an object from a word, it is inferred that there exists a relationship between word and object which serves as the cause of such determination.
For if there were no relationship, it would follow that any word whatsoever could produce a cognition of any object whatsoever.
Therefore, the existence of this relationship cannot be denied.
On this point, the resolution is as follows:
[Nyāyasūtra 2.1.55] "No, because the comprehension of the meaning of a word is occasional."
The determination of the relationship between word and meaning is not caused by an inherent connection;
rather, it is caused by convention (*samaya*).

As we have stated: "That which is expressed by the sentence qualified by the genitive case, namely 'this belongs to that,' is the specific meaning recognized as the relationship between word and meaning"—it is this convention that we have described.

What, then, is this "convention" (samaya)? It is the application of a rule that determines the relationship between signifier and signified, such that for this word, this collection of meanings is the object to be expressed.
When that [convention] is employed, the comprehension of the meaning arises from the word.
For in the opposite case, there would be an absence of cognition even upon hearing the word;
moreover, this [objection] is unavoidable even for one who maintains the theory of the relation [between word and meaning].
Furthermore, because people grasp [the word] as it is being used, the application of convention belongs to worldly persons.

And for the sake of preserving the tradition (*samaya*), this is the grammatical exposition (*vyākaraṇa*) which explains speech characterized by words, [and] the definition of meaning for speech characterized by sentences;
[it is] the definition of meaning for the definition...
[of words]. A sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of words (*padasamūha*) wherein the meaning is complete.
Thus, in this way, the relationship between word and meaning, characterized by apprehension (*prāpti*), does not serve as a basis for inference even in the slightest degree. //55//
And because there is no restriction regarding specific classes [of causes].
The comprehension of meaning from a word is conventional, not inherent.
Among seers, Aryans, and Mlecchas, the application of words for the purpose of conveying meaning proceeds according to their will.

For if the capacity of a word to convey meaning were inherent, it would not be subject to such arbitrary usage; just as the luminous quality of light, which is the cause of the cognition of form, does not deviate from its function across different species. //56//
Regarding the repeated performance of sacrifices such as the *putrakāmeṣṭi*:
NyS 2.1.57 states that their lack of authority [as means of valid knowledge] results from the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and tautology.
The Blessed One, the Seer, refers specifically to the word "of that" (*tasya*).
The status of the word as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not possible.
Why? Because of the fault of falsehood—as in the *Putrakāmeṣṭi* sacrifice: "One desiring a son should sacrifice with the Putreṣṭi."
When the *iṣṭi* sacrifice has been completed, the birth of a son is observed;

because of the falsity of such statements concerning perceptible matters, it is understood that even statements concerning imperceptible matters—such as "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra*"—are false.
Furthermore, this is due to the fault of contradicting what has been enjoined.

Having prescribed in the section on oblation that "one should offer when the sun has risen, one should offer before sunrise, or one should offer at the time of twilight," [the scripture] contradicts what was thus enjoined: "A dark dog devours the oblation of him who offers after sunrise;
a brindled dog devours the oblation of him who offers before sunrise; or both a dark and a brindled dog devour the oblation of him who offers at twilight.
Because of this contradiction, one or the other must be false.
Furthermore, there is the fault of tautology;

for when repetition is being taught—such as in the injunction, "He recites the first verse three times" and "the last verse three times"—the fault of tautology arises. And that which is tautological is the speech of a careless person.
Therefore, verbal testimony is not a means of valid cognition, because of the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and tautology. //57//
[The non-perception of the object] is not [due to the object's absence], but rather due to a deficiency in the action, the agent, or the instrument.
There is no fault of falsehood in the *putrakāmeṣṭi* sacrifice.
Why? Because of the deficiency in the ritual action, the agent, and the means.
[The view is] that by means of the sacrifice, the parents, having united, procreate a son.
The instrument (karaṇa) of the sacrifice is the means (sādhana);
the parents are the agents (kartārau); the conjunction is the action (karma).
The birth of a son results from the conjunction of three factors; conversely, its absence results from their deficiency.
First, regarding the ritual sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), deficiency in action consists of an error in the intended effort.
The deficiency of the agent consists in the performer being ignorant or of evil conduct;
the deficiency of the means consists in the sacrificial oblation being unprepared or defiled,
and the mantras being deficient or excessive, or lacking in proper accent and phoneme.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) may be improperly acquired, deficient, or censured.
Furthermore, defects in the ritual act pertaining to the officiants consist of improper application;
defects pertaining to the agent consist of abnormalities of the womb and damage to the seed.

Deficiency in the means (*sādhanavaiguṇya*) has been stated in the case of the desired result. And in the world, there is the injunctive sentence: "One desiring fire should rub two pieces of wood. In that context, deficiency in the action (*karmavaiguṇya*) consists of rubbing the wood incorrectly.
Deficiency in the agent consists of negligence regarding wisdom and effort;
deficiency in the means consists of [the wood being] wet, hollow, or burnt by forest fire.
In such cases, because the result is not produced, there is no fault of falsehood.

Because the production of results is observed through the application of qualities (*guṇa*), and this does not differ from worldly practice, as in the case of the injunction: "One desiring a son should sacrifice with the Putreṣṭi. //58//
NyS 2.1.59: Because a fault is stated even after having accepted [the opponent's position], provided there is a difference in time.
The phrase "there is no contradiction regarding the oblation" (na vyāghāto havane) carries over [from the previous sūtra].

When one violates the accepted time for the oblation and offers it at another time, this fault is stated regarding that deviation from the accepted time: "A dark [creature] consumes his oblation, he who offers after sunrise.
This is a statement of censure regarding the failure of the ritual injunction. //59//
And because the justification for restatement is established.
The topic at hand is that repetition is not a fault when it serves a purpose. Repetition that is devoid of meaning is tautology;
repetition that possesses meaning is restatement (anuvāda).
This repetition—namely, the restatement "He recites the first thrice, the last thrice"—is appropriate because it possesses purposeful meaning;
for by means of the triple recitation, the first and the last [verses] become fifteen in number among the *sāmidhenī* verses. (The *sāmidhenīs* thus attain the number fifteen. p. 555

And likewise, there is a mantra for salutation: "With this thunderbolt of speech consisting of fifteen [verses], I strike down this rival—him who hates us and whom we hate. This mantra of the thunderbolt refers to the fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses;
that [purpose] would not be achieved without repetition. //60//
And because the division of sentences is understood through the inclusion of the term "meaning" (artha).
Verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition, just as it is in the world. //61//
Furthermore, the classification of Brahmana statements is threefold—NyS 2.1.62:
because of their application as injunctions (vidhi), explanatory passages (arthavāda), and restatements (anuvāda).
Indeed, the statements of the Brahmins are classified into three types: injunctive statements, explanatory statements, and reiterative statements. //62//
In this regard—NyS 2.1.63: An injunction is that which prescribes.
That sentence which is prescriptive and impelling is an injunction (*vidhi*).
An injunction, moreover, is either a mandate (*niyoga*) or a permission (*anujñā*), such as "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice," and so forth. //63//
Praise, censure, the deeds of others, and ancient legends constitute explanatory passages (arthavāda).
The praise characterized by a statement of the fruit of the injunction is "stuti" (commendation); it serves the purpose of generating conviction,
so that one may have faith in what is being praised, and it is also an incitement to action.

One engages [in action] because of hearing about its fruit: "By means of the Sarvajit, the gods indeed conquered all; for the attainment of all, for the conquest of all, by this very [sacrifice] one attains all and conquers all.

A statement regarding an undesirable result is a censure intended for avoidance, according to the principle that "one should not practice what is censured. Such [statements] as "This Jyotiṣṭoma is indeed the first of sacrifices; he who, having performed this, performs another sacrifice, falls into a pit or dies" constitute [this category].

*Parakṛti* is the mention of a ritual act performed by another person that is contradicted [by the established rule], such as: "Having offered the omentum, they first sprinkle it with clarified butter;

then [they sprinkle] the speckled butter. But the Caraka-Adhvaryus, indeed, first sprinkle the speckled butter, saying, 'The speckled butter is the vital breaths of Agni, it is the Stoma,'" and so forth.
A rule practiced through tradition is called a *purākalpa* (ancient precedent).
For example: "Therefore, with this [sāman], the Brahmins should chant the *bahiṣpavamāna* stotra; we shall extend the sacrifice from its source," and so forth.
How are *purākṛti* and *purākalpa* considered explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)?
It is called an *arthavāda* because it is connected with a statement of praise or censure and because it illuminates some matter that serves as the basis for an injunction. //64//
NyS 2.1.65: Anuvāda (reiteration) is the restatement of that which has been enjoined by a rule.
Reiteration (anuvāda) consists of both the restatement of an injunction and the restatement of what has been enjoined.
The former is a restatement of words, while the latter is a restatement of meaning. Just as repetition (punarukta) is of two kinds, so too is reiteration.
But for what purpose is that which has been enjoined restated?
It is for the sake of providing a qualification (*adhikāra*);
having taken up what has been enjoined, either praise or censure is made known.

Or it is stated as a supplement to an injunction; furthermore, even that which follows immediately after what has been enjoined may be a restatement (anuvāda). In this same manner, other cases should also be inferred.

In the world as well, there are three types of sentences: injunctive (*vidhi*), explanatory (*arthavāda*), and reiterative (*anuvāda*). "One should cook rice" is an injunctive sentence. An explanatory sentence is: "Longevity, luster, strength, happiness, and eloquence are established in food."
The translation is as follows: "Cook! Cook! is repetition;
"Let it be cooked quickly" is likewise;
"Indeed, let it be cooked" is for the purpose of entreaty.
And the phrase "it must indeed be cooked" is for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

Just as in worldly sentences there is validity because the meaning is grasped through division [of words], so too Vedic sentences ought to possess validity because their meaning is grasped through division. //65//
There is no distinction between a restatement (*anuvāda*) and a tautology (*punarukta*), because both are justified as repetitions of words.
The distinction that "repetition is incorrect, whereas restatement is correct" is not tenable.
Why? Because in both cases a word whose meaning has already been understood is repeated; since there is a repetition of a word whose purpose has already been fulfilled, both are incorrect. //66//
Just as there is an instruction regarding a faster mode of movement, there is no lack of distinction due to repeated practice.
There is no lack of distinction between restatement (anuvāda) and tautology (punarukta).
Why? Because repetition that possesses meaning constitutes restatement;
repetition that possesses meaning is restatement.
It is like the instruction for moving more quickly:
"Go faster and faster"— the excellence of the action is expressed solely through repetition.
This is given as an illustration;
likewise, other types of repetition include "he cooks, he cooks," which denotes the non-cessation of an action,
and "every village is beautiful," which denotes pervasion.
"Pari pari trigartebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ" (It has rained all around the Trigartas) indicates exclusion;
"adhy adhi kuḍyaṃ niṣaṇṇam" (He is seated right up against the wall) indicates proximity;
"tiktaṃ tiktaṃ" (Bitter, bitter) indicates manner or kind.

Thus, it is established that a restatement (anuvāda) serves the purpose of providing a governing context (adhikāra) in cases of praise, censure, and all injunctions, as well as the purpose of referring to what immediately precedes the enjoined act. //67//
But is the validity of the word established merely by the removal of the reasons for its negation? No; and for this reason:
"Its validity is like the validity of mantras and Ayurveda, because of the validity of the authoritative person (āpta). (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.68)
Furthermore, what is the authority of Āyurveda?
It is that which is taught by Āyurveda: "By doing this, one attains the desired;
by avoiding this, one abandons the undesired."

The "being thus" (*tathābhāva*) of that which is being performed is the non-contradiction of its truthfulness. And when the words of a mantra—whose purpose is the warding off of a thunderbolt as their object—are employed, the fact that the matter is "thus" constitutes its authority.
By what is this [authority] produced?
It is established by the authority of a reliable person (āpta). But what is the authority of reliable persons?
It consists in having directly realized the nature of reality (dharmatā), compassion for living beings, and the desire to explain things as they truly are.
[Regarding the phrase "the desire to make known the object as it truly is"]:

Those who are authoritative (āpta) have indeed directly realized the Dharma; they feel genuine compassion for beings, thinking, "This is to be abandoned, this is the cause of its abandonment; this is to be attained, this is the cause of its attainment.
For those living beings who do not understand by themselves, there is no cause for understanding other than instruction from them.
Indeed, for living beings who are themselves not awakened, there is no cause for awakening other than instruction.
Furthermore, in the absence of awakening, there can be neither striving nor avoidance;
nor can there be a state of well-being without having acted.
Nor is there anyone else who can be of benefit to him.

Well then, let us instruct them according to our vision and according to reality; having heard this and practicing it, they will abandon what is to be abandoned and attain that which is to be attained.
Thus, the instruction of a reliable person (āptopadeśa), when embraced by these three kinds of reliability of the authority and put into practice, becomes the means for accomplishing the goal.
Thus, the instruction of a reliable person (*āptopadeśa*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
thus, reliable persons are a means of valid cognition.

By means of the portion of the Veda concerning perceptible objects—namely, Ayurveda, which is the instruction of a reliable person—one should infer that the portion of the Veda concerning imperceptible objects is also a means of valid cognition, because the reason for the reliability of the source is the same.
Furthermore, a portion of this [scriptural injunction], such as "one desiring a village should sacrifice," has a perceptible purpose;
therefore, it should be inferred [that other parts do as well]. Moreover, in the world, the majority of worldly practice is based upon instruction.

Even for a worldly teacher, there is validity through their knowledge of the object to be taught, through their desire to favor others, and through their wish to communicate the object as it truly is; because of the acceptance of that [teacher], the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, there is an inference based on the identity of the seers and the expounders:

those very same trustworthy persons who were the seers and expounders of the meanings of the Vedas were also the seers and expounders of the *Āyurveda* and other sciences; therefore, just as the authority of the *Āyurveda* is established, the authority of the Veda should be inferred.

[Objection: Since the Vedic sentences are eternal, their status as a means of valid cognition does not derive from the authority of trustworthy persons; thus, it is incorrect to say that their authority arises from the authority of trustworthy persons.
The status of sound as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the comprehension of meaning arises from its capacity to denote, not from its eternity.
For if it were eternal, since everything would be expressed by every [sound], the fixed relationship between word and meaning (*śabdārtha-vyavasthā*) would be untenable.
If it is argued that there can be no denotative power if it is non-eternal, we say no.
If it is argued that they too are eternal because they are not observed among worldly things, we say no;
for since they are not the teaching of an authoritative person, it is impossible for them to be non-contradictory with reality.
For it is because of its eternity that sound is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued:
"But it [sound] is non-eternal"?
This is a statement made without distinction.
One must state the reason why worldly instruction from an unreliable source is not eternal:
because names and words convey their meaning according to their application, they possess authority in the world; however, since [the Veda] is eternal, its authority is untenable.
In this world, a word is employed for a specific meaning, and it becomes a communicator of that meaning through the power of its application,
not because of its eternity. Furthermore,
the eternity of the Vedas consists in the uninterrupted continuity of their tradition, study, and usage throughout past and future intermediate Manvantaras and Yugas.

The eternity of the Vedas consists in the uninterrupted continuity of their tradition, practice, and application regarding the past and the future; furthermore, their authority derives from the authority of the trustworthy person (āpta), and this is the same for worldly words as well. //68//
Thus ends the first daily lesson of the second chapter in the *Nyāyabhāṣya* of Vātsyāyana.
Now begins the second daily lesson of the second chapter.
Considering that the enumeration of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not in accordance with reality, he says:

NyS 2.2.1: Nor is there a fourfold [number of means of valid cognition], because tradition (aitihya), presumption (arthāpatti), probability (sambhava), and non-existence (abhāva) are also means of valid cognition.
There are not only four means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
What then? Tradition (aitihya), presumption (arthāpatti), probability (sambhava), and non-existence (abhāva)—these also are means of valid cognition.
Why are those [other means of knowledge] not mentioned?
*Aitihya* is a tradition of report whose original speaker is unspecified, expressed as "so they say. *Arthāpatti* is the implication of a fact by virtue of another fact.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is an implication (*prasaṅga*).
When a certain meaning is being expressed, another meaning that necessarily follows is presumption.
For example: "When clouds are absent, rain does not occur."
What is implied here by the statement "it exists"? That it exists when [the causes] are present.
Presumption (*sambhava*) is the apprehension of the existence of one thing based on the apprehension of the existence of another thing that is inseparably connected (*avinābhāvin*).

For example, from the apprehension of the existence of a *droṇa* measure, there is the apprehension of the existence of an *āḍhaka*; and from the apprehension of the existence of an *āḍhaka*, [there is the apprehension of the existence] of a *prastha*.
Non-existence is the opposite of existence; that which has not come into being serves as the indicator of that which has come into being.

The non-existent activity of raining indicates the existent conjunction of wind and clouds, for when there is a restraining conjunction of wind and clouds, the activity of falling does not occur in water due to its weight. //1//
These are indeed valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but they are not distinct means of knowledge.
Yet, by one who considers them to be distinct means of knowledge, a refutation is stated; this is as follows:

NyS 2.2.2: There is no refutation [of inference] because oral tradition (*aitihya*) is not distinct from verbal testimony (*śabda*), and because presumption (*arthāpatti*), postulation (*sambhava*), and absence (*abhāva*) are not distinct from inference (*anumāna*).
The refutation is untenable. How so? [Because] "verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person" (āptopadeśaḥ śabdaḥ).
And the definition of verbal testimony does not exclude traditional lore (aitihya).
Thus, this particularity is subsumed under the universal.
Inference is the cognition of an imperceptible object through its connection with a perceptible one.
[Inference is the cognition of that which is connected. p. 576
Likewise, there is no such thing as *arthāpatti* (presumption) or *sambhava* (possibility).
Because the apprehension of a meaning not explicitly stated occurs through its being the opposite of the understood meaning of a sentence, *arthāpatti* is nothing other than inference (*anumāna*).
And *sambhava* is the apprehension of one member of a whole by means of the whole, between two related things that exist in a relation of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).

Furthermore, when two entities—one being a collection and the other its constituent—are connected through their respective functions, it is possible for one to be apprehended by means of the collection;
that too is indeed inference.
When opposition is established in the sense that "this being present, that is not tenable," an obstructing factor of the cause is inferred from the non-occurrence of the effect.
Thus, this enumeration of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is indeed according to their actual nature. //2//
It has been stated that these are indeed valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but they are not distinct means of knowledge;
however, in this regard, the admission of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as a valid means of knowledge is untenable. For instance:
NyS 2.2.3: Presumption is not a means of valid cognition because it is inconclusive.
When there is no rain when clouds are absent, it follows by implication that it occurs when they are present; yet, even when they are present, it does not occur at times.
Thus, this *arthāpatti* (presumption) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). //3//
There is no inconclusiveness regarding presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), because what is not actually a presumption is mistakenly taken to be a presumption. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.4)
From the statement "when the cause is absent, the effect does not arise," the opposing meaning—that "when the cause is present, the effect arises"—is established by implication;
for existence is the opposite of non-existence.
Thus, this arising of the effect, being established by implication when the cause is present, does not deviate from the existence of the cause.
Indeed, an effect does not arise when its cause is absent; therefore, [the reason] is not inconclusive.

As for the claim that an effect does not arise despite the presence of its cause due to an obstruction of the instrumental conditions (*nimitta-pratibandha*), this is a property of the cause itself, and it is not the object of inference by implication (*arthāpatti*).
What, then, is the object of this [inference]?

When a cause exists, the effect arises; thus, this arising of the effect does not deviate from the existence of the cause, and that is its object of cognition (*prameya*). However, since there is no actual *arthāpatti* (presumption) here, the refutation is stated by one who has merely formed the misconception that it is *arthāpatti*. [The phrase "since there is no actual *arthāpatti*, the refutation is stated by one who has formed the misconception that it is *arthāpatti*" appears twice in the source. p. 580
And the invalidity of the negation [of the probans] is due to its being inconclusive (anaikāntika).
The statement "Presumption (arthāpatti) is not a valid means of knowledge because it is inconclusive" is a negation;
by this, the validity of presumption is negated, but not its existence.
In this way, it becomes inconclusive.
Because it is inconclusive, no object whatsoever is negated by this non-authoritative [reasoning]. //5//
Now, if you think that there is deviation [of inference] regarding objects whose scope is restricted to their own specific domain,

and that the existence of a negation is not its object, then in that case— NyS_2,2.6: Or, if that [negation] is a valid means of knowledge, then the validity of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) does not follow.
The scope of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is also the non-deviation of the existence of a cause from the production of its effect;
nor is it the case that the nature of the cause is to fail to produce an effect due to an obstruction of the instrumental conditions. //6//
In that case, the admission of non-existence as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not tenable. Why?
NyS 2.2.7: Non-existence is not a means of valid cognition because its object of cognition (prameya) is not established.

Since non-existence (*abhāva*) is an abundant object of cognition established in the world, [the opponent] out of impudence says: "Non-existence is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because its object of cognition is not established. //7//
Now, because this subject matter is extensive, only a portion of it is illustrated:
NyS 2.2.8: Since those not yet characterized are characterized by the absence of a characteristic among those already characterized, that object of knowledge is established.

The object of cognition (prameya) consisting of that non-existence is established. How so? Among garments that have been characterized and are not to be taken, the objects to be taken are those uncharacterized ones; they are characterized by the absence of characteristics, because they are characterized by the non-existence of characteristics. When one is commanded, "Bring the uncharacterized garments," while both types are present, one recognizes those garments in which no characteristics exist precisely through the absence of characteristics.
And having practiced, one brings [the goal] about;
furthermore, valid cognition is the cause of practice. //8//
NyS_2.2.9: If it is argued that non-existence cannot occur when an object is absent, we say no, because another defining characteristic is applicable.
Where something, having existed, does not exist, there its non-existence is established.
However, in the case of unmarked garments, they do not cease to exist after having been marked;
therefore, the absence of marks in them is untenable.

[The phrase] "is not established" [is used] because other characteristics are established—just as one perceives the establishment of characteristics in other garments, one does not do so in those that are uncharacterized.
Thus, perceiving this absence of characteristics, one understands the object through its non-existence. //9//
Because that [non-existence] is established, it is not a valid reason regarding those things that have not been characterized.
Regarding those characteristics that are observed in those [objects] where perfection and existence are found, there is no absence of those characteristics;
and as for those characteristics which exist in the observed, their absence in the unobserved is not a valid reason, for the absence of those things which actually exist is contradicted. //10//
Not so, because establishment occurs in dependence on that which exists according to its defining characteristic.
We do not say that there is an absence of those characteristics which exist;
rather, some characteristics are established while others are not established.
Considering this, one realizes the absence of those characteristics in relation to which one does not perceive the presence of characteristics. //11//
And because non-existence prior to production is logically established.
Indeed, non-duality of absence (abhāvadvaita) exists: first, there is non-existence prior to origination;
second, there is non-existence due to the loss of the self once it has originated.
Among these, in the case of unmarked garments, it is the absence of marks characterized by non-existence prior to origination that is meant, and not the other [kind of absence]. //12//

By stating the qualification regarding its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—namely, "Verbal testimony (śabda) is the instruction of a reliable person (āpta)"—it is made known that verbal testimony is of various kinds.
Regarding it, there is a general inquiry: is it eternal (nitya) or non-eternal (anitya)?
And when the cause for such deliberation is questioned, doubt arises due to conflicting views (vipratipatti).
Some maintain that sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*), all-pervasive (*vibhu*), eternal (*nitya*), and characterized by manifestation (*abhivyakti*).
Others hold that it resides within substances in association with odor and other qualities, remaining there like odor itself and characterized by manifestation.
Still others maintain that sound is a quality of space, characterized by origination and cessation, like cognition (*buddhi*).
Others hold that sound arises from the agitation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), is non-dependent, and possesses the nature of origination and cessation;
therefore, there is doubt as to what the truth in this matter is.
"Sound is impermanent" is the reply. How so?
Because it possesses effort, because it is perceptible by the senses, and because it is treated as being produced. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.13)
The "origin" (ādi) is the source or cause, from which something is derived.
That which possesses a cause is observed to be non-eternal.
Furthermore, sound is produced by conjunction and disjunction; therefore, because it possesses a cause, sound is non-eternal.
What, then, is this demonstration of meaning by means of a reason?
It is because it possesses the property of arising;
that is, sound is impermanent—having come into being, it ceases to be, for it possesses the property of destruction.

This is a matter of doubt: are conjunction and disjunction the causes of the production of sound, or rather the causes of its manifestation? To this he says: "Because it is perceptible by the senses" (*aindriyakatvāt*).
That which is grasped through proximity to the sense organs is "perceptible by the senses" (*aindriyaka*).

Is this [sound] manifested while occupying the same location as its manifestor, like color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; or rather, when a series of sounds arises from a sound produced by conjunction, that which is proximate to the ear is perceived?

Since sound is perceived even when the conjunction has ceased, it is not perceived as occupying the same location as its manifestor—for instance, when wood is being cut, once the conjunction between the wood and the axe has ceased, the sound is still perceived by one standing at a distance.
Furthermore, the perception of the manifested does not occur in the absence of the manifestor.
Furthermore, the apprehension of the manifested [sound] does not occur in the absence of a manifestor; therefore, conjunction is not a manifestor.

Rather, when conjunction is productive, a series of sounds arises from the sound born of that conjunction, and there is the apprehension of that which has reached the vicinity of the ear. Thus, it is logical that the sound is apprehended upon the cessation of the conjunction.
