Furthermore, sound is produced and not manifested— because it is treated as something produced (*kṛtaka*). It is treated as produced when one says "intense" or "weak," just as one speaks of "intense pleasure, weak pleasure, intense pain, or weak pain."
And one speaks of "intense sound" and "weak sound.

If it is argued that the intensity or weakness of the apprehension occurs because the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is likewise [intense or weak], just as with color-form (*rūpa*), we say no; for this would entail the possibility of suppression (*abhibhava*).

Due to the intensity or weakness of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) which acts as the manifestor, there arises an intensity or weakness in the apprehension of the sound, but the sound itself does not differ.

Just as the perception of form [is affected] by the intensity or dullness of light, that is not so; for in this way, the suppression [of one sound by another] is logically established: a loud sound of a drum suppresses a faint sound of a lute, but a faint sound does not.
Furthermore, the apprehension of sound is not the subduer,
nor is the sound itself divided;
rather, subdual is logical only when the sound is divided.

Therefore, sound is produced, not manifested. Furthermore, obscuration (abhibhava) is impossible; for if manifestation occurs where [the sound] is co-located with the manifestor, there would be no contact—on the view that "sound is manifested in the same location as the manifestor," it is not possible, because the sound of the lute strings is not reached by the sound of the drum.

If it is argued that "overpowering occurs without contact," there follows the undesirable consequence of the overpowering of all sounds. If one should think that overpowering occurs even in the absence of contact, then just as the sound of a drum overpowers a certain sound of a lute string, so too the sound of a drum situated at a distance would overpower the sounds of lute strings situated near the listener, because of the lack of contact.
Consequently, when a drum is struck in only one place, the sounds of lute strings occurring simultaneously throughout the entire world would not be heard.
Since there exist various distinct series of sounds, it is logical that for some sound, due to its proximity to the auditory organ, there may be an overpowering of another sound—
either intense or weak. But what, indeed, is this so-called "overpowering"?
Overpowering (*abhibhava*) is the non-perception caused by the perception of something belonging to the same class as the object to be perceived;
for example, the light of a torch, though capable of being perceived, is [not perceived] because of the light of the sun. //13//

NyS 2.2.14: [The term "non-eternal" is applied] neither because of the non-existence of a jar, nor because of the eternality of the universal [of "non-existence"], nor because of the metaphorical application of "non-eternal" even to eternal things.
Sound is certainly not impermanent because it has a beginning.
Why? Because of deviation.
For the non-existence of a jar, which indeed has a beginning, is observed to be permanent.
How can it have a beginning?
For a jar does not exist apart from the division of its causes.
How, then, could it be eternal?
That which does not arise from the disintegration of its causes can never have its non-existence overturned by existence;
as for the argument based on being perceptible by the senses, that too is inconclusive.
Furthermore, the universal (sāmānya) is both perceptible by the senses and eternal.
As for the claim that it is "designated as if it were produced," this too is subject to deviation.

The metaphorical treatment of eternal things as if they were non-eternal is observed; for instance, one says "a portion of a tree," "a portion of a blanket," and likewise, "a portion of space" and "a portion of the self. //14//
NyS 2.2.15: There is no deviation [from the definition] because of the distinction between that which possesses the essence and that which participates in it.
Regarding the term "eternal" (*nitya*), what is its true nature?
Eternality is the impossibility of the destruction of one's own essence for that which is characterized by the non-arising of any other entity;
and that [destruction] is not possible in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*).

But that which is figurative (*bhākta*) is as follows: when one ceases to be oneself—that is, having been, one no longer exists—and never comes to be again, there the non-existence of a jar is treated as if it were eternal; such is the nature of this category (*padārtha*).
In that regard, since no effect whatsoever is observed to be eternal in the same manner as the [eternal] word, there is no deviation [from the rule].

As for the claim that "because the universal is eternal, that which is grasped through sensory proximity is sensory"—[this is refuted] by the qualification [of the inference] regarding the continuum (santāna). (NyS 2.2.16)
The subject under discussion is that there is no deviation regarding eternal things.
It is not because of the capacity of the sense organs to grasp [the object] that sound is non-eternal;
rather, because it is grasped through proximity to the sense organs, there is an inference of a continuum (santāna), and by means of that, its non-eternality is established.

As for the claim that [the term "non-eternal"] is applied even to eternal things by way of metaphorical usage, this is not so; for (NyS 2.2.17) the word "part" (*pradeśa*) denotes a causal substance (*kāraṇadravya*).
"Even in the case of eternal things, there is no deviation.

Thus, in [the expressions] "space-point" (*ākāśapradeśa*) and "self-point" (*ātmapradeśa*), the causal substance of space or the self is not being denoted here in the same way as it is for a produced thing.
For how could that which does not exist be denoted?
And its non-existence [as a substance] follows from its non-perception by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
What, then, is asserted in that regard?
It is the non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*) of conjunction: the conjunction of space with a delimited substance does not pervade space; it exists without pervading it.
Therefore, this [term] has a commonality with a produced substance;
for the conjunction of two *āmalaka* fruits does not pervade its substratum.
And it is by virtue of this commonality that there is the figurative designation (*bhakti*) of "space" as a "location" (*pradeśa*).
By this, the [existence of] spatial divisions of the self has been explained.
Furthermore, just as with conjunction, sound, cognition, and so forth, possess non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*).
And it has been examined that the intensity and dullness of sound are properties of the essence of sound itself, and are not produced by figurative attribution (*bhakti*).

But why is it that no sūtra is heard from the author of the sūtras regarding this matter? This is the custom of the venerable author of the sūtras: in many instances, he does not establish two opposing positions; rather, one should ascertain the truth there based on the established tenets of the treatise (*śāstra*).
And the established tenet of the treatise is inference, which is designated as "reasoning" (*nyāya*), is accepted, and has many branches. //17//
Furthermore, how is it to be understood that "this exists" and "this does not exist"?
It is to be understood through the apprehension and non-apprehension of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
In that case, the word (*śabda*) would be non-existent—
NyS 2.2.18: [Sound is eternal] because it is not perceived prior to its utterance, and because no such thing as an obstruction is perceived.
Before its utterance, the word does not exist.
Why? Because it is not perceived.
[The opponent's claim that] "the non-perception of an existent thing is due to such factors as concealment" is untenable.

Why? Because the causes of non-perception, such as obstruction and the like, are not apprehended— since no cause for non-perception, such as "the sound is not perceived because it is obstructed" or "it is not perceived because it is not in contact with the sense organ due to an intervening barrier," is grasped, this [sound] which was not uttered is therefore considered non-existent.
"Utterance is its manifestor; therefore, there is non-perception prior to utterance due to the absence of that [manifestor].
What, then, is this so-called "utterance"?
It is the impact upon the throat, palate, and other points of articulation by the internal air impelled by the effort produced by the desire to speak.

Through effort, there is the striking against the throat, palate, and other locations by the abdominal air that has been impelled; from such striking at the respective places, the manifestation of the phonemes occurs.
Indeed, this "striking" is a specific kind of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Furthermore, the capacity of conjunction to manifest [an object] has been refuted;
therefore, the non-perception [of sound] is not due to the absence of a manifester,
but rather due to its [sound's] very non-existence.
This [word], while being uttered, is heard; and while being heard, it is inferred that "having not existed, it comes to be.
Furthermore, after the utterance, it is no longer heard; having come to be, it ceases to be, and because of its non-existence, it is no longer heard.
How so? It has been stated that this is due to the non-perception of an obstruction and so forth.
Therefore, sound possesses the nature of origination and disappearance. //18//

This being the case, as if scattering dust upon the truth, he says this: NyS 2.2.19: "The existence of an obscuration is established because that [obscuration] is not perceived due to its non-perception."

If there is no obscuration because it is not perceived, then the non-perception of obscuration must also not exist because it is not perceived; therefore, due to its absence, obscuration would be unrefuted.
How, then, do you know that the non-perception of obscuration is not perceived?

What is to be known here? Because it is to be personally realized, it is the same: indeed, one who does not perceive an obscuration personally realizes for oneself, "I do not perceive an obscuration," just as one who is obstructed by a wall and perceives that obscuration personally realizes for themselves [that they are obstructed].
Thus, this non-perception of an obstruction is itself to be experienced just like the perception of an obstruction;
and this being the case, there exists a subsequent statement whose subject matter has been removed [by the preceding]. //16//
However, by way of a concessive argument, the proponent of the genus (jāti-vādin) says:
"Even from non-perception, because of the existence of non-perception itself, there is no impossibility of an obstruction, since it is not perceived. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.20)

Just as there exists the non-perception of an obstruction even while it is not being perceived, if you concede that there likewise exists an obstruction even though it is not being perceived— by conceding that "there exists the non-perception of an obstruction which is not being perceived"—
and yet you say, "There is no obstruction because it is not perceived," [you contradict yourself].
Even in this doctrine of permission, a restriction regarding practice is not tenable. //20//
Because non-apprehension consists in the nature of non-perception, it is not a valid reason.
"That which is perceived exists, and that which is not perceived does not exist"; thus it is established that what is non-existent is characterized by non-perception.

And non-apprehension is the absence of apprehension; thus, because it is an absence, it is not apprehended. Furthermore, since an obstruction is indeed something existent, it ought to be apprehended by means of its own apprehension; yet it is not apprehended. Therefore, it does not exist. [Since an obstruction is indeed something existent, it ought to be apprehended by means of its own apprehension; yet it is not apprehended. Therefore, it does not exist. p.619
In this regard, what was stated—that the impossibility of an obscuration [is not established] because of non-perception—is incorrect. //21//
Now, asserting the eternity of sound, for what reason does he assert it?
— Because it is intangible. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.22)
Just as space is seen to be eternal and intangible, so too is sound. //22//
Thus, this [reason] is "deviant" (savyabhicāra) from both sides: an atom is seen to be tangible and yet eternal, while action is seen to be intangible and yet non-eternal.
Regarding the reason "because of being intangible," here is an example by way of similarity with the probandum (sādhyasādharmyeṇodāharaṇam):
NyS 2.2.23: No, because action is impermanent.
An example by way of dissimilarity with the probandum (sādhyavaidharmya):
"Because it is not eternal" (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.24).
In both examples, it is not a valid reason because of deviation. //24//
In that case, the reason is this:
"Because of tradition" (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.25).
It is observed that what is being handed over remains stationary;
and sound is being handed over by the teacher to the pupil;
therefore, it is stationary. //25//
Because that which lies between them is not perceived, this is not a valid reason.
By what mark is its existence perceived in the interval between that by which something is given and that to whom it is given?
For it is an unavoidable fact that the object being given, while remaining stationary, departs from the giver and reaches the recipient. //26//
NyS 2.2.27: There is no prohibition [of the Veda] because of its being taught.
Study is the indicative mark; for if there were no tradition, teaching would not exist. //27//
NyS 2.2.28: There is no refutation [of the argument], because one or the other of the two positions has been taught.
The teaching is the same for both positions, because the doubt has not been removed:
does the word residing in the teacher pass over to the student—that is the teaching—or does it not pass over to him—that is the teaching? (p. 623)
Or rather, is teaching the imitation of what has been learned, like instruction in dancing? Thus, teaching is not a mark [indicative] of the recipient. //28//
In that case, the reason is this:
[Nyāyasūtra 2.2.29] "Because of practice."
That which is being practiced is seen to be stable;
when one says "he sees five times," it means the form is seen again and again as something stable.
Furthermore, there is repetition with respect to sound—as in "the hymn has been recited ten times" or "it has been recited twenty times."
Therefore, the repeated utterance of that which is already established is called practice (abhyāsa). //29//
It is not so, because even when there is difference, there is a figurative application of the term "repetition."

Even when there is no fixed limit, repetition is expressed, as in: "May you dance twice, may you dance thrice," or "He danced twice, he danced thrice," or "He performs the Agnihotra twice," or "He eats twice. (30)
Thus, because of the fallacy of deviation, the use of the word "other" (*anya*) in a prohibited reason is refuted:
"If one thing is other than another because of its non-otherness, then there is an absence of otherness. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.31)
That which you consider to be "other" does not actually become other because it is non-different from its own nature;
thus, there is an absence of otherness.
In this regard, what was stated—that even in the case of otherness, [the term is applied] through the metaphorical usage of repeated practice—is incorrect. //31//
For one who denies the employment of a word, the employment of another word is also denied:
"In the absence of that [word], there is no non-difference between the two, because they are established in mutual dependence. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.32)

You establish the non-difference of one thing from another; having established it, you then deny that there is any difference, yet you acknowledge the word "non-different" and employ this compound term "ananyat."
This word *anya* is compounded with a negation.
If, however, there were no subsequent term here, with what would this [word] be compounded by means of negation?

Therefore, between those two words, *anya* and *ananya*, the other—the word *ananya*—is established in dependence upon the other, the word *anya*. Thus, what was stated—that there is an absence of difference—is incorrect.
Let it be, then, that sound is eternal now—because no cause for its destruction is perceived. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.33)
Whatever is impermanent, its destruction arises from a cause, as in the case of a clod of earth, which results from the disjunction of its constituent substances.
If sound were impermanent, that cause from which its destruction arises would be perceived; however, it is not perceived. Therefore, [sound] is eternal. //33//
NyS 2.2.34: Since no cause for non-hearing is perceived, it would follow that there must be constant hearing.

Just as there would be the consequence of non-destruction because no cause of destruction is perceived, so too there would be the consequence of constant audition because no cause for the absence of audition is perceived.
If it is argued that there is no audition due to the absence of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), [we reply that] the manifestor has already been refuted.
Now, [the opponent might argue that] there is no hearing of something existing because it lacks a cause, just as there is destruction of something existing without a cause.
But this objection is equally inconsistent with observed fact, whether regarding destruction or non-hearing in the absence of a cause. //34//
And since non-perception is absent when [the object] is being perceived, it is not a valid reason.

Furthermore, when the cause of the destruction of sound is apprehended through inference, the argument that "it does not exist because no cause of destruction is perceived" is not a valid reason (*anapadeśa*), just as [the argument] "therefore it is a horse because it has horns.
If it is asked, "What is the inference? [the answer follows].
The production of a series [of sound]:
the series of sound has been established as follows—from a sound produced by conjunction and disjunction (saṃyoga-vibhāga), another sound arises; from that, yet another; and from that, still another.
In this process, the effect-sound suppresses the cause-sound, while the conjunction with a resistant substance (pratighāti-dravya) is the suppressor of the final sound.
However, conjunction with a resistant substance (*pratighātidravyasaṃyoga*) is the cause of the cessation of the final sound.

For it is observed that when there is an obstruction such as a wall, a sound is not heard even by one standing nearby, whereas it is heard even by one standing at a distance provided there is no obstruction.

Furthermore, when a bell is struck, a series of various sounds is heard without interruption—appearing as loud, louder, soft, and softer—due to the differences in their auditory perception. Thus, a succession of distinct sounds is perceived.

In that case, regarding the eternal sound, one must state whether the cause of its manifestation resides in the bell, or elsewhere, or remains stationary, or functions as a continuous series (*santānavṛtti*), or acts as the cause of manifestation; for it is by means of this that a continuous stream of auditory perception occurs, and since there is no difference in the sound itself, the distinction between various auditions must be accounted for.

But since sound is impermanent, there exists in the bell another instrumental cause, consisting of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), which operates as a continuous series and functions in conjunction with the contact [of the striker]; this follows in intensity—whether sharp or dull—and through its persistence, the series of sounds persists.
Furthermore, because that [impression] varies in being sharp or dull, the sound itself possesses intensity or dullness, and it is this that produces the difference in its auditory perception. //35//
Is it not the case that no other cause for the formation [of sound] is perceived, and because it is not perceived, it does not exist? [Response:
No, for there is no non-perception [of the cause], since sound ceases upon the contact with the hand.
Through the action of the hand, there occurs contact with the bell, and when that occurs, the series of sounds does not arise;
therefore, hearing is impossible.
In this regard, it is inferred that the conjunction with a resistant substance obstructs another causal factor of the sound, which exists as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
And due to its cessation, the series of sound does not arise;

in the absence of arising, there is an interruption of hearing, just as when the *saṃskāra*—the cause of the arrow's motion—is destroyed through contact with a resistant substance, there is an absence of movement. Likewise, there is the cessation of the series of vibrations which is perceptible by the sense of touch.
The contact of the hand with bronze vessels and the like is the mark of the continuity of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, there is no non-perception of another cause that consists of a mental impression. //36//
And because no cause of destruction is perceived, if [the sound] were to persist, it would follow that it is eternal.
If that for which no cause of destruction is perceived remains, then by virtue of its remaining, its eternity follows as a logical consequence;
thus, indeed, regarding these hearings of sound, it is held that they are the manifestations of sound.
No cause for their destruction is established by you;
because no such cause is established, they must persist, and from that persistence, it follows that they are eternal.
If this is not the case, [then...]
In that case, since no cause for destruction is perceived, sound persists; therefore, it is eternal. //37//
The resonance that has a substrate identical to that of the vibration ceases upon contact with the hand, just like the vibration itself, because its cause has ceased.
For if they were in different substrates (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), then due to contact with a resistant substance, only that which is in the same substrate (*samānādhikaraṇa*) would cease.
[Nyāyasūtra 2.2.38: There is no refutation [of sound] because it is intangible (*asparśatva*).
As for this [objection], that "sound is not a quality of space"—this negation is untenable, because the substratum of sound is intangible (*asparśatva*).

Since sound is not perceived in the same location as color and other qualities, it is understood that sound has as its substratum an intangible, all-pervading substance (*vyāpidravya*), on account of the occurrence of a series of sounds (*śabdasantāna*), and not a substratum common to vibration (*kampa*). //38//

It is not tenable that sound, which resides together with color and other qualities in each substance, is manifested while occupying the same location [as them]. Why? Because in a compound, there would be the occurrence of different case endings. (NyS 2.2.39)
And the meaning of "because of the occurrence of a continuum" has been explained.
If form and so forth, as well as sounds, were all present together and combined in every substance, then they would be combined in that aggregate.
In a collection, whatever is situated as belonging to a certain genus must be apprehended as belonging to that very same genus, just as [colors] such as form are in the case of sound.

In this regard, there is this distinction: within a single substance, various forms of sounds possessing different articulations (*bhinnaśruti*) and distinct properties (*vidharma*) are heard as being manifested; and there is another distinction consisting of sounds possessing similar forms, identical articulations (*samānaśruti*), and common properties (*sadharmā*), by virtue of their qualities of intensity (*tīvra*) and dullness (*manda*).
They are heard as distinct; therefore, both [of those views] are untenable.

This property belongs to elements that arise as manifold things, not to a single thing being manifested. [This property belongs to elements that arise as manifold things, not to a single thing being manifested. p.638
Furthermore, there is this distinction and another distinction;
therefore, because such distinctions are established, we consider that sound is not manifested as being inherently present within each substance together with color and the other qualities. //39//

This sound is of two kinds: consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*) and mere resonance (*dhvani*). Regarding that which consists of phonemes first: NyS 2.2.40: There is doubt because of the teaching of both modification (*vikāra*) and substitution (*ādeśa*).

Regarding the example *dadhy atra*, some consider this a "modification" (*vikāra*), thinking that the vowel *i* abandons its quality of *itva* and undergoes the state of *yatva*. Others maintain that when the vowel *i* ceases to be employed because the context has been established, they speak of the employment of *y* in its place.
Thus, both views are taught: that in the context of *saṃhitā*, the vowel *i* is not employed, and in its stead, the substitute *y* is employed.
In that regard, it is not known what the reality (tattva) is.
The reality is the instruction of the primary material cause (ādeśopadeśa).

For if there were an instruction regarding a transformation (vikāropadeśa), the transformation could not be inferred because the underlying continuity (anvaya) would not be perceived; [only] if there were continuity could one infer a transformation by noting that "something ceases and something else arises."
Furthermore, no positive concomitance (anvaya) is perceived; therefore, there is no modification [of one phoneme into another].

Moreover, when two phonemes produced by different articulatory organs are not employed together, their employment is logically established: the phoneme *i* is produced with an open articulation (*vivṛta-karaṇa*), while the phoneme *y* is produced with a slightly contacted articulation (*īṣatspṛṣṭa-karaṇa*).
These two must be articulated by means of distinct efforts known as "articulatory positions" (*karaṇa*).
Thus, it is logical that when one of these two is not applied, the other is applied;
and there is no distinction in the case of non-modification.
Wherever these two—the vowel *i* and the consonant *y*—are not subject to modification, as in the word *yatate*, [the rule applies].
He restrains it;
he was restraining it;
thus, the vowel *i* [is used], as in the word *idam*.

Furthermore, in cases where a modification has occurred, such as when one says "bring curd for the sacrifice," there is no difference between the two instances regarding the effort of the speaker or the hearing of the listener; thus, the designation [of the substitute] is justified.
Moreover, this is because the actual word being employed is not perceived [as the original].
Indeed, it is not that the phoneme *i* is perceived as undergoing a transformation into the phoneme *y*.
What then? When the phoneme *i* is employed, the phoneme *y* is employed [in its place];
therefore, it is called "unchanged" (*avikāra*).
And if there were no modification, there would be no loss of the grammatical derivation of words;
for it would be established that "phonemes do not undergo modification.
Furthermore, on this view, since the grammatical derivation of words would be impossible, we would have no basis for accepting the modification of phonemes.
Indeed, one phoneme does not have another phoneme as its effect;
for the letter *y* is not produced from the letter *i*, nor is the letter *i* produced from the letter *y*.
For these phonemes are produced by distinct places of articulation and efforts; it is therefore logical that they may be employed in each other's place.
This transformation must be either a change of state (*pariṇāma*) or a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*);
yet neither of these exists. Therefore, there are no transformations of phonemes (*varṇa*).

And just as the transformation of a collection of phonemes is untenable, so too is the transformation of individual phonemes untenable—as in the rules "for *as*, *bhū*" and "for *brū*... [and so forth].

Regarding the term *vacir*: just as in certain instances a collection of phonemes that possesses the characteristic of a verbal root (*dhātu*) is neither a transformation nor an effect [of that root], but rather another word is employed in place of a different word, so too is it with one phoneme being replaced by another phoneme. //40//
For this reason as well, there are no modifications of phonemes:
when the original material increases, the modification increases. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.41)
In the case of transformations, conformity to the original material (prakṛti) is observed;
however, in the case of the letter *ya*, there is no conformity to short or long vowels by which its status as a transformation might be inferred. //41//
NyS 2.2.42: Because modifications are perceived as being less, equal, or greater [in quantity], this is not a valid reason [for the claim that the cause and effect are identical].
Just as material modifications are perceived as being less than, equal to, or greater than [the original], so too this modification might be less [than the original]. //42//
Because both kinds of reason are absent, the example is not a means of proof.
In this case, there is no reason based on similarity with the example, nor one based on dissimilarity;
and since the example is not connected by the reason, it is not a means of proof.
Furthermore, an inconsistency would result regarding the counter-example.

Just as a horse, when employed to carry a load in place of an ox, does not become a modification (*vikāra*) of that ox, so too the letter *y* employed in place of the vowel *i* is not its modification.
Furthermore, there is no restrictive reason here to the effect that "the supporting example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is valid, but the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) is not. (43)
And an example of a modification of substance:
"Not [from substances] of dissimilar material causes, because of the diversity of their modifications" (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.44).
The fundamental nature (*prakṛti-bhāva*) of incomparable substances is subject to variation, and their modifications (*vikāra*) conform to that fundamental nature.
However, the sound *ya* does not conform to the sound *i*.
Therefore, the modification of a substance is not a valid illustration [for this case]. //44//
The alternative regarding the modification of phonemes is like the diversity of modifications of substances.

Just as there is a diversity of transformations despite the prakṛti being identical in terms of its substantiality, so too is there a variety of modifications despite the prakṛti being identical in terms of its lack of color. //45//
NyS 2.2.46: No, because the properties of a modification are not possible [in that case].
This property of transformation pertains to the substantial universal (dravyasāmānya);
when the substance— whether clay or gold— which constitutes that [universal], persists in its essential nature, its previous configuration ceases and another configuration arises.
He explains that modification:

there is no essence of sound (*śabdātman*) that persists through the commonality of phonemes (*varṇasāmānya*) such that it could thus abandon its state of being *yat* and undergo transformation into *tat*.
In this regard, just as when a substance exists, a horse is not a modification of an ox because the properties of modification are impossible [in that case], so too here.
Thus, there is no substitution of *y* for the vowel *i*, because the nature of undergoing modification is not applicable to it. //46//
For this reason as well, there are no modifications of phonemes:
because those that have undergone modification do not return to their original state. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.47)
Furthermore, a re-occurrence of an offense is untenable.
Why? Because there is no inference of a re-occurrence.
The vowel *i* has transitioned into the state of *y*, yet it becomes *i* again.
Furthermore, there is no inference here regarding the use or non-use of the letter *y* in place of the letter *i*. //47//
It is not [the case] that there is no inference;
for this is indeed an inference:
"The recurrence of gold and other such substances is not a reason [for their being eternal]. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.48)
Just as gold, having abandoned the state of being an earring, attains the state of being a necklace, and having abandoned the state of being a necklace, again attains the state of being an earring;
so too the phoneme *i*, having attained the state of being *y*, becomes the phoneme *i* once more. //48//
Because of deviation [from the rule], there is no inference: for example, milk that has reached the state of curd does not become milk again; why then should there not be a reversion of phonemes?
Or, if there is a reversion like gold—then the application of the example of gold is as follows:
"No, because the modifications of that [gold] do not deviate from the nature of gold. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.49)
Gold remains constant while becoming a substrate (dharmin) through its diminishing qualities (dharmas) and its emerging qualities;
however, no such essence of sound (śabdātmā) is perceived as a substrate through its diminishing "it-ness" (itva) and its emerging "yat-ness" (yatva).
Therefore, the example of gold is not tenable.
There is no refutation of the modifications of phonemes because they do not deviate from the nature of being a phoneme (*varṇatva*);
even the modifications of phonemes do not fail to conform to the nature of being a phoneme, just as a modification of gold does not deviate from the nature of being gold.
The application of properties belongs to that which possesses the universal, not to the universal itself.
The earring and the necklace are attributes of gold, not of "gold-ness";
likewise, of what phoneme-nature (*varṇātman*) could the sounds *i* and *y* be the attributes?
Since "phoneme-ness" (*varṇatva*) is a universal (*sāmānya*), these two cannot be its attributes.
Furthermore, a ceasing phenomenon is not the material cause of an arising phenomenon; in this case, the ceasing phoneme *i* is not the material cause of the arising phoneme *y*. //49//
For this reason as well, the modification of phonemes is untenable:
because there is no modification if they are eternal, and instability if they are non-eternal. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.50)
On the view that phonemes are eternal, since both the phoneme *i* and the phoneme *y* are eternal, a modification is impossible;
for if they are eternal, they are indestructible, so what could be the modification of which?
Now, as for the view that phonemes are non-eternal:
[The opponent's position: Even so, there would be an infinite regress of phonemes (*varṇa*).
What is this "infinite regress of phonemes"?

"Having arisen, there is cessation; when the *ikāra* has arisen and ceased, the *yakāra* arises; and when the *yakāra* has arisen and ceased, the *ikāra* arises. Which one is the modification of which?
This should be understood as applying both to the elision (*avagraha*) in the process of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), and to the euphonic combination in the process of elision. //50//
Regarding the position that [the phonemes] are eternal, the resolution is as follows:
*Nyāyasūtra* 2.2.51: "Because eternal things are beyond the senses, and because there is a conceptual variation regarding their properties, the modification of phonemes is not refuted."
The contradiction is that letters are eternal and yet are not subject to modification;
for while they are eternal, some things are beyond the senses and some are perceptible by the senses,
and letters are indeed perceptible by the senses.
Thus, while that which is eternal undergoes no modification,
the phonemes (*varṇa*) do undergo modification;
because of this contradiction, the distinction of their properties is not a valid reason.

That which is eternal is neither produced nor does it perish; being characterized by the absence of production and destruction, it is eternal. That which is non-eternal, however, is joined with production and destruction.
Furthermore, change is not possible without production and destruction.
Therefore, if phonemes were to undergo modification, [they would necessarily be non-eternal].
Their permanence is precluded;
or, if they are permanent,
their nature of undergoing modification is precluded.
Thus, this contradictory fallacy of the reason is called "the differentiation of properties" (dharmavikalpa). //51//
The argument for the position that [sound] is impermanent:
NyS 2.2.52: And if there were non-duration, then its modification would arise, just like the perception of phonemes.

Just as there is the hearing of phonemes (*varṇa*) that do not persist, so too does their modification (*vikāra*) occur. Because they are unrelated and thus incapable [of conveying meaning], the perception of phonemes is not incapable [of conveying meaning] due to its relation to modification; for if it were grasped as such, it would lead one to infer a modification of the phonemes.
In this regard, just as the earth possesses the quality of odor, so too do [the elements] possess the qualities of sound, pleasure, and so forth.
"It becomes such as this":
[the qualities are earth itself; thus, even the qualities such as sound and pleasure become such as this. p. 650
Furthermore, the perception of a phoneme does not cause the cessation of the application of another phoneme when that [first] phoneme has ceased.

If this application of the letter *y* upon the cessation of the vowel *i* were to cease because of the perception of the phoneme, then one would have to hold that the vowel *i*, being perceived there, undergoes a transformation into the state of *y*.
Therefore, the perception of a phoneme is not the cause of the modification of a phoneme. //52//

NyS 2.2.53: Since there is an absence of permanence when there is the nature of undergoing modification, and since modification is established at a later time, [the opponent's position] is not refuted.
The refutation [of the permanence of phonemes] based on the argument that they possess the property of modification (*vikāra*) is not tenable;
for indeed, nothing possessing the property of modification is ever perceived as eternal. Thus, the refutation by the example of the perception of phonemes (*varṇa*) is not tenable.

For when one uses the phrase "dadhi atra" with a pause (*avagraha*), and after remaining silent for a long time, subsequently employs it in *saṃhitā* (continuous flow) as "dadhy atra," [the phoneme /i/ is clearly perceived].
Having practiced for a long time and remained [in that state], one then applies the *saṃhitā* [rule] as in "dadhy atra.
Now, since this letter *y* is employed when the vowel *i* has long since ceased, it is not understood as a modification (*vikāra*) of anything;
thus, the objection arises that "in the absence of a cause, there can be no effect" (kāraṇābhāvāt kāryābhāvaḥ). //53//
For this reason as well, the modification of phonemes is untenable:
because there is no fixed rule regarding their original forms (prakṛti). NyS 2.2.54.
In the place of the letter *i*, the letter *y* is heard; indeed, in the place of the letter *y*, the letter *i* is prescribed, as in the word "vidhyati.
If there were such a relationship of original form (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikāra*) between phonemes, then there would be a fixed rule for that original form.
It is observed that there is a restriction regarding the fundamental nature (prakṛti) even when subject to modification (vikāra). //54//
Since there is a restriction regarding what is unrestricted, there is no such thing as being unrestricted.

This "non-restriction" (aniyama) of *prakṛti* that was mentioned is actually restricted; it is established according to its respective domain, and because it is restricted, it is called "restriction" (*niyama*).
This being so, there is no such thing as non-restriction.
Therefore, as for what was stated [in the objection], "because of the non-restriction of *prakṛti*," [that is incorrect].
This is incorrect. //55//
There is no refutation [of our position] because of the contradiction between restriction and non-restriction, and because there is restriction even in the case of non-restriction.
In this context, "rule" (*niyama*) signifies the authorization of a matter, while "non-rule" (*aniyama*) signifies its prohibition.
Since there is a contradiction between what is authorized and what is prohibited, they cannot be identical in meaning.
And since non-restriction is itself restricted, it does not constitute a restriction; thus, what is being negated here is not the existence of the object as such.
What then? It is that for an object existing in such a manner—which is designated by the word "restriction"—the very word "restriction" is appropriate because of its restricted nature.
Therefore, this is a negation of non-restriction based on restriction. //56//
And this production of phonetic modification does not arise from transformation (*pariṇāma*) or from the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). What then?

[Nyāyasūtra 2.2.57: But the modifications of phonemes arise from the occurrence of other qualities (*guṇāntarāpatti*), suppression (*upamarda*), diminution (*hrāsa*), increase (*vṛddhi*), partial contact (*leśa*), and complete contact (*śleṣa*).

The meaning of the term "modification" (vikāra) is the non-occurrence [of the original] due to the relationship between the original element (sthānin) and its substitute (ādeśa); that [non-occurrence] is differentiated.
It consists in the acquisition of another quality, such as an acute vowel becoming grave, and so forth.
"Suppression" (upamarda) means the arising of another form upon the cessation of one form.
"Diminution" (hrāsa) is the shortening of a long vowel;
"augmentation" (vṛddhi) is the lengthening of a short vowel.
Or rather, *pluta* refers to those two;
*leśa* means lightness (*lāghava*), and *sta* is a derivative (*vikāra*) of the root *as*.
Accretion is the addition of either a root-vowel or an affix;
these very things are the specific modifications.
These very ones are the substitutes; if these modifications are logically established, then they are called "phoneme-modifications" (varṇavikāra). //57//
Those [sounds], ending in a case-suffix, constitute a word (pada).
According to their appearance, modified phonemes ending in case-suffixes receive the designation "word" (*pada*).
There are two kinds of suffixes: nominal and verbal;
examples are *brāhmaṇaḥ* and *pacati*.
Those [phonemes], ending in an inflectional suffix, constitute a word (pada).
According to their appearance, modified phonemes ending in case-terminations (vibhakti) receive the designation of "word" (pada).
There are two kinds of case-terminations: nominal and verbal;
examples are *brāhmaṇaḥ* and *pacati*.

In that case, prefixes (upasarga) and particles (nipāta) would not receive the designation "word" (pada), and another rule would have to be stated; yet indeed, the elision of the nominative case-ending after an indeclinable is taught for the purpose of granting them the designation "word. //58//
The purpose is that the meaning is understood through the word; the investigation is conducted with reference to the nominal word (*nāmapada*),
and "cow" (*gaur*) is indeed the example for that word and its meaning.
NyS 2.2.59: Because of the figurative application [of a term] when the individual, the configuration, and the genus are present together, there arises doubt.

Proximity (*sannidhi*) is the occurrence of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). When the word "cow" (*gaur*) is employed with respect to individuals, forms, and universals that exist through inseparable connection,
it is not known therein whether any one of these is the referent of the term, or whether all of them together are.
The determination of the meaning of a word follows from the capacity of its usage. Therefore—NyS 2.2.60:

Individuality [is the meaning of a word], because the application of the terms "collection," "relinquishment," "acceptance," "number," "increase," "decrease," "color," "compound," and "conjunction" occurs with reference to the individual.
The individual (vyakti) is the meaning of a word. Why? Because words such as "cow" (yā) and others are applied metaphorically to the individual;
"metaphorical application" (upacāra) means usage.

The sentence "the cow that stands" and "the cow that sits"— this sentence does not denote the universal (jāti), because there is no difference [between the two cows]; rather, it denotes the substance (dravya), because there is a difference [between the individual cows].
[This refers to] that which denotes a substance (*dravya*).

For example, in the expression "a herd of cows" (*gavāṃ samūhaḥ*), there is a denotation of a substance because of its plurality; it is not [a denotation] of a genus (*jāti*), because a genus is non-differentiated.

Furthermore, in the expression "giving a cow to the physician" (*vaidyāya gāṃ dadāti*), there is the relinquishment of a substance, not of a genus, because a genus is incorporeal (*amūrta*) and because [in the case of a genus], neither sequential progression nor regression is possible.
Possession (*parigraha*) is the connection with the status of ownership,
as in "Kauṇḍinya’s cow" or "the Brāhmaṇa’s cow";
when a substance is denoted, a difference in relation is established due to the difference in the substances, which is thus logically justified.
But the genus (*jāti*) is indivisible.
As for number: when one says "ten cows" or "twenty cows," it is the distinct substance that is numbered, not the genus, because the genus is without division.
Growth is the accumulation of parts in a substance that possesses causes, as in the expression "the cow grew"; however, a genus (jāti) is partless. By this, decrease is also explained.
Color—such as "the cow is white" or "the cow is tawny";
this is the connection of a quality with a substance, not with a universal.
Compound—such as "benefit for the cow" or "happiness for the cow."

The connection with pleasure and so forth belongs to the substance (*dravya*), not to the genus (*jāti*). The underlying reason is as follows: a cow, being a continuous series of similar offspring, produces another cow;
because it possesses the property of producing that [result], this is appropriate for the substance, but not for the genus, due to the opposite being the case.
For "substance" and "individual" are not different things. //60//
The refutation of this [is stated]:
NyS 2.2.61: No, because that would lead to an infinite regress.
The individual (vyakti) is not the meaning of a word.
Why? Because of the lack of finality (anavasthāna).
That which is qualified by [words] such as "white" and so forth is the meaning of the word "cow," as in "the cow that stands" or "the cow that sits."
A substance alone, without being qualified by a genus, is not denoted; what then? It is denoted as qualified by a genus. Therefore, the individual is not the word-meaning.
In this same way, it should be understood regarding aggregates and so forth. //61//
If the individual is not the word-meaning, how then is there figurative usage with respect to the individual?
Figurative usage occurs on account of a cause, even when the thing is not actually that [which it is called].
Indeed, this is observed—

NyS 2.2.62: Metaphorical designation (upacāra) of a term for something else occurs—despite the absence of that actual identity—with respect to [the following grounds]: association, location, purpose, function, measure, support, proximity, connection, instrumentality, and sovereignty; as in the cases of "Brāhmaṇa," "bed," "mat," "king," "barley meal," "sandalwood," "Ganges," "cloth," "food," and "man."
"Even in the absence of that [actual] state, there is a metaphorical application of it"; this means that a word not denoting something is expressed by a word that does denote it.
This occurs through association—as in "feed the staff," where the Brahmin associated with the staff is what is intended.
By way of location (*sthāna*): in the expression "the beds cry out," it is the persons situated on the beds who are denoted.
By way of purpose (*tādarthya*): when the *vīraṇa* grass intended for a mat is being arranged, one says, "he is making a mat.
By way of behavior (*vṛtta*): as in "Yama is the king" or "Kubera is the king," because he behaves like them.
From measure: "barley flour measured by an *āḍhaka*" (*āḍhakasaktavaḥ*) means flour measured with an *āḍhaka* container.
From holding: "sandalwood held on a scale" (*tulācandana*) means sandalwood placed upon a scale.
From proximity: when it is said, "the cows are grazing in the Gaṅgā," the nearby region is denoted.
Through conjunction (*yoga*): a cloth conjoined with the quality of blackness is designated as "black.
Through accomplishment (*sādhana*): food is [said to be] the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Through sovereignty (*ādhipatya*): this person belongs to such-and-such a family, he belongs to such-and-such a lineage.
In this regard, this genus-term is applied to the individual either through association or through connection. //62//

If the individual instance (*vyakti*) is not the meaning of this word "cow," then let it be so: *NyS 2.2.63*: The form (*ākṛti*) [is the meaning], because the establishment of the existence [of an entity] depends upon it.
The generic form (*ākṛti*) is the meaning of a word. Why? Because the establishment of the existence of a substance is dependent upon it.
The generic form is the fixed arrangement of the parts of a substance and their own constituent parts.
When that [exclusion] is apprehended, the determination of entities—such as "this is a cow" or "this is a horse"—is established, but not when it is not apprehended.
That which, by being apprehended, establishes the determination of entities, is what the word is capable of denoting; that is its meaning. //63//

That [word] is appropriate which denotes that which possesses a connection with a genus; in this context, it is said to be "qualified by the genus," as in the case of the word "cow. Furthermore, the arrangement of parts does not possess a connection with the genus.
To what, then, does it belong?
[This refers to] a substance whose constituent parts are arranged in a fixed configuration.
Therefore, the form (ākṛti) is not the word-meaning.
Let it be, then, that the universal (jāti) is the word-meaning.

NyS 2.2.64: Even though [the term "cow"] applies to both the individual and the configuration, it is the genus that is the object of sprinkling and other such rites, because these would not otherwise apply to a clay cow.
The universal (jāti) is the word-meaning.
Why? Because sprinkling and other such rites do not apply even to a clay cow, despite its being endowed with both individuality (vyakti) and configuration (ākṛti).
One does not employ such commands as "Sprinkle the cow," "Bring the cow," or "Give the cow" in reference to a clay cow.
Why? Because of the absence of the universal (*jāti*).

For in that case there is the individual (*vyakti*) and there is the configuration (*ākṛti*); that whose absence results in the lack of cognition [of the object] therein is the word-meaning (*padārtha*). //64//
NyS 2.2.65: It is not so, because the manifestation of the universal depends upon the form and the individual.
The manifestation of the genus depends upon both the form and the individual;
for when neither the form nor the individual is perceived, the genus alone is not apprehended in its purity.
Therefore, the genus is not the meaning of a word. //65//
Indeed, it is not possible for there to be no category of object (padārtha); what, then, is the category of object?
NS 2.2.66: The individual, the configuration, and the genus are the categories of objects.

The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of specification. What is specified? That the status of being a constituent element (*padārthatva*) belongs to the relationship between the primary and its subsidiary (*pradhānāṅgabhāva*) without restriction.

For when there is an intention to express distinction and a comprehension of particulars, then the individual (vyakti) is primary, while the genus (jāti) and the configuration (ākṛti) are subordinate.
But when distinction is not intended and there is a comprehension of the universal, then the genus is primary, while the individual and the configuration are subordinate.
This is frequently seen in actual applications;
however, it should be understood that the primary status belongs to the generic form (ākṛti). //66//
But how is it known that there are distinct individual entities (*vyakti*), forms (*ākṛti*), and universals (*jāti*)?
It is because of the difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*). To begin with:
An individual manifestation (vyakti) is a corporeal form (mūrti) that serves as the substratum for specific qualities (guṇaviśeṣa).
That which is manifested is the manifest (vyakti), meaning that which is perceivable by the senses; thus, not every substance is the manifest.

That substance which, as the case may be, is the substratum for the specific qualities ending with touch—namely, gravity, density, fluidity, and the latent impressions (saṃskāra)—as well as for non-pervasive dimension (parimāṇa), is "mūrti" because its constituent parts are congealed (NyS 2.2.68).
"Configuration" (ākṛti) is defined as the indicator (liṅga) of a genus (jāti).
One should understand that *ākṛti* (form) is that by which genus (*jāti*) and the gender-markers (*liṅga*) of the genus are manifested;
and it is nothing other than the fixed arrangement (*vyūha*) of the parts of a living being (*sattva*) and their constituent parts.
[Regarding "of the parts of a living being"... p. 692.
Indeed, the limbs of a living being, when arranged in a fixed configuration, constitute the mark of the genus; for one infers that it is a cow by means of its head or its foot.
And it is only when there is a fixed arrangement of the limbs of a living being that "cowness" (gotva) becomes manifest.

In the case of a genus that is not manifested by a form—such as in the instances of "clay," "gold," or "silver"—the form is excluded; [therefore] the genus loses its status as the meaning of the word. //68//
Genus (jāti) has as its nature the production of similar [cognitions].

That which produces a uniform cognition regarding diverse substrates, by virtue of which many things do not exclude one another—that object which is the cause for the recurrence of a single cognition across multiple instances is the universal (sāmānya).
And that which effects non-difference among some things and difference from others is the particularized universal (sāmānyaviśeṣa), namely, the genus (jāti). //69//
Thus ends the second daily lesson of the second chapter in the Nyāyabhāṣya of Vātsyāyana.
And thus the second chapter is completed. //2//
The Third Chapter, First Daily Lesson. The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have been examined; now the object of valid cognition (*prameya*) is being examined.
And since that [self] is the "Self" and so forth, the Self is now being analyzed:
is the Self merely the aggregate of body, sense-faculties, mind, intellect, and feelings, or is it something distinct from those?
Why is there this doubt? Because it is established in both ways through conventional designation.
*Vyapadeśa* is the designation of the relationship between the action (*kriyā*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) with the agent (*kartṛ*).
It is of two kinds.
The designation of a whole by means of a part— as in "the tree stands by its roots" or "the palace is supported by its pillars.
The designation of one thing by means of another— as in "he cuts with an axe."
One sees by means of a lamp.
And there is this conventional designation: "one sees with the eye," "one cognizes with the mind," "one deliberates with the intellect," and "one experiences pleasure and pain with the body.
In that regard, it is not determined whether [the action belongs] to a part of the whole—the aggregate consisting of the body and so forth—[or to the whole itself].
Now, [the question arises] whether it belongs to another, distinct from that, or to something else entirely.
This designation of "improper method" (anaya) is made by another [author]. Why?
Because of the apprehension of a single object through both seeing and touching (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.1).

A certain object is grasped by sight, and that same object is also grasped by touch— thinking, "That which I saw with the eye, I now touch with the sense of touch," and "That which I touched with the sense of touch, I now see with the eye. Furthermore, these two cognitions, having a single object and a single agent, are joined together in recollection.
These two conditions are neither produced by a composite agent, nor are they produced by a single agent consisting of the sense faculty.

Therefore, that which synthesizes two cognitions— produced by different causes and having different agents— that grasp a single object through the eye and the tactile faculty as having the same objective domain, must be a distinct entity [from those faculties].
How, then, could these two not have a single agent?
Indeed, a sense faculty is capable of synthesizing its own respective graspings of objects, which have no other agent, but it cannot synthesize the grasping of an object by another sense faculty.
How, then, are these not produced by a composite (saṅghāta)?
For this single [self] experiences two successive states—having distinct causes and having itself as their agent—as synthesized together, but a composite does not.

Why? Because, as long as the [cognition] has not ceased within the aggregate, there is no non-connection with the apprehension of each individual object, just as there is none by means of another sense organ. //1//
NyS 3.1.2: No, because of the fixed determination of objects.
There is no conscious being other than the aggregate of the body and so forth.
Why? Because of the fixed determination of objects;
the sense organs have fixed objects.
When the eye is absent, form is not perceived; when it is present, it is perceived.
And when something does not exist in the absence of another, but exists when that other is present, it is understood to belong to that [other].
[It exists when it is present... p.713
Therefore, the apprehension of form belongs to the eye; the eye sees the form.
The same applies to the nose and the other [senses].
These sense-faculties are conscious because they grasp their respective objects, since the grasping of objects occurs only when the sense-faculties exist and not when they do not.

This being so, what is the need for another conscious entity? [The opponent replies: This reason is inconclusive because of doubt—namely, this fact that the grasping of objects occurs only when the sense-faculties exist and not otherwise.
Is it because [the body] is conscious, or rather because it is the cause for the apprehension of the instruments of consciousness?
Even though the sense organs are instruments of consciousness, [the body] must be the cause for their apprehension. //2//

As for what was stated [in NS 3.1.2], "because of the determination of objects" (viṣayavyavasthāna), [NS 3.1.3 states]: "Because the self exists precisely due to that determination, there is no refutation."

If, indeed, a single sense organ were all-knowing, capable of grasping all objects, and conscious while having no fixed object, who then could infer any other conscious being? However, since the sense organs have fixed objects, therefore another conscious being is inferred—one who is all-knowing, the grasper of all objects, and who transcends the limitations of those fixed objects. Indeed, one who perceives a visible form infers a taste or odor previously apprehended; and one who experiences an odor infers a visible form or a taste. The same should be stated for the remaining sense objects as well.
Having seen a form, one smells a fragrance;
and having smelled a fragrance, one sees a form.
Thus, it is this very [self] that synthesizes the apprehension of all objects— which occurs through indefinite successions of states, rests upon a single consciousness, and has no other agent—

as well as perceptions, inferences, verbal cognitions, doubts, and various cognitions regarding different objects, synthesizing them as having its own self as their agent, and thereby experiences them.
And one comes to comprehend the entire range of the treatise;
having heard the sequentially occurring phonemes— which are not objects of the ear— by way of their synthesis into the form of words and sentences,
and while understanding the established relationship between word and meaning, one grasps a manifold collection of meanings that cannot be apprehended by each individual sense-organ alone.
This systematic treatment of the objects of knowledge for the Omniscient One cannot be traversed word by word;
rather, only a mere outline has been presented.
In this regard, what was stated—that if the sense organs themselves were conscious, what would be the use of a separate consciousness—is untenable. //3//
For this reason as well, the self is distinct from the body and so forth,
and is not merely the aggregate of the body and its constituents:
because there is no sin when the body is burned.
By the term "taking up a body" (śarīragrahaṇa), a living being consisting of an aggregate of body, sense organs, intellect, and sensations is understood.
For one who burns a living body, the sin committed through the injury of a living being is called a transgression (pātaka);
the absence of that [transgression] is [what is meant].
Because the agent has no connection with the fruit thereof, while the non-agent does have such a connection;
for indeed, within the continuum of body, sense-faculties, intellect, and sensation, one aggregate arises and another ceases.
That continuum, consisting of a succession of arising and ceasing, does not contradict [the notion of] identity, because it is the basis for the identity of the aggregate of the body and so forth;
for this [continuum] is perceived as having identity as its basis.
And this being the case, that collection of the body and so forth which, as a living being, commits violence is not connected with the fruit of that violence;
and he who is connected with it did not commit the violence.
Thus, when there is a difference in the sentient being, the fallacies of the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāna*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) would follow.
Furthermore, if the arising and cessation of a sentient being were not caused by karma, it would follow that the creation of sentient beings occurs without a karmic motive;
in that case, the practice of celibacy for the sake of liberation would be purposeless.
Moreover, if a sentient being were merely the aggregate of the body and so forth, there would be no sin in burning a corpse.
And this is undesirable.
Therefore, the self is eternal and distinct from the aggregate of the body and so forth. //4//
NyS 3.1.5: Its absence [of the property of being produced] exists even when that which possesses a self is burned, because of its eternality.
Even for one whose body is burned while being possessed of a permanent self, there would be no sin for the burner upon the burning of that body. Why? Because the self is eternal.
No one can ever truly harm another;
for if one were harmed, that person's permanence would cease to exist.
Thus, this violence is fruitless in one case, but untenable in the other. //5//
No, because of the destruction of the agent who is the substratum of the effect.

We do not say that violence is the killing of an eternal sentient being; rather, violence is the injury, affliction, or impairment characterized by deficiency, or else the destruction of the continuum characterized by slaughter, directed toward the body— which is the locus of activity— and the sense faculties— which are the agents of the perception of their respective objects— of a sentient being whose nature is indestructible.

The effect (*kārya*), however, is the experience of pleasure and pain; its locus (*āyatana*), support (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and substratum (*āśraya*) is the body. The destruction (*badha*) of the sense-faculties—which are the agents of the perception of their respective objects as well as of the body, which is the substratum of that effect—is violence (*hiṃsā*).
It does not belong to an eternal self.
In that regard, what was stated—"its non-existence [does not follow] even when a living being is burned, because of its eternity"—is incorrect.
For one for whom violence is the destruction of the *sattva*, there is the fault of the loss of what has been done (*kṛtahāna*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*).

This must be one of two possibilities: either violence is the annihilation of a sentient being, or it is the destruction of the substratum of action and the agent of a sentient being whose nature is indestructible;
there is no other alternative.
And the annihilation of sentient beings has been refuted;
in that regard, what else remains?
The rest is "as it truly is."
Alternatively, regarding the phrase "due to the killing of the agent who is the substratum of the effect":
the substratum of the effect is the aggregate of body, sense-faculties, and intellect;
therein occurs the experience of pleasure and pain by the eternal self.

Its basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), its support (*āśraya*), and its locus (*āyatana*) is that [body]; it is not other than that, and thus it alone is the agent. For the cessation of the experience of pleasure and pain is caused by that [body], and does not occur without it. Its "killing" (*vadha*) is injury (*upaghāta*), affliction (*pīḍā*), or destruction (*pramāpaṇa*); it is violence (*hiṃsā*), and not the annihilation of the self (*ātma-uccheda*) due to its being eternal.
Regarding that which was stated—"The absence [of smoke] occurs even when something possessing a self (sātmaka) is burned, because of its permanence"—this is not so. //6//
For this reason as well, the self is distinct from the body and so forth:
because of the recognition by one [eye] of what was seen by the other. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.7)

Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is the linking cognition (*pratisandhijñāna*) regarding a single object between two successive cognitions— such as [the thought], "I now see that very same thing which I previously knew," or "This object is that very same one"; or from the recognition by the other eye of what was seen by the left eye,
[as in the thought], "I now see that very same thing which I saw."
Regarding the sentience of the sense organs: that which was seen by one cannot be recognized by another; thus, recognition would be impossible.
Yet this recognition does exist; therefore, the conscious being is distinct from the sense organs. //7//
It is not [the case that there is only one nose], because there is the conceit of duality regarding [the two nostrils] which are separated by the bone of the bridge of the nose.

This eye is one, situated in the middle and separated by the bone of the nose; its two ends, when perceived, give rise to the conceit of duality, just as in the case of a long object that is obstructed in the middle. //8//
NyS 3.1.9: Because the second does not perish upon the destruction of one, there is no oneness.
When one eye is impaired or removed, the second eye remains as the means for perceiving objects;
therefore, the obstruction of one [eye] is impossible. //9//
Even when the parts have perished, the whole is still perceived; therefore, [the opponent's reason] is not a valid proof.
"The non-destruction of the second [part] upon the destruction of one is not a valid reason.
Why? Because when some branches of a tree have been cut, the tree is indeed still perceived. //10//
NyS 3.1.11: There is no refutation [of our position] because it contradicts the illustrative example.
When the substance that is the cause undergoes disjunction, the substance that is the effect does not persist, because that would entail its being eternal.
Among many composite substances, that whose causes have undergone disjunction perishes, while those whose causes have not undergone disjunction persist.
Alternatively, contradiction with what is observed is contradiction with the example (*dṛṣṭāntavirodha*).

For on the skull of a dead person, two cavities are perceived distinctly in the place of the eyes, separated by the bone of the nose; and this is not possible if there were only one [cavity] separated by the bone of the nose.
Alternatively, because the destruction of a single [object] is not restricted, these are two distinct objects.
And those two distinct impairments of the obstructions are inferred to be different. Furthermore,
due to the pressure on one eye, because of the resulting difference in the contact between the visual ray and its object, a difference in the perceived object is apprehended as it were.
And that [recognition] is contradicted if there were oneness;
for when the pressure has ceased, there is a non-differentiated synthesis.
Therefore, it is impossible for a single entity to be obstructed. //11//
And this conscious being is inferred to be distinct from the aggregate of the body and so forth—because of the transformation of another sense organ. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.12)

When the color or odor of a certain sour fruit is perceived by some sense organ while its taste has been previously experienced through association, a modification of another sense organ—the tongue—is perceived; this consists of a flow of saliva induced by the memory of the taste and the longing for it.
This phenomenon would be impossible if the senses were sentient.
What is seen by one is not remembered by another. //12//
NyS 3.1.13: No, because memory has as its object that which is to be remembered.
The mental factor called memory arises from a sign; its object is that which is to be remembered, and the modification of another sense organ caused by it is not produced by the self. //13//
NyS 3.1.14: There is no refutation [of the self] because of the existence of its qualities within the self.
Since it exists as a quality of the self, there is no refutation of the self.
If memory is a quality of the self, then memory is logically possible; otherwise, it would be impossible for one who has seen something to remember it as someone else.

If, however, the senses were conscious, there would be no unification of the apprehensions of objects by various agents; or, if such unification did occur, the distinct determination of objects would be impossible.

But a single conscious being, perceiving multiple objects through different causes, remembers an object previously seen; thus, because of the unification of perceptions and the existence of memory, [consciousness] must be a quality of the Self, which is a single entity that perceives multiple objects.

Its existence [is established], and its non-existence is untenable in the contrary case. Because of the connection [of past and present experiences], all the worldly transactions of living beings depend upon memory. Memory, in turn, depends upon a substratum. Therefore, the substratum of memory exists. This is the proof. Furthermore, since memory is observed to be of the nature of recollection, it must have a cause; and because there is no other cause possible, it follows that the self (ātman) exists as the substratum of memory. Thus, the existence of the self is established. Moreover, the existence of the self is proven by the fact that memory is impossible otherwise. All the worldly activities of living beings are based on memory. Since memory is impossible without a single agent who experiences various objects at different times, the self exists as the substratum of memory. Therefore, the self exists. This concludes the section on the existence of the self. Furthermore, the existence of the self is proven by the fact that memory is impossible otherwise. All the worldly activities of living beings—such as eating, drinking, moving, and so forth—are preceded by memory. For example, one who has previously experienced the pleasure of eating rice and the like will, upon seeing rice later, remember the previous experience and desire it again. One who desires it will then engage in the activity of eating. Thus, all worldly activities are preceded by memory. And since memory is impossible without a single agent who experiences various objects at different times, the self exists as the substratum of memory. Therefore, the self exists. This concludes the section on the existence of the self. Furthermore, the existence of the self is proven by the fact that memory is impossible otherwise. All
The "modification of another sense-organ" (*indriyāntaravikāra*) is merely an illustrative example of the mark of the self (*ātman*).

Furthermore, because the objects of memory are innumerable, this statement—"It is not [the case that the self is inferred] from memory, because memory has as its object that which is to be remembered"—is made after having taken into account the innumerability of the objects of memory.
This memory, which occurs when an object is no longer being perceived, takes the form: "I knew that object."

The object of this [subsequent cognition] is an object previously known, qualified by the knower and the act of knowing, and not the mere object; for one thinks, "I have known that object," or "That object was known by me."
The fourfold statement, "In this matter, my knowledge arose," indicates knowledge regarding an object of memory; it is equivalent in meaning [to the other forms].
Indeed, in every case, the knower, the knowledge, and the knowable are apprehended.
Now, in the case of an object that is directly perceived, the memory [of that perception] links together three cognitions concerning a single object, having a common agent.
They are not produced by different agents, nor are they without an agent; rather, they have a single agent. I saw that very object which I see now.
"I saw" refers both to the act of seeing and to the awareness of seeing;
for indeed, if one's own seeing were not cognized, the thought "I saw" would not occur.
These two, moreover, are distinct forms of knowledge.
"The very one whom I see now"—this is the third cognition.
Thus, a single object, when associated with these three cognitions, is neither without an agent nor possessed of multiple agents;
rather, [it is known] by means of the three cognitions... p. 736.
Regarding the phrase "having a single agent":

this object of memory, which exists as a known entity when not being specifically enumerated, is denied [by the opponent] with the argument, "The self does not exist, because memory has as its object only that which is to be remembered.

However, this is not merely memory, nor does it have merely that which is to be remembered as its object; for, like the synthesis of cognitions, the synthesis of memories belongs to a single [agent], since he possesses all things as his object.
This single knower, whose object is everything, synthesizes his own cognitions: "I shall know this object;
I know this object; I have known this object. Desiring to know this object, after not knowing it for a long time, he determines: "I have known it.
In this way, he also synthesizes memory, which is distinguished by the three times and distinguished by the desire to remember.
If a sentient being is merely a continuum of conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*), then as these factors arise again and again, they pass away.
There is not even a single conditioned factor that could experience knowledge and memory distinguished by the three times.
Furthermore, without such an experience, the reconnection of knowledge and memory—and the notions of "I" and "mine"—would not arise, just as they do not in the case of another body.

Therefore, it is inferred that there exists a single [self] which, in every body, connects its own series of cognitions and series of memories; for, due to the absence of its activity in other bodies, no such connection occurs. //14//
Not so, because the means for the cognition of the self are present in the mind.
The self is not distinct from the aggregate of the body and so forth.

Why? Because the grounds for establishing the self are possible in the mind; that is, because the grounds for proving the self—such as "because a single object is apprehended by both seeing and touching," and so forth—are possible in the mind.
For the mind has all things as its object;
therefore, there is no self distinct from the aggregate of body, senses, mind, and intellect. //15//
NyS 3.1.16: Since the means of knowledge are established for the knower, there is merely a difference in terminology.
Indeed, instruments of knowledge are appropriate for a knower: one sees with the eye, smells with the nose, and touches with the sense of touch;

likewise, for a thinker who has all things as his object, there exists an instrument of thought consisting of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which has all things as its object, by means of which he thinks.
This being so, while the designation "self" (ātman) is not tolerated for the knower, the designation "mind" (manas) is permitted.
Furthermore, while the notion of "mind" (*manas*) regarding the mind is not tolerated, its function as an instrument of cognition (*matisādhana*) is admitted.
Thus, this is merely a difference in terminology; there is no dispute regarding the underlying reality.
Alternatively, if [the mind] were rejected, it would follow that all the sense faculties (*indriya*) must likewise be abolished.

Now, if it is asserted that the means of cognition for all objects—which pertains to all objects—is denied by saying "it does not exist," then it follows that the means of apprehending objects such as form and so forth also do not exist, which results in the total abolition of all the sense organs. //16//
And restriction is without inferential proof.
As for this restriction that is asserted— that while there exist means for the apprehension of form and so forth,
there is no means of cognition whose object is everything—
This restriction is without inference;
there is no inference here by which we might apprehend the restriction.
Furthermore, pleasure and so forth are objects distinct from color-form and the rest; therefore, the existence of another instrument [the internal organ] is required for their perception.

Just as smell is not perceived by the eye, and thus there must be another instrument, namely the nose; and just as taste is not perceived by the eye or the nose, and thus there must be another instrument, namely the tongue; so it is for the remaining [senses] as well.
Likewise, since pleasure and the like are not perceived by the eye and the other [senses], there must necessarily be another instrument [for their perception].
There must be another cause [for this]. And that is the mark of the non-simultaneity of cognitions (*jñānāyaugapadya*).

Furthermore, that which is the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the perception of pleasure and so forth is the mark of the non-simultaneity of cognitions; because of its proximity to or distance from each sense organ (*indriya*), cognitions do not arise simultaneously.
In this regard, that which was stated—namely, "because the means for the realization of the self are possible in the mind"—is incorrect. //17//
