But is this [self] distinct from the aggregate of the body and so forth, and is it eternal or non-eternal?
Whence does this doubt arise?
The doubt arises because both possibilities are observed.
That which exists is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal.
Furthermore, when the existence of the self has been established, doubt is not dispelled;
thus, by the very same reasons for the existence of the self, its persistence prior to the dissolution of the body is proven, and it persists even after the dissolution of the body. Why?
NyS_3.1.18: [The self exists] because a newborn infant manifests joy, fear, and sorrow due to the continuity of memories previously practiced.

Indeed, this newborn boy, in this very life, experiences joy, fear, and sorrow even when the causes of joy, fear, and sorrow have not been grasped [in this life], as these are to be inferred from their signs.
And these arise from the continuity of memory (*smṛtyanubandha*), and not otherwise.
Furthermore, the continuity of memory does not occur without prior practice.
And since prior practice is possible only if there was a previous birth and not otherwise, this is established; thus it remains that "this [self] continues after the dissolution of the body. //18//
The modification [of the soul] is like the modifications of opening and closing observed in lotuses and other such things.

Just as there occurs the modification of opening, closing, and transformation in impermanent things such as lotuses, so too there would be the modification of experiencing joy, fear, and sorrow in the impermanent self.

This is untenable due to the absence of a reason; for by this reason—that the experience of joy and so forth in the impermanent self is like the modifications of opening and closing in lotuses—there is no proof of the probandum from the similarity of the example, nor is there proof from its dissimilarity.
It is said that [the argument] is "meaningless" (*apārthaka*) because it lacks a logical reason and its meaning is incoherent.

Furthermore, there is no cessation of the causes of joy and so forth based on the example: this experience of joy and so forth toward objects that have been habitually indulged in—which is perceived within each individual self and is produced by the persistence of memory—is not removed by the example of the closing of lotuses and the like.
And just as this [motion] does not cease, so it is even for that which has been born;
for in the production of action, there are the disjunction and conjunction of the leaf, like the opening and closing [of an eye],
and the cause of the action is to be inferred from the action itself.
And this being the case, what is there to be refuted by means of an example? //19//

Now, if it is thought that the modifications of opening, closing, and so forth in lotuses and the like occur without a cause, and that similarly the soul's experience of joy and the rest occurs without a cause—this is not so;
because the modifications of the five elements are caused by heat, cold, rain, and the seasons. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.20)

Since [the lotus and other plants] exist when heat and so forth are present, and do not exist when they are absent, their transformations—namely, their opening and closing—are caused by those [factors] and brought about through the favor of the five elements; thus, they are not without cause. In the same way, transformations such as joy and the like must also arise from a cause; they cannot occur without a cause.
And there is no other cause for this than the continuity of memory from previous practice;
nor is there an inference regarding the causes of its arising and disappearance based on the example of the self,
for joy and the like do not arise without a cause.
Joy and the like do not take up other causes in the same way that heat and so forth do;
therefore, this [objection] is incorrect. //20//
For this reason as well, the self is eternal:
because of the craving for mother's milk resulting from the habituation to food [in previous lives] after passing away. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.21)
In a newborn calf, a desire for milk is observed as an indicator of its natural inclination;
and that cannot exist without a prior habituation to food.
By what reasoning?

For it is observed that among embodied beings who are afflicted by hunger, there arises a desire for food due to a continuous stream of memory produced by the habitual practice of eating in previous lives. And this [desire] would not be possible for one who has just been born without the prior habituation of a previous body.
[It is possible for one who has just been born. (p. 746)
From this it is inferred that there was a previous body in which food was practiced by him.
Indeed, this self, having passed away from a former body and entered another body, being afflicted by hunger and recollecting the food previously practiced, desires mother’s milk.
Therefore, the self is not divided by the division of the body; rather, it certainly continues to exist beyond the division of the body. //21//
Its approaching [the sense-object] is like the movement of iron toward a magnet.
Just as iron approaches a magnet even without prior practice, so too does an infant desire breast milk even without prior practice with food. //22//
Is this movement of iron toward a magnet without a cause, or is it due to a cause?
First, it is not without a cause, because there is no activity elsewhere [where such a cause is absent]. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.23)
If it were without a cause,
even clods of earth and the like would be attracted to a magnet;
for there can never be a lack of a cause for a fixed restriction.
Now, if it is from a sign, by what is that perceived?
It has action as its mark and action as its cause.
The mark of the restriction of action is the restriction of the cause of action;
by means of that, there is an absence of activity toward anything else.
Even in the case of an infant, a restricted act of approaching is observed.
And there is no sign of a desire for breast-milk other than a continuous stream of memory produced by the habituation to food;
this cause is established by means of an illustration.
[The cause is established by means of an illustration. p. 748
Furthermore, nothing arises in the absence of a cause;
nor does an example invalidate a perceived cause for desire.
Therefore, the movement of iron toward a magnet is not a non-example [of such a process].
Furthermore, iron indeed does not function elsewhere; iron never approaches a clod of earth—
by what cause is this restriction established?
If it is due to a restriction of causes,
and that [restriction] has the restriction of activity as its mark,
then likewise the desire of an infant, having a restricted object, must also arise from a restriction of causes.
And that cause—whether it be habitual memory or something else—is distinguished by what is observed; for among embodied beings, the desire for food is observed to arise from habitual memory. //23//
For this reason as well, the self is eternal. Why?
Because the birth of one who is free from passion is not observed. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.24)
It follows by implication that one is born with lust;
this one being born is born bound by lust,
and the source of lust is the recollection of objects previously experienced.
Furthermore, the prior experience of objects is not possible without a body in another birth.
This very self, recollecting the objects experienced in a previous body, becomes attached to those various [objects].

And thus, this reconnection occurs between two births; in this way, the connection of the conscious being with a body is beginningless—through the previous body with a prior one, that with a more prior one, and so on—and the persistence of attachment is also beginningless; therefore, its permanence is established. //24//

But how is it known that the passion of one who is born is produced by the recollection of objects previously experienced, and not rather— NyS_3.1.25— as the production [of a substance] with its qualities, is the production of that [passion]?

Just as the qualities of a substance subject to origination arise from a cause, so too does passion arise from some source in the self subject to origination. Here, this restatement of what has already been said is for the purpose of illustration. //25//
No, because desire and the like have conceptual construction as their cause.
Indeed, the arising of the self and of passion is not like the arising of a substance possessing qualities.
Why? Because passion and the rest have conceptualization as their cause.
For this passion, produced by conceptualization, is observed in living beings who indulge in sense objects.
And *saṅkalpa* (volitional construction) has its origin in the recollection of objects previously experienced.
By this, it is inferred that even for one who has been born, passion (*rāga*) is produced by the recollection of objects previously experienced.

However, since the production of passion occurs based on the locus of the self's arising, if there were a cause of passion other than *saṅkalpa*, its production would have to be stated as being like that of an effect-substance or a quality.
The production of a self is not established,
nor is there any cause for passion other than conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*).
Therefore, it is illogical that the production of those two [passion and its object] occurs in the manner of the production of a substance possessing qualities (*saguṇadravya*).
Furthermore, even if one were to posit an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) characterized by merit and demerit as a cause of passion other than volition (*saṅkalpa*),
even so, connection with a previous body cannot be denied;
for its manifestation occurs there [in that previous state], not in this present birth.
"Passion [arises] from being absorbed in that": indeed, this habitual practice toward sense objects is the cause of cultivation, which is called "being absorbed in that.
Furthermore, specific types of passion arise from specific types of birth.
Indeed, this [desire] is karma that brings about a specific birth; because it serves that purpose, it is understood to be designated by that term.
Therefore, it is untenable to claim that there is any cause for passion other than volition (saṅkalpa). //26//

It has been stated that the connection of the conscious principle with a body is beginningless, and that its body—serving as the locus for pleasure and pain—is caused by its own previously performed actions.
That [body] is now examined: is it of a single material nature, like the sense of smell and so forth, or is it of multiple material natures?
Whence the doubt?
Doubt arises from conflicting views;
for there are those who assert, through various numerical alternatives, that the elements such as earth and the rest constitute the material cause of the body.
What is the truth in that matter? [Nyāyasūtra 3.1.27: It is composed of earth, because other qualities are perceived.
Among these, the human [body] is composed of earth.
Why? Because other qualities are perceived;
earth possesses smell, and the body likewise possesses smell.
Since water and the other elements lack odor, [the body] would be odorless by their very nature.

However, this [body] is not produced from earth alone when it is unmixed with water and the others; rather, it is conceived as the substratum for the activities of the sense organs and their objects. Therefore, the body comes into being when there is a conjunction of the five elements, for the mutual conjunction of the five elements is not prohibited.
In other worlds, there are bodies composed of water, fire, and air; even in those cases, the conjunction of the elements is dependent upon the purpose of the person.
Even in the production of objects such as cooking pots, it is certain that production does not occur without the conjunction of clay and other materials. //27//
NyS 3.1.28: It consists of the earthy, the watery, and the fiery, because its qualities are perceived.
And because inhalation and exhalation are perceived, [the body] consists of the four elements.
It consists of the five elements because it possesses the functions of odour, moisture, maturation, support, and providing space.
The author of the Sūtra has disregarded these reasons because they are doubtful.
In what way are they doubtful?

[Because] when the primordial nature (prakṛti) exists, the properties of the elements (bhūta) are perceived; yet even when it does not exist, they are present because there is no prohibition against their conjunction with those things that are in proximity.
Just as in a pot there are water, fire, air, and space;
so too this body, whose nature consists of multiple elements, would—by following its own nature—be odorless, tasteless, formless, and intangible.
By following its own nature, it would be formless and intangible.
But this is not so;
therefore, [the earth is established as] "consisting of earth, because other qualities are perceived" (VS 4.1.1–3).
And because of the authority of scripture.
In the mantra, "Let your eye go to the sun," the phrase "let your body go to the earth" is heard. This,
therefore, is a statement of the dissolution of the modification (vikāra) into its material cause (prakṛti).
In the mantra "I protect your eye with the sun," another mantra is heard stating, "I protect your body with the earth.
This indicates that the protection of the effect is expressed by means of its cause.

Furthermore, since we observe that things of the same genus initiate a single effect in cases such as cooking pots and the like, it is illogical for things of different genera to initiate a single effect. //31//
Now, the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are investigated according to the sequence of objects of knowledge: are they unmanifest (*avyaktika*) or are they elemental (*bhautika*)?
From what source does this doubt arise?
NyS 3.1.32: Because it is perceived when the black antelope skin is present, and because it is perceived even apart from it, there is doubt.
The black antelope skin is material;
when it is unimpaired, there is perception of form, and when it is impaired, there is no perception.
It is not the case that an object situated apart from the black antelope skin is perceived, nor is it the case that an object reaching the black antelope skin is perceived.
Nor is it the case that the sense organs function without reaching their objects;
this [non-reaching] would be possible only if they were non-material due to being all-pervading.
Thus, because both properties are perceived, there is doubt. //32//
[Because of the non-apprehension [of their cause], there is doubt.
(NS 3.1.32) He says they are not composed of the elements (*abhautika*). Why?
NS 3.1.33: Because of the apprehension of both the large and the minute.
"Great" (mahat) is perceived as larger and largest, such as a banyan tree or a mountain; "subtle" (aṇu) is grasped as smaller and smallest, such as a banyan seed.
Both of these, being perceived, contradict the material nature of the eye.
For that which is material pervades only as far as its own extent;
however, that which is non-material, by virtue of its all-pervasiveness, is omnipresent. //33//
The non-materiality and omnipresence of the sense organs cannot be established merely by their grasping large and small objects. Indeed—NyS 3.1.34:
Their perception [of objects] occurs due to a specific contact between the ray and the object.
The perception of those two large atoms occurs due to a specific kind of contact between the visual ray and the object, just as it does for the ray of a lamp and its object.
Furthermore, the contact between the ray and the object is indicated by the presence of an obstruction.
For the visual ray does not illuminate an object obstructed by walls and the like, just as the ray of a lamp [does not]. //34//
Since [the object] would be inferable from its obscuration, he says this:
"Because that is not perceived, it is not a reason" (NyS 3.1.35).
For fire possesses color and touch;
since it is large, composed of multiple substances, and possesses color, it would be perceived through direct perception like a lamp if its visual ray were present. //35//
The non-perception through direct perception of that which is being inferred is not a valid reason for its non-existence.

The non-perception through direct observation of a ray of light—which is inferred by the mark (liṅga) of an obstruction intended to prevent contact—does not establish its non-existence, just as in the case of the far side of the moon or the lower part of the earth. //36//
And there is a restriction on perception due to the distinction between the properties of substances and qualities.
Indeed, this is a distinct property of substance and a property of quality:
a watery substance that is large, composed of many constituent parts, and has detached components is not perceived through direct perception; however, its cold touch is apprehended.

Because of the persistence of that substance, the winter and dewy seasons are postulated. Similarly, a fiery substance of that same kind, with its form unmanifested, is not perceived along with its color.
In that same way, [the two seasons] are postulated; yet such [a substance] is not perceived.
However, its heat is perceived; because of the persistence of that substance, summer and spring are postulated. //37//
But where this [perception] occurs—NyS 3.1.38:
There is the perception of color due to its inherence in multiple substances and due to a specific quality of color.
In this regard, both color-form (*rūpa*) and the substance (*dravya*) which is its substrate are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

However, that specific quality of color-form—due to the presence of which color-form is perceived in some cases, and due to the absence of which the substance is not perceived in some cases—is called "manifestation" (*udbhava*).
Furthermore, this visual ray (*nāyana-raśmi*) possesses non-manifest color-form (*anudbhūta-rūpa*).
Therefore, it is not perceived through direct perception;
yet, a distinction in the properties of light is observed.
Fire is perceptible when both its color and touch are manifest, as in the case of the rays of the sun;
it is perceptible when its color is manifest but its touch is unmanifest, as in the case of the rays of a lamp;
and it is imperceptible when its touch is manifest but its color is unmanifest, as in the case of fire in contact with water.
The visual ray is imperceptible because its color and touch are unmanifested. //38//
And the arrangement of the sense organs, brought about by karma, is dependent upon the purpose of the person (puruṣa).
Just as the purpose of a conscious being is conceived as consisting in the perception of objects and the perception of pleasure and pain, so too are the sense organs arrayed;
and the array of the visual ray is for the purpose of reaching the object.
Furthermore, the non-manifestation of color and touch is for the sake of establishing conventional usage.
Furthermore, the occurrence of obstruction due to resistance in specific substances serves a practical purpose.
The manifold arrangement of all substances, like that of the sense organs, is produced by action and is dependent upon the purposes of the Person (puruṣa).
Action, consisting of merit and demerit, exists for the sake of the experience of the conscious being.
Furthermore, resistance is a property of material (bhautika) things because it is non-deviant [with respect to them].

That resistance which belongs to a sense faculty toward a particular substance, due to its being obstructed by that substance, is a property of material things; it does not deviate from material things, for nothing that is non-material is observed to possess the property of resistance.
However, non-resistance is inconclusive, because it is common to both that which is derived from the elements (*bhautika*) and that which is not derived from the elements (*abhautika*).
Furthermore, if one should think: "The sense-faculties are derived from the elements because they possess resistance;
it follows that they are not derived from the elements because they lack resistance"?
Furthermore, non-obstruction is observed because objects are perceived even when separated by glass, clouds, films, or crystal;
therefore, that [objection] is not tenable.
Why? Because even material things are not obstructed.
There is no obstruction of the rays of a lamp by glass, mica, or crystal, nor of the digestive heat within cooking vessels and the like. //39//
And non-apprehension is possible due to a difference in causes:
like the non-apprehension of the light of a torch at midday, there is no apprehension of that [object]. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.40)

Just as it is said, "Perception [of color] occurs due to its inherence in multiple substances and due to a specific quality of color," yet even when the causes for perception are present, the light of a torch at midday is not perceived because it is overwhelmed by the light of the sun;

in the same way, although perception occurs due to the presence of multiple substances in a large object and due to a specific quality of color—such that the causes for perception are present—the visual ray is not perceived because of another cause.
And that has been explained: there is no perception by direct observation of a substance whose color and touch are unmanifest. //40//
Furthermore, absolute non-perception is a cause for [inferring] non-existence.
For would this not apply to one who says: "The light of a clod of earth is not perceived at midday because it is overwhelmed by the light of the sun"?
No, because it is not perceived even at night.
"Also because it is not perceived through inference.
Thus, due to absolute non-perception, there is no light from a clod of earth, but it is not so with the ray of the eye. //41//
And this [non-perception] is logically consistent:
because the perception of an object occurs through the assistance of external light, there is non-perception due to its lack of manifestation.
The eye, assisted by external light, is the grasper of its object; in the absence of that [light], there is no perception.

And when there is assistance from light and the perception of cold touch occurs, the substance which is the substratum of that [touch] is not grasped by the eye because its color-form (*rūpa*) is unmanifest (*anudbhūta*).
[In the case of] assistance from light... p.771
This non-perception of the substance which is the substratum of color is observed due to the non-manifestation of that color;
therefore, what was stated—that "it is not a reason because of its non-perception"—is incorrect. //42//
But why is it that "overpowering" (abhibhava) is not stated to be the cause for the non-perception of the visual ray? [Nyāyasūtra 3.1.43:
Because there is overpowering even when [the object] is manifested.
And the word "ca" (and) has the sense of "also in the case of independence from the assistance of external light.
That form which is manifested (*abhivyakta*), prominent (*udbhūta*), and does not depend on the assistance of external light— that is the object of *abhibhava* (overpowering),
because in the opposite case there is no overpowering.

And because its form is not manifest, it is unperceived; yet, being perceived through the assistance of external light, it is not overwhelmed. Thus, it is established that the visual ray exists. //43//
And because the rays from the eyes of nocturnal creatures are observed.
For the rays of the eyes are indeed seen at night in nocturnal animals such as cats and the like;
therefore, there is an inference regarding the remaining [beings].
If it is argued that, just as there is a difference in species, there is likewise a difference in the sense organs?
Furthermore, a mere differentiation of the nature of phenomena is untenable, because we observe that obscuration has the purpose of counteracting [the truth]. //44//

The impossibility of the contact between the sense organ and its object being the cause of cognition. Why? Because perception occurs even without reaching [the object], as is evident from the perception of things separated by glass, a layer of clouds, or crystal. (NyS 3.1.45)
Grass and other moving objects are seen when obstructed by glass or a cloud; thus, the contact [of the sense organ] with that which is not separated is indeed impeded by an intervening medium.
And if the contact between the ray and the object were the cause of perception, there would be no perception of what is obstructed, because there is no contact in that case.

Furthermore, there is this perception of objects through glass, mica, clouds, or crystal; this indicates that the sense organs function without reaching their objects, and for this very reason they are non-material (abhautika), since the property of functioning by reaching an object is characteristic of material things. //45//
There is no refutation [of the argument] because of the non-perception of things obstructed by a wall.
If the sense organs function without reaching their objects, there would be no non-perception of an object obstructed by a wall. //46//
But even if [the sense organ] functions by reaching [its object], how is it that objects separated by glass, a film of cloud, or crystal are perceived?
[Answer: Because there is no obstruction, contact [between the sense organ and the object] is possible. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.47)
Neither glass nor a layer of clouds obstructs the visual ray; thus, being unimpeded, it approaches its object. //47//
And as for the one who thinks that there is no non-obstruction for that which is composed of the elements, that is not so;
for the rays of the sun are not obstructed even when the object to be burned is behind a crystal. (NyS 3.1.48)
Because the rays of the sun are not obstructed, and because they are not obstructed even when passing through crystal, and because they are not obstructed by that which is to be burned;
and since the word "because of non-obstruction" is connected to each [of these] terms, there is a division of sentences.
And as for the distinction in meaning regarding each statement:
the ray of the sun is not obstructed by jars and such; because it is unimpeded, it heats the water contained within the jar.
For when there is contact, there is the perception of the quality of heat belonging to another substance, and by that, the suppression of the sensation of cold.
Likewise, even when an object to be illuminated is separated by a crystal, there is no obstruction of the lamp's rays;
and because there is no obstruction, there is the perception of the object once it has been reached.

Furthermore, a substance situated in a frying pan or similar vessel is burned by fiery heat; in that case, there is contact because there is no obstruction, and since burning occurs upon contact, fire does not act without reaching its object.
Thus, the word "because there is no obstruction" (*avighātāt*) is employed as a standalone term.

What is this so-called non-obstruction (*avighāta*)? It is the non-restraint of a substance from all sides by another substance whose parts are not being displaced and which acts as an interposer; it is the absence of an impediment to the cause of motion, meaning there is no prevention of its reaching [its destination].
For it is observed that water poured into a jar can be perceived externally through the sensation of coldness.
Furthermore, there is no perception of the touch of a substance that is not in contact with the sense organ;
yet, in the case of vision, both trembling and flowing [of the visual ray] are observed.

In that regard, because the visual ray is not obstructed by glass, clouds, thin veils, and the like, it reaches out and comes into contact with the object; thus, its apprehension is logically established. //48//
Not so, because it would entail the mutual exchange of their respective properties.
Otherwise, it would follow that there is no obstruction by walls and the like, just as there is none by glass or clouds;
or, conversely, there would be obstruction by glass, clouds, and so forth, just as there is by walls.
Therefore, the reason for this restriction must be stated. //49//
Just as there is the perception of form in a mirror or in water due to their inherent clarity, so too is that [perception of the self].
The clarity (*prasāda*) of a mirror or water is its own specific quality (*svo dharmaḥ*), as is observed by rule; or rather, the perception of form is the specific quality of that clarity.

Just as when the visual ray, having struck the mirror and been reflected back, comes into contact with one's own face, there occurs the perception of one's own face—which is called the apprehension of a reflection—due to the assistance provided by the form of the mirror.
That becomes the cause;
for when there is a deficiency...
[p. 779] due to the impairment of the form of the mirror, that [reflection] is absent.

Furthermore, the reflection of objects does not occur in walls and such; likewise, there is no obstruction of the visual ray by glass, mica, or thin cloth, while there is obstruction by walls and the like, due to the restrictive nature of the substance itself.
For it is impossible to impose or prohibit [the properties] of things that have been perceived or inferred. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.51)
Because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has reality as its object;
for indeed, O sir, objects that have been seen or inferred by one who is investigating cannot be commanded, "Let them be thus," nor can they be commanded, "Let them be thus. (p. 780)
Nor can it be refuted by saying "it is not so," for it is not tenable to claim that smell, like visible form, should be perceptible to the eye,
or that visible form, like smell, should not be perceptible to the eye.
Let there be the apprehension of water by means of smoke, just as there is the apprehension of fire;
or, let there not be the apprehension of fire by means of smoke, just as there is no apprehension of water.
What is the reason?

Indeed, just as objects exist according to their own nature and their own specific properties (*svadharma*), so too are they apprehended by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for valid cognition has as its object that which exists in such a state. Now, these two—prescription (*niyoga*) and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*)—have been taught by you; let there be non-obstruction by walls and the like, just as with glass or clouds, or let there be non-obstruction by glass, clouds, and the like, just as with walls and the like.
[The opponent says: "Let it not be so.

[The author replies: No; for these properties of substances are indeed perceived through both direct observation and inference, since the perception of resistance and non-resistance serves as the defining criterion.
Obstruction by walls and the like is inferred from the non-perception of what is screened;
non-obstruction by glass, clouds, veils, and the like is inferred from the perception of what is screened. //51//
Furthermore, is this [body] a single sense-organ (*indriya*), or are there many sense-organs?
Whence arises this doubt?
NyS 3.1.52: Doubt arises because there is multiplicity when the locations are different, and because a whole (*avayavin*) occupies multiple locations.

Many substances are seen to occupy various locations, yet the single whole (avayavin) also occupies those various locations; therefore, there is doubt regarding the sense organs because they occupy distinct locations. //52//
There is one sense-organ—
the skin— because it is not distinct [from the others].
He says that the skin is the single sense-faculty. Why? Because there is no separation;
there is no location of a sense-faculty that is not reached by the skin.
Furthermore, when the skin is absent, no apprehension of objects occurs;
since it pervades the locations of all the sense-faculties and only when it is present does the apprehension of objects take place, this skin is a single sense-faculty.
It is not a separate sense-faculty, because there is no perception of the objects of other [distinct] sense-faculties.

When the characteristic of perceiving touch is present and touch is being grasped by the tactile organ (*tvag-indriya*), other objects of the senses such as visible form (*rūpa*) and so forth are not grasped by those who are blind and so on.

Since there is no separate sense organ distinct from the one that grasps touch, visible forms and the rest would have to be grasped by the blind and others just like touch; yet they are not so grasped.
Therefore, the tactile organ is not a single [all-encompassing] sense organ.
The perception of that [color] occurs through a specific part of the skin, just like the perception of smoke.

For example, just as a certain specific part of the skin, when in contact with the eye, perceives the touch of smoke while other parts do not, so too there are specific parts of the skin that grasp color and other qualities; because these are impaired, color and the rest are not perceived by those who are blind and so forth.
The reason is invalid because it is contradictory.

Having stated that "there is only one sense organ because there is no difference from the skin," you then say, "the perception of color and so forth occurs through a specific part of the skin, just like the perception of smoke.

This being the case, the perceivers of objects must be distinct, because the objects are established separately, because the apprehension of an object occurs when that [specific part] exists, and because it does not occur when it is impaired.
And thus, the preceding argument is contradicted by the subsequent argument;
furthermore, the negative concomitance (avyatireka) is doubtful,
since the locations of the sense organs are also pervaded by the elements such as earth and the rest.
Furthermore, in the absence of these [elements], there is no apprehension of objects;
therefore, neither the skin nor any other single sense organ can be all-pervasive with respect to all objects. //53//
Not so, because objects are not perceived simultaneously.
The self is connected with the mind; the mind with the sense organ;
and the sense organ is in contact with all objects.
If there were only one sense organ, simultaneous cognitions would arise from the contact of the self, the sense organs, the mind, and the objects;
yet color-form and other qualities are not perceived simultaneously. Therefore, there is no single sense organ that has all things as its object.
Furthermore, because the apprehensions of objects do not occur together, there is no single sense organ that possesses all objects.
For if there were concomitance [of the senses with their objects], the apprehension of objects would be impossible for those who are blind and so forth. //54//
And because of contradiction, the skin is not one.

The skin is certainly not a single sense-faculty, because that would lead to a contradiction: if forms were perceived by the skin without being reached, then by the same principle of acting without contact (*aprāpyakāritva*), the same consequence would apply to touch and the other objects as well.
Furthermore, since touch and the others are perceived when they have been reached, it follows that forms and the others must also be perceived when they have been reached.
If you argue that [the skin] acts both by reaching and without reaching [its object]?
Because an obstruction is impossible, there is the apprehension of the mere object.

Now, if it should be thought that tangible objects such as touch are apprehended by the skin when they have come into contact [with it], whereas visible forms are apprehended without having come into contact,
then in that case, no obstruction exists.
Furthermore, because there would be no possibility of obstruction, there would be the perception of mere color-form (rūpa) whether it is obstructed or unobstructed.
Moreover, the conformity of the perception and non-perception of color-form to distance and proximity would not occur;
for if color-form were perceived by the skin without being reached [by the sense organ], then the non-perception of color-form at a distance and its perception nearby would be impossible. //55//
And because plurality is established through negation, a supporting reason is also adduced:
"Because of the fivefold nature of the sense organs and their objects" (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.56).
The "purpose" (artha) is the functional motive;
that is fivefold for the sense organs.

When the object of touch is apprehended by the tactile organ (sparśanendriya), form is not apprehended by that very same organ; thus, the eye is inferred as the means for the purpose of apprehending form.

Since form is perceived by that very [organ], the eye is inferred as the instrument for the perception of form. Furthermore, since odor is not perceived by those two [the eye and the body] during the perception of touch and form, the nose is inferred as the instrument for the perception of odor. Since taste is not perceived by those three [the eye, body, and nose] during their respective perceptions, the tongue is inferred as the instrument for the perception of taste.
Furthermore, since sound is not heard by those [other organs] even when the four [objects] are being perceived, the ear is inferred as the means for perceiving sound.
Thus, because the function of each sense organ cannot be accomplished by the others, there are exactly five sense organs. //56//
No, because the objects of those [senses] are manifold.
Indeed, it is not established that there are five sense-faculties simply because there are five types of sense-objects.
Why? Because those objects are many;
for these sense-objects are indeed numerous.
Tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*) are, first of all, cold, hot, or neither-hot-nor-cold;
visible forms (*rūpa*) are white, green, and so forth;
and odors (*gandha*) are desirable, undesirable, or indifferent.

Tastes such as pungent and so forth are distinct, and sounds—consisting of phonemes as well as mere resonance—are distinct. Therefore, for one who [asserts] five sense organs on the basis of the fivefold nature of sense objects, it would follow that there must be many sense organs due to the multiplicity of sense objects. //57//
There is no refutation of odors and so forth, because they are not distinct from the nature of odor-ness and so on.

The apprehensions of odors and so forth—which have been established as such by their own respective general properties (sāmānya), namely "odor-ness" and so on—do not necessitate other [distinct] apprehending subjects, because they are to be accomplished by means of non-common instruments (*asamānasādhanasādhyatvāt*). It has been stated that an aggregate of objects constitutes an inference, not a single part of an object. [End of quote. p. 790
Relying on only a portion of the meaning, you negate the mere fivefold nature of the objects; therefore, this negation is incorrect.
How, then, are odors and the rest established by their own specific universals (svasāmānya) such as "odor-ness" (gandhatva)?
Indeed, this touch is threefold—cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold—and it is subsumed under its own universal, "touch-ness" (sparśatva).

Furthermore, when a cold touch is being perceived, it does not necessitate another perceiver for the perception of either a hot or a neither-hot-nor-cold touch, because different types of touch are accomplished by a single instrument; that very same [instrument] by which the cold touch is perceived also perceives the other two. The same applies to odors by way of their nature as odor.
As form-ness of forms, as taste-ness of tastes, and as sound-ness of sounds.
Furthermore, the apprehensions of odor and so forth necessitate other distinct perceivers, because they are to be accomplished by means that are not common [to one another].
Therefore, it is established that there are five sense organs because their objects and instruments are fivefold. //58//
If the universal is the unifier,
it follows that there is unity among the sense organs, because they are not distinct from their object-ness.
For odors and the other [objects] are subsumed under the general category of "being an object" (viṣayatva). //59//
No, because of the fivefold nature of their characteristics, substrata, movements, forms, and genera.
Indeed, objects established by their general property of being "objects" are not inferred to be apprehended by a single means of cognition independently of other apprehending agents;
yet, the five [qualities] such as odor, which are established by their own specific universals such as "odor-ness," are inferred to be apprehended by different sense organs.
Therefore, this [argument] is irrelevant.

And this very same point is restated by the phrase "because there are five characteristics defined as cognitions" (*buddhilakṣaṇapañcatvāt*). Cognitions themselves are the characteristics because they serve as the marks for the apprehension of objects, which [in turn] indicates the sense organs.
This has already been explained in the commentary on that sūtra: "because there are five sense objects and sense organs" (*indriyārthapañcatvāt*).
Therefore, because there are five characteristics of cognition, there are five sense organs.
Furthermore, the seats of the five sense organs are also fivefold;
the seat of the tactile organ is the entire body, as its characteristic mark is the apprehension of touch.
The eye has its locus in the black-and-white deer-skin (kṛṣṇasāra) and, having issued forth externally, is the instrument for perceiving form;
the nose has its locus in the nose;
the tongue has its locus in the tongue.
The sense of hearing has the ear-cavity as its locus, because it is characterized by the apprehension of odors, tastes, forms, tangibles, and sounds;
furthermore, there is a distinction among the senses due to the difference in their modes of operation.
The eye, fixed upon the black pupil (kṛṣṇasāra), goes outward and reaches those substances which are the substrata of visible form;
however, the sense organs such as touch approach their objects by moving toward their own bases.
In the case of sound, its proximity to the ear occurs through the process of a continuous series (santānavṛtti).
Size (*ākṛti*) is indeed dimension (*parimāṇa*), which is of five kinds.
The sense organs of smell, taste, and touch have their own respective locations and are inferred by the perception of their objects.
The eye has its locus in the black pupil (*kṛṣṇasāra*); it extends outward and pervades the object.

The auditory organ is not other than space; it is all-pervasive, and its existence is inferred from the experience of sound alone. By means of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person, it manifests sound through a restriction to specific locations. "Jāti" (genus/source) is said to mean "yoni" (source/birthplace).
Indeed, the five elements, earth and the others, are the sources of the sense organs;
therefore, it is established that there are five sense organs because of the fivefold nature of the primary constituents (prakṛti). //60//

But how is it known that the sense organs have the elements as their material cause (*bhūtaprakṛti*) and not the unmanifest (*avyaktaprakṛti*)? [The answer is: Because of the perception of specific qualities of the elements, they are of the same nature as them. (NyS 3.1.61)
For a rule regarding the manifestation of specific qualities in the elements, such as air and the rest, is observed:
air is the manifester of touch,
and water is the manifester of taste.
Light is the manifestor of color;
a certain substance of the earth is the manifestor of the odor of another substance.

Furthermore, there exists this rule regarding the sense organs: that each perceives a specific quality of its corresponding element. Therefore, because they perceive the specific qualities of the elements, we consider the sense organs to have the elements as their material cause (*prakṛti*), and not the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) as their material cause. //61//

It has been stated that odor and the other qualities are the attributes of earth and the other elements; however, since this enumeration applies equally whether earth and the others possess a single quality or multiple qualities, he says:
*Nyāyasūtra* 3.1.62: "Of odor, taste, color, touch, and sound, those ending with touch belong to earth."
Having excluded each preceding one among water, fire, and air, the subsequent one belongs to space.
Regarding the phrase "of those ending with tangibility," there is a change of case-ending:
[the meaning is] "the subsequent sound of space is from those ending with tangibility.
[End of quotation. p. 796.
How, then, is there the use of the suffix *tarap*?
It is due to the capacity for independent application (*svatantra-viniyoga*).
By that, it is understood that the word "uttara" denotes something for the sake of another.
For in the *uddeśasūtra*, sound is mentioned after those [elements] ending with contact (*sparśa*).

Alternatively, it is due to the intended meaning of "contact" (*tantram vā sparśasya vivakṣitatvāt*): when those ending with contact have been assigned [their respective positions], sound is that which follows them. //62-63//
Not so, because not all qualities are perceived.
This application of qualities is not correct. Why? Because not all the qualities of a given element are perceived by a sense organ composed of that same element.

For instance, by the olfactory organ, which consists of earth, everything from touch down to the other qualities is not grasped; only smell alone is grasped. The same applies to the remaining [senses] as well. //64//
How, then, are these qualities to be applied?
NS 3.1.65: Because each successive quality exists in each preceding one, the subsequent qualities are not perceived in those [preceding ones].
Each one among smell and the others is, respectively, the quality of each one among earth and the others;
therefore, "their non-perception" means the non-perception of those [smells], of those two [earths], and of that [earth].
[The sense organs do not perceive all qualities: the nose does not perceive taste, color, or touch; the tongue does not perceive color or touch; and the eye does not perceive touch.
How, then, are the elements perceived as possessing multiple qualities? [They are so perceived] because of their association (*saṃsarga*).
And because of contact with water and the other elements, taste and the other qualities are indeed perceived in earth; the same applies to the remaining elements as well. //65//

In that case, a fixed rule (niyama) would not obtain because there is no restriction regarding their association; for it might be argued that earth has four qualities, water three, fire two, and air one.
Yet, such a fixed rule is indeed established. How so?
NS 3.1.66: "For the subsequent is pervaded by the preceding."
Since earth and the other elements are pervaded by each preceding one by each succeeding one, there is a rule of combination;
this should be understood as pertaining to the creation of the primary elements (bhūtas), not to the present state. //66//
NyS 3.1.67: It is not so, because both the earthen and the watery [substances] are perceptible.
"No," he says, rejecting the three-sūtra argument.
Why? Because this earthy substance and this watery substance are both perceptible.

According to the principle that "perception [occurs] due to largeness, being composed of multiple substances, and color," only a fiery substance would be perceptible, and not an earthy or watery one, due to the absence of color [in the latter two].
However, because the earthy and watery [substances] are perceptible like the fiery, it is not the case that multiple qualities are perceived in the elements due to their mutual contact.

For one who asserts that the perceptibility of the earthy and watery [substances] is caused by the form (color) of other elements, it follows that air would also be perceptible; or else, a restrictive cause must be stated.
Or rather, because the tastes of the earthy and watery [substances] are perceptible—the earthy taste being of six kinds—[the same logic applies].
Water is indeed sweet;
and this cannot arise from a mixture [of other tastes],
because the two colors— those of the earthy and the watery [substances]— are perceived when they are assisted by the color of fire.
For in a mixture, it is only the manifesting form that exists, and not the manifested;
and because the forms of earthy and watery substances are perceived as being of both single and multiple kinds—
the earthy form being of many kinds, such as green, red, yellow, and so forth.
Water, however, is white and non-luminous;
and this [property] is not possible when there is a conjunction of elements possessing only a single quality.
This is merely an illustration.
Beyond this is the detailed elaboration:
because of the perceptibility of two types of touch— namely, those belonging to earth and those belonging to fire—
the touch of earth is neither hot nor cold.
Heat is perceived as belonging to fire, and this is not possible through contact with air, which possesses the single quality of touch that is neither hot nor cold;
or alternatively, because the substances of earth and water, which possess fixed qualities, are directly perceived.
The perceptible substance of earth possesses four qualities, while that of water possesses three;
by means of this [perceptible effect], its cause is inferred to be of such a nature.
For the effect is the mark [of the cause], since the existence of the effect follows from the existence of the cause.

Thus, because the two substances consisting of fire and air are perceptible, the determination of their qualities allows for the inference of the determination of those qualities in their causal substance. Furthermore, the distinction between the earthy and the watery is observed through perception;
an earthy substance is perceived by direct observation as being distinct from water and other elements.
The watery [element] is grasped by the other two,
and the fiery [element] is grasped by the wind.
Nor is each individual quality perceived;
thus, the statement "the lower is pervaded by the higher" is without inference.
For no inferential mark (*liṅga*) that could lead us to understand this in such a way is perceived here.

As for what was said— that "the subsequent is indeed pervaded by the prior" should be understood as applying to the creation of the elements and not to the present state— that is incorrect because there is no restrictive reason [for such a limitation].
Moreover, it is observed in the present that the subsequent is pervaded by the prior,
as for example, fire is pervaded by air.
Pervasion is conjunction,
and that is common to both;
since fire is possessed of touch because it is pervaded by air, but air is not possessed of color because it is pervaded by fire, there is no restrictive cause [for such a distinction].
And it is observed that the tactile quality of air is not perceived due to its being overwhelmed by the tactile quality of fire; yet, a thing cannot be overwhelmed by itself. //67//
Thus, having refuted that popular doctrine which contradicts reason, the objection raised in [Nyāyasūtra 3.1.67], "because not all qualities are perceived," is resolved as follows:
"On account of the progressive excellence of each preceding quality, each subsequent one is predominant. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.68)
Therefore, there is no perception of all qualities;

because each preceding sense organ, such as the nose and so forth, possesses a superior excellence regarding its respective quality—smell and so on—it is designated as "predominant" (pradhāna). What constitutes this predominance?
The state of being the grasper of objects.
What is the excellence of the quality? It is the capacity for manifestation.

Just as external substances— terrestrial, aqueous, and fiery— which possess four, three, and two qualities respectively, do not manifest all qualities, but rather manifest smell, taste, and form respectively due to the predominance of those specific qualities; even so, the olfactory, gustatory, and visual organs, which possess four, three, and two qualities respectively, do not perceive all qualities.
However, due to the excellence of fragrance, taste, and form respectively, the olfactory and other senses possess the capacity to grasp fragrance, taste, and form.
Therefore, all qualities are not perceived by the nose and the other senses.
As for one who asserts that the nose grasps only fragrance because it has fragrance as its quality, and likewise for the tongue and the others—
It would follow that there would be a perception of qualities by the sense of smell and the other organs, according to their respective association with those qualities. //68//
But by what is this distinction established—that some sense organs are composed of earth and not all, while some are composed of water, fire, or air and not all?
[Nyāyasūtra 3.1.69: That distinction, however, is due to the predominance [of a particular element].
The "abundance" (*bhūyastva*) is the conjunction of distinct substances capable of accomplishing a purpose, brought about by the refinement of the person.
For the word "abundance" is seen to denote excellence (*prakarpa*), just as an excellent object is called "abundant."

Just as substances such as poison, medicine, and gems—which are capable of performing distinct purposeful actions—are produced by the power of human refinement, and not every substance is capable of every action;
so too, the olfactory and other sense organs are produced as being capable of apprehending their respective distinct objects, and not as being capable of apprehending all objects. //69//
The sense organs do not perceive their own qualities.
If one asks why,
it is because the sense organs exist only when they possess their respective qualities (NyS 3.1.70).
The olfactory and other sense organs do not perceive their own odors and so forth.
If one asks for what reason,
it is because the olfactory and other organs function as sense faculties only in conjunction with their own respective qualities.

The nose, together with its own odor which performs the same function as an external one, perceives the external odor; however, its perception of its own odor does not occur due to the absence of a cooperative condition.
The same applies to the remaining [senses] as well. //70//
If, moreover, odor were both a concomitant cause for the nose and its object of perception, then it says: "And because that [odor] is not perceived by that very [nose]. (NyS 3.1.71)
There is no perception of the qualities of the sense organs.
As for one who says: "Just as an external object is perceived by the eye, so too should that very eye be perceived by that same eye."
This case is exactly like that; for in both instances, there is an absence of a cause for comprehension. //71//
Not so, because sound is perceived as a quality.
It is not the case that the sense organs do not perceive their own qualities;
for the sound, which is its own quality, is indeed perceived by the auditory organ. //72//
The perception of that [ether] is due to its qualitative difference from other substances and their qualities.
Space does not become a sense-faculty by virtue of possessing the quality of sound;
nor is sound the manifester of sound;
and the perception of their own respective qualities by the olfactory and other faculties does not occur.
Nor is it inferred;
rather, it is inferred that sound is perceived by the auditory faculty, which is space,
and that space possesses the quality of sound.
And the remainder should be understood as inference (*anumāna*).
To begin with, the self (*ātman*) is not the hearer, nor is it the instrument; for if the mind were the sense of hearing, deafness would be impossible.
Earth and the other elements possess the capacity for the state of being the olfactory organ and so forth, but they lack the capacity for the state of being the auditory organ.
This is their capacity.
And [if it were] in the absence of the auditory organ, there would be incapacity.
But this auditory organ exists and space remains; by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), space is the auditory organ. //73//
Thus ends the first Āhnika of the third Adhyāya in the Nyāyabhāṣya of the venerable Vātsyāyana.
Now begins the second daily lesson (āhnika) of the third chapter.
The sense organs and their objects have been examined;
now follows the sequence for the examination of cognition (buddhi).
Is it impermanent or permanent?
Whence does this doubt arise?
NyS 3.2.1: Doubt arises from the similarity [of sound] with action and space.
In that cognition, a common property— namely, the state of being intangible— is perceived through those two [the self and the body],
as is a specific property— the state of possessing the qualities of arising and passing away—
and their respective opposites, suchness and non-eternality, are not perceived in that cognition.
Therefore, there is doubt. //1//
Indeed, this doubt is untenable;
for to all embodied beings, cognition is individually experienced as impermanent, just like pleasure and the rest.
And there occurs the awareness: "I shall know," "I know," and "I have known.
Furthermore, without arising and passing away, there can be no manifestation across the three times;
therefore, it is established that because of this manifestation across the three times, cognition is impermanent.

And this is established by valid means of knowledge; it has also been stated in the *Śāstra*: "That which arises from the contact of a sense organ with its object," and "The non-simultaneity of cognitions is the mark of the mind," and so forth.
Therefore, the process of doubt is untenable.
This treatise is for the purpose of refuting the doctrine of [wrong] views;
for it is thus that the Sāṅkhyas perceive and proclaim: "The intellect (*buddhi*), which constitutes the internal organ of the person (*puruṣa*), is eternal. And they set forth the proof:
NyS 3.2.2: Because there is recognition of the object.
What, then, is this recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)?
It is the synthesizing cognition (*pratisandhijñāna*) regarding two cognitions with respect to the same object, in the form: "I know this very object that I previously knew.
And this is possible only if the intellect (*buddhi*) is permanent.
But if there were plurality—that is, if there were distinct cognitions that arise and perish—recognition would be impossible; for one person does not recognize what has been known by another. //2//
NyS 3.2.3: It is not a valid reason because it is equivalent to the probandum.
Just as the permanence of the intellect (buddhi) is to be proven, so too is recognition (pratyabhijñāna).
What is the reason?
Because it is impossible for the property of a conscious agent to reside in an instrument.

This— namely, knowledge (*jñāna*), seeing (*darśana*), apprehension (*upalabdhi*), awakening (*bodha*), cognition (*pratyaya*), and determination (*adhyavasāya*)— is indeed the property of the self (*puruṣadharma*).
For it is the conscious one who recognizes an object previously known.
For this reason, its eternity is logical.

However, if consciousness is admitted to belong to the instrument [the internal organ], then the essential nature of the conscious being must be stated; it is not possible to establish that there exists another self whose nature has not been specified.

If cognition is admitted to belong to the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the internal organ, then what is the essential nature of the conscious being now, what is its property, and what is its reality?
And what does this conscious being do by means of cognition residing in the intellect (*buddhi*)?
If it is said that "it wills," no;
for that would be stating something different from cognition—namely, that "the person wills while the intellect cognizes"—but this is not stated as being something other than cognition.
"To will, to know, to perceive, to see, and to apprehend" have this one and the same meaning.
If you say that "intellect makes known," certainly so; it is true that the person knows while the intellect makes it known.
And if this is accepted, it is established that knowledge belongs to the person, not to the internal organ, the intellect.
And regarding the proposition that there is a distinction between different words for each individual person, the statement of the reason for the refutation is as follows:
whoever asserts that "one person perceives" and "another understands," [is refuted by the following].
"One perceives" and "one sees"—
these are indeed distinct persons, namely the conscious one, the cognizer, the perceiver, and the seer; since these attributes do not belong to a single entity, what is the reason for your denial?
If you argue that there is no difference in meaning, then the same [objection] applies.

If you think that because these words have non-different meanings, the established distinction between them is untenable, then the same [consequence] follows: in the case of "the person cognizes" (*puruṣaś cetayate*) and "the intellect knows" (*buddhir jānīte*), the meaning does not differ; since both possess consciousness (*cetanatva*), one or the other would have to be discarded.

If, on the other hand, it is called "intellect" (*buddhi*) because one awakens by means of it— that is, awakening itself— then it is simply the mind (*manas*) that is being referred to, and that is eternal. Let this be so.
But the permanence of the mind does not follow from the recognition of objects,
for it is observed that recognition occurs despite a difference in instruments, because the knower is one— as in the case of "the recognition by the other [eye] of what was seen by the left"—
just as with the eyes or a lamp.
"The recognition of a lamp seen by one lamp through another lamp"—therefore, this is the reason for the permanence of the knower. //3//

And as for the view that while the intellect (*buddhi*) remains constant, cognitions— which are its modifications (*vṛtti*)— issue forth according to their respective objects, and that the modification is not distinct from the possessor of the modification—
that too is incorrect, because there is no simultaneous perception [of both].

If there were non-difference between the modification and that which possesses the modification, then because the possessor of the modification persists, the modifications would also persist; thus, these apprehensions of objects would remain, and it would follow as a logical consequence that all objects are apprehended simultaneously. //4//
And in the absence of recognition, there would follow the consequence of destruction.
Furthermore, if recognition were directed toward the past, then even that which possesses activity would be past, which entails the destruction of the internal organ;
and in the opposite case, there would be a plurality [of cognizers]. //5//

And the mind, being unitary and non-omnipresent, comes into contact with the sense organs successively; thus, because its operation is sequential, there is no simultaneous perception. — Nyāyasūtra 3.2.6: "Because of its successive functioning, there is no simultaneous apprehension."
There is a distinction between the sense organs and their objects, as well as between the function and that which possesses the function.
Furthermore, there is non-recognition [of the same object] due to the engagement with another object.
Non-recognition is non-apprehension.

And non-apprehension of some object occurs when the mind is occupied with another object, because of the difference between the function and that which possesses the function; for if there were identity [between them], such occupation would be purposeless. //7//
Regarding the omnipresence of the internal organ, [the opponent claims] there is a successive conjunction with the sense organs;
[this is] not so, because of the absence of motion.
Since the sense organs have been reached by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there is an absence of "going," which is the meaning of "reaching.
In that case, because there is no sequential functioning, the impossibility of non-simultaneous perception [of objects] follows.
Furthermore, since movement is absent, the non-simultaneous perception of the all-pervading internal organ—which was previously refuted—is not inferred by any other mark (*liṅga*).

Just as the movement of the eye is denied because it perceives both near and distant objects simultaneously, and its obstruction by an intervening object—such as a hand—is inferred [in the case of the moon], this dispute concerns the instrument (*karaṇa*), not its eternity. This dispute concerns the instrument, not its eternity. (p. 819)
For it is established that the mind is an internal organ and eternal.
Where, then, is there a dispute?
It concerns its all-pervasiveness (vibhutva).
And that [position] is refuted by the non-perception of such a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is one, whereas these various functions (*vṛtti*), which consist of cognition, are manifold:
visual consciousness, olfactory consciousness, consciousness of form, and consciousness of odor.
And this [distinction] is untenable if there were identity between the function and that which possesses the function;
thus, it is the *puruṣa* who knows, not the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
By this, the objection regarding distraction toward other objects is refuted.

The attachment to another object, characterized by the apprehension of that other object, belongs to the person and not to the internal organ; however, this attachment—consisting in proximity to one sense-organ and non-proximity to another—is admitted to belong to the mind. //8//
"The internal organ is one, while its modifications are many.

Even though there is no actual difference [in the internal organ], this is said regarding its modifications: "The misconception of its being different is like the misconception of the crystal being different [from itself]. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.9)

In that state, there is the conceit of diversity, just as there is the conceit of otherness— such as "blue" or "red"— in a crystal when it is overlaid by another substance; likewise, [this occurs] due to the overlaying of different objects.
It is not so, because there is no reason [for it].

This misconception of multiplicity regarding cognitions is metaphorical, like the misconception of difference in a crystal; however, there is no reason why it should not be like the misconception of difference in odors and so forth.

If you argue that the lack of a reason is the same [in both cases], we say no, because we observe the successive arising and passing away of cognitions—namely, that cognitions arise and pass away successively with respect to sense objects.
And it is observed that they cause [the senses] to function;
therefore, this notion of multiplicity regarding cognitions is like the conceit of distinctness regarding odors and so forth. //9//
Not tolerating the argument that "it is like the misconception of difference in a crystal," the proponent of momentariness (kṣaṇikavādin) says:
"Even in the case of a crystal, [the argument] is not a valid reason, because individual entities are momentary due to the production of one after another. (NyS 3.2.10)
The position that the illusion of multiplicity arises from the differences in adjuncts (upadhāna) while the crystal remains undifferentiated is one for which the reason is non-existent.
Why? Because even in the case of the crystal, there is a continuous arising of successive [moments];
that is, in the crystal as well, distinct manifestations arise and others cease.
How so? Because individual entities are momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
A *kṣaṇa* is the shortest duration of time; those that exist for only a *kṣaṇa* are "momentary.
But how is it known that individual entities are momentary?
Because an accumulation, a diminution, and a continuity are observed in the body and so forth:
the nourishment derived from food, once processed by digestion, undergoes a continuous process of accumulation and diminution within the body in the form of blood and other constituents.
From this accumulation, there is the production of individual entities.
From diminution comes the cessation of manifestation.

This being the case, growth of the body is perceived over time through the differentiation of the transformation of its constituent parts; thus, this property belonging to a particular manifestation is to be understood as belonging to manifestation in general. //10//
NyS 3.2.11: Since there is no cause for restriction, everything is permitted according to what is observed.
The rule that in all individual entities there is a continuous process of increase and decrease, as in the case of the body, is not absolute.
Why? Because of the absence of a reason;
for here there exists neither perception nor inference to establish it.
Therefore, permission is granted according to what is observed:
wherever a continuous process of increase and decrease is seen,
there the arising of successive individuals is permitted on the basis of observing that continuous process of increase and decrease.
It is admitted where an uninterrupted continuity of increase and decrease is observed,
as in the case of bodies and the like;
whereas it is rejected wherever such a continuity is not observed, as in the case of stones and similar objects.
Even in the case of crystal, no continuity of increase and decrease is observed;
therefore, it is incorrect to claim that another [substance] arises in the crystal.
This is just as when the bitterness of the arka plant imparts bitterness to all other substances. //11//

For one who maintains that there is momentariness in the substance-series (*dravya-santāna*)—namely, that through the cessation of everything without remainder there is a production of what was previously non-existent, devoid of any continuity—the following [objection applies]:
"Because causes for both arising and destruction are perceived. (NyS 3.2.12)
First, a cause of origination is observed, namely the accumulation of parts in the case of anthills and the like;
and a cause of destruction is observed in the case of jars and the like, namely the disjunction of parts.
[The disjunction of parts of jars and the like is observed. p. 827

But for one [who holds that] that whose parts are not diminished ceases and that whose parts are not augmented arises, there is no cause perceived in either case—neither when there is a cessation without residue nor when there is an arising of what was previously non-existent. This is established by the analogy of the destruction of milk where no cause is perceived, and by the analogy of the arising of curd. *Nyāyasūtra* 3.2.13.

Just as the cause of the destruction of milk and the cause of the production of curd are admitted even though they are not perceived, so too, in the case of a crystal, there are causes for its destruction and causes for its production among successive individual manifestations; [this is so] because it is apprehended through inference, and thus it is not a case of non-perception. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.14)

The signs of the destruction of milk and the causes of the destruction of milk, as well as the signs of the production of curd and the causes of the production of curd, are perceived; therefore, it is not a case of non-apprehension.

However, in the case of substances such as crystal, since there is the production of successive individuals [rather than a single persisting substance], there is no sign [of such persistence]; thus, there is indeed no production [of a new substance]. //14//
Regarding this, someone offers a rebuttal:
"No, because of the appearance of other qualities through the transformation of the milk. (NyS 3.2.15)
One says that the transformation of milk is not its destruction;
and "transformation" is the emergence of another property upon the cessation of a previous property of a persisting substance.
Another says it is the manifestation of a different quality.
When a substance exists, upon the cessation of its previous quality, another quality arises;
this indeed is like the state of becoming one-sided. //15//
But here there is a refutation: NS 3.2.16: "The observation of the production of another substance from a rearrangement [of parts] is an inference for the cessation of the previous substance."

When a distinct substance, curd, is perceived to have arisen from a reorganization of parts characterized by coagulation (*saṃmūrchana*), it is inferred that the previous substance, milk, has ceased to exist due to the separation of its parts.

This is just as when a distinct substance, a pot, has arisen in a vessel from a different arrangement of clay particles, the previous substance, the lump of clay, ceases to exist due to the separation of the clay particles. Furthermore, just as with clay, there is a continuity of parts between milk and curd; for the arising of a new substance through a cessation without any continuity (*niranvaya*) is not possible if there were a total destruction [of the prior substance]. //16//
Having granted that the destruction of milk occurs without a cause, the following objection is stated regarding the production of curd:
NyS 3.2.17: "Because the cause of destruction is not perceived in some cases and is perceived in others, [the argument] is inconclusive."
The claim that the destruction and arising of individual instances of crystal are causeless, like [the transformation of] milk into curd, is not an absolute rule.
Why? Because there is no reason [for it].
There is no reason here for the destruction and arising of individual instances such as crystals to be causeless, as in the case of milk and curd.

Furthermore, it is not as in the case where the destruction of a jar occurs due to the presence of a cause of destruction and its production occurs due to the presence of a cause of production; likewise, the existence of destruction and production in individual instances such as crystals cannot be due to the presence of causes for their destruction and production. Moreover, the statement of the example is without a basis. This example would have a basis only if destruction and production were perceived in the crystals themselves—just as the destruction of milk is unperceived while the production of curd is perceived.
But those two are not perceived;
therefore, this example lacks a substratum.
Furthermore, since you have conceded that the production and destruction of the crystal exist, and since you have accepted the proof for this point, there is no refutation [of our position].
Just as with a pot, the destruction and arising of crystals and the like are not without cause; therefore, this example must be accepted because it cannot be refuted.

However, the claim that the destruction and arising [of milk and curd] are without cause—like that of milk and curd—is capable of being refuted, because one observes that destruction and arising occur from causes.
One who observes the destruction and arising of milk and curd must infer their cause, for a cause is indeed known through the mark of its effect. //17//
It has been established that cognition is impermanent.
However, this is now considered: to whom does this cognition belong? Is it a quality of the self, the sense organs, the mind, or the objects?
Although this matter is indeed well-known, it is being elaborated upon so that the remaining points of investigation may be carried out.
Thus, this doubt arises because of the occurrence of contact with the intellect (*buddhi*) due to the non-apprehension of the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*).
Regarding that, the specific characteristic [is defined] in NyS 3.2.18:
"It is not [the case that the object is the cause], because even when the sense organ and the object have perished, the cognition persists."
Nor is knowledge a quality of the sense organs, for knowledge persists even when they have perished;
indeed, this cognition "I saw" occurs even when both the sense organ and the object have perished.
Furthermore, it is not possible for knowledge to exist once the knower has perished.
Indeed, that cognition which arises from the contact of a sense organ with its object ceases when the sense organ and the object perish; this [other cognition],
however,
arises from the contact of the self and the mind.
"Its existence is logical" means as follows:
this memory, namely "I saw," has as its object that which was previously seen.
And it is not logical for there to be a recollection of a prior perception if the knower has perished.
Furthermore, what is seen by one is not remembered by another;
nor, when the mind is accepted as the knower, can it be maintained that the sense organs and their objects possess the status of being knowers. //18//
Let it be, then, that cognition is a quality of the mind—NyS 3.2.19: And because cognizable objects are not perceived simultaneously, [cognition] does not belong to the mind.

The non-simultaneous perception of objects of knowledge is the mark of the internal organ; in that regard, the internal organ which is inferred from the non-simultaneous perception of objects of knowledge—
knowledge is not a quality of that [organ].
To whom, then, does it belong?
To the knower, because of his mastery;
the knower is the master, and the instrument is that which is mastered.
Furthermore, if [the mind] were a quality of knowledge, its status as an instrument would cease.

Since the knower possesses the cognition of odor and so forth through instruments such as the nose, it is inferred that the cognition of pleasure and so forth, as well as memory, belong to that which has the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) as its instrument.
In that regard, the mind, which is a quality of knowledge, is the self (ātman).
As for that which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) serving as the means for the apprehension of pleasure and so forth, it is merely a difference in designation and not a difference in substance;
or rather, the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) is "and because of the simultaneous apprehension of objects of knowledge by the yogin.

Indeed, when supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) has manifested, the yogin, possessing the quality of non-obstruction (*vikaraṇadharman*), creates other bodies equipped with sense organs, and through them, he perceives objects of knowledge simultaneously.

And this [simultaneity of cognitions] is possible only when the knower is all-pervading (vibhu), not when the mind (manas) is atomic; for if the mind were all-pervading, there would be no refutation of the fact that cognition is a quality of the self.

Furthermore, if the mind were all-pervading—that is, if it were coextensive with the internal organ—then because of its simultaneous contact with all the sense organs, cognitions would arise simultaneously. //19//
Even if it were a quality of the self, the same [objection] would apply.
If the self were all-pervading and conjoined with all the sense organs simultaneously, it would follow that cognitions would arise at once. //20//
NyS 3.2.21: Because of the absence of contact between the sense organs and the mind, that [cognition] does not arise.
Just as the contact between the sense organ and its object is a cause for the perception of odor and so forth, so too is the contact between the sense organ and the mind (manas) a cause.
And because the mind is atomic, this [contact] is not simultaneous.
Due to this non-simultaneity, there is no simultaneous arising of cognitions, even though they are qualities of the self. //21//
