If, on the other hand, the cognition of odor and so forth were to arise from the mere contact of the self, the sense organ, and the object, [it would be untenable];
for no cause for such production has been specified. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.22)
"The cognition of odor and so forth arises from the mere contact of the self with the sense organ; no cause for its production is specified here by which we might understand this. //22//
And because no cause of destruction is perceived, if [sound] were to persist, it would follow that it is eternal.
The phrase "this is the same even if they are qualities of the self" is conjoined with this [point].
For there are two kinds of causes for the destruction of qualities: the disappearance of the substratum of the qualities and a contrary quality.
Because the self is eternal, the former [position] is untenable;

furthermore, a quality of the intellect that is contradictory [to its nature] is not perceived. Therefore, if the intellect were a quality of the self, it would follow as a logical consequence that it is eternal. //23//
NyS 3.2.24: Because cognition is apprehended as impermanent, it is destroyed by a subsequent cognition, just like sound.
That "the intellect is impermanent" is something to be personally experienced by every embodied being.

Furthermore, the continuum of the intellect is perceived; therein, one cognition is inferred to be a contrary quality to another cognition, just as in the continuum of sound, one sound is a contrary to another sound. //24//

If cognition were a quality of the self, then since there would be no lack of simultaneity among causes— given that there exist innumerable conditioned factors produced by knowledge which serve as causes for memory, and these are inherent in the self, while the contact between the self and the mind, which is also a cause of memory, is equally present— multiple memories would arise simultaneously.
In this regard, someone wishing to establish that contact [of the mind] is not simultaneous says:
"Because memory arises from the contact of the mind with a portion of the self in which cognition is inherent, there is no simultaneous production [of cognitions]. (NyS 3.2.25)

The impression (*saṃskāra*) which is the means for knowledge is called "knowledge. By means of the regions of the self (*ātmapradeśa*) refined by knowledge, the mind (*manas*) comes into contact with them in succession. Due to this contact between the self and the mind, memories also arise in succession. //25//
NyS 3.2.26: [The soul is not eternal], because the mind functions within the body.
The conjunction of the embodied self with the mind, accompanied by the ripening latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*), is held to be "living.
In that state, for one who exists within the body prior to death, a conjunction of the mind with regions of the self outside the body—refined by the impressions of cognition—is not possible. //26//
NyS 3.2.27: It is not a valid reason because it is itself that which is to be proven.
Life consists merely in the maturation of the latent impressions of karma;
this being the case, it follows that the mind exists within the body. //27//
There is no refutation [of the soul's existence] because the maintenance of the body is possible for one who remembers.
Indeed, by directing the mind with the desire to remember, one recalls some object even after a long time;
and for one who is remembering, the maintenance of the body is observed. Furthermore, the effort born from the contact between the self and the mind is of two kinds: sustaining and impelling.
And once the mind has issued forth from the body, it would fall due to its weight because of the absence of the sustaining effort; [this is not so] for one who remembers.
//28// Not so, because of the mind's rapid movement. //NyS_3.2.29//

The mind’s swift movement consists of its contact with an external portion of the self through a faculty refined by cognition, and once it has returned, the production of effort; both of these are logical.
Alternatively, having produced a sustaining effort, there is the mind's departure from the body.
Therefore, it is established that there is retention (dhāraṇā) in that state. //29//
NyS 3.2.30: No, because there is no fixed rule regarding the time of recollection.
Some things are remembered quickly, while others are remembered after a long time.

When [remembrance occurs] after a long time, then— while a continuous stream of thought (*cintā-prabandha*) is being maintained in the mind with the desire to remember (*susmūrṣā*)— the contemplation of some sign (*liṅga*) of the object becomes the cause of that remembrance.

In this regard, it is argued that this [memory] is not possible when the mind has been long departed, because the conjunction of the self and the mind, independent of the body's conjunction, cannot be the cause of memory; for the body is the locus of experience.

The body is the locus of experience for the knowing person; therefore, for one who has departed from it, the mere conjunction of the mind with the self is not sufficient for the production of cognition, pleasure, and so forth.
Or, if [the body] were merely for the purpose of fashioning [the organs], the body would be useless. //30//
Nor is there a specific conjunction [of the self with the mind] due to the self's impulsion, chance, or ignorance.
Would there be a particular conjunction of the mind with something external to the body through the impulsion of the self,
or by chance, or by accident, or through the cognition of the mind?
In every respect, however, [the self] is untenable.
How so? Because it would be an object of memory, because memory would occur at will, and because knowledge would be impossible.

If the self, being the cause of the memory of that object, impels the mind— thinking, "Let the mind be conjoined with that mental impression (saṃskāra) which is inherent in this particular location of the self"— then that object has already been remembered and is not something yet to be remembered; moreover,
neither the location of the self nor the mental impression is perceptible to the self.

In that case, there is no perception of the self through direct experience because it is not logically established. Furthermore, when one applies the mind with the desire to remember, one recalls some object after a long time, not spontaneously;
moreover, the mind lacks the quality of being a knower, as knowledge is denied to it. //31//
And this is the same as [the case of] the pain in the foot of one whose mind is distracted, due to a particular kind of contact. — NyS 3.2.32.

Indeed, when this person, whose mind is distracted elsewhere, experiences a piercing of the foot by a pebble or a thorn in a certain place, then a specific conjunction of the self and the mind must be postulated,
for pain and the sensation of pain are observed there. In that case, the same refutation applies.
But [if you argue] that there is no distinction based on chance, and that neither action nor conjunction is accidental—[we reply:
if you claim that karma, which is the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), is the cause of action for the sake of experience, then it is the same [for us].

If you think: "The unseen force residing in the person is the cause of action in the mind for the sake of the person's experience; in this way, suffering and the sensation of suffering are established," [then we respond as follows:]
The same applies here: even in the case of memory, a specific conjunction must exist as its cause.
Therefore, what was stated—that "there is no specific conjunction [of the self with the mind] due to the self’s impulsion, chance, or ignorance"—is not a valid refutation.
However, the previous refutation—"because the mind functions within the body"—remains valid. //32//
What, then, is the cause for the non-simultaneous recollection despite the simultaneous existence of the causes?
NS 3.2.33: Non-simultaneous recollection occurs because the cognitions of the mental application (praṇidhāna), the inferential mark (liṅga), and so forth, do not exist simultaneously.

Just as the contact between the self and the mind and the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) are the causes of memory, so too is the act of resolution (*praṇidhāna*), as well as the cognitions of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth; and since these do not occur simultaneously, the memories produced by them do not arise at once.
However, if memory were to occur through mere presence [of the object] without depending on resolution and the rest, there would be the undesirable consequence of simultaneous memories.

Indeed, regarding this memory that sometimes arises as if it were intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*), independent of application of the mind (*praṇidhāna*) and so forth: there would be the undesirable consequence of its arising simultaneously [with other memories], because of the absence of a cause;
for since the existing cause of memory is not perceived, there is a misconception that it is identical to intuitive knowledge.
In a continuous stream of thought concerning many objects, only a certain object serves as the cause of memory for someone at a certain time.
In a continuous stream of thought, a certain object serves as the cause for someone's memory;
through the repeated reflection upon it, the memory of that object arises.
Yet this rememberer does not perceive every cause of memory, thinking, "In this way, my memory has arisen."
Because it is not consciously perceived, this knowledge is mistakenly thought to be intuitive (*prātibha*), like [the intuition] of a seer;
however, there is no such thing as memory that does not depend on mental application (*praṇidhāna*) and so forth.
If it is asked how this applies to intuitive knowledge, the restriction is due to a specific quality of the person's karma, just as in the case of experience.
Now, why does intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-jñāna*) not arise simultaneously?

Just as karma intended for experience does not produce experience all at once, so too the specific merit of the person (*puruṣa-karma-viśeṣa*), which is the cause of intuition, does not produce multiple instances of intuitive knowledge simultaneously.
If it is argued that this is untenable due to the absence of a cause, [we reply: no.
It is not so, because of the capacity of the instrument (karaṇa) for the succession of cognitions.
If you think that there is no reason or example for the rule "like experience," [we reply]:
no, because of the capacity of the instrument for the succession of cognitions.
Multiple cognitions do not arise simultaneously with respect to a single object of knowledge, nor do they arise with respect to multiple objects.

Thus, this capacity of the instrument [the internal organ]—which is of such a nature—is to be inferred from the observed succession of cognitions; for there is no simultaneity of cognitions despite the multiplicity of bodies for a cognizer whose nature is devoid of instruments.

The capacity of the instrument [the internal organ] is to be inferred through the sequence of cognitions as being of such a nature; it is not known [to belong] to the knower, whose nature is devoid of instruments, because cognitions are simultaneous despite the multiplicity of bodies.
This is the second refutation:
furthermore, if multiple cognitions were to inhere in a single, stationary body, there would be a simultaneous recollection of multiple objects in a single location.
In some cases, the manifold cognitions of a knower whose body is situated in one place—involving a continuous stream of sense-objects—would inhere in a single region of the self (*ātman*).

Consequently, when the mind (*manas*) comes into contact with that [single] region, it would follow that there is simultaneous recollection of many previously known things, because there is no sequential distinction (*paryāya*) in the contact with that region.

Since the various regions of the self are not distinct substances, and since the inherence in a single object is indistinguishable across them, it is impossible to deny the simultaneity of recollections.

In the case of the series of sounds, however, just as sound is heard due to its proximity to the locus of the auditory organ, memory arises in the mind due to its proximity to the mental impression (*saṃskāra*); thus, there is no consequence of simultaneous production.
As for the previous refutation—that there would be the consequence of simultaneous memory in a single location because multiple cognitions are inherent therein—that remains [valid]. //33//

The view held by some—that knowledge is a property of the self (puruṣadharma), whereas desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, and pain are properties of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇadharma)—is here refuted:
"Because the commencement and cessation [of activity] are caused by the desire and aversion of the knower. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.34)

Indeed, this person first knows: "This is a means to my happiness; this is a means to my suffering. Having known this, he desires to obtain the means to his own happiness and desires to abandon the means to suffering.
For one impelled by the desire for attainment, the specific exertion directed toward acquiring the means to happiness is *ārambha* (undertaking).
For one impelled by the desire to abandon [suffering], the avoidance of the means to suffering is cessation (*nivṛtti*).
Thus, there is a single connection among knowledge, desire, effort, aversion, pleasure, and pain;
that is, they possess a single agent and a common substratum.
Therefore, desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, and pain are attributes of the conscious knower, not of the insentient.

Furthermore, since the commencement and cessation [of activity] are observed in the internal self (pratyagātman), it should be understood that there is an inference [of these same attributes] in other [beings]. //34//

On this point, the proponent of the view that consciousness belongs to the elements (bhūtacaitanika) says: "Because desire and aversion have those [elements] as their mark, [consciousness] is denied in earth and the other [elements]. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.35)
Desire and aversion have the characteristics of engagement and withdrawal; for one who has engagement and withdrawal, there is desire and aversion, and for him there is knowledge.

Thus it follows that since engagement and withdrawal are observed in bodies composed of earth, water, fire, and air, they possess desire, aversion, and knowledge; this constitutes consciousness. //35//
Because the commencement and cessation [of action] are observed in the case of axes and similar tools.
There is an absence of consciousness in the body.

Since the commencement and cessation [of activity] are observed, it follows that there is a conjunction with desire, aversion, and cognition; for since the commencement and cessation of instruments such as axes and the like are observed, one might [erroneously] conclude they possess consciousness.
Now, if it is argued that the body possesses a conjunction with desire and so forth...

However, since the commencement and cessation of an instrument such as an axe are subject to deviation [from the agent's will], this reason—that there is a conjunction with desire, aversion, and cognition because the commencement and cessation of earthy, watery, fiery, and airy bodies are observed—is not [valid].
Rather, the meaning is this: there is no prohibition against [the presence of] desire and aversion in earthy and other [bodies], because they have those [commencement and cessation] as their marks.

The "commencement" (*ārambha*) of the elements, such as earth and the rest, is a specific activity characterized by the arrangement of their constituent parts within the bodies of mobile and stationary beings. Since this characteristic is absent in clods of earth and similar objects, they lack such specific activity.

Desire and aversion are the indicators of the cessation of such commencement; because these are observed in the atoms of earth and other elements, it is established that there is a conjunction with desire and aversion, and from that conjunction, a conjunction with cognition follows—thus, the sentience of the elements is proven.
[Objection: This is not a valid reason, because it is not perceived in jars and the like.

"Commencement" (ārambha) is a specific activity characterized by the arrangement of the constituent parts of clay, such as those of a jar; "cessation" (nivṛtti) is the absence of such specific activity in substances like sand.
Furthermore, the mere observation of commencement and cessation in clay and sand does not imply their conjunction with desire, aversion, effort, or cognition.
Therefore, because desire and aversion have that as their mark, [the argument] is not a valid reason. //36//
But restriction and non-restriction are the qualifiers of that [cause].
The regularity and irregularity of those two— desire and aversion— are the differentiators and the factors that distinguish them.
For the knower, activity and cessation are caused by desire and aversion, but they do not reside in [the knower] himself.
What then? [The activity] resides in the substratum of the agent.

In that case, since the engagement and withdrawal occur only with respect to those elements being employed [by the agent] and not with respect to all of them, the lack of restriction is logically established.

However, for one who holds that because the elements possess sentience, their undertaking and cessation are caused by desire and aversion and reside in their own substrata, there would necessarily be such a restriction.

Just as the activity of material elements (bhūta) occurs invariably due to the influence of other qualities (guṇa), and their cessation occurs due to the obstruction of those qualities, so too would activity and cessation caused by knowledge, desire, and aversion occur in the material elements themselves, residing in their own substratum;
however, they do not so occur. Therefore, knowledge, desire, aversion, and effort reside in the instigator (prayojaka).
It is established, therefore, that activity and cessation depend upon the substrate of the one being impelled.
However, the plurality of knowers within a single body is without inferential proof.

For the proponent of elemental consciousness (*bhūtacaitanika*), since there are many elements within a single body possessing the qualities of cognition, desire, aversion, and effort, it follows that there would be a plurality of knowers.
There is no valid proof for one who says "om" [i.e., that there is only one knower];
for just as there are multiple knowers in various bodies due to the distinct distribution of qualities such as intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth,
so too, even in a single body, there would be an inference of a plurality of knowers based on the distribution of intellect and the rest.
Furthermore, a specific activity of the elements caused by the qualities of another is observed; this is an inference applicable elsewhere as well.

A specific activity caused by the qualities of another is observed in the elements characterized as instruments, such as axes and the like, and in those characterized as raw materials, such as clay and the like.
This serves as an inference for other cases as well, namely, the bodies of mobile and immobile beings.
The specific activity of the elements, which is characterized by the arrangement of their parts, must have a cause other than [their own] qualities.

That cause is a quality co-located with effort, known as *saṃskāra* (latent impression), designated as *dharma* and *adharma*, which serves all purposes and, like effort, impels the elements toward the fulfillment of the person's ends.

It should be understood that the refutation of the view that the elements themselves possess consciousness has already been established by the reasons proving the existence of the self and the reasons proving the permanence of the self.
And the refutation is the same [in the case of the senses and their objects], because even when those have perished, the cognition persists; thus it is said:
"Because they are the marks of that [cognition], there is no refutation [of the existence of the soul] with respect to desire and aversion in earth and the other elements.
However, these two—commencement and cessation—are explained otherwise as being merely action and the mere cessation of action.

And such [qualities] are not observed in earth and the other elements. Therefore, it is incorrect to say: "Because they have that as their mark, there is no denial of desire and aversion in earth and the rest. (37) The refutation applies equally to the elements, the sense organs, and the mind.
The mind, however, is merely an illustration.

NyS 3.2.38: [Pleasure and pain do not arise] from the mind, because [the reasons] already stated apply, because of its dependence on another, and because of the arrival of what was not previously produced.
From the point where it is stated, "Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks of the self," everything that has been explained is summarized;
by this, the consciousness of the elements, the senses, and the mind is denied.
Because they are dependent: the elements, the senses, and the mind are dependent, for they operate in the acts of holding, impelling, and expanding only through the force of effort.
Furthermore, [if they were] conscious, they would be independent.

And because of the "attainment of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*): since "activity is the undertaking of speech, intellect, and body," if the elements, senses, and mind were conscious, a person would experience the fruit of karma performed by another;
however, if they are unconscious, it is logical that the person experiences the fruit of the karma performed by himself through the means of those [unconscious instruments]. //38//
Now, this is the summary of the established conclusion:
NyS 3.2.39: Because of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) and because the previously stated reasons are applicable.
The subject under discussion is that knowledge is a quality of the self (*ātman*).
"Elimination" (*pariśeṣa*) is defined as "the conviction regarding what remains when all other possibilities have been excluded after the refutation of those that were applicable.
Since the elements, the sense organs, and the mind have been refuted, no other substance is applicable; yet the self remains, and it is thus known that knowledge is its quality.

"And because of the establishment of the reasons as stated" means that there is no refutation of the reasons for establishing the self, such as "because a single object is apprehended through both seeing and touching," and so forth.

The statement regarding the establishment of the reasons as stated is intended to indicate the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) and to provide knowledge of the subject under discussion, such as its establishment and so on.
Alternatively, "and because of the establishment" is simply another reason (*hetvantara*).
This self is indeed eternal,
because after practicing righteousness in one body, upon the dissolution of that body, it is reborn among the gods in heaven;
and after practicing unrighteousness, upon the dissolution of the body, it is reborn in the hells.

Rebirth, characterized by the attainment of another body, is possible only when there is a permanent self that serves as its substratum; however, if there were merely a continuum of cognitions devoid of a self, rebirth would be untenable as it would lack any substratum.

Furthermore, it is logically consistent that *saṃsāra* occurs when a single sentient being possesses multiple bodies, and that *apavarga*, or liberation, occurs through the severance of the continuity of those bodies.

However, if there were merely a continuum of cognitions (*buddhisantati*) and no single sentient being, it would be impossible for anyone to traverse the long path of cyclic existence, nor could anyone be liberated from the continuity of bodies; thus, both *saṃsāra* and *apavarga* would be untenable.
Furthermore, if there were merely a continuum of cognitions, then because each sentient being would be distinct, this entire collection of worldly activities of living beings would be disconnected,
uncoordinated, and lacking finality; for,
due to the absence of memory, one [cognition] does not remember what was seen by another.
Furthermore, recollection (*smaraṇa*) is indeed the grasping by a single cognizer of an object previously known, thinking, "I knew this object to be known.
This very same cognizer grasps the object previously known, and that grasping of his is recollection;
this is not possible if there is merely a continuum of cognitions (*buddhiprabandha*) devoid of a self (*nirātman*). //39//
Memory, however, belongs to the self because of its nature as a knower.
"It is possible" means that recollection belongs to the self alone, and not to the mere continuum of consciousness;
the word "tu" (but/however) is used for emphasis.
How so? Because its intrinsic nature is that of a knower (*jña*).
"Knower" is its intrinsic nature, its own essential property (*sva-dharma*).
Indeed, this [Self] is connected with manifold cognitions pertaining to the three times—[cognitions such as] "it will know," "it knows," and "it has known."
He will know, he knows, [he has known]; that knowledge of his, which has the three times as its object, is to be personally experienced, occurring as "I shall know," "I know," and "I have known.
Therefore, this recollection belongs to one for whom this is his own dharma, and not to a mere continuum of cognition devoid of a self. //40//
It has been stated that because the causes of memory do not occur simultaneously, there is no simultaneous recollection.
Now, from what does memory arise?
Memory, indeed—

NyS 3.2.41: Memory is caused by [the following: resolve, connection, repetition, signs, characteristics, similarity, inclusion, the relationship between the container and the contained, conjunction, separation, a single effect, contradiction, excellence, attainment, intervention, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, fear, seeking, action, passion, merit, and demerit; furthermore, the fixing of the mind through the desire to remember (*susmūrṣā*)—known as resolve—and the contemplation of the signs of what is desired to be remembered, are causes for the recollection of objects.
Connection (*nibandha*), indeed, is the grouping of meanings within a single treatise.

Indeed, meanings that possess a single unified structure serve as causes for mutual recollection, whether they occur in sequential order or otherwise. Alternatively, "connection" (*nibandha*) refers to the placement of things to be remembered among well-known topics, as established by the authors of mnemonic treatises (*dhāraṇā-śāstra*).
Practice (*abhyāsa*), however, is the recurrence of cognitions regarding the same object;
the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by practice, which is a quality of the self, is denoted by the word "practice," and it is the cause of memory when it is similar [to its original object].

Furthermore, the mark (liṅga) is of four kinds: that which is conjoined (saṃyogin), that which is inherent (samavāyin), that which is inherent in the same object (ekārthasamavāyin), and that which is contradictory (virodhin).
For example: smoke [is the mark] of fire;
a horn [is the mark] of a cow.
The hand [is the cause] of the foot, and form [is the cause] of touch; that which has not yet come into being is the cause of that which has already come into being.
A characteristic residing in the parts of an animal is the cause for the recollection of its genus.
"This belongs to the Vidas, this to the Gargas," and so forth; or likeness, such as a portrait or an image of Devadatta;
and through possession, either an owner remembers his property by means of himself, or one remembers one's own property by means of the owner.

From the basis, one recollects the village headman who is dependent upon him; from that which is dependent, one recollects the village headman by means of what is dependent upon him. From a relationship, one recollects the teacher who is associated with the pupil.
"The officiating priest [is for] the one to be sacrificed for"—
that is, "the one to be sacrificed for" [is for] the purposes that are to be performed, because of their immediate succession.
Due to separation, one intensely remembers that with which one is separated, experiencing that very separation.
Due to a common purpose, the sight of one agent brings about the memory of another agent.
Due to opposition, upon seeing one of two persons desiring victory, the other is remembered.
Because of excellence, one frequently remembers that by which an excellence has been produced;
because of attainment, one frequently remembers that from which something has already been attained or is yet to be attained;
and because of concealment, swords and other such items are remembered through their sheaths and so forth.
The sword and other such weapons are remembered by means of their sheaths and so forth;
pleasure and pain cause one to remember their causes;
and through desire and aversion, one remembers that which one desires and that which one hates.

One remembers [a person] from whom one fears out of fear; one remembers [a benefactor] by means of which one is a petitioner, such as food or clothing; and one remembers a chariot-maker by means of his action, namely the chariot.
Due to passion (*rāga*), one frequently remembers that woman toward whom one has become lustful.
Due to merit (*dharma*), there is the recollection of previous births as well as the retention of what was studied and heard in this life.
Due to demerit (*adharma*), one remembers the means to suffering previously experienced.
Furthermore, since cognitions do not occur simultaneously regarding these signs, there is no simultaneous recollection;
and this is merely an illustration of the causes of memory, not an exhaustive enumeration. //41//

And since cognition is impermanent, there arises a doubt regarding those things that are impermanent: is cognition something that perishes as soon as it arises, like sound, or does it persist for a period of time, like a jar? The position that it perishes as soon as it arises is accepted. Why?
NyS 3.2.42: Because action is perceived as non-persistent.
"Because of the perception of action as non-abiding":

just as the continuum of action (kriyāsantāna) of a discharged arrow is perceived until its fall, and because cognitions are restricted to their respective objects, the existence of a continuum of cognition (buddhisantāna) is established in the same manner as the continuum of action.
Furthermore, when grasping a persisting object, perception ceases for that which is being obstructed.

While the jar remains and is being perceived, cognition proceeds as a continuous stream until the obstruction occurs; therefore, once it is obstructed, perceptual knowledge ceases, just as the cognition [ceases] by way of its continuity.

[If it were so,] one would cease [to act] while knowing; however, if cognition were to persist for a period of time, then perception would continue to exist even when the object of sight is obstructed.
Furthermore, memory is not a valid inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the persistence of cognition, because the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by cognition is the cause of memory.

And as for the one who might think: "The intellect (*buddhi*) persists, for memory is observed to have the intellect as its object; and that [memory] would not exist if the intellect were impermanent, due to the absence of a cause"—this is not a valid logical mark (*aliṅga*). Why? Because it is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), which is a distinct quality (*guṇāntara*) produced by the intellect, that is the cause of memory, not the intellect itself.
If it is argued that this is untenable due to the absence of a cause, [we reply]:
if [an object] were perceptible by virtue of the persistence of cognition, there would be an absence of memory.
As long as the cognition persists, so long is that object of cognition perceptual; and when something is perceptual, memory is logically impossible. //42//
The non-apprehension of the unmanifest [object] is due to its lack of stability, like the non-apprehension of form during a flash of lightning.

If cognition were to perish as soon as it arises, then the apprehension of the object of knowledge would necessarily be indistinct—just as, during a flash of lightning, the perception of form is indistinct because the lightning's light does not persist;
yet, the apprehension of substances is actually distinct. Therefore, this [position] is untenable. //43//
NyS 3.2.44: By the employment of a reason, there is the admission of that which is to be negated.

That "cognition which perishes as soon as it has arisen" must be refuted; yet that very point is admitted [by you] in the case of the perception of form during a flash of lightning, according to the principle:
"Where there is indistinct perception, there cognition perishes as soon as it has arisen.
However, this variation in perception results from a variation in the causes of perception, not from a variation in cognition itself.

This apprehension—which is sometimes unmanifest and sometimes manifest—is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because it arises from the conceptualization that serves as the cause of apprehension. Where the cause of apprehension is not fixed, there the apprehension is unmanifest; where it is fixed, there it is manifest.
This is not, however, due to the mind’s own fixation or non-fixation.

Why? Because cognition is indeed the grasping of an object; that which is the grasping of an object—whether unmanifest or manifest—is cognition. And when there is no grasping of specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), there is merely the grasping of general characteristics (*sāmānya*); that is unmanifest grasping. In that case, the non-arising of another cognition regarding another object is due to the absence of a cause.
Where an object (*dharmī*) is grasped as possessing both common characteristics and specific characteristics, that is manifest grasping.

However, where a particularity is not apprehended and there is only the apprehension of a generality, that is an indistinct apprehension. Furthermore, the possession of specific properties is a different object from the possession of common properties;
the fact that there is no apprehension of that [specific property] is due to the absence of the causes for such apprehension, and not because of a lack of stability in the intellect.
And apprehension is indeed manifest according to its respective object, because cognitions are restricted to their specific objects.

Apprehension whose object is a universal is manifest with respect to its own object, and apprehension whose object is a particular is manifest with respect to its own object; for cognitions are restricted to their respective objects.
Therefore, in what domain could this "unmanifest apprehension" that has been taught be caused by the non-settling of cognition?

The establishment of the diversity of cognitions regarding a substratum (dharmin) due to the difference in its properties (dharmabheda) occurs through the presence or absence [of those properties]. For indeed, in the case of an object that is a substratum, there are both common and specific properties; regarding these, there arise various cognitions restricted to each respective object.
If both [the universal and the particular] reside in the substratum (dharmin), then the apprehension is "manifest" with reference to that substratum;
however, when there is merely the apprehension of the universal, then it is an "unmanifest" apprehension.
Thus, the occurrence of manifest and unmanifest apprehensions is established with reference to the substratum. //44//
Nor is this indistinct apprehension of either the intellect (*buddhi*) or the object of cognition possible because of their non-stability; for this—NyS 3.2.45:
...is not like the apprehension of what is manifested by a continuous series of lamp-flames.
Even though cognition is non-durable, its apprehension of those [objects] must be understood as clearly manifest.
How so? Like the apprehension manifested by the continuity of a lamp’s flame.

Although there is non-duration in the apprehension of the lamp’s flames as they proceed in a continuum, and non-duration in the objects to be apprehended—because cognitions are restricted to their respective objects—there are as many cognitions as there are lamp-flames.
And here, the perception of the flames of a lamp is clearly observed. //45//
Volition is a quality of the body because it exists when the body exists and is absent when it is absent.
[Nyāyasūtra 3.2.46: There is doubt regarding a substance because its own qualities and the qualities of others are perceived therein.
That which is subject to doubt is its existence;
for while its own quality, fluidity, is perceived in water,
the heat [of fire] is a quality belonging to another.
Therefore, this doubt arises: is consciousness a quality of the body that is perceived in the body, or is it a quality of some other substance? //46//
Consciousness is not a quality of the body; why?
Because color and other qualities persist as long as the substance exists (NyS 3.2.47).
A body devoid of form and so forth is not perceived, whereas that which is devoid of consciousness is perceived—just as water devoid of heat [is perceived].
Therefore, consciousness is not a quality of the body.
If it is argued that it is like a mental formation (*saṃskāra*), we say no, because its cause is not cut off.
Just as there is a formation (*saṃskāra*) in a substance of a certain kind, so too is its cessation (*uparama*);
however, in that case, due to the destruction of the cause, there occurs an absolute non-occurrence of formation.
Just as consciousness (*cetanā*) is perceived in a body of a certain kind, so too is the absolute cessation of consciousness perceived in that very same kind [of body].
Therefore, the argument "like the formative forces (saṃskāra)" is an unequal analogy.
Furthermore, would the cause for the arising of consciousness reside within the body,
or would it reside in some other substance?
Or does it reside in both?
That is not so, because there is no cause for such a restriction.
There is no cause for a rule that consciousness should sometimes arise when residing in the body and sometimes not.
Furthermore, there is no reason for the restriction that consciousness arises only in the body and not in clods of earth or other objects when [the soul] resides in another substance;

for if the [soul] residing in both were the cause, there would be no reason for the restriction that consciousness does not arise in substances of the same genus as the body, but arises only in the body. //47//
And as for the thought that, just as the cessation of qualities such as blackness is observed in a substance while it still exists, so too might there be a cessation of consciousness—
[it is] not so, because of the arising of another quality produced by heating (*pākaja*).
There is no absolute cessation of the substance's form;
when the dark color ceases, another quality produced by heating, namely red color, arises.
However, in the case of the body, there is an absolute cessation of consciousness alone. //48//
Moreover:
"Because their opposites are established, there is no refutation of things produced by heating. (NyS 3.2.49)

In as many substances as there is the establishment of a quality that is the opposite of a prior quality, in those cases the production of qualities born of heating (*pākaja*) is observed, because the coexistence of qualities born of heating with the prior qualities is not perceived. However, in the case of the body, when consciousness (*cetanā*) is established as being opposed [to something], no other quality is perceived that is non-coexistent with it, by which one might infer a contradiction of consciousness. Therefore, since consciousness is not refuted, it should persist as long as the body exists.
But it does not so function; therefore, consciousness is not a quality of the body. //49//
For this reason as well, consciousness is not a quality of the body:
because it pervades the entire body. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.50)
Since both the body and all its constituent parts are pervaded by the arising of consciousness, there would be no place where consciousness does not arise;
and since the parts of the body possess consciousness just as the body itself does, it follows that there is a multiplicity of conscious entities.
In that case, just as the distribution of pleasure, pain, and cognition serves as a mark for the multiplicity of conscious entities across different bodies, so too would it be within a single body.
But it does not exist [in that way];
therefore, consciousness is not a quality of the body. //50//

As for what was stated—that there is no part of the body where consciousness does not arise—that is refuted by the following: "Not so, because it is not perceived in the hair, nails, and so forth" (NyS 3.2.51).
If consciousness does not arise in the hair, nails, and so forth, then its pervasiveness throughout the body is untenable. //51//
NyS 3.2.52: Because the body extends only as far as the skin, there is no application [of the definition] to the hair, nails, and so forth.
The defining characteristic of the body is that it is the locus of the sense faculties;
the body is that which extends to the skin and serves as the basis for the experience of life, mind, pleasure, and pain.
Therefore, consciousness does not arise in the hair and other such parts.
However, the connection of the hair and so forth with the body is due to their functional utility. //52//
For this reason as well, consciousness is not a quality of the body:
because it possesses characteristics contrary to those of the qualities of the body. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.53)
The quality of the body is of two kinds: that which is imperceptible, namely gravity;
that which is graspable by the sense organs, namely color and so forth; and a different category, namely consciousness.
It is not imperceptible because it is experienced;
nor is it graspable by the [external] sense organs because its object is the mind.
Therefore, it is a quality belonging to a distinct substance. //53//
NyS 3.2.54: No, because of the mutual difference between color and the other [sensory objects].

Just as form and the other [sensory qualities], though possessing mutually distinct characteristics, do not abandon their status as qualities of the body, so too consciousness, by virtue of its difference from form and the rest, shall not abandon its status as a quality of the body. //54//
Nyāyasūtra 3.2.55: There is no refutation [of the existence of the self], because color and other qualities are perceptible by the senses.
And because it is imperceptible:

just as color and the other qualities, which possess mutually distinct characteristics, do not transcend the two-fold classification, so too consciousness would not transcend the two-fold classification if it were a quality of the body due to its dissimilarity to color and the rest;
however, it does transcend it.
Therefore, it is not a quality of the body.
Since the negation of cognition in the elements, the sense organs, and the mind has already been established, this new undertaking is for the purpose of providing specific clarification;
for a reality that is examined in many ways becomes more thoroughly ascertained. //55//
The intellect has been examined; now follows the sequence for examining the mind.
In this regard, there is an inquiry as to whether [the mind] is one or many in each body.
NyS 3.2.56: Because cognitions do not occur simultaneously, the mind is one.
Indeed, there is a non-simultaneity of cognitions for each individual sense organ according to its respective object, because a sense organ has the capacity to produce only a single cognition;
this is not a mark for the unity of the mind.
As for this fact that there is no simultaneity of cognitions regarding different objects by means of the various sense organs—that is the inferential mark [of the mind].
Why? Because if there were multiple minds, a simultaneity of the contact between the sense organs and the mind would be possible, and consequently, there would be a simultaneity of cognitions;
yet such does not occur.
Therefore, the mind is one, because it is synonymous with the cognition of objects. //56//
[Objection: No, because multiple actions are perceived simultaneously.

Indeed, this teacher, while reciting, walks, holds his water-pot, sees the path, hears the sounds of forest-dwellers, and—fearing them—desires to know the signs of wild beasts and remembers that he must go to his destination.
Since these actions are not perceived as occurring in a sequence, it follows that they are simultaneous; thus, it is established that there must be a plurality of minds. //57//
The perception of that [succession] occurs due to rapid movement, like the sight of a whirling firebrand.
Because of the rapid movement of a whirling firebrand, the existing sequence is not perceived;
due to the non-perception of the sequence, there arises a cognition of a circle through the notion of non-interruption.

Likewise, because cognitions and actions occur with such rapidity, their existing sequence is not perceived; due to this non-perception of sequence, there arises the misconception that actions occur simultaneously. Now, is it because of the non-perception of sequence that there is the misconception of simultaneous action, or is it because of their actual simultaneous existence that multiple actions are perceived as occurring at once? Since no distinction can be established here, the reason for [this misconception] is stated.
It has been stated that cognitions of other objects arise in succession for the other sense-faculties, and this cannot be denied because it is directly perceived by the self.
Furthermore, when one reflects upon objects seen or heard, cognitions occur successively and not simultaneously; this must be inferred from the following:
the sequence is not perceived because the cognitions of letters, words, and sentences, as well as the cognitions of their meanings, occur with such rapidity.
How so? Indeed, as the phonemes contained within a sentence are being uttered, there is first of all the audition of each phoneme;
having heard one or more phonemes, he synthesizes them into the form of a word; having synthesized them, he determines the word.
Through the determination of words by means of memory, one understands the word-meanings; through the recollection of the collection of words, one determines the sentence;
and having grasped the related word-meanings, one understands the sentence-meaning.
Furthermore, because these cognitions occur in succession, their sequence is not perceived due to their rapid occurrence;
thus, this inference [of simultaneity] applies elsewhere to the misconception of the simultaneity of cognitive acts.
Moreover, there is no cognition produced simultaneously and free from doubt by which one might infer the multiplicity of minds within a single body. //58//
And because it possesses the aforementioned cause, it is atomic.
The mind is one and atomic; this is a conjunction of properties [stated] because cognitions do not occur simultaneously.
If the mind were large, there would be a simultaneous grasping of all objects due to its contact with all the sense organs. //59//
Indeed, sir, the mind, together with the senses, acquires its functional activity within the body and not outside the body.

For the knowing Puruṣa, whose abode is the body, the functions beginning with cognition, as well as the enjoyment of objects, the avoidance of what is undesirable, and the attainment of what is desired—all worldly activities whatsoever—depend upon the body.

Regarding this, because of conflicting views, there arises a doubt: is this creation of the body caused by the karma of the Puruṣa, or is it caused solely by the material elements independently of karma?
Indeed, it is heard that there is a disagreement on this point;
in this regard, the truth is as follows:
its arising [of the body] occurs due to the connection with the fruits of previously performed actions. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.60)
The activity in a previous body, characterized by the initiation of speech, intellect, and the physical body, is what is called "previously performed karma" (*pūrvakṛta-karma*);
its fruit consists of the merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) produced thereby.
The persistence of the result of that [action] consists in its remaining inherent in the self;
by means of that [persistence], the body arises from the elements as impelled by it,
and not from independent [elements].

That which serves as the substratum for this self—which, conceiving "this is I," is engaged therein and, through thirst for enjoyment, perceives objects and thereby forms *dharma* and *adharma*—is its body.
By means of that formation (*saṃskāra*), characterized as *dharma* and *adharma*, when this body falls along with the primary elements (*bhūta*), a subsequent body is produced;
and for this produced body, there occurs the performance of human purposes (*puruṣārtha*) just as in the previous body.
And since the activity of the person proceeds as it did in previous bodies, this [creation] is possible when the production of a body occurs from the elements dependent upon karma. Furthermore,

it is observed that from the elements impelled by the effort (prayatna) which is a quality of the person, there arises the production of objects such as chariots, which are capable of performing functions for the sake of the person.

In the same way, it should be inferred that the body also, being produced as capable of performing actions for the sake of the Person (puruṣārtha), arises from the elements which depend upon other qualities of the Person. //60//
On this point, the nihilist says:
"The assumption of that [body] is like the assumption of form from the elements" (NyS 3.2.61).
Just as forms such as sand, gravel, stones, red ochre, collyrium, and so forth— which are produced from elements independent of karma—
are utilized because they serve the purposes of man, so too the body, though produced from elements independent of karma, is utilized because it serves the purposes of man. //61//
No, because it is equal to the point to be proven.

Just as the production of a body is to be proven as being caused by no karma (*akarmanimitta*), so too the creation of sand, gravel, stones, red ochre, collyrium, and so forth must be proven as being caused by no karma; because it is equivalent to what is to be proven (*sādhyasamatvāt*), it is not a valid proof. Furthermore, the argument "like the taking up of forms from the elements" is also [merely] that which is to be proven. //62//
NyS 3.2.63: [The self is not produced by the parents], because they are merely the cause of its birth.
Moreover, this comparison is unequal.
Why? Because these forms arise without a seed, whereas the production of a body is preceded by a seed.
By the words "mother" and "father," the blood and semen, which constitute the seed, are intended.

In that regard, the karma of the sentient being to be experienced through dwelling in the womb, and the two karmas of the parents to be experienced as the fruit of having a son, cause the production of the body within the mother’s womb from the primary elements; thus, it is established that there is conformity with the seed. //63//
Likewise, [the same applies] to food.
The phrase "because it is the cause of origination" is the subject under discussion.

Food that has been eaten and drunk is digested; the resulting substance, the nutrient essence (*rasadravya*), accumulates in the mother’s body and within the seed located in the womb, undergoing a maturation similar to that of the seed itself.
This accumulation occurs in measured proportions within the seed until it becomes capable of formation, which is called "growth" (*sañcaya*).

And that which has been accumulated is organized through a structural arrangement consisting of the *kalala*, *arbuda*, *māṃsapeśī*, *kaṇḍarā*, head, hands, and so forth, according to the differentiation of the seats of the sense faculties;
and within this arrangement, the substance of nutritive essence (*rasadravya*) introduced via the umbilical cord of the embryo is further built up until it is capable of birth.
Furthermore, this process is not possible for food and drink remaining in a vessel or similar container.
For this reason, it is understood that the body has karma as its cause. //64//
And because there would be no restriction regarding [the simultaneous] attainment.

Not every union of husband and wife is seen to be the cause of conception; in that regard, since [conception] does not occur when the [specific] action (*karman*) is absent, but does occur when it is present, the absence of a restrictive rule (*niyamābhāva*) is untenable.
A restrictive rule would apply only if the elements (*bhūta*) were the causes of the body's production independently of *karman*, for in this case [of our view], there is no lack of a cause. //65//
Moreover:
"Action is the cause of the production of conjunction, just as it is the cause of the production of the body. (NyS 3.2.66)
Indeed, just as this body—with its channels conveying the elements and vital breaths, its elements ending with semen, its tendons, skin, bones, veins, muscles, embryo-tissues, and sinews;

its head, arms, belly, and thighs; and its internal cavities containing wind, bile, and phlegm, along with the mouth, heart, stomach, intestines, and lower passages—is arranged in a configuration that produces extreme suffering, it is impossible for the earth and other elements, independent of karma, to have fashioned it.
It is understood that the production of a body is caused by karma;

and thus, because there is no cause restricted to each individual, and because bodies are produced from earth and other elements which are common to all selves due to their connection with unsurpassed selves, and because there is no cause for restriction residing within earth and the other elements, [the resulting bodies would be identical].
It follows that the locus for the experience of pleasure and pain would be common to all selves.
However, as for the fact that [experience] is established individually for each self, it is understood that karma is the cause of this restriction, being the cause for the production of a body.

For when a latent disposition of karma (*karmāśaya*), which is restricted to an individual self, reaches maturity, it produces and establishes a body as the locus of experience for that very self alone.
Thus, it is understood that "action is the cause of conjunction, just as it is the cause of the production of the body";
however, we maintain that the specific determination of each individual body depends upon its conjunction with a self. //66//
By this, the argument of non-restriction has been refuted.

That which was stated—namely, that there is no fixed rule regarding the production of the body when it is not caused by action—is refuted by the statement: "Action is the cause for the production of conjunction, just as it is the cause for the production of the body. (p. 908)
What, then, is this rule?

The rule is that as the body belongs to one self, so it belongs to all. The absence of such a rule—where for one it is thus and for another it is otherwise—is non-rule, which is to say difference, distinction, or particularity.
—[Thus: "non-restriction," "distinction," "exclusion," and "particularity.
And the exclusion of birth is observed, such as [the distinction between] one of noble lineage and one of lowly lineage, or that which is praiseworthy and that which is contemptible.
[perceiving] that which is full of disease as being free from disease, that which is complete as being deficient,
and that which is full of suffering as being full of happiness;
One perceives that which is endowed with the marks of a superior person as being the opposite; one perceives what has praiseworthy marks as having censurable marks;
and one perceives those with keen faculties as having dull faculties.
And the subtle distinction is immeasurable.
This very diversity of births arises from the diversity of karma, which is restricted to each individual self (*pratyātmaniyata*).

In the absence of such individually restricted karma, since selves are without distinction and are equal by nature, and because there would be no cause for restriction residing in earth and the other elements—such as the specific character of earth and so forth—everything would belong to all selves in every respect.
But this birth is not of such a nature;
therefore, the arising of the body is not caused by karma alone. Furthermore, its separation [from the body] is logical, because the exhaustion of karma is logically possible.
Since the production of the body is caused by karma, the dissociation of the self from that body is logically established.
Why? Because the exhaustion of karma is logically established.
Indeed, the exhaustion of karma is established through right vision; when delusion has been destroyed, one who is free from passion no longer possesses karma that is a cause for rebirth.

Because one does not perform [actions] through body, speech, and mind, there is no further accumulation of future karma; and because one experiences the maturation (*vipāka*) of what was previously accumulated, there is its exhaustion.

Thus, due to the absence of a cause for production, there is no rebirth (*apratisandhi*) in this body, as another body is no longer produced. However, if the creation of the body were caused by *karman*, then since the exhaustion of the primary elements (*bhūta*) would be impossible, their separation from the self would likewise be impossible. //67//
If it is argued that this [movement] is caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), then the same consequence would follow regarding liberation (*apavarga*).
Indeed, non-perception is called the "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*). The production of the body from the elements is brought about by the unseen.
For as long as the body has not been produced, the seer, lacking a locus, does not perceive the object of sight.
And that object of his is twofold: the external objects and the diversity of the unmanifest self.

If you think that the creation of the body is for that purpose [of experience], and that once that [purpose] is accomplished, the elements—having fulfilled their function—no longer produce a body, and thus the separation from the body is logically established;
[we reply: "In that case, there would be a recurrence of that [body] even upon liberation"—that is, the production of a body would follow once again.

The non-arising of perception when the body has not yet arisen, which is considered "non-perception," and the non-arising of perception upon liberation through the cessation of the body, which constitutes "non-perception"—
there is no distinction between these two types of non-perception. Thus, because non-perception has not been eliminated,
there follows the undesirable consequence that the body would arise again even after liberation.

If it is argued that the distinction lies in having fulfilled their purpose (*caritārthatā*), we say no, because we observe the commencement [of new bodies] both when [the elements] have performed their function and when they have not.

If it is claimed that this is indeed the distinction—that the elements, having fulfilled their purpose by terminating with the experience of the object, do not initiate another body—we say no, because we observe the commencement [of new bodies] both when [the elements] have performed their function and when they have not; for the elements, even after having fulfilled their purpose, serve as the instruments for the perception of objects.

The repeated commencement of a body is observed; since there would be no cause for the perception of the difference between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, the repeated commencement of a body would be purposeless. Therefore, in the creation of the elements which is not caused by karma, it is not logical that the production of a body is for the sake of perception.
However, in a creation caused by karma, the production of a body has the purpose of perception;
for perception is the experiencing of the ripening of karma.
If it is argued that this [perception] is brought about by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), [we reply:]...

According to the view of some, there is a specific quality of atoms called *adṛṣṭa* (the unseen), which is the cause of motion; impelled by this, the atoms coalesce and produce a body. Then, the mind enters that body, and impelled by its own quality of *adṛṣṭa*, the perception of the seer occurs within the body endowed with the mind.
In this view, because the qualities are not destroyed, there would be the recurrence of that [bondage] even in liberation;
for in liberation, the production of a body would follow, since the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), which is a quality of the atoms, cannot be destroyed. //68//
And because mental action is the cause [of rebirth], the non-cessation of conjunction [with a new body] follows.
If the mind were permeated by the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of mental qualities, there would be no severance of the conjunction [between the mind and the body];
and how, then, could that withdrawal of the mind from the body be brought about?
However, when the store of karma (karmāśaya) is exhausted, the withdrawal becomes possible due to another store of karma that is ripening.

If it is argued that departure [from the body] occurs solely from the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)—that is, the very same unseen force which is the cause of approaching the body is also the cause of departing from it—this is not so, because it is impossible for a single [unseen force] to be the cause of both living and dying. For if this were the case, it would follow that a single unseen force is the cause of both living and dying, and this is not tenable. //69//
And there would follow the consequence of eternality, because death would be impossible.
Death is the falling away of the body when the storehouse of karma is exhausted through the experience of its maturation;
from another storehouse of karma, there is rebirth.
But if the body were produced from the mere elements independently of karma, then upon the exhaustion of what would death—the falling away of the body—occur?
Indeed, we recognize that if death were not established [as having a specific cause], it would follow as a logical consequence that [the soul] is eternal;
however, if death were accidental, the distinction between different types of death would be untenable. //70//
Desiring to resolve the objection that "liberation would thus entail the recurrence of that [bondage]," he says:
"This would be like the non-eternality of the blackness of atoms. (NyS 3.2.71)

Just as the blackness of an atom, though eternal, is prevented from arising again once it has been abolished by contact with fire, so too the body, brought about by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), does not arise again upon liberation. // 71 //
Not so, because it would entail the consequence of experiencing the results of actions not performed.
This is not a valid example.
Why? Because it would entail the fallacy of encountering the results of what one has not done (*akṛtābhyāgamaprasaṅga*).
That which is "not done" is logically untenable according to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Its arrival, its acceptance,
and its determination— this must be considered established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) by one who has faith in it.
Therefore, this is not a mere example, nor is it perception, nor is any inference being stated.
Thus, this is stated to be the "equality of the example with the probandum" (*sādhyasamatva*).
Alternatively, it is because it would entail the consequence of experiencing the results of actions not performed (*akṛtābhyāgamaprasaṅga*).

For one who attempts to resolve the origin of the body as being caused by no action (karma) by means of the example of the blackness of atoms, there follows the consequence of experiencing the results of actions not performed.
If it were the case that pleasure or pain comes upon a person even when the karma that is the cause of pleasure or pain has not been performed, an absurd conclusion would follow.
For one who says "yes" [to this], there is a contradiction with perception, inference, and scripture.
First, the contradiction with perception: this diversity of pleasure and pain is perceptible to all embodied beings because it is experienced by each individual self.
What is the difference? It consists of such distinctions as intense or mild, long-lasting or brief, manifold or single-fold, and so forth.
Yet, there is no specific cause for pleasure and pain that is restricted to each individual;
and in the absence of a specific cause, no specific result is observed.

However, when pleasure and pain are contingent upon action (*karman*), the distinction between various kinds and a single kind of pleasure and pain is established because actions can be intense or mild, because there is an increase or decrease in the accumulation of actions, and because actions themselves possess diverse or uniform natures.
Since this observed distinction between pleasure and pain would not exist if there were no distinction in their causes, there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Likewise, there is a contradiction with inference (*anumāna*): for it is observed that the distribution of pleasure and pain follows from the specific arrangement of human qualities (*puruṣaguṇa*).

Indeed, one who possesses consciousness, having understood that pleasure is to be accomplished by means of an instrument and desiring it, exerts effort to obtain that instrument; such a person is joined with pleasure, but not its opposite.

And one who, having understood that pain is to be accomplished by means of an instrument and wishing to abandon it, exerts effort to avoid that instrument; such a person is abandoned by pain, but not its opposite.
Since this determination of pleasure and pain for conscious beings exists even without [visible] effort, there must also exist another quality of consciousness [as its cause]; this is the inference.
This [position] contradicts the connection with pleasure and pain when that is not caused by action (*karman*).

Furthermore, because it is imperceptible, that other quality (*guṇāntara*) is "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*); and because the time of its maturation (*vipākakāla*) is not fixed, it is indeterminate (*avyavasthita*).

But [if you argue that] intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest are both objects of cognition and subject to liberation, then there is a contradiction with scripture (*āgama*). For indeed, this vast body of teachings from the seers (*ṛṣis*) consists of injunctions for performance and avoidance;
and the fruit of those teachings is the activity characterized by performance by embodied beings according to the divisions of caste (*varṇa*) and stage of life (*āśrama*).
Cessation is characterized by avoidance;
and both of these are contradicted in this view that "there is no such thing as good or bad conduct, nor is there for persons any connection with pleasure or pain caused by karma."
This is the most wicked of false views: that the creation of the body is not caused by karma, and that the experience of pleasure and pain is not caused by karma. //72//
Thus ends the second Āhnika of the third Adhyāya in the Nyāyabhāṣya of the venerable Vātsyāyana.
And this third chapter is completed. 3.
The Nyāya Darśana: Now begins the first Āhnika of the fourth Adhyāya. Following the [examination of] the mind, activity (pravṛtti) must be examined.
In this regard, everything up to the body and so forth, which serve as the substrata for merit and demerit, has indeed been examined.
He states that all of this is an examination of activity:
"Activity is as previously described. (NyS 4.1.1)
Thus it has been examined. //1//
"In that case, let the defects (doṣas) be examined immediately after [the examination of] activity (pravṛtti). To this he says:
"Likewise, the defects. (NyS 4.1.2)
Thus they have been examined:
because they reside in the same substratum as cognition, they are qualities of the self;
and because they are the cause of activity and possess the capacity for the reconnection of rebirth, they are the causes of saṃsāra.
Because saṃsāra is beginningless, [the defects] proceed by way of a beginningless continuity.
Through the cessation of false knowledge—arising from the knowledge of reality—and through that cessation, when the continuity of passion and aversion is severed, there is liberation (apavarga).
Thus, it has been stated regarding the defects that they possess the nature of manifestation and concealment, and so forth. //2//
It has been stated that faults (doṣas) are characterized by setting [the mind] in motion;
such being the case, why are these—namely pride (māna), envy (īrṣyā), malice (asūyā), doubt (vicikitsā), avarice (matsara), and so forth—not also enumerated? To this, he says:
In that regard, there are three categories, because passion, hatred, and delusion are distinct entities.
These faults consist of three groups or three categories:
the category of attachment (*rāga*)—namely, desire, stinginess, longing, craving, and greed;
the category of aversion (*dveṣa*)—namely, anger, envy, malice, hostility, and resentment; and the category of delusion (*moha*).
False knowledge, doubt, pride, and negligence—these are not included because they belong to three categories.
[Objection: In that case, since there is no difference in their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), is it not untenable for them to be three?
This is not untenable,
because passion, hatred, and delusion are distinct entities;
passion is characterized by attachment.
Hatred is characterized by intolerance, and delusion is characterized by wrong practice.
This is to be personally experienced by all embodied beings: this embodied being recognizes a desire that has arisen, thinking, "The quality of desire exists within me."
And he discerns dispassion, thinking: "There is no quality of passion within me.
The same applies to the other two [qualities].
However, pride, envy, malice, and so forth are not enumerated here, as they fall under the three categories [of passion, delusion, and virtue]. //3//
Not so, because there is no state of being a single counter-thesis.
Passion and the other afflictions are not distinct entities.
Why? Because they have a single adversary: the knowledge of reality, right understanding, noble wisdom, and perfect awakening—these constitute one adversary to the three [afflictions]. //4//
It is not a valid reason because of its deviation.
On earth, substances such as the dark-colored (śyāma) and others are produced by a single cause, namely contact with fire;
and those born of maturation (pākaja) have a single origin. //5//
And since they exist as distinct entities:
"Among these, delusion is the worst, because the others do not arise in one who is not deluded. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.6)
Delusion is evil, or rather more evil; this was said with reference to two [types of evil].
Why? Because the other does not arise in one who is not deluded.
—Because of the non-arising [of delusion]: passion and hatred do not arise in one who is undeluded, whereas for one who is deluded, they arise according to his conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*).
Regarding sense objects, conceptualizations that are provocative give rise to passion.
The intentions that provoke anger are the causes of hatred;
and both types of intentions, because they are characterized by false engagement, are nothing other than delusion.
Thus, these two—attachment and aversion—have their origin in delusion.
Furthermore, when delusion ceases through the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), passion and aversion do not arise; thus, there is the establishment of their being mutual opposites.

And having established this, the [sūtra] is explained as follows: "From the knowledge of reality, upon the successive disappearance of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, there is liberation due to the non-existence of each immediately preceding member. //6//
Then it follows that:
because of the relationship between cause and effect, there is a state of being a distinct entity [of the self] from the defects. (NyS 4.1.7)
For the cause is one thing and the effect is another; thus, because delusion has defects as its cause, it is not itself a defect. //7//
[Reply: No, because delusion is included within the definition of a fault.
By this definition of defects—that their characteristic is "setting in motion"—delusion (moha) is included among the defects. //8//
And because the relationship between cause and effect is established, there is no refutation of those things belonging to the same class.
It is observed that among substances or qualities of the same genus, there exists a manifold variety of distinctions in the relationship between cause and effect. //9//

Following the defects [of the self] is the state after death (*pretyabhāva*). Its non-establishment follows from the eternity of the self—for indeed, nothing that is eternal is ever born or dies—and thus, because birth and death are impossible for an eternal self, the state after death (which consists of both) is untenable. To this, there is the following restatement of an established position: [The opponent argues: Birth and death are observed in the world; therefore, the self must be non-eternal. Furthermore, since the self is not perceived at birth, it must have come into being from something else. And since it is not perceived at death, it must have passed away into something else. Thus, the self is subject to birth and death, and its state after death is established. [The proponent replies: This is not so. Because the self is eternal, there is no establishment of the state after death. For it is not the case that anything eternal is born or dies; thus, due to the eternity of the self, birth and death are impossible. Moreover, the state after death consists of both [birth and death]. In this regard, the following is a restatement of what is already established: [The opponent asks: What is this "state after death"? [The proponent replies: It is the attainment of a new body after the destruction of the previous one. [The opponent asks: How is this known? [The proponent replies: By inference. [The opponent asks: From what kind of inference? [The proponent replies: From the inference based on the observation of similarity between the preceding and succeeding states. Just as a person who has been asleep awakens with the same consciousness, so too does one who has died take up another body with a consciousness similar to the former. Therefore, the self is eternal, and the state after death is established. [The opponent objects: If the self were eternal, then why is it not perceived at birth? [The proponent replies: Because it is subtle and not perceptible by the senses. [The opponent asks: But if it is eternal, how can it be said to be born? [The proponent replies: It is called "born" when it enters into a new body and assumes a new configuration. [The opponent asks: And how is it said to die? [The proponent replies: It is said to "die" when it leaves the body and ceases its association with it. Thus, although the self is eternal, the designations of "birth" and "death" are applied to it based on its connection with the body. Therefore, the state after death is established. [The opponent asks: If the self is eternal, then why is it not perceived during life? [The proponent replies: Because it is obscured by the body and the internal organs. [The opponent asks: But if it is eternal, how can it be said to undergo change? [The proponent replies: It undergoes change through its association with merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), which cause it to assume various bodies and experiences. Thus, the self is eternal, yet it is subject to the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) through its connection with the body and the internal organs. Therefore, the state after death is established. [The opponent asks: If the self is eternal, then why is it not perceived at the time of death? [The proponent replies: Because it is departing from the body and is not yet fully manifest. [The opponent asks: But if it is eternal, how can it be said to pass away? [The proponent replies: It is said to "pass away" when it relinquishes its current body and moves toward another. Thus, although the self is eternal, the designations of "birth," "death," and "passing away" are applied to it based on its transition between bodies. Therefore, the state after death is established. [The opponent asks: If the self is eternal, then why is it not perceived in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)? [The proponent replies: Because it is extremely subtle and difficult to perceive. [The opponent asks: But if it is eternal, how can it be said to be born in the next world? [The proponent replies: It is born in the next world when it takes up a new body in accordance with its past karma. Thus, although the self is eternal, it undergoes rebirth through the power of its latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and karma. Therefore, the state after death is established. [The opponent asks: If the self is eternal, then why is it not perceived in deep sleep? [The proponent replies: Because it is merged with the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and is not yet awakened. [The opponent asks: But if it is eternal, how can it be said to wake up? [The proponent replies: It wakes up when the conditions for awakening—such as the cessation of the exhaustion of sleep and the influence of past karma—are met. Thus, although the self is eternal, it experiences states of waking and sleeping through the influence of its mental impressions. Therefore, the state after death is established. [The opponent asks: If the self is eternal, then why is it not perceived in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*)? [The proponent replies: Because in liberation, the self is free from all adjuncts (*upādhi*) and is not perceived by the senses. [The opponent asks: But if it is eternal, how can it be said to attain liberation? [The proponent replies: It attains liberation when it is released from the cycle of rebirth and realizes its true nature. Thus, although the self is eternal, it attains liberation through the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the realization of the truth. Therefore, the state after death is established. [The opponent asks: If the self is eternal, then why is it not perceived in the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*)? [The proponent replies: Because in meditative absorption, the self is absorbed in the supreme reality and is not perceived by the ordinary mind. [The opponent asks: But if it is eternal, how can it be said to emerge from meditation? [The proponent replies: It emerges from meditation when the force of its concentration is exhausted and it returns to the realm of the senses. Thus, although the self is eternal, it experiences states of meditation and emergence through the power of its mental focus. Therefore, the state after death is established. [The opponent asks: If the self is eternal, then why is it not perceived in the state of death?
