[The proponent replies: Because at the moment of death, the self is transitioning and is not yet fully manifest. [The opponent asks: But if it is eternal, how can it be said to enter the next life? [The proponent replies: It enters the next life when it takes up a new body in accordance with its past karma. Thus, although the self is eternal, it undergoes the process of death and rebirth through the power of its latent impressions and karma. Therefore, the state after death is established. [The opponent asks: If the self is eternal, then why is it not perceived in the state of dissolution (*pralaya*)? [The proponent replies: Because in dissolution, the self is merged with the primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and is not perceived by the senses. [The opponent asks: But if it is eternal, how can it be said to be created again? [The proponent replies: It is created again when the cycle of creation begins and it takes up a new body in accordance with its past karma. Thus, although the self is eternal, it undergoes the cycles of creation and dissolution through the power of its latent impressions and karma. Therefore, the state after death is established. [The opponent asks: If the self is eternal, then why is it not perceived in the state of unconsciousness (*mūrchā*)? [The proponent replies: Because in unconsciousness, the self is overwhelmed by the disturbance of the humors (*doṣa*) and is not perceived by the senses. [The opponent asks: But if it is eternal, how can it be said to regain consciousness? [The proponent replies: It regains consciousness when the disturbance of the humors subsides and it returns to its normal state. Thus, although the self is eternal, it experiences states of consciousness and unconsciousness through the influence of its physical and mental conditions. Therefore, the state after death is established. [The opponent asks: If the self is eternal, then why is it not perceived in the state of extreme pain? [The proponent replies: Because in extreme pain, the self is overwhelmed by the intensity of suffering and is not perceived by the senses. [The opponent asks: But if it is eternal, how can it be said to experience relief? [The proponent replies: It experiences relief when the pain subsides and it returns to a state of relative comfort. Thus, although the self is eternal, it experiences pleasure and pain through the influence of its past karma and the conditions of its body. Therefore, the state after death is established. [The opponent asks: If the self is eternal, then why is it not perceived in the state of extreme joy? [The proponent replies: Because in extreme joy, the self is absorbed in the intensity of bliss and is not perceived by the senses. [The opponent asks: But if it is eternal, how can it be said to experience sorrow? [The proponent replies: It experiences sorrow when the joy fades and it encounters adverse circumstances. Thus, although the self is eternal
NyS 4.1.10: The proof of rebirth is established through the permanence of the self.
This self is eternal; it departs, meaning it leaves the previous body and dies;
and having departed—that is, having abandoned the previous body—it comes into being, meaning it is born and takes up another body.

And both of these were stated in the passage, "Rebirth is re-arising after death" (*punar-utpattiḥ pretyabhāvaḥ*). Rebirth (*pretyabhāvaḥ*) is the assumption of another body after discarding the previous body; and this is possible only if [the self] is eternal. For one, however, for whom rebirth is the arising of a new being (*sattva*) and the cessation of a being, there is the fault of the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāna*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*).
Furthermore, under a doctrine that asserts annihilation as the cause [of existence], the instructions of the Sages (*ṛṣi*) would be rendered meaningless. //10//
If it is asked how there is production:
[The answer is] from the manifest, the manifest [arises], because perception is the means of valid cognition (NyS 4.1.11).
In what manner and from what kind of cause does the manifest body and so forth arise?

From the manifest—designated as the elements, such as earth and the rest—which are supremely subtle, eternal, and manifest, there arises the manifest substance known as the substratum of the body, the senses, the objects, and the instruments.
Furthermore, that which is manifest is indeed perceptible by the senses; because of this commonality, the cause as well is manifest.
What is the commonality?

It is the conjunction with qualities such as form (*rūpa*). From eternal [substances] such as earth, which are conjoined with qualities such as form, bodies and so forth arise, likewise conjoined with qualities such as form.
On account of the validity of direct perception— for it is observed that from earth and other substances endowed with qualities such as color, a substance of a similar nature arises;
and by means of that, there is inference of what is not perceived.
This is because the persistence of color and other qualities is seen in both the material cause and its modification.
The causal nature of eternal and supersensible entities such as earth and the rest is inferred. //11//
NyS 4.1.12: No, because a jar is not produced from a jar.
This too is a matter of direct perception: indeed, a manifest pot is never seen being produced from a manifest [pot];
since it is observed that the manifest does not arise from the manifest, the manifest is not the cause. //12//
Nyāyasūtra 4.1.13: There is no refutation [of our position] because a jar is produced from a manifest [cause].
We do not say that everything is the cause of everything;
rather, whatever manifest substance (*vyakta-dravya*) arises, it arises from that which is of the same nature.
And that manifest substance from which a jar arises is the clay-substance known as potsherds.
And one who denies this is not entitled to obtain permission anywhere;
such is the truth. //13//
Hereafter, the views of the various teachers are presented:
"The arising of an entity from non-existence [is not possible], because nothing manifests without having destroyed [its cause]. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.14)

The position that "the existent arises from the non-existent" is held because of manifestation following destruction; for the sprout arises after the seed has been destroyed, not without its being destroyed.
If the destruction of the seed were not the cause of the sprout, then the sprout would arise even when the seed is not destroyed. //14//
To this it is replied: "Because of contradiction, there is no application [of the reason]. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.15)
The formulation "because of appearing after having destroyed" is incorrect due to contradiction:
that which destroys cannot appear after having destroyed it, because it already exists;
and that which appears cannot be a destruction by means of what has not yet appeared and does not exist. //15//
Not so, because the term "agent" (kāraka) is applied to both the past and the future.
Even when the past and the future do not exist, words denoting an agent are employed; for example:
"A son will be born," or "He rejoices in the son who is about to be born."
He gives a name to his son who is yet to be born; he says, "The jar existed," and he grieves over a broken jar.
The shards of a broken jar,
and "unborn sons cause their father distress"— such metaphorical (bhākta) usages are frequently observed. But what is this "metaphorical" usage?
"Immediate succession" (*ānantarya*) is a figurative expression (*bhakti*); its meaning is that [the seed] manifests after having been destroyed by the power of immediate succession.
Since the sprout, while about to manifest, destroys [the seed], this agency is figurative (*bhākta*). //16//
Not from those that have perished, because [the effect] does not arise [from them].
A sprout does not arise from a seed that has perished; therefore, there is no arising of an entity from non-existence. //17//
NyS 4.1.18: There is no refutation [of our position] because of the sequential instruction.
Sequence is the fixed order of priority and posteriority between destruction and manifestation;
indeed, it is pointed out as the cause for the arising of existence from non-existence,
and that [sequence] is not denied.
The production of a substance from a different configuration occurs when the previous configuration of the constituent parts that were obstructing it ceases, and not from non-existence.
The parts of the seed, having acquired motion due to some cause, abandon their previous configuration and assume another configuration; from this new configuration, the sprout arises.
Indeed, the parts and their conjunctions are observed to be the causes for the production of the sprout.

Furthermore, as long as the previous arrangement has not ceased, it is impossible for the parts of the seed to assume another arrangement; thus, the necessity of the sequence between the destruction [of the cause] and the manifestation [of the effect] is what constitutes "succession" (*krama*).
Therefore, an entity does not arise from non-existence.
And since no cause for the production of the sprout exists other than the parts of the seed, the restriction that the seed is the material cause is established. //18//
Then another says:
"God is the cause, because human actions are seen to be fruitless. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.19)
This person, though exerting effort, does not necessarily obtain the fruit of that effort; therefore, it is inferred that the attainment of the fruit of action by a person is dependent on another.
That upon which it depends is God.
Therefore, God is the cause. //19//
NyS 4.1.20: No, because the fruit is not produced in the absence of human effort.
If the production of results were dependent solely upon God, then even without human effort, the result would nevertheless be produced. //20//
That is not a valid reason, because it is brought about by that [very same thing].
The Lord favors human effort; when a person strives for a result, the Lord brings that result to fruition.
When He does not bring it about, then the human action becomes fruitless.
Therefore, because it is caused by God, human action is not the cause, since results do not arise in the absence of [the activity of] God.
God is another self (ātman) distinguished by his qualities;
for him, no other conceptualization (kalpa) is possible than that which is consistent with his own nature.

Īśvara is a distinct self distinguished by the destruction of unrighteousness, false knowledge, and negligence, and by the perfection of righteousness, knowledge, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
His fruit, resulting from righteousness and concentration, is the eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇiman*.
Furthermore, his righteousness conforms to his will and sets in motion the individual accumulations of merit and demerit, as well as the elements such as earth.
Thus, by not losing the results of one's own actions (*svakṛtābhyāgama*), the Lord’s power of creation (*nirmāṇaprākāmya*) should be understood as the fruit of his own performed karma.
And this [authority] is like that of a trustworthy person (*āptakalpa*); just as a father is to his children, so the Lord, being their father, is to all beings.
Nor is any other analogy possible than the analogy of the self.
First of all, no property capable of serving as a logical mark (*liṅga*) can be established for him apart from his intellect (*buddhi*).
Furthermore, according to scripture, he is the seer, the knower, the omniscient Lord.
And who is capable of establishing an indefinable Lord—beyond the scope of perception, inference, and scripture—by means of marks of the self such as intellect and the like?
Who is capable of establishing an indefinable Lord (*īśvara*) who transcends the scope of perception, inference, and scripture?

Furthermore, for one who proceeds by abandoning the principle that one reaps what one has sown (*svakṛtābhyāgama*), all those refutations previously stated regarding the creation of the body being caused by past actions (*karman*) would follow as a logical consequence. //21//
Now another says:
"The production of entities occurs without a cause, as seen in the case of the sharpness of thorns and so forth. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.22)
Why is the production of bodies and so forth signless?
Because of the observation of the sharpness of thorns and the like;
[this applies] to the thorn.

Just as sharpness, the variegation of mountain minerals, and the smoothness of stones are observed to be both without a visible cause and yet produced from material causes, so too is the creation of bodies and other things. //22//
Because it has the signless as its sign, it is not [established] by way of being signless.

It is said that the arising of entities occurs from a causeless state (*animitta*); however, that from which something arises is itself a cause. Since that which is causeless cannot function as a cause, the arising of entities does not occur from a causeless state. //23//
NyS 4.1.24: There is no refutation [of our position] because there is a difference in meaning between the "causal" (nimitta) and the "non-causal" (animitta).
For the sign is one thing and the negation of the sign is another; nor is the negation itself the object to be negated,
just as when one says "the water-pot is without water," the prohibition of water does not become water itself.
Indeed, this doctrine—that the creation of the body and so forth has no cause other than karma—is not distinct from the [previous] position;
therefore, because they are non-different, it should be understood as refuted by the very refutation of that [position]. //24//
Others, however, think:
"Everything is impermanent because it possesses the nature of arising and perishing. (NyS 4.1.25)
What is called "impermanent"?
That which exists at some time is impermanent;
that which has the nature of arising does not exist when unarisen, and that which has the nature of perishing does not exist once it has perished.
What, then, is everything?
It is both the derivative [matter], such as the body and so forth, and the non-derivative, such as the intellect and so forth.
Both of these are known to have the nature of arising and perishing;
therefore, all that is impermanent. //25//
Not so, because impermanence itself is impermanent.
If, first of all, the impermanence of everything were permanent, then because of that permanence, not everything would be impermanent;
or if it were impermanent, then in its absence, everything would be permanent. //26//
That impermanence of fire is like the destruction [of fire] following the destruction of the combustible object.
Even that impermanence is itself impermanent.
How so? Just as fire, having destroyed the combustible object, perishes along with it, so too does the impermanence of all things perish after having destroyed everything. //27//
NyS 4.1.28: There is no rejection of the eternal, because it is established according to how it is perceived.
Indeed, this doctrine constantly refutes permanence, yet the refutation of permanence is untenable.
Why? Because the establishment [of things] occurs according to their perception.
That which is perceived through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as having the nature of arising and perishing is impermanent;
that which is not so perceived is the opposite.

Furthermore, the nature of arising and perishing is not established by valid means of knowledge for the most subtle elements—space, time, direction, self, and mind—nor for some of their qualities, nor for generality, particularity, and inherence.
Therefore, these are eternal. //28//
This is another extreme view:
"Everything is eternal, because the five elements are eternal. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.29)
All this is merely the primary elements, and those are eternal, because the annihilation of the primary elements is impossible. //29//
NyS 4.1.30: [Sound is non-eternal] because the causes of its production and destruction are perceived.
Furthermore, both a cause of origination and a cause of destruction are perceived;
this would be contradicted if everything were eternal. //30//
There is no refutation [of the definition], because it is included within that definition.
Regarding that which you think has its causes of origination and destruction perceived:

that is not apprehended as a distinct entity devoid of the characteristics of the primary elements (bhūta); because it is subsumed under the characteristics of the primary elements, this is stated to be a negation of the claim that "this is merely the primary elements. //31//
NyS 4.1.32: [The self exists] because its production and its causes are perceived.
The production of an effect possessing qualities identical to those of its cause is observed, and the cause itself is also perceived;
neither of these two facts pertains to eternal entities,
nor can the observation of production and its cause be denied.
Furthermore, there is no perception whatsoever that lacks an object.
By the power of perception, it is inferred that an effect arises possessing qualities identical to its cause;
indeed, that [cause] is the object of perception.
And thus, there is the logical establishment of its inclusion within that definition:
for it is observed that the effort of a cognizer is prompted by the causes of arising and destruction;
and the composite whole (avayavin) is well-known to possess those properties.
Furthermore, it is established that the whole (avayavin) possesses the properties of arising and perishing.
Moreover, there is non-pervasion (avyāpti) regarding sound, action, cognition, and so forth.

Because the five elements are eternal and because [these phenomena] do not fall under their defining characteristics, by this [reasoning], sound, action, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort are not pervaded; therefore, [the reason] is inconclusive (anekānta).
If it is argued that perception [of elements] is a false apprehension, like the conceit regarding objects in a dream, this applies equally to the perception of the elements.
Just as in a dream there is a conceit regarding objects, so too is there a conceit regarding the causes of their production.
And thus, this is equally applicable to the perception of the elements; for the perception of earth and the other elements would also result in being like the conceit regarding objects in a dream.

If it is argued that "in the absence of earth and the other elements, all worldly transactions would collapse," then that is the same in the other case as well: in the absence of the objects perceived as the causes of production and destruction, all worldly transactions would likewise collapse.

Therefore, because eternal things are beyond the senses and thus not objects [of perception], this argument—that production and destruction are like the false attribution of objects in a dream—is not a valid reason. //32//
Of the substrate (*upādāna*) that remains constant, a mere phenomenon (*dharma-mātra*) ceases and a mere phenomenon arises; this indeed is the domain of arising and destruction.
And that which arises exists even prior to its arising.
And as for the claim that "whatever ceases exists even when it has ceased," and thus everything is eternal—is this so?
NS 4.1.33: No, because such a fixed order is untenable.
The distinction that "this is an origination" and "this is a cessation" is not tenable, because there is no difference in the existence of both the originated and the ceased;
for since the mere fact of their being present is common to both, the distinction that "this property has originated" and "this has ceased" cannot be established.
Now, the determination of time— namely, that "origination and cessation occur now, not then"— is untenable because this dharma exists at all times. Consequently,
the distinction that "origination and cessation belong to this [dharma], but not to that" is untenable,
because there is no difference between the two.
Furthermore, the temporal distinction between "the future" and "the past" would be untenable,
because the present is characterized by actual existence.

However, if one holds that "origination" is the acquisition of self-nature for that which was non-existent and "cessation" is the loss of self-nature for that which was existent, then these faults do not arise.
Therefore, what was stated previously—that [the self] exists even before its manifestation and that it continues to exist after its cessation—is incorrect. //33//
This is another extreme view:
"Everything is distinct, because the characteristics of entities are distinct. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.34)
Everything is manifold; not a single entity exists.
Why? Because of the distinctness of the characteristics of entities. The characteristic of an entity is its designation—the term by which the entity is characterized, that is, its name.
Because its objects are distinct:
every word that designates an entity expresses a collection;
for instance, the technical term "jar" (kumbha) applies to a collection of smell, taste, color, and touch, as well as to a collection of the base, sides, neck, and so forth.
And this is merely an illustration. //34//
NyS 4.1.35: [The object] is not [non-existent], because a single entity is produced by multiple characteristics.
The term "anekavidhalakṣaṇaiḥ" is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (madhyamapadalopī samāsaḥ).
A single entity is produced as being connected with various characteristics such as odor and so forth, as well as qualities (guṇas) and parts (avayavas) such as the base and so forth;
thus, substance (dravya) is distinct from its qualities, and the whole (avayavin) is distinct from its parts.
And both of these follow the principle of differentiation. //35//
Moreover:
"There is no refutation [of our position] precisely because of the established definition [of the means of knowledge]. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.36)
The negation that "no single entity exists" is improper.
Why? Precisely because of the establishment of defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Whatever here is the defining characteristic of an entity, consisting of its name and word, that is established in a single [entity].
"I touch that very jar which I saw; I see that very thing which I touched"—thus it is not a collection of atoms (*aṇu-samūha*) that is perceived.
And since no collection of atoms is being perceived, that which is perceived must be a single entity.
Furthermore, this has been stated: "There is no single entity because of which there could be a collection."
Because a single [entity] is not possible, the collection does not exist at all— since there is no single entity upon which the word "collection" could be applied;
and because a single [entity] is not possible,
the collection is not tenable, for a collection is indeed a unification of the one.

This is untenable because it is self-contradictory: when you state the reason that "the word 'entity' (bhāva) is applied to a collection," you thereby admit the very thing whose negation is being asserted— that there is no single entity—
since a collection is indeed a unification of singulars.

And because the term "entity" (*bhāva*) is used in reference to a collection, the negation of each individual member within that collection—namely, that "there is no single entity"—is established by relying upon the collection itself. Thus, this is a trivial argument, as it results in a contradiction on both counts. //36//
This is another extreme view:
"Everything is non-existence, because the existence of things is established through their mutual non-existence. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.37)
Whatever collection of entities there may be, all that is non-existence (abhāva).
Why? Because among entities, mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva) is established:

"A cow is non-existent in the form of a horse" means "The cow is not a horse," and "A horse is non-existent in the form of a cow" means "The horse is not a cow. This is because the cognition of non-existence and the negation are in grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the word for an entity.
Everything is non-existence. //37//
This is untenable because there is a contradiction between the two terms in the proposition and between the proposition and the reason.
The meaning of the word "all" (*sarva*) is the state of being without remainder,
whereas the meaning of the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is the negation of existence.

If the former is with designation (*sopākhyam*) and the latter is without designation (*nirupākhya*), how could that which is being designated therein be without designation, i.e., a non-entity (*abhāva*)?
A non-entity without designation can never be asserted as having multiplicity or totality.
If you say that "all this is non-existence"—that is, do you mean that what you consider to be "all this" is non-existence?
If this is so, the contradiction remains unresolved; for it is impossible for the notion of "the manifold" and "without remainder" to exist within non-existence.
Furthermore, this cognition "all" exists;
therefore, it is not non-existence. Moreover, there is a contradiction between the proposition and the reason: the proposition "all is non-existence" is a negation of existence.
The reason is "because the mutual non-existence of entities is established.
Having admitted and relied upon the mutual non-existence of entities, it is said that "everything is non-existent" by virtue of the establishment of that mutual non-existence.
If everything were non-existent, then the statement "because the mutual non-existence of entities is established" would not be tenable.
Now, if the establishment of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) occurs among existing things (*bhāva*), then the claim that "everything is non-existence" is not tenable;
furthermore, this connects with the [preceding] Sūtra.
Not so, because things are established by way of their own intrinsic nature.
Not everything is non-existent.
Why? Because things exist by virtue of their own being;
it is asserted that things exist by means of their own specific characteristics (*dharma*).
And what is the intrinsic nature (*svadharma*) of entities?
It is the commonality such as "existence" (*sat*) and so forth for substances, qualities, and actions;
and for substances, it is the specific property such as "possessing motion" (*kriyāvat*), and so on.
And it is said that [the qualities] ending with touch belong to earth;
furthermore, there is an infinite variety for each [element],
and the specific properties of generality, particularity, and inherence are also apprehended.
Since non-existence is indefinable, would this distinct object that causes comprehension not fail to exist?
Yet it does exist; therefore, not everything is non-existence.
Alternatively, "because things are not established by way of intrinsic nature" means because their own-form (*svarūpa*) is not established.
When the word "cow" is employed, a substance qualified by a universal (*jāti*) is apprehended, not a mere non-existence.
Furthermore, if everything were non-existence, then "cow" would be perceived as non-existence, and non-existence would be expressed by the word "cow.
However, since a specific substance is perceived upon the employment of the word "cow," and not non-existence, [the claim that everything is non-existence] is therefore untenable.
Alternatively, [the phrase] "because it is not established by way of intrinsic nature" means: why is it not said that "the cow is non-existent in the form of a horse"?
Since it is not so stated, the cow exists in its own form; thus, there is establishment by way of intrinsic nature.
Why is it not said that "what is horseless is a horse" or "what is non-cow is a cow"?
Because such expressions are not used, it is understood that the substance exists by its own form (*svarūpa*).

Furthermore, when there is a negation of non-distinction (*avyatireka-pratiṣedha*), there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the notion of existence (*bhāva*); for in the case of existence, distinction (*vyatireka*) consists in relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

In this context, non-distinction (*avyatireka*) is the relation termed identity (*abheda*). When that is negated, there is always grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the cognition of "non-existent," as in the example: "There are no jujube fruits in the bowl. Furthermore, in the case of "The cow is non-existent in the form of a horse" or "The cow is not a horse," the non-distinction between the cow and the horse is negated, meaning that there is no oneness between the cow and the horse.

When that [non-existence] is being negated by means of an entity, such as a cow, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the cognition of non-existence and the word "non-existent," as in "the non-existent cow is not of the nature of a horse.

This is just as when the conjunction of jujube fruits with a bowl is being negated, there is coreferentiality between the cognition of non-existence and the existing [locus], as in "there are no jujube fruits in the bowl. //38//
There is no establishment of intrinsic nature, because of its relativity.
That which is produced through dependence is relative:
length is produced in dependence on shortness, and shortness is produced in dependence on length;
nothing exists by way of its own intrinsic nature.
Why? Because of the efficacy of dependence.
Therefore, there is no establishment of intrinsic nature for entities. //39//
It is untenable because it is self-contradictory.
If length is produced in dependence on shortness, while shortness is non-dependent,
then in relation to what is "short" now apprehended?
Or, if shortness is produced in dependence on length...
Is [the sequence] long and independent?
In this way, since one of two mutually dependent things would be absent if the other were absent—resulting in the absence of both—the establishment of dependence is untenable. (p. 984)
If intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were not established, why would length and shortness—which are relative—fail to exist in two substances that are equal or circular?
Whether there is dependence or non-dependence, there is no difference between the two substances;
for as much as exists in the substance when it is being depended upon, just so much exists when it is not being depended upon, and there is no distinction in either case.
If, however, [the distinction] were merely relative, then a specific excellence would have to arise in one of the two.
If it is asked, "What is the efficacy of relativity?"— it is the possibility of perceiving a degree of excellence when both are perceived.

Perceiving two substances existing together in one place, one grasps that which possesses a superior [dimension] and determines it to be "long," and grasps that which is inferior and determines it to be "short.
This is what is meant by the capacity of relativity (apekṣāsāmarthya). //40//
Now, the monistic doctrines concerning number:
everything is one, because there is no distinction in existence;
everything is twofold, due to the division between the eternal and the non-eternal.
Everything is threefold: the knower, knowledge, and the object of knowledge.
Everything is fourfold: the cognizer, the means of cognition, the object of cognition, and the resulting cognition.
In this manner, other categories may also be applied as appropriate.
In this regard, the examination [is as follows]:
NyS 4.1.41: The absolute determination of number is not established, because of the impossibility and possibility of causes.
If there is a difference between the probandum and the probans,
then certainty is not established because of their distinctness; or,
if there is no difference between the probandum and the probans?
Even so, exclusivity is not established due to the absence of a proof;
for indeed, nothing whatsoever is established without a reason (hetu). //41//
Not so, because [the whole] exists as a constituent part of its cause.
Why is there no non-establishment for those who hold the extreme view that [the whole] is identical with the number?
Because the cause exists as a constituent part (*avayava*).
Since a certain constituent part serves as the means of proof (*sādhana*), there is no exclusion (*avyatireka*).
The same applies to dualism and the other [views] as well. //42//
Because it is partless, [the reason] is not a valid logical ground.
The reason "because the cause exists as a constituent part" is not a valid reason.

Why? Having asserted the proposition that "everything is one" without exception, one speaks of the oneness of some particular thing; in that case, a distinct constituent part serving as the means of proof is not possible.
The same applies to dualism and other such views.
Indeed, if these extremist numerical doctrines proceed by rejecting the expansion of the diversity of objects produced by specific causes,
they become false doctrines due to their contradiction with perception, inference, and scripture.
Or do they proceed by way of permission?
[The answer is: The acquisition of wealth is brought about by common factors, while the differentiation of wealth is brought about by specific factors; thus, they abandon absolutism.
Indeed, these absolutisms have been examined for the sake of discerning the knowledge of reality. //43//
The fruit follows immediately after the state after death; regarding that [fruit], there is doubt because its production occurs both immediately and at a later time. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.44)
In "he cooks" and "he milks," the fruit is immediate, namely the boiled rice and the milk; whereas in "he ploughs" and "he sows," the fruit is obtained at a later time, namely the harvest of grain.
And there exists this action, "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra"; regarding its fruit, there is doubt:
it is not immediate, because it is to be experienced at a later time.

Heaven is heard of as the fruit, and that arises from this [action] once it has been differentiated by means of a different body; it is not an immediate result, such as the fruit of a desire for a village and the like. //44//
NyS 4.1.45: There is no production at a later time because the cause has perished.
When the process of manifestation has been destroyed, the fruit of that manifestation cannot arise without a cause;
for indeed, nothing whatsoever is produced from a cause that has perished. //45//
Prior to its production, it would exist like the fruit of a tree [before it has ripened].

Just as one who desires fruit performs preparatory work such as watering at the root of a tree, and when that [superficial layer] has perished, the earth element— sustained by the water element and ripened by internal heat—

produces the substance of sap; and that sap, having become a substantial entity, pervading the tree and being distinguished by its ripening, settles itself through a particular arrangement and produces leaves and other parts up to the fruit.
Thus, ritual acts such as sprinkling and so forth are purposeful;
yet, the production of a fruit does not arise from what has perished.
Rather, through such activity, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) characterized as merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*) is produced.
Once born, it—being assisted by other auxiliary factors—produces its fruit at a later time.
And this has been stated: "Its arising occurs due to the connection with the results of previous actions. (46)
This very [effect], while being produced prior to its actual production—NyS 4.1.47:
is neither non-existent, nor existent, nor both existent and non-existent, because of the difference in nature between the existent and the non-existent.
Prior to its production, that which possesses the nature of being produced does not exist, because of the restriction of material causes (*upādāna*).
For the production of a particular thing, only a specific material cause is required, not everything for everything; thus, if [the effect] were non-existent, such a restriction would not be possible.
"It is not existent, because the arising of that which already exists prior to its production is untenable.
No; [it is] "existent," because existence and non-existence are of different natures (vaidharmya), and thus existence is admitted as the meaning.
"Non-existent" is the negation of the object;
the contradiction between these two is their dissimilarity (vaidharmya), and because of this contradiction, the impossibility of non-exclusion [from the class of objects] follows. //47//
Prior to its arising, that which is subject to arising is certainly non-existent. Why?
Because we observe both arising and passing away. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.48)
As for what was stated previously— that before its production the effect is not non-existent because of the restriction of its material cause (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.49)—
that [non-existence] is established by cognition.

"This [cause] alone is capable of producing this [effect], not everything"—thus, prior to its production, the effect is established by the intellect as having a restricted cause, because one observes a restriction in its production.
Therefore, the restriction of the material cause (*upādāna*) is logically justified; however, if the effect already existed prior to its production, there would be no production at all. //49//
"Because of the distinction of the substratum, like the production of fruit from a tree," is not a valid reason.
The preparatory treatment such as watering the roots and the fruit both depend upon the tree;
however, since the action is here in this body while the fruit is there in the next world, [the reason] is not a valid probans due to the difference in their substrata. //50//
NyS 4.1.51: There is no refutation [of pleasure], because pleasure has the self as its locus.
Pleasure, because it is directly perceived by the self, has the self as its locus;
action designated as *dharma* has that very [self] as its locus, since *dharma* is a quality of the self. Therefore, a separation from the locus is impossible. //51//
NyS 4.1.52: [The opponent argues that] it is not so, because there is an indication of fruits such as sons, cattle, women, household goods, gold, food, and so forth.
The fruit is specified as sons and so forth, not as pleasure;
since it is stated in such injunctions as "one desiring a village should sacrifice" and "one desiring a son should sacrifice," the claim that pleasure is the fruit is incorrect. //52//
Because the fruit is produced through connection with them, there is a metaphorical designation of "fruit" applied to those [auxiliaries].

Because a result characterized by joy arises from the relationship with sons and others, there is a metaphorical designation of "result" applied to sons and others, just as the word "life-breaths" is used for food in the statement, "Food, indeed, is the life-breaths. //53//
Suffering was indicated immediately after the fruit,
and it was stated that "suffering is characterized by affliction.
Is this, then, a denial of pleasure, which is personally experienced and directly perceived by all living beings?
"Or is it another [type of] kalpa?
"It is another," he said.
"How so? For indeed, happiness witnessed by the entire world cannot be denied."

But this instruction on the cultivation of the perception of suffering is for the purpose of abandoning suffering for one who is weary of the suffering caused by the experience of the continuous succession of birth and death, and who desires to relinquish that suffering. By what reasoning?

Indeed, all classes of sentient beings, all places of birth, and all forms of rebirth are accompanied by affliction; because they are associated with suffering, the seers have declared that the characteristic of suffering is affliction.
Here, the cultivation of the perception of suffering is taught, and the reason for this is set forth:
"The arising of birth is indeed suffering, because it is joined with manifold afflictions. (NyS 4.1.54)
Birth consists of the body, the sense organs, and the intellect; and "origination" (utpatti) is the manifestation of these—the body and so forth—characterized by their specific configurations.
Furthermore, affliction is of various kinds: inferior, middling, and superior.
It is superior for those in the hells, middling for animals,
but inferior for humans.
For even the gods are inferior to those who are free from passion.

Thus, for one who perceives every place of rebirth as being beset by various afflictions, the perception of suffering becomes established toward pleasure, its means, and toward the body, the senses, and the cognitions. [The perception of suffering becomes established toward the cognitions. p.1008
From the establishment of the perception of suffering, there arises the perception of non-delight in all worlds.
For one who dwells upon the perception of non-delight, craving for the objects of all worlds is severed;
through the abandonment of craving, one is liberated from all suffering.
Just as one who, perceiving milk to be poison because of its contact with poison, does not take it, and by not taking it, does not undergo the suffering of death; //54//
But the enumeration of suffering is not a denial of pleasure; why?
Because pleasure is produced in the intervals [between sufferings]. (NyS 4.1.55)
Indeed, this enumeration of suffering is not a denial of pleasure.
Why? Because pleasure is produced in the intervals [of suffering].
For pleasure, which is to be personally experienced by embodied beings, is indeed produced in the intervals between afflictions.
Therefore, it is impossible to reject this. //55//
Furthermore, from the perspective of its meaning:
NyS 4.1.56: There is no refutation [of the definition of perception] because, for one who experiences [an object], the affliction does not cease due to the fault of seeking it further.
Regarding pleasure, "by way of the designation of suffering" refers to the context; "seeking" (paryeṣaṇā) means longing or craving for the acquisition of objects.
The fault of seeking is this: that which one craves while experiencing [pleasure] may not be attained, or even if it is attained, it perishes.

Thinking, "It has turned out deficient," or "It has turned out with many obstacles," from this fault of seeking (*paryeṣaṇā-doṣa*), various kinds of mental anguish arise. For one who experiences this, there is no cessation of affliction due to the fault of seeking. Because there is no cessation of affliction, the cultivation of the perception of suffering (*duḥkha-saṃjñā*) is taught.
For this reason, birth is suffering, not because of the absence of happiness. Furthermore, it has been said:
"When the desire of one who longs for pleasure is fulfilled..."
"Then another desire quickly oppresses him:

'Even if one should obtain this entire earth, bounded by the ocean, together with its cattle and horses, that seeker of wealth is not satisfied by that wealth; how then can there be happiness for one who desires wealth? (56)
And because there is a misconception of pleasure within the variety of suffering.
The instruction for the cultivation of the perception of suffering is being given.
For this person, established in the experience of pleasure, considers pleasure to be the supreme human goal;
he thinks there is no higher good than pleasure, and upon attaining pleasure, he feels his purpose has been fulfilled and his task accomplished.
Due to false resolve, one becomes attached to pleasure and to the objects that serve as its means; being thus attached, one strives for pleasure.

As he so strives, manifold suffering arises for him—caused by birth, old age, disease, death, union with the unpleasant, separation from the beloved, and the failure to obtain what is desired—extending to all its various forms.
One mistakenly conceives that conceptualization of suffering to be happiness;
for suffering is an integral part of happiness,
and it is not possible to attain happiness without encountering suffering.

Because it is for the sake of that [pleasure], one whose wisdom is impaired by the perception of pleasure thinks, "This is indeed pleasure," and thus runs toward rebirth with the thought, "Be born! and does not transcend cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, the cultivation of the perception of suffering is taught as the antidote to this perception of pleasure.
Birth is suffering because it is accompanied by suffering.
It is not because of the absence of pleasure.
If that is so, why is it not said that "birth is suffering"?

Since this [term] could have been stated in that way, the fact that he says instead "birth is indeed suffering" (duḥkham eva janma) indicates the absence of pleasure; for this particle *eva* has the function of restriction (*vinigrahārthīya*).
How so? Birth is not suffering by its own nature, but rather it is designated as suffering through metaphorical attribution;
likewise with happiness. This very point is established by this [sūtra], and not that birth is suffering itself. //57//
Immediately after the enumeration of suffering, liberation (apavarga) is addressed; it is refuted as follows:
"There is no liberation because of the continuous succession of debts, afflictions, and worldly activity" (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.58).

There is no liberation due to the bondage of debts—according to the text: "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born with three debts: he owes the sages [the debt] of studentship, the gods [the debt] of sacrifice, and the ancestors [the debt] of progeny. These are the debts;
their "bondage" is the connection with one's own duties.

Because of the statement regarding the connection with karma— namely, "This sacrificial session (*satra*), namely the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa, lasts until old age and death," and "By old age indeed one is released from that sacrificial session, and by death indeed"—
[this is so] because of the binding of debts (*ṛṇānubandha*).

There is no absence of liberation because there is no time for the practice of liberation; due to the persistence of afflictions, there is no liberation. This person dies still bound by afflictions and is born still bound by afflictions; no severance of the continuity of his afflictions is perceived.
Because of the continuity of activity, there is no liberation—this [self] is perceived as being unliberated from birth until death due to the undertaking of speech, intellect, and body;

therefore, that which was stated—"Upon the successive disappearance of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, there is liberation because of the absence of each preceding one upon the disappearance of the next"—is untenable. //58//
To this it is replied:

as for the statement "because of the connection with debts" (*ṛṇānubandhāt*), [the phrase] "as if by debts" (*ṛṇair iva*)—this is a figurative reference using a term for a subordinate quality (*guṇa-śabda*) because the primary term (*pradhāna-śabda*) is inappropriate; such usage is justified for the purpose of censure or praise. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.59)
The term "debts" (ṛṇaiḥ) is not a primary word.
For it is observed that this word "debt" is primarily applied where one person gives what is to be received back and another receives what is to be given back.
And this is not tenable here,
because the word "pradhāna" (primary) is inappropriate;
rather, this is a figurative restatement using the word "guṇa" (subordinate), as in the expression "by debts as it were by debts."
Because [the literal sense] is untenable, this is a figurative restatement (*anuvāda*) by means of a word denoting a quality (*guṇa-śabda*), namely, "as if by debts, as if by debts.

This is a metaphorical application (*prayuktopama*), just as one says, "The boy is fire. Furthermore, this word "debt" (*ṛṇa*) is employed here having been observed elsewhere, just as the word "fire" is used for a boy.
How is there a restatement by means of a word denoting a quality?
Because censure and praise are thereby established:
when a ritual action is omitted, one is censured like a debtor for failing to pay a debt.
And in the performance of ritual duties, he is praised like a debtor because of the payment of his debt; this alone is the meaning of the simile.

The word "being born" (*jāyamāna*) is a term denoting a specific quality (*guṇa-śabda*), because there is no entitlement [to such duties] in its opposite state. Furthermore, in the passage "a Brāhmaṇa, indeed, being born," the word "being born" refers to one who has become a householder.
When this person becomes a householder, he is then qualified for ritual acts (*karma*), because one who is merely born from his mother lacks such qualification.
However, when the boy is born from his mother, he is not yet qualified for ritual acts, because qualification belongs only to one who is both desirous [of results] and capable.

One is qualified for ritual acts by virtue of being desirous, as the injunctions for rituals involve a connection with desire, as seen in such passages as "One desiring heaven should offer the *Agnihotra*," and so forth. This applies until death.
And because activity is possible for one who is capable, one who is capable has the qualification for ritual acts, since activity is possible for him;
indeed, it is the capable person who engages in the prescribed ritual act, and not anyone else.
However, the absence of both [desire and capacity] occurs in the primary sense of the word;
for instance, in the case of a boy being born from his mother, both desire and capacity do not exist.
Furthermore, a Vedic sentence does not differ from a worldly sentence insofar as it is composed by a person who acts with deliberation.
In this regard, even an ordinary worldly person, though lacking discernment, would not say to a child immediately upon birth: "Study! Sacrifice! Lead the life of a religious student!"
Why, then, does the seer—who is free from fault and speaks with propriety—engage in teaching for the sake of instruction?
Indeed, a dancer does not perform for the blind, nor does a singer sing for the deaf;
furthermore, the object of instruction is the understanding of the meaning taught.
Instruction is given to one who understands the meaning of what has been taught;
this [instruction] does not apply to a newborn infant.
Furthermore, the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, which are the marks of the householder stage, speak of ritual action.
Furthermore, that ritual action which the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas prescribe is consistent with the marks of the householder state, such as the connection with a wife;

therefore, it is said that "this person, being born, is [born] as a householder. Moreover, the statement regarding "ending with old age" (*jarāmarya*) is logically tenable only if one's desire for worldly life does not undergo transformation.

As long as one’s desire for the fruit [of ritual action] does not change or cease, so long must that karma be performed; thus, the doctrine of "until old age" (*jarāmaryavāda*) is established with respect to him.
The statement, "By old age indeed," refers to the fourth quarter of life—that which is joined with renunciation (*pravrajyā*). It is said, "By old age indeed he is released from this";
the fourth quarter of life, joined with renunciation, is called "old age."
For in that context, renunciation is prescribed; thus, [the statement] "in the case of absolute conjunction with old age, by means of old age indeed" would be meaningless.
Furthermore, the claim that "one who is incapable is liberated" is also untenable.

He states an external means for one who is himself incapable: "Or a pupil may offer the oblation, having been purchased by means of the Veda; or a milk-offerer may offer it, having been purchased by means of wealth.
Now, is that which is enjoined being restated, or is a purpose being postulated out of desire?
It is logical that there should be a restatement of what has been enjoined;
for it is appropriate that the capacity of the statement implies that the householder, like one who is indebted, engages in ritual acts while lacking independence.
For the means of accomplishing a result are the object of effort, not the result itself; when these are perfected, they conduce to the result.
And that which is being born is prescribed.
And that which is being born is enjoined;
therefore, he who is connected [with the rite] is "the one being born.
If it is argued that this is not so because there is no direct injunction (*pratyakṣavidhāna*), we say no.
"Because there is also no direct scriptural injunction for its prohibition; rather, the householder's life is enjoined directly by perception [of scripture].
*Gārhasthya* is enjoined through direct perception.
If there were another stage of life (āśrama), the Brahmin would have established it as well through direct perception.
[Objection: There is no other stage of life (āśrama) because there is no direct scriptural injunction for it.
[Reply: No, because even a prohibition lacks direct scriptural injunction.

Indeed, a prohibition is not directly enjoined by a Brāhmaṇa text—such as "there are no other stages of life; there is only the householder's stage"—because such a prohibition is not heard directly in scripture.
"This is improper," [one might say].
But the injunction follows from its specific domain (*adhikāra*), just as in other branches of knowledge.

Just as other treatises are direct authorities within their own respective domains because there is no other source for that meaning, so too this Brāhmaṇa, which is a treatise on the householder's life, is a direct authority within its own domain.
"It is not prescriptive for other stages of life because they do not exist," [it is argued]. Furthermore, the *Ṛgveda* and the *Brāhmaṇas* are said to proclaim liberation (*apavarga*).
Both the *Ṛks* and the *Brāhmaṇas* contain declarations regarding liberation.
And as for the *Ṛgveda* verses:
"By means of ritual acts, the seers attained death, being possessed of progeny and desiring wealth;
then other wise seers attained immortality, which is beyond ritual acts."
"Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality—
that which shines forth, placed beyond the heavens in the secret cave, which the ascetics enter. "I know this Great Person, resplendent like the sun, beyond the darkness."
"Only by knowing Him does one go beyond death; there is no other path for the journey.
Now, the Brāhmaṇas:
"There are three pillars of dharma—the sacrifice, study, and giving constitute the first; austerity alone is the second; the student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī)..."

"The third is one who dwells in the teacher's family, exhausting himself completely in the teacher's family; all these indeed attain worlds of merit, but he who is established in Brahman attains immortality.
"Desiring this very world, mendicants go forth as wanderers."
Now, moreover, they say: "This person consists entirely of desire. As is his desire, so is his resolve; as is his resolve, so is the deed he performs; and whatever deed he performs, that he attains.

Having thus described transmigration through actions, they teach another subject relevant to the context: "Thus indeed is one who still desires. But as for one who does not desire—him who is without desire, free from desire, whose desire is the Self, whose desire is attained—for him the vital breaths do not depart; right here they are merged."
"Being Brahman, one attains Brahman.

In this regard, what was stated—that there is an absence of liberation due to the binding of debts—is incorrect. Furthermore, because of the scriptural testimony regarding the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*) in the passage, "There are four paths leading to the gods," the position of a single stage of life (*aikāśramya*) is untenable. //59//

And for one who desires the fruit, there is this Brāhmaṇa passage: "This Agnihotra is a sacrificial session (*sattra*) that lasts until old age or death; so too are the New and Full Moon sacrifices. How is this so? [The answer is:
"Because of the ritual depositing (*samāropaṇa*) [of the fires] into oneself, there is no prohibition [against the cessation of rites]. (NyS 4.1.60)

It is heard in the Śruti: "Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, having offered all his possessions (*sarvavedasa*) in it, and having consigned the fires into himself (*ātmani*), a Brāhmaṇa should go forth [as a wandering ascetic].
By this we understand that the consigning of the fires is enjoined for one who has turned away from the desire for offspring, wealth, and worlds, and whose seeking of fruits has ceased.

And thus the Brāhmaṇas say: "Yājñavalkya, being about to undertake another vow, said to Maitreyī: 'Truly, I am about to depart from this state; come now, let me divide this [wealth] between you and [my other wife] Kātyāyanī.'"*
"I shall make an end together with Kātyāyanī.
Furthermore, it is said: "O Maitreyī, you have been instructed; this much indeed, my dear, is immortality," and having said this, Yājñavalkya departed as a wandering mendicant.
(NyS 4.1.61) Moreover, because the ritual of placing the sacrificial vessels (*pātracaya*) does not occur [at the time of death], there is an absence of fruit [from the sacrifice].
If ritual action were prescribed without distinction as something to be performed until old age and death, it would follow that the rites for all people must end with the piling of the funeral pyre;
in that case, the renunciation of desires would not be heard of in scripture.
[For it says: "In this regard, indeed, the ancient Brahmins who had studied the Vedas and possessed knowledge did not desire offspring, thinking: 'What is the use of offspring?'"
"Thinking, 'This self is ours; this world is ours,' they indeed rose above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, and then lived the life of mendicants.

Since for one who has risen above these desires, actions ending with the collection of alms-bowls are no longer appropriate, it follows that the fruit of an action does not belong to the agent as an indistinct result.

Because the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*) are prescribed in the *Itihāsas*, *Purāṇas*, and *Dharmaśāstras*, the existence of only one stage of life is untenable. If it is argued that these [texts] are not authoritative, we say no; for their authority is recognized by means of valid authority—indeed, the authority of the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* is established by a Brahmin who is himself a source of valid knowledge.
It is authorized [in scripture]: "Now these very Atharvāṅgirasas recited this Itihāsa-Purāṇa; the Itihāsa-Purāṇa is the fifth Veda among the Vedas.
Therefore, it is incorrect to claim that it lacks authority.
Furthermore, if the Dharmaśāstra were invalid, there would follow the consequence of the destruction of the world due to the cessation of the legal transactions of living beings.
Moreover, its invalidity is untenable because the seers and expounders are the same;
for those very ones who were the seers and expounders of the Mantra and Brāhmaṇa [portions] are [the seers and expounders of the Dharmaśāstra].
These indeed consist of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, as well as the Dharmaśāstras. Their authority is established according to their respective domains,
for the domain of the Mantra and Brāhmaṇa is one thing, while that of the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras is another.
The subject matter of the Mantra and Brāhmaṇa is sacrifice; that of Itihāsa and Purāṇa is worldly conduct; and that of the Dharmaśāstra is the establishment of worldly legal procedures.
In that regard, since everything is not established by a single [means], these means of valid cognition function according to their respective domains, just like the sense organs and so forth. //61//
As for the argument that [liberation does not occur] because the continuity of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is never severed—NyS 4.1.62 states:
"For one who is in deep sleep and perceives no dreams, there is liberation due to the absence of afflictions."

Just as for one who is in deep sleep, the connection with passion and the connection with pleasure and pain are severed when no dreams are seen, so it is also in liberation (*apavarga*); and this is cited as the nature of the liberated self by those who know Brahman. //62//
As for the argument that [rebirth occurs] "due to the persistence of activity" (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.63): activity does not lead to rebirth for one whose afflictions have been eliminated.
When passion, hatred, and delusion have been destroyed, there is no activity leading to rebirth.
Rebirth, however, is the arising of a new birth after the cessation of a previous life,
and that is brought about by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa).
When that [ignorance] has been abandoned, there being no further birth after this life, there is the absence of another birth; this non-relinking is liberation (*apavarga*).
If it is argued that this leads to the consequence of the fruitlessness of karma, we say no, because the experience of the maturation of karma is not denied.
It is said that when previous births cease, rebirth does not occur; however, the experience of the maturation of karma is not denied, for all previous karmas indeed ripen in the final birth. //63//
No, because the continuum of afflictions is inherent by nature.
The severance of the continuity of the afflictions is not possible; why?
Because the continuity of the afflictions is inherent in their nature.
This continuity of the afflictions is beginningless.
And that which is beginningless cannot be eradicated. //64//
Regarding this, someone offers a rebuttal:
"Just as there is non-eternality due to non-existence prior to origination, so too is there non-eternality even when [the property] is inherent. (NyS 4.1.65)
Just as the beginningless non-existence prior to arising is brought to an end by an arisen entity, so too is the natural continuity of afflictions impermanent. //65//
Another says:
"Or it is like the blackness of an atom and its impermanence. (NyS 4.1.66)
Just as the blackness of an atom is beginningless and yet impermanent due to contact with fire,
so too is the continuum of afflictions;
for indeed, the properties of an existing thing are both permanence and impermanence.
The claim that reality exists in both existence and non-existence is merely figurative.
The notion that the blackness of an atom is beginningless is untenable due to the absence of a cause.
Furthermore, the assertion that what is characterized by non-origination is impermanent lacks any supporting reason here. //66//
But this [objection regarding] concentration is not valid—NyS 4.1.67: because passion and the like have conceptual construction as their cause.
The word "and" (ca) signifies a conjunction, meaning "because they have karma as their cause" and "because they have each other as their cause.
From false conceptualizations—those which are provocative of passion, provocation of anger, and provocation of delusion—attachment, aversion, and delusion arise;
furthermore, karma, which brings about the various classes of beings, produces the regular [manifestations of] attachment, aversion, and delusion.
Because of the observation of a fixed rule:
for it is observed that some class of beings abounds in passion (*rāga*), some in hatred (*dveṣa*), and some in delusion (*moha*);
furthermore, the arising of passion and the other afflictions is caused by one another.

The deluded person feels attachment; the deluded person feels aversion. One who is attached becomes deluded; one who is averse becomes deluded. Through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), all false conceptualizations (*mithyā-saṅkalpa*) cease to arise; and because the cause does not arise, the effect does not arise. Thus, there is the absolute non-arising of passion and the other afflictions. Furthermore, it is untenable [to claim] that the continuum of afflictions (*kleśa-santati*) is beginningless.
Indeed, all these internal entities, such as the body and so forth, proceed by way of a beginningless continuity;
herein, nothing that has never previously arisen ever arises for the first time, except through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
And this being so, it is not asserted that anything possesses the nature of non-arising or the nature of imperishability.

Furthermore, karma that brings about a particular class of sentient beings does not become a cause for the arising of passion and other afflictions once false conceptualizations have been destroyed by the knowledge of reality; rather, it results only in the experience of pleasure and pain. //67//
Now begins the second daily lesson of the fourth chapter.
Now, indeed, sir, does the knowledge of reality arise with respect to each and every one of as many objects as there are, or does it arise in some [particular] case?
And what is the distinction here?
It is not that [cognition] arises in each case for as many objects as there are, because knowable things are infinite;
nor does it arise in some cases [only].
In that case where [knowledge] does not arise, delusion remains unceased; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of a residue of delusion.
Furthermore, it is not possible for delusion regarding one object to be negated by knowledge of reality regarding another object.
Indeed, delusion is false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), not merely the non-arising of knowledge of reality.
And that object upon which false knowledge operates—functioning as the seed of saṃsāra—is what must be known in its true nature.
What, then, is that false knowledge? It is the grasping of a self in that which is not-self.
The delusion "I am" is the conceit of "I.
Indeed, the view of one who perceives what is not the self as "I am" is the conceit of "I.
But what is that collection of things which is the object of the conceit of "I"?
How is it that the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), which has as its objects the body, the sense organs, the mind, sensations, and cognitions, becomes the seed of saṃsāra? [It does so.

Indeed, this person, having resolved that "I am" with respect to the collection of objects such as the body, and perceiving the destruction of the self through the destruction of those [objects], is overwhelmed by the thirst for non-destruction and repeatedly grasps them.
Grasping them, he exerts himself for the sake of birth and death; because of his lack of separation from that, he is not ultimately liberated from suffering.
But he who sees that suffering, the basis of suffering, and even pleasure that is connected with suffering—all this is suffering—he thoroughly understands suffering.
And when suffering is thoroughly understood, it is abandoned through non-clinging, like poisoned food.
In this way, he perceives that faults and karma are the causes of suffering.
And since it is not possible for there to be an end to the continuity of suffering as long as the defects have not been abandoned, one abandons the defects;
and it has been stated that when the defects are abandoned, there is no further activity leading to rebirth.
Furthermore, one establishes the objects of knowledge—the sufferings that are the fruits of existence after death—as well as the actions and defects that are to be abandoned.
Liberation (apavarga) is that which is to be attained; the means for its attainment is the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna).

Thus, for one who cultivates, practices, and meditates upon the objects of valid cognition as divided into these four categories, there arises right vision—the knowledge of reality, which is the comprehension of things as they truly are.
And thus—
NyS 4.2.1: Through the knowledge of reality regarding the causes of defects, there is the cessation of the ego-sense.
The objects of valid cognition (prameya), beginning with the body and ending with suffering, have their cause in defects (doṣa), because false knowledge (mithyājñāna) has them as its object.

This true knowledge (tattvajñāna), when it arises having those same things as its object, brings about the cessation of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), because of the opposition between the two when they share a common object.

Thus, from true knowledge, there follows liberation (apavarga) "through the successive disappearance of false knowledge, defects, activity, birth, and suffering, due to the absence of each subsequent one upon the disappearance of the one preceding it."
And this summary of the meaning of the treatise is restated; it is not being prescribed as something previously unestablished. //1//
Now, as for the sequence of thorough discernment (prasaṅkhyāna):
"The objects, such as form and so forth, which are the causes of defects, are produced by conceptual construction (saṅkalpa). (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.2)
The objects of the senses, which are the domains of desire, are called form and so forth.
When these are falsely conceptualized, they give rise to passion, hatred, and delusion;
therefore, one should first examine them.
And for one who practices discernment (*prasaṅkhyāna*) toward those [objects], false conceptualization (*mithyā-saṅkalpa*) regarding objects such as form ceases.
When that has ceased, one should practice discernment toward the internal, such as the body.
Through that discernment, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) directed toward the internal object ceases.
This ego-sense has the internal as its object;
he who dwells with a mind detached both internally and externally is said to be liberated. //2//

Henceforth, it is taught that some designations are to be abandoned while others are to be cultivated; this is neither for the sake of rejecting the Lord nor for the sake of grasping at objects. How so?
— NyS 4.2.3: But the misconception of a whole has that [collection] as its cause.

The cause of those faults, however, is the conceit of a whole (avayavin). That indeed consists of the notion of "woman" together with its equipment for a man, and the notion of "man" together with its equipment for a woman; it is the notion of signs (nimitta-saṃjñā) and the notion of secondary characteristics (anuvyañjana-saṃjñā).
The perception of signs: the tongue and the ear, the teeth and the lips.
The eyes, the nose,
and the minor marks— such as "the staff-like [eyebrows]" or "the lips are thus"—
this perception increases desire and the faults associated with it that ought to be abandoned.

The avoidance of this [perception] consists in the designation of its parts by way of differentiation— the designations of hair, body hair, flesh, blood, bone, sinew, vessels, phlegm, bile, excrement,
and so forth.
This is called the perception of the foul (*aśubhasaṃjñā*). As he cultivates it, sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) is abandoned.
Furthermore, it is taught that even when both kinds of objects exist, some perceptions are to be cultivated while others are to be avoided.
Just as when food is mixed with poison, one forms the perception of "food" for the sake of taking it up, and the perception of "poison" for the sake of abandoning it. //3//
Now, in order to refute the object [of cognition], the refutation of the composite whole (avayavin) is established:
"Because knowledge and ignorance are each twofold, there is doubt. (NyS 4.2.4)
Knowledge is twofold because of the perception of both the existent and the non-existent;
likewise, ignorance is twofold because of the non-perception of both the existent and the non-existent.
When a whole (avayavin) is being perceived, doubt arises due to this twofold nature of knowledge.
And since it is not being perceived, there is doubt due to the twofold nature of ignorance;
this is that composite whole which is perceived.
Moreover, even if it is not perceived, one is not released from doubt in any way whatsoever. //4//
There is no doubt regarding that, because it has been established by the previous reason.
In this regard, doubt is not appropriate.
Why? Because the previously stated reasons have not been refuted, it follows that there is the commencement of a distinct substance. //5//
Nor is there doubt [regarding the self] because its functioning is untenable.
Furthermore, because its occurrence is untenable, doubt is also untenable; thus, there is no whole (avayavin). //6//
He analyzes this:
"Because the parts do not subsist either in their entirety or in part, the whole does not exist. (NyS 4.2.7)
Each individual part does not reside in the whole in its entirety,
because of the difference in their dimensions and because it would follow that there would be no connection with other parts;
nor does it reside in a single portion of the whole.
For it has no other parts that exist as constituent portions. //7//
Now, if the whole exists only in its parts— [then it follows that] because of its non-existence in them, there is no whole.
It does not reside in each individual part,
because of the difference in their dimensions and because it would follow that the substance would consist of multiple substances;
nor does it reside in all parts collectively through its own parts, because there are no further parts [of the whole] beyond those [parts].
Thus, in this way, the doubt that "the composite whole does not exist" is not tenable.
And because it does not exist separately from its parts.
The phrase "the absence of the whole" (avayavyabhāva) carries over [from the previous context].
Furthermore, this [whole] does not exist separately from its parts, because it is not perceived and because it would entail the consequence of being eternal.
Therefore, the whole does not exist.
Nor are the parts the whole.

Nor is the whole (avayavī) a property (dharma) of the parts. Why? Because, as before, it is impossible for a mere property to have a relationship with its substrata, the parts; and because a property is not perceived separately from its substrata, the parts—the argument is the same. //10//
NyS 4.2.11: Since there is no differentiation within a single entity, the application of words denoting differentiation is untenable; therefore, the question is invalid.
The question—whether the whole resides in each individual part or by way of a single portion—is untenable.
Why? Because since there is no division within a single entity, the employment of words implying division is inappropriate.
The term "whole" (*kṛtsnam*) denotes the entirety of that which is manifold.
"One part" (*ekadeśa*) is a designation for something that exists as a plurality.

These two terms, "whole" (*kṛtsna*) and "part" (*ekadeśa*), have difference as their domain and are not applicable to a single composite whole (*avayavin*), because in that case there is an absence of difference. //11//
Because there is an absence of other parts, [the whole] does not exist in one part; thus, [the opponent's reason] is not a valid reason—NyS 4.2.12:
Even if there were other parts, because [the whole] does not subsist [in them], it is not a valid reason.
"Because there is no other constituent part.

Even if a single portion were itself another constituent part, nevertheless, it is the constituent part that exists within [another] constituent part, and not the whole; thus, the whole would be something else.
Even if other parts exist, the whole does not subsist [in them], because it does not subsist in a single part due to the absence of other parts; thus, this is not a valid reason.
If it is asked, "How does it subsist?"—it is an attainment characterized by the relationship between a support and that which is supported, wherein a single entity resides in multiple locations.
If it is asked how there is the relationship of the substratum (*āśraya*) and the dependent (*āśrita*), [the answer is]:
that from which another cannot obtain its own existence elsewhere is the substratum.
An effect-substance does not obtain its own existence apart from the cause-substances; however, the reverse is true for the cause-substances [in relation to the effect].
If it is asked, "How [is this] in the case of eternal things?", [we reply:
since it is established by observation in the case of non-eternal things, how could there not be a relationship of substratum and superstratum in the case of eternal substances? If this is asked:
Since the relationship of support and supported is observed among impermanent substances and qualities, its existence in permanent [substances] is established.
Therefore, for one who desires the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), the conceit of a "whole" (*avayavin*) is refuted,
not the whole itself.
Just as there is false conceptualization regarding form and so forth, [yet] form and so forth do not [themselves constitute that conceptualization]. //12//
Even when one objects that "there is no apprehension of anything because the whole (avayavin) is not established," he says this in reply:
"The apprehension of that [the whole] is like the perception by one with ophthalmia of a mass of hairs" (NyS 4.2.13).

Just as a single hair is not perceived by one with ophthalmia, whereas a mass of hairs is perceived, so too a single atom is not perceived, whereas a collection of atoms is perceived; thus, this apprehension has the aggregate of atoms as its object. //13//

NyS_4.2.14: Due to the sharpness or dullness of a sense organ, there is a corresponding variation in the apprehension of its own object; it does not, however, function with respect to what is not its object.
Just as the perception of objects becomes sharp or dull according to the sharpness or dullness of the sense organs with respect to their respective domains,
so it is that the eye, even when intensified, does not perceive an object that is outside its domain,
and even when diminished, it does not deviate from its own domain.
Thus, among those with cataracts, one does not perceive a single hair within the range of vision, while another perceives a mass of hairs;
for both are perceived by an eye free from cataracts.

However, atoms are beyond the senses; being objects that do not fall within the range of any sense organ, they are not perceived by any sense organ individually, whereas they are perceived when aggregated.
Thus, it would follow that the sense organ functions with respect to what is not its proper object.
An object distinct from atoms is never perceived.
Indeed, these very atoms, when perceived in conjunction, abandon their transcendental nature;
and when separated and not being perceived, they do not attain the status of sense-objects.
Thus, since no other substance is produced, there would be a very great contradiction; therefore, it is logical that there must be another substance which is the object of perception.

If it is argued that the object is merely an accumulation (*sañcaya*), we say no; for an accumulation is a state of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and since conjunction is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), its perception is untenable.
An aggregate (sañcaya) is indeed the conjunction of many things;
and that [conjunction] is perceived when its substratum is perceptible, not when its substratum is beyond the senses, for one perceives:
"this is conjoined with that."
Therefore, this is logical:
for when an object is being perceived by a sense faculty, no cause for its non-perception—such as an obstruction—is observed.
Consequently, the non-perception of atoms is not due to a deficiency in the sense faculty.
Just as there is no non-perception of odors and so forth by the eye due to the weakness of the sense organ. //14//
And in this way, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress of parts and wholes until the dissolution of the universe.

Indeed, that non-existence which results from the negation of the existence of a whole (*avayavin*) in its parts (*avayava*), when applied to a part being in its own parts, would either lead to the dissolution of everything,
