or it would exclude [the concept] from the partless atom (*paramāṇu*).
In both cases, there would be an absence of anything within the range of perception.
In the absence of that [object], there is an absence of the perceivable;
and this negation of mental modification has the perceivable as its basis.
Thus, by destroying its own basis, it leads to self-destruction. //15//
Moreover:
"There is no dissolution, because of the persistence of the substrate. (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.16)

Since the negation of existence [of a composite] based on the division of its parts results in non-existence, this [non-existence] is excluded from the partless atom and does not apply to a universal dissolution;
for the partlessness of the atom is established because there is no further reduction to something smaller than that, as it is the limit where no smaller part can exist.
Indeed, when the parts of a clod of earth are divided, each subsequent part becomes smaller and smaller.
And this is the point where further reduction would lead to an infinite regress, because that which is the ultimate minimum, beyond which nothing smaller exists, is where the process ceases;
and since there is nothing smaller than that, we designate it as the "ultimate atom" (*paramāṇu*).
16. Or [the atom is] beyond the *truṭi*. NyS_4.2.17.
Because the division of parts is not infinite and because substances are innumerable, there is a cessation of the state of being an atom (truṭi). //17//
Now, the proponent of non-apprehension (*anupalambhika*), thinking that everything does not exist, says:
"That [existence] is untenable because of the penetration of space" (NyS 4.2.18).
The existence of such an atom—partless and eternal—is untenable.
Why? Because of its interpenetration by space.
An atom is pervaded and interpenetrated by space both internally and externally.
Because of its interpenetration, it has parts;
because it has parts, it is non-eternal. //18//
Or else, space would not be omnipresent.
Now, if this is not accepted—that there is no space within the atom—it follows that [the atom] would lack omnipresence. //19//
NyS_4.2.20: Since it is stated that there are other causes for a product-substance both internally and externally, that [interiority and exteriority] is absent in what is not a product.
"Internal" refers to a cause that is concealed by other causes; "external," on the other hand, refers to a cause that is either intervening or non-intervening.
This [distinction] is possible in the case of a substance that is an effect.
Because the atom is not an effect;
for in that which is not an effect, such as the atom, there is an absence of "inside" and "outside."
And that wherein its existence is to be imitated is not the atom,
for that which has nothing smaller than itself is an atom. //20//
And because sound and conjunction are all-pervading, [space] is omnipresent.
Wherever sounds arise, they manifest in space; they have space as their substratum.
Conjunctions of minds, atoms, and their products manifest in space;
for no corporeal substance is perceived that is not conjoined with space.
Therefore, it is not non-omnipresent. //21//
Non-expansion, non-obstruction, and omnipresence are the properties of space.
It is not obstructed by a substance that is mobile and possesses resistance, just as water is not obstructed by wood;
why? Because it is partless (*niravayavatvāt*).
And a serpent does not obstruct it—that is, it does not impede its quality which is the cause of its action.
Why? Because it is intangible (*asparśatva*).
For obstruction is observed in the opposite case; therefore, you ought not to expect a phenomenon observed in a composite, tangible substance to occur in its opposite.
The negation of the atom follows from the consequence that the constituent part of an atom would itself be subtler;
for if the atom possessed parts, it would follow that the part of the atom is subtler than the atom.
Why? Because a difference in magnitude is observed between a causal substance and its effect.
Therefore, while the part of an atom is subtler, that which possesses parts is the object to be imitated;
thus, this object to be imitated is what is being negated here.
The impermanence of an effect arises from the disjunction of its causes,
not from its penetration by space;
the impermanence of a clod of earth arises from the disjunction of its constituent parts.
Not because of the pervasion by space. //22//
And because the occurrence of configuration is possible for those things possessing form, there exists the reality of constituent parts.
For among those things that are delimited and possess tangibility, a configuration—such as triangular, quadrangular, even, or circular—is possible;
that which is the configuration is the arrangement of parts.
And since atoms are spherical, they must therefore possess parts. //23//
And because conjunction is possible.

An atom situated in the middle, when conjoined with two atoms— one preceding and one following— creates a separation between them. By means of this separation, it is inferred that it is conjoined with the preceding atom by its front part, and conjoined with the subsequent atom by its rear part.
Those two parts, the prior and the posterior, are its constituents;
likewise, for that which is joined on all sides, the parts on all sides are its constituents.
As for the claim that "the existence of constituents follows from the possibility of the configuration of corporeal things," this has already been addressed.

What has been said? That there is a refutation of the atom as an effect because, upon division, it would follow that it becomes smaller and smaller; since it cannot become smaller than that [limit], there is cessation [of division] there, and because an atom without parts would entail the consequence of being even more minute.
Furthermore, as for the argument "because conjunction is possible":
there is an obstruction due to the possession of touch, and there is a figurative attribution of parts due to the non-pervasion of the substratum.
And it has been said in this regard: "An atom possessing tangibility is an obstructer of two atoms possessing tangibility because of their mutual resistance, not because of its having parts.

And because of its possession of tangibility, when an obstruction occurs, the conjunction of atoms does not pervade the substratum; thus there is a figurative attribution of parts, as if it were possessed of parts.

And it has also been stated here that, regarding the consequence of further reduction in size through division, since there is no smaller than that [the atom], and because it would entail the consequence of the constituent part being even more minute, the status of the atom as an effect is negated. //24//

Regarding the two reasons—"because the configuration of corporeal things is possible" and "because conjunction is possible [of atoms]"—there is no refutation [of the existence of atoms], because these would lead to an infinite regress, and an infinite regress is untenable. (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.25)
"Whatever possesses form and whatever is joined, all that has parts"— these two reasons lead to an infinite regress (anavasthā),
and such an infinite regress is not tenable;
for only if the infinite regress were real would these two reasons be valid.
Therefore, this [objection] does not constitute a refutation of the partlessness [of atoms].
Furthermore, it is not possible for there to be a division without the loss of that which is being divided; therefore, the state of having dissolution as its end is not tenable.

Moreover, in the case of infinite regress, because the parts of substances would be infinite in each instance, there would be no perception of differences in magnitude or of weight, and the part and the whole would possess identical magnitudes, due to the division of the atom from its own parts.
"Upwards," thus [it is said]. //25//
As for this which you maintain—relying on the intellect—that objects of the intellect exist, these are false cognitions;
for if they were cognitions of reality, the true nature of the objects of the intellect would be perceived upon their analysis by the intellect.

[Nyāyasūtra 4.2.26: But because the true nature of entities is not perceived through analysis by the intellect, it is not perceived, just as the existence of a cloth is not perceived when the threads are pulled away.
Just as when each individual thread is analyzed—thinking "this is a thread, this is a thread"—no distinct entity whatsoever is perceived that could be the object of the cognition of a cloth;
since its true nature is not perceived, the cognition of a cloth occurring in the absence of such an object is a false cognition (mithyābuddhi), and so it is in all cases. //26//
It is not a valid reason because it is contradictory.
If there is an analytical investigation of entities by means of the intellect, there is no non-perception of the true nature of all entities;
if, on the other hand, there is non-perception of the true nature of all entities, there is no analytical investigation of entities by means of the intellect.
Thus, the claim that there is both an analytical investigation of entities by means of the intellect and a non-perception of their true nature is contradictory.
And [the claim that] there is no perception of the true nature [of things] is contradicted.
As it has been said: "In this way, the consequence of an infinite regress of parts and wholes would follow until the final dissolution. (27)
Because it has that as its substratum, there is no separate apprehension.

An effect-substance (kāryadravya) rests upon its cause-substances (kāraṇadravya) and is not perceived separately from those causes; for if it were otherwise, there would be a separate apprehension [of them].
Wherever the relationship of support and supported does not exist, there is a separate apprehension.
However, through the discernment by the intellect, there is a separate apprehension of entities even among atoms that transcend the senses;
for that which is grasped by the sense organ, when being discerned by this intellect, is seen as something else. // 28 //
And because the comprehension of an object occurs through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

The realization of the true nature of things through the discernment of the intellect consists in knowing what exists and how it exists, and what does not exist and how it does not exist; all of this is established through the apprehension of valid means of cognition (pramāṇa),
and that apprehension by means of valid cognition is itself the discernment of things by the intellect.
By that [means of knowledge], all treatises, all actions, and all the worldly dealings of embodied beings are pervaded.
For one who investigates determines through the intellect, "this exists" and "this does not exist"; thus, there is no impossibility regarding the existence of all things. // 29 //
NyS 4.2.30: [The non-existence of the soul is established] by means of the impossibility and possibility of the means of valid cognition.
And this being the case, the claim that "everything does not exist" is not tenable; why?
Because of the non-establishment and establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If the statement "everything does not exist" were established by a means of valid cognition, [then everything would exist].
The claim that "everything does not exist" is contradicted.
Furthermore, if no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is tenable,
how can the proof of the statement "everything does not exist" be established?
Now, if establishment occurs without a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), how is it that the [proposition] "everything exists" is not established? // 30 //
This conceit regarding the means of valid cognition and the objects of cognition is like the conceit regarding the objects of a dream.

Just as in a dream objects do not exist and yet there is a conceit [of their existence], so too the means of valid cognition and the objects of valid cognition do not exist, and yet there is a conceit of means and objects of valid cognition. // 31 //
Or rather, it is like an illusion, a city of Gandharvas, or a mirage.
NyS 4.2.33: There is no proof because of the absence of a reason.

There is no reason why the conceit regarding the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge at the end of a dream should be like the conceit regarding objects [in a dream], and not like the perception of objects at the end of the waking state.
Due to the absence of a reason, [the opponent's position] is unestablished.
Furthermore, there is likewise an absence of a reason for the claim that non-existent objects are perceived at the end of a dream.
If it is argued that [objects do not exist] because they are not perceived upon awakening, we reply:
there is no negation [of their existence] because objects are perceived during the state of awakening.
If you mean that objects do not exist in a dream because they are not perceived upon awakening, [we respond as follows].
In that case, these objects which are perceived by one who has awakened [from sleep] exist because they are perceived;
for the efficacy of a reason lies in its contrapositive.
When existence is established through perception, non-existence is proven through non-perception.
But if there is an absence in both ways, non-apprehension has no efficacy,
as in the case where color is not seen due to the absence of a lamp; in that situation, the absence is established by means of a presence.
Regarding the conceptualization within a dream, a statement of the reason must be provided.
By saying "like the conceit regarding objects in a dream," the reason for the conceptualization within a dream must be stated.
Some dreams are accompanied by fear.
One [dream] is accompanied by joy,
another is the opposite of both,
and sometimes one does not see a dream at all.
But for one who possesses a causal basis, the occurrence of conceptual construction arises from the conceptual differentiation of that causal basis regarding the conceit of dream-objects. // 33 //
And the conceit regarding the objects of a dream is like memory and conceptualization.
The object [of cognition] has been previously perceived;

just as memory and conceptualization have previously perceived objects and are not capable of denying them, so too the apprehension of objects in a dream has a previously perceived object and is not capable of denying it.
[The word *kalpate* means:
Thus, the state of dreaming, which has its objects perceived [within itself], is analogous to the waking state.
For it is the very same person who, while asleep, sees a dream, who—upon waking—recalls those dream-visions, thinking, "I saw this."
In that regard, the determination that the conceit regarding dream objects is false arises by virtue of the waking state's cognitive function (*buddhivṛtti*).
Furthermore, when there is a subsequent recognition (*pratisandhāna*), this determination—that the conceit regarding dream objects is false—arises by virtue of the waking person's cognitive function.
However, if there were no distinction between the two states, the means of proof would be redundant.

For one for whom there is no distinction between the states of dreaming and waking, the proof that "it is like the conceit regarding objects in a dream" is useless, because its very basis has been rejected. Furthermore, the determination that "this is that" when it is not that depends upon a primary substratum; for example, the determination that "this is a person" in regard to a post that is not a person.
That [cognition] has the primary object as its basis;
for indeed, when a person is not perceived, there can be no determination that "this is a person" regarding what is not a person.
Likewise, the determination regarding an object in a dream—such as "I saw an elephant" or "I saw a mountain"—must likewise have the primary object as its basis. 34.
And this being the case:
"The destruction of false perception results from the knowledge of reality, just as the disappearance of the conceit regarding objects in a dream occurs upon waking. (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.35)

The determination that "this is a person" with respect to a post is a false perception (*mithyopalabdhi*), being a cognition of something as what it is not (*atasmiṃs tad iti jñāna*). The determination that "this is a post" with respect to a post is knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
And by means of knowledge of reality, false perception is sublated.
The object does not consist of the common characteristics of a post or a person.

Just as, upon awakening, the misconception regarding dream objects is sublated by the mental state of knowledge, but the object itself— characterized by its common features— is not [sublated], so too, in the case of illusions, cities of Gandharvas, and mirages, those cognitions which determine "that is this" (where it is not) are likewise destroyed through the destruction of false perception by means of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
It is not a negation of the object.
Furthermore, there is false cognition regarding illusions and the like because of their material cause (*upādāna*).
Having taken as a material cause a substance that resembles the thing to be manifested, one who possesses the means produces a false determination in another; that is an illusion (*māyā*).

In the case of frost and similar phenomena, when they are arranged in a formation resembling a city, the cognition of a "city" arises from a distance; in the absence of such an arrangement, that cognition does not occur.

Similarly, when the rays of the sun are mixed with terrestrial heat and are flickering, the cognition of "water" arises due to the perception of common features; for one standing nearby, this cognition does not occur in the absence of those features.

Since false cognition occurs at some time, in some place, and for someone because of the existence [of an object], it is not without a cause. Furthermore, a duality of cognitions is observed between the one who employs the illusion and another person,
as in the case of a city of Gandharvas or a mirage seen from afar or nearby.
And [this] regarding the object of a dream for one who has just woken from deep sleep is not tenable if everything were non-existent, indefinable, and devoid of self-nature. // 35 //
And it is so with cognition as well, because the existence of its cause is perceived.
And there is no refutation of false cognition, just as there is none of the object;
why? Because its cause is perceived and its existence is perceived.
For the objective basis of false cognition is indeed perceived, and the false cognition itself, having arisen within each individual, is apprehended because it is experienced;
therefore, false cognition also exists. // 36 //
And because of the distinction between the real and the primary, the twofold nature of false cognition is established.

The reality is "it is a post" or "it is primordial matter (pradhāna)"; however, because the reality and the primary object are not excluded from one another, a false cognition arises— such as "it is a man at the post"— due to the perception of their commonality.

Thus, just as there is the cognition of a "crane" regarding a banner and the cognition of a "pigeon" regarding a clod of earth, there is no coexistence of false cognitions regarding the same object, because their determination is based on the apprehension of specific common features (sāmānya).
However, for one for whom everything is soulless (nirātmaka) and indefinable (nirupākhya), such a coexistence [of contradictory cognitions] would necessarily follow.

Furthermore, regarding objects of cognition such as odor, the cognitions of odor and so forth that are considered erroneous actually become cognitions of reality (*tattva-buddhi*) themselves, because there is no grasping of a universal (*sāmānya*) between the reality and the predominant [quality].
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that the cognitions of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are false. // 37 //
It has been stated that the cessation of egoism results from the knowledge of reality regarding the causes of the defects.
Now, how does this knowledge of reality arise? [Nyāyasūtra 4.2.38:
From the practice of a specific form of meditative concentration.
That [state], however, is the conjunction of the mind— which has been withdrawn from the senses and is being held steady by a sustaining effort— with the self,
characterized by the desire to know reality.
For when that [conjunction] exists, cognitions do not arise with respect to the objects of the senses.
Through the power of that practice, the cognition of reality arises. // 38 //
Regarding what was stated— "For when that [mind] exists, cognitions do not arise with respect to the sense objects"—
this is not so, because of the intensity of a particular object (NyS 4.2.39).
This is not tenable because cognition arises even for one who does not desire it.
Why? Because of the intensity of the specific object.
It is observed that cognition arises even for one who does not wish to perceive it, as in the case of the sound of thunder and the like.
In that case, a distinction in meditative concentration is not tenable. // 39 //
And because [the activity] is instigated by hunger and other such factors.
Since cognitions arise even against one's will due to hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and diseases, therefore the attainment of one-pointedness is impossible. // 40 //
Let this be granted—that there is emergence from concentration, the cause of emergence, and that which is antagonistic to concentration;
however, when these exist—NyS 4.2.41:
their arising occurs due to the connection with the fruits of previous actions.

The discernment of phenomena (*dharmapraviveka*)— which is the cause for the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), accumulated through actions performed in previous lives and characterized by the continuity of its fruit— is the capacity for the practice of yoga; for if practice were fruitless, people would not take care to engage in it.
For the power of practice is indeed observed among worldly activities. (41)
And for the purpose of avoiding obstacles:
*Nyāyasūtra* 4.2.42: "Instruction on the practice of yoga in forests, caves, on sandy banks, and so forth."
The quality (*dharma*) produced by the practice of yoga persists even in another birth.

When that quality, which is the cause of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), reaches its highest degree of accumulation—namely, when there is an intense cultivation of meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—the knowledge of reality arises.

Furthermore, the suppression of specific objects by means of concentration is observed in common experience, as a worldly person says: "I did not hear this; I did not know this; my mind was elsewhere. (42)
If it is granted that cognition arises even against one's will due to the intensity of a particular object,
then the same consequence would follow regarding liberation as well.
Even for one who is liberated, cognitions might arise due to the power of external objects. // 43 //
No, because what has already been established necessarily occurs.

When the body, which is the substratum for movement, the sense organs, and their objects, has been produced through the power of karma, the arising of cognitions necessarily occurs because [the external object] serves as its instrumental cause.

Furthermore, even though an external object may be powerful, it is not capable of producing a cognition in the self; rather, its capacity for producing cognition is observed to exist only through its conjunction with a sense organ. // 44 //
And the absence of that [suffering] occurs in liberation.

Since the body and sense organs, which serve as the substratum for the causes of cognition, cease to exist due to the absence of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), they are non-existent in the state of liberation (*apavarga*).
Therefore, what was stated— that "the same undesirable consequence would apply even in liberation"— is incorrect.
Therefore, liberation (*apavarga*) is the release from all suffering.
Since in liberation the seed of all suffering and the locus of all suffering are severed, liberation is the freedom from every form of suffering;
for suffering does not arise when it is without seed and without locus. // 45 //
For that purpose, there is the refinement of the self through restraint (*yama*) and observance (*niyama*), and through the means of the internal rules of yoga.

For the attainment of that liberation, there is the refinement of the self through restraint (*yama*) and observance (*niyama*). Restraint is the means for achieving dharma common to all those in the stages of life (*āśrama*), whereas observance is specific to each.
Furthermore, self-purification consists in the abandonment of unwholesome states (*adharma*) and the accumulation of wholesome states (*dharma*).
The internal method of practice is to be understood from the *Yogaśāstra*;
it consists, moreover, of austerity (*tapas*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and fixed attention (*dhāraṇā*).
The practice of discernment regarding the objects of the senses is for the purpose of abandoning attachment and aversion;
the means, however, is the prescribed method of the practitioner of yoga (yogācāra). // 46 //
The repeated practice of grasping knowledge and engaging in discussion with those who possess that knowledge.

"For that purpose" refers to what has been previously mentioned. "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is that by which something is known; it is the scripture of the science of the Self (*ātmavidyā*). Its "acquisition" (*grahaṇa*) consists of study and retention;
its "practice" (*abhyāsa*) consists of constant application, namely study, hearing, and reflection.
"Engaging in discussion with those who possess that knowledge" is for the sake of maturing one's wisdom;

maturation, moreover, consists of the cutting away of doubt, the comprehension of previously unknown objects, and the acceptance of what has been determined. Discussion conducted according to established rules is "saṃvāda. (47)
The statement "a discussion with those possessing that knowledge" is analyzed as having an undivided meaning:
"One should approach such a person [for discussion] along with disciples, teachers, fellow students, and those seeking excellence, provided they are free from malice. (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.48)
This has been explained according to its definitive meaning by the literal recitation itself. // 48 //

And if one should think that the adoption of a position and its counter-position is unfavorable to the opponent—[then it is not so], for even if [the proponent] lacks a counter-position, it is [still valid] when there is a purpose and a desire [for the truth]. (NyS 4.2.49)
The phrase "he should approach him" carries over [from the previous verse].

Desiring to acquire wisdom from another, one should purify one's own philosophical system by demonstrating a desire to know reality, without establishing one's own position on a fixed basis; for the views of various teachers are mutually contradictory. (49)

Furthermore, some deviate from logic due to attachment to their own side; regarding this: NyS 4.2.50: "Wrangling (jalpa) and cavil (vitaṇḍā) are for the purpose of protecting the determination of truth, like the covering of thorny branches for the protection of the growth of seeds."
This [is for] those who have not yet produced the knowledge of reality, whose defects are not yet abandoned, and who are striving for that purpose. // 50 //

And for one who is being treated with contempt by another due to [the latter's] knowledge, world-weariness, and so forth—[this is] "discourse after having entered into a dispute" (vigṛhya-kathana) with those two.
NyS_4.2.51: [This is] discourse after having entered into a dispute with those two.
"Having engaged in debate" means with the desire for victory, not with the desire to know the truth;
this [debate] is for the sake of protecting one's learning, not for the sake of gain, honor, or fame. // 51 //
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Nyāyabhāṣya of the venerable Vātsyāyana. 4.
The Nyāya Darśana;
now begins the first Āhnika of the fifth Adhyāya.
It has been stated in brief that "the multiplicity of *jātis* arises from the variations in opposition based on similarity and dissimilarity";
this is now analyzed in detail: these *jātis*, indeed, constitute twenty-four refutations when a probative reason (*sthāpanāhetu*) is employed. They are:

similarity (*sādharmya*), dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), superiority (*utkarṣa*), inferiority (*apakarṣa*), the eulogized (*varṇya*), the non-eulogized (*avarṇya*), variation (*vikalpa*), the attainable (*sādhyaprāpti*), the unattainable (*aprāpti*), the consequence (*prasaṅga*), the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*), non-origination (*anutpatti*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), the topic (*prakaraṇa*), the non-reason (*ahetu*), presumption (*arthāpatti*), non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*), occurrence (*upapatti*), perception (*upalabdhi*), non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), the eternal (*nitya*), the non-eternal (*anitya*), and the effect (*kārya*). These are the *samās* (equalities). NyS 5.1.1.
An opposition based on similarity that is not distinguished from the original probans is "balancing the similar" (*sādharmyasama*).
We shall provide examples of this non-distinction in various places.
In the same way, "balancing the dissimilar" (*vaidharmyasama*) and the others are also to be defined. //1//
The definition, however, is as follows:

NyS 5.1.2: When a conclusion has been drawn through similarity or dissimilarity, the two sophistries known as *sādharmya-sama* (balancing the similarity) and *vaidharmya-sama* (balancing the dissimilarity) arise from the alleged occurrence of the opposite of that property.

When a conclusion is drawn through similarity, the refutation by means of similarity itself—which consists in the demonstration of the opposite of the property to be proved—is called *sādharmyasama* (balancing the similarity), provided it is not distinguished from the original argument. For example:
"The self possesses action, because it is endowed with qualities that are the cause of action in a substance."
A substance, such as a clod of earth, is possessed of action because it is endowed with qualities that are the causes of action;
and the self is likewise; therefore, the self is possessed of action.
When it has been thus established, the opponent objects by means of similarity alone: "The self is inactive because an all-pervading substance is inactive;
and space is both all-pervading and inactive, and so too is the self."
Therefore, it is inactive.
Nor is there any specific reason why, because of its similarity to that which possesses action, it must itself possess action.
Furthermore, it is not the case that [the soul] is inactive simply because of a similarity in the absence of action;
for since there is no specific reason [for such a conclusion], this constitutes a "balancing of the similar" (*sādharmyasama*) refutation.
Now, as for the "balancing of the dissimilar" (*vaidharmyasama*): a clod of earth is seen to be limited and endowed with qualities that cause action, yet the self is not like that.
Therefore, it is not the case that [the soul] possesses action like a clod of earth.

Nor is there any specific reason why, because of its similarity to that which possesses action, it must possess action, rather than being actionless due to its dissimilarity to that which possesses action; since there is no specific reason [to prefer one over the other], this is the "balancing the heterogeneity" (vaidharmyasama) fallacy.
And the conclusion by way of dissimilarity: the self is inactive because it is all-pervading;
a substance possessing activity is seen to be non-pervasive, as for example a clod of earth, and the self is not like that.

Therefore, [the opponent argues] it is inactive. This is an objection based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa pratyavasthānam*): the substance space (*ākāśa*) is seen to be inactive while being devoid of qualities that cause action, yet the self (*ātman*) is not like that.
Therefore, it is not devoid of action.

Nor is there a specific reason [to conclude] that because of its dissimilarity to that which possesses action, it must be devoid of action, rather than—because of its dissimilarity to that which is devoid of action—it must possess action; since there is no specific reason [for either], this is "balancing the dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyasama*).
Now, as for "balancing the similarity" (*sādharmyasama*): a clod of earth is seen to possess action and to be endowed with qualities that are the causes of action.
Likewise, the self [is] so;
therefore, it possesses action.

And there is no specific reason [to conclude] that it is inactive because of its dissimilarity to that which possesses action, rather than being active because of its similarity to that which possesses action. Due to the absence of a specific reason, this is the "balancing the similarity" (sādharmyasama) fallacy.
The answer to these two is as follows:
Nyāyasūtra 5.1.3: Its establishment is like the establishment of a cow through the universal "cowness."

If the proof of the probandum were asserted merely through similarity or merely through dissimilarity, there would be a lack of definitive certainty; however, that [certainty] is not possible when the specific property is taken into account. For instance, a cow is established as such because of its similarity to cows, due to the specific universal of "cowness" (*gotva*).
But it is not from the connection with the dewlap and so forth;
rather, a cow is established solely through "cowness" (*gotva*) because of its dissimilarity to horses and the like, and not from distinctions such as qualities (*guṇa*).
This has already been explained in the section on the members [of a syllogism]:
"Because the means of valid cognition are interconnected, their joint performance of a single purpose constitutes a 'sentence' (vākya).
Indeed, this lack of settled order is based upon fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa).

Nyāyasūtra 5.1.4: Through the variation of properties in the subject and the example, and because both are to be proven, there arise the fallacies of *utkarṣasama*, *apakarṣasama*, *varṇyasama*, *avarṇyasama*, *vikalpasama*, and *sādhyasama*.
The "balancing by addition" (*utkarṣasama*) occurs when one attempts to attach a property of the example to the subject of the thesis.

For instance: "If the self possesses action because it is endowed with the quality that is the cause of action, like a clod of earth, then it follows that, just like the clod of earth, it must also possess touch."
If, on the other hand, it does not possess tangibility, then like a clod of earth, it would likewise not possess action;
or else, a distinction must be stated in the case of the opposite.
*Apakarṣasama* (the equalization by subtraction) is the objection that, based on the example, one points out the absence of the property to be proven [in the subject]. For instance:
"A clod of earth is indeed seen to possess action and to be non-omnipresent; [is the self likewise seen to be non-omnipresent? (p. 1110).
Granted that the self may be active yet non-omnipresent,
or conversely, a distinction must be stated;
it is to be proclaimed and praised, whereas by the opposite [it would be] unpraiseworthy.
These two, which reverse the properties of the probandum and the example, are the "equal by description" (*varṇyasama*) and the "equal by non-description" (*avarṇyasama*).

When one points out a discrepancy in the property to be proven based on a variation in another property within an example that is already endowed with the property of proof, it is the "equal by alternative" (*vikalpasama*).
For instance, some thing endowed with the quality of being a cause of action is heavy, such as a clod of earth.
Just as air is somewhat light,
so too some things, being endowed with the quality that is the cause of action, may possess action, like a clod of earth;
while some things, like the self, are devoid of action.
Or rather, a distinction must be stated:

the property (dharma) that is connected with the power of the members [of the syllogism], such as the reason (hetu), is the probandum (sādhya); one who applies that [property] to the example commits the fallacy of "equivalence to the probandum" (sādhyasama).
If the self is like a clod of earth,
then it follows that the clod of earth is like the self;
and since this self is to be proven as possessing activity, the clod of earth must likewise be proven [to possess activity].
If, however, it is not so, then the self is not like a clod of earth. //4//
The reply to these is: "Because the establishment of the conclusion follows from some similarity, there is no refutation on account of dissimilarity. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.5)
The concealment of what has been established is impossible.
Furthermore, an established [object] serves as an analogy on account of some common property, such as "as is a cow, so is a gavaya.
[End of quotation. p.1114
In that case, it is not possible to raise an objection regarding a discrepancy in the properties (*dharma-vikalpa*) between the cow and the gavaya.

Likewise, when the probans (*sādhaka-dharma*) is endowed with the efficacy of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and other factors, it is not possible to state a refutation based on a discrepancy in the properties between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the example due to their dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). //5//
And because the example is established through the extension of the property to be proven.
Where there is a consensus of understanding among worldly investigators, by that [consensus] the non-erroneous object is extended [by analogy] for the purpose of making it known.
Thus, since the extension of the probandum is established in the example, the status of being a probandum is untenable [in the case of the subject]. //6//

NyS 5.1.7: Because a reason is indistinguishable whether it reaches the probandum or does not reach it—since it cannot establish the conclusion if it does not reach it—the two [objections] based on reaching and non-reaching are called *prāptisama* and *aprāptisama*.
Does the reason establish the probandum by reaching it, or without reaching it?
First, it does not establish it by reaching it, because there is no distinction in their state once they have reached one another;
when two things already exist and have reached each other, which of them is the establisher and which is the established?
It does not exist without reaching the object to be accomplished; a lamp does not illuminate without having reached it.
To counter-argue on the basis of this "reaching" is the "equivalence by reaching" (prāptisama).
The "balancing by non-attainment" (aprāptisama) is an objection based on non-attainment. //7//
The answer to these two is as follows:
NyS 5.1.8: There is no prohibition [of the production of sound] because we observe the production of jars and other objects, and because [sound] is produced by pressing and by sorcery (abhicāra).

Indeed, the negation [of the instrument] is untenable in both ways: for the agent, the instrument, and the locus produce the effect, such as a jar from clay, by reaching it; and furthermore, it is observed that in the case of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), when pain is inflicted, the means of accomplishment functions without reaching [the object]. //8//

NyS 5.1.9: Because of the failure to state the reason for the example and because of the counter-objection by means of a counter-example, there are the two [futile rejoinders] known as *prasaṅgasama* and *pratidṛṣṭāntasama*.
The "balancing by consequence" (*prasaṅgasama*) refutation is an objection raised on the grounds that the means of proof for the proof itself must also be stated.
[For example: "A clod of earth possesses action because it is endowed with the quality that is the cause of action"—this reason is not stated;
yet there can be no establishment [of a point] without a reason.
The "balancing by a counter-example" (*pratidṛṣṭāntasama*) is an objection based on a counter-example.

When it is stated, "The self possesses action because it is endowed with qualities that are causes of action, like a clod of earth," a counter-example is adduced: "Space is seen to be devoid of action despite being endowed with qualities that are causes of action.
But what quality in space is a cause of action?
Conjunction with air depends upon a latent impression (saṃskāra), like the conjunction between air and a tree. //9//
The answer to these two is as follows:
*Nyāyasūtra* 5.1.10: "Just as there is the cessation of the consequence regarding the material cause of a lamp, so too is there the cessation of that [consequence]."
First, when asked this, he ought to say: who takes up a lamp, and for what purpose?
"Desiring to see, for the purpose of seeing what is visible.
Now, why do those desiring to see a lamp not take up another lamp?
For a lamp is seen even without another lamp.
In that case, the taking up of a lamp for the purpose of seeing would be useless.
Now, for what purpose is the example stated?
It is for the purpose of making known that which is not yet known.
Now, for what purpose is the indication of the cause taught in the case of the example?
If it is for the sake of making it known, then the example has already been made known.
Indeed, "an example (dṛṣṭānta) is that object regarding which there is a consensus of understanding among ordinary people and experts";
the statement of a reason for the purpose of making that known is useless—this is the response to the *prasaṅgasama* [balancing the consequence] objection. //10//
Now, the response to the "counter-example" (pratidṛṣṭāntasama) fallacy: NyS 5.1.11: And when a counter-example functions as a reason, the [original] example is not without a reason.
By one who states a counter-example (pratidṛṣṭānta), no specific reason (viśeṣahetu) is indicated— namely, that in this manner the counter-example is the prover and not the [original] example.
Thus, when the counter-example functions as the reason, it follows that the example is not a non-reason (ahetu).
And how could that [reason] not be "without a cause"?
[It would be so] if it were unrefuted and established [as a valid reason]. //11//
NyS 5.1.12: "The 'equalizing by non-arising' (anutpattisama) [occurs] because of the absence of a cause prior to the arising [of the effect]."

When it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar," another person says: "Prior to its production, while the sound has not yet arisen, the state of following immediately upon effort—which is the cause of impermanence—is absent;
therefore, by the absence of that [cause], permanence is obtained, and for that which is permanent, there is no production."
The "balancing by non-arising" (anutpattisama) is an opposition based on non-arising. //12//
The answer to this is: "Because that which has arisen exists in such a manner, and because the cause is established, there is no negation of the cause. (NyS 5.1.13)
"Because it exists as such once produced":
for this sound indeed comes to be as "produced";
prior to its production, the sound itself does not exist.

Since sound exists once it has arisen, the fact that sound—which already exists—is produced immediately following effort is established as the cause of its impermanence; therefore, because this causal basis is established, the objection that "prior to its production there is an absence of a cause" is untenable. //13//

NyS 5.1.14: When the general property and the example are equally perceptible by the senses, [the fallacy] "balancing the doubt" (saṃśayasama) occurs because of the commonality of both permanence and impermanence.

When the reason "sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort, like a pot" has been stated, one objects by way of doubt: "Even though it follows immediately upon effort, it possesses the common property of being perceptible by the senses (*aindriyakatva*) with respect to the eternal universal (*sāmānya*);
and it also possesses that same property with respect to the impermanent pot."
Therefore, because of the commonality of both permanence and impermanence, doubt does not cease. //14//
The answer to this is:

NyS 5.1.15: "When there is doubt due to similarity, there is no doubt due to dissimilarity; or, if there were doubt in both cases, it would lead to an infinite regress of doubt. Furthermore, since permanence is not admitted, there is no refutation of the universal.
When the object is determined as 'a person' based on a particular characteristic, namely dissimilarity,"
Doubt does not find an opportunity based on the similarity between a post and a person;

likewise, when the impermanence of sound is determined through its dissimilarity—the specific property of being produced immediately after an effort—doubt does not find an opportunity based on the similarity between the permanent and the impermanent. If it were to find such an opportunity, [it would be untenable].

Consequently, because the similarity between a post and a person would not be excluded, there would be perpetual doubt. Furthermore, when a specific feature is being perceived, it is not accepted that similarity alone is the cause of doubt;
for when the specific features of a person are being perceived, the similarity between a post and a person does not become a cause of doubt. //15//
NyS 5.1.16: The "neutralized" (prakaraṇasama) [reason] is that which establishes the subject matter through similarity to both sides.
The process (*prakriyā*) is the engagement of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) due to their similarity (*sādharmya*) through both the eternal and the non-eternal.

One person advances the thesis: "Sound is non-eternal because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar"; and the second person advances the counter-thesis by way of similarity with the eternal: "Sound is eternal because it is audible, like the nature of sound (*śabdatva*)."

This being the case, when the reason "because it follows immediately upon effort" is stated by way of similarity with the impermanent, it does not transcend the context; and because it does not transcend the context, it does not transcend the lack of a definitive conclusion.
This is the same even when the reason is stated by way of similarity with the permanent.
This counter-position, which does not go beyond the original context, is *prakaraṇasama*.
This is the same even in the case of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*);
because the process of proof is established through the dissimilarity to both [sides], it is called *prakaraṇasama*. //16//
The answer to this is:

"Since the establishment of the subject matter (*prakaraṇa*) occurs through a counter-position, the negation [of that position] is untenable, because the counter-position is logically established. (NyS 5.1.17)
By one who asserts that the establishment of the process occurs through similarity to both, the establishment of the process from the counter-position is effectively stated.
If there is similarity to both, then one of the two is the counter-position; this being so, the counter-position becomes logically established.
The negation is untenable because of the establishment of the counter-position;
for if the establishment of the counter-position occurs, the negation does not occur,
and if the establishment of the negation occurs, the counter-position does not occur.

"The establishment of the counter-argument and the establishment of the refutation are mutually contradictory. Furthermore, the progression [of the debate] is not established due to the lack of determination of the truth; for the debate concludes upon the opposite [determination], since it is only when there is a determination of the truth that the debate comes to an end. //17//
NyS 5.1.18: Because the reason is not established in the three times, there is the "equal to the non-reason" (ahetusama).
The cause is the means of proof;
it must exist either before, after, or simultaneously with that which is to be proven.
If the means of proof exists first, [then...]
If the probandum does not exist, of what is there a proof?
Or if it exists later,
when the proof does not yet exist, of what is this the probandum?

Now, if the probandum and the proof were established simultaneously, then between two things that exist at the same time, which would be the proof of which, and which would be the probandum of which? Thus, the reason is not distinguished from what is not a reason. Opposition based on this similarity with what is not a reason is "balancing the non-reason" (*ahetusama*). //18//
The answer to this is:
"Because the probandum is established by means of the reason, there is no non-establishment [of the reason] across the three times. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.19)
There is no failure to establish [the existence of things] across the three times.
Why? Because the probandum is established by means of the reason.
Both the production of that which is to be produced and the cognition of that which is to be known are observed to arise from a cause.
Thus, this great object of direct perception serves as the illustrative example (*udāharaṇa*).

As for what was said—that if the probandum (*sādhya*) does not exist, of what is there a proof (*sādhana*)?—it is of that which is being produced (*nirvartya*) and that which is being made known (*vijñāpya*). //19//
And because a negation is impossible, there is no negation of that which is to be negated.
Whether the negation occurs before, after, or simultaneously [with the probans], it is not tenable;
since the negation itself is untenable, the reason for the establishment [of the thesis] is proven. //20//
Nyāyasūtra 5.1.21: Arthāpattisama (the equal by implication) occurs when the opponent's position is established through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

When the thesis has been established that "sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar," the *arthāpattisama* (balancing the implication) occurs for one who seeks to prove the opposite side by means of an implication (*arthāpatti*).

If it is argued that sound is impermanent due to its similarity with the impermanent in terms of following immediately upon effort, then it follows by implication that it must be permanent due to its similarity with the permanent.
And it possesses a commonality with the eternal, namely, the quality of being intangible. //21//
The answer to this is:

NyS 5.1.22: Since it has not been stated, the occurrence of the defeat of one's own position through implication (arthāpatti) does not follow; for implication is non-conclusive because it has not been stated.
For one who asserts that "even without explicitly stating the capacity [of a reason], it follows by implication," the loss of one's own position is established because [the reason] was not stated;
for when the non-eternal position is proven, the loss of the eternal position follows by implication. Furthermore, such an implication is inconclusive.
This presumption (*arthāpatti*) is equal for both sides:

if sound is eternal because it possesses the property of being intangible like space due to its similarity with what is eternal, it follows by implication that it is non-eternal because it possesses the property of arising immediately after an effort due to its similarity with what is non-eternal.
Nor does this constitute a definitive presumption based solely on the mere opposite.
Indeed, it does not follow as a matter of course that because there is a falling of a solid stone, there is an absence of falling for liquid water. //22//

NyS 5.1.23: "The equalization based on the occurrence of existence" [is the sophistical rejoinder] because, if there were no distinction due to the occurrence of a single property, it would follow that everything is non-distinct.

If one property—namely, the state of occurring immediately after an effort—is applicable to both sound and a jar, then since there is no distinction between the two regarding their impermanence, it would follow that everything is without distinction.
How so? Because [the property] is equally applicable to all existing things.

The counter-argument that "one property, namely existence, applies to everything, and because existence applies [equally], it follows that there is no distinction between all things" is the *aviśeṣasama* (balancing the non-distinction). //23//
The answer to this is: "There is no [valid] negation because that property is applicable in some cases and inapplicable in others. (NyS 5.1.24)

Just as, because the single property of being produced immediately after effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is established for both the probandum and the example, "impermanence" is a further property that constitutes their non-difference;
it is not so with all entities, for there is no other property that serves as the cause for the establishment of their existence by virtue of which they could be non-different.
Now, if it is thought that impermanence itself would be another property (*dharmāntara*) serving as the cause for the existence of entities everywhere,
then, when such a conception is indeed entertained, the thesis (*pakṣa*) follows that "all entities are impermanent because their existence is established.
In that case, there is no example other than the very meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*).
Furthermore, there is no reason (*hetu*) that lacks an example (*anudāharaṇa*).
Moreover, it is untenable for a single part of the thesis (*pratijñaikadeśa*) to serve as the example; [it is untenable for a part of the thesis... p.1135.
For that which is to be proven cannot serve as an example.
Furthermore, since that which exists possesses both the states of being eternal and non-eternal, the property of non-eternality is untenable.
Therefore, because the existence [of the probandum] is established, it would follow that all things are indistinguishable; thus, this statement is devoid of meaning.
By stating that "impermanence follows from the establishment of the existence of all entities," the impermanence of sound is admitted; therefore, the denial [of its impermanence] is untenable. //24//
NyS 5.1.25: "Equal to the proof" (upapattisama) occurs because the reasons for both [sides] are equally applicable.

If a cause for the non-eternality of sound is established, such that sound is non-eternal, then a cause for its eternality—its intangibility—is also established, and thus its eternality is likewise established.
To counter-argue by means of the establishment of causes for both non-eternality and eternality is the "balancing of the reason" (*upapattisama*).
The answer to this is:
NyS 5.1.26: There is no refutation [of the opponent's position] because their logical justification has been admitted.
By stating "because both causes are established," the establishment of the cause of impermanence is not being denied;
for if it were denied, there would be no establishment of both causes.
By the statement that both causes are established, the establishment of the cause of impermanence is admitted.
The negation is untenable because it has been permitted;
if you say that the negation is due to contradiction, then the contradiction is the same [for both sides].
If it is argued that by stating a contradiction—namely, the consequence that a single entity would be both eternal and non-eternal—one has stated a "refutation" (pratiṣedha), [we reply:
the contradiction is equal for both one's own position and the opponent's position; and that [contradiction] is not a proof for either side. //26//
NyS 5.1.27: The "balancing by perception" (upalabdhisama) occurs because [the probandum] is perceived even in the absence of the stated cause.

Even in the absence of the stated cause of impermanence—namely, being produced immediately after an effort—the impermanence of sound arising from the snapping of a tree branch due to the impact of the wind is observed.

1138] Objection based on the observation of the property to be proven (the *sādhyadharma*) despite the absence of the stated probans (*sādhana*) is called "balancing the perception" (*upalabdhisama*). //27//
The answer to this is:
"There is no refutation [of our position], because that property can also arise from another cause" (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.28).
By stating "because it follows immediately after an effort," the production [of sound] from a cause is being asserted, not a necessary restriction of the effect to that specific cause.
And if the impermanence of sound is established even when it is produced from another cause, [then the argument holds].
What is it that is being negated here? //28//
It is not the case that a sound which exists prior to its utterance is unperceived; why?
Because no such obscuring factor as a covering is perceived.

Just as there is non-perception of existing objects like water due to the presence of a covering or similar obstacle, it is not so with sound, for its non-perception is not caused by an obscuring factor such as a covering.
This [non-apprehension] would be apprehended as the cause for the non-apprehension of that [sound], just like water and so forth; however, it is not apprehended.
Therefore, sound is the opposite of water and such things, even though it is not being perceived.

(Nyāyasūtra 5.1.29) "When the absence [of a thing] is established through the non-perception of its perception, the rejoinder based on the possibility of the opposite is 'balancing the non-apprehension' (anupalabdhisama)."
The non-apprehension of those [factors] such as obscurations is not apprehended.
Because it is not apprehended, its non-existence is established by the principle that "what is not perceived does not exist.
Since there is no cause for establishing its non-existence, the opposite—namely, the existence of those obscurations and so forth—is determined.
Because the opposite of that [reason] is established, the thesis—that "there is no non-perception of an existing sound prior to its utterance"—is not proven.

This reason, "because of the non-perception of an obstruction and so forth," becomes "equal to non-perception" (*anupalabdhisama*) when it is countered by the non-perception of the obstruction itself and the non-perception of the non-perception of the obstruction. //29//
The answer to this is:
"Because non-apprehension is of the nature of non-apprehension, it is not a valid reason. (NyS 5.1.30)
The non-perception of obstructions and so forth does not exist, because [it itself] is unperceived; thus, it is not a valid reason. Why? Because non-perception has the nature of being unperceived.
Because non-apprehension is merely the absence of apprehension:
whatever exists is the object of apprehension,
and it is by means of apprehension that it is asserted to exist.
That which does not exist is the object of non-apprehension;
it is asserted that what is not apprehended does not exist.

This very non-apprehension, being itself an absence of apprehension due to the non-apprehension of an obstruction and so forth, operates within its own domain when there is no apprehension; yet, while operating within its own domain, it does not negate that domain.
Furthermore, the non-perception of an obstruction and so forth, being unrefuted, is fit to serve as a logical reason (*hetu*).
Obstructions and the like, however, because they exist, are objects of perception;
therefore, there ought to be a perception of them.

That those [obstructing factors] are not perceived is due to the absence of a perception that could establish its own object; because of this non-perception, the object of non-perception is understood—namely, that there are no causes for the non-apprehension of sound such as obstructions.
Furthermore, it is from non-perception that non-perception itself is established.
That is its object. //30//
And because one internally experiences the presence and absence of conceptual cognitions.
The term "without cause" carries over [from the previous sūtra].
Within each body, the presence and absence of various types of cognitions are to be experienced through direct awareness, such as:
"I have a cognition of doubt," or "I do not have a cognition of doubt."
The same applies to the cognitions of perception, inference, scripture, and memory.

This non-apprehension of an obstruction and so forth is the absence of apprehension, which is self-cognized—namely, "I have no apprehension of an obstruction of sound. Thus, the causes for the non-grasping of sound are not perceived.
In this regard, it has been stated that the establishment of non-existence follows from the non-apprehension of that [non-apprehension].
This is not tenable. //31//

NyS 5.1.32: The "balancing by non-eternality" (anityasama) occurs when, because of similarity (sādharmya), a common property is established, leading to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that everything must be non-eternal.

For one who says "sound is impermanent because of its similarity to an impermanent pot," since there is a similarity between the impermanent pot and all entities, it follows that the impermanence of all things results—which is undesirable.
This is called the "balancing of impermanence" (*anityasama*) because it is an opposition based on impermanence. //32//
The answer to this is:
"Because it is not established on the basis of similarity, the negation is not established, since [the negation] possesses similarity with that which is to be negated. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.33)

A "refutation" (pratiṣedha) is a statement consisting of members such as the proposition (pratijñā) that negates the subject-pakṣa; it is characterized by being a counter-position (pratipakṣa). Its similarity with the pakṣa—which is the object to be negated—consists in its possession of the same members, such as the proposition and so forth.
If, on account of this similarity with the impermanent, the non-eternality [of sound] were not established, [then the same would apply to the opponent's case].
Because the similarity [of the probans] is unestablished, the negation is also unestablished, since it too shares a similarity with that which is to be negated. //33//
And since, in the example, a property known through the relationship of probandum and probans serves as the reason, and since that [property] exists in both ways, there is no lack of distinction.
In an example, that property which is known through the relationship of the probandum and the probans is designated as the reason (*hetu*);
and it exists in two ways.
It exists in both ways:
it is similar in some respects and distinct in others.
From the general comes similarity (*sādharmya*), and from the particular comes dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
Thus, the reason (*hetu*) is a specific similarity,
not mere similarity in its undifferentiated form, nor mere dissimilarity.

Relying merely upon similarity and mere dissimilarity, you have stated: "Because of similarity—that is, because of the occurrence of a common property—there follows the undesirable consequence that everything would be non-eternal; therefore, this is the 'balancing of the non-eternal' (anityasama).
This is incorrect.
Furthermore, whatever was said in the refutation of the 'balancing of non-distinction' (aviśeṣasama) should also be understood to apply here. //34//
The "balancing the eternal" (nityasama) [fallacy] occurs because, since the eternal possesses an impermanent state, permanence is established in the impermanent.
It is proposed that sound is impermanent.
Is that impermanence permanent in sound or impermanent? If, first of all, it exists at all times, [then...]

Because the property (dharma) exists at all times, the substratum (dharmī) must also exist at all times; thus, sound is eternal. Alternatively, if it does not exist at all times, then because the property of impermanence is absent, sound is eternal.
Thus, because it is countered by means of permanence, it is the "balancing of permanence" (nityasama). //35//

The answer to this is: NyS 5.1.36: Because the non-eternal nature [of sound] always exists in that which is to be negated, and because non-eternality is established in what is non-eternal, there is no negation [of non-eternality].
When it is stated that "impermanence always exists in the sound which is to be negated," the impermanence of sound is thereby admitted;
and since impermanence is thus established, the negation "sound is not impermanent" is untenable.
If, on the other hand, this is not accepted, [the reason remains unestablished].
Because non-eternality exists eternally, it cannot serve as a logical reason (*hetu*); since there is no such reason, the negation [of sound's eternality] is untenable.
Furthermore, the non-existence of sound due to the cessation of what has arisen constitutes its non-eternality; in that case, the counter-question is untenable.
This inquiry—whether that impermanence exists in sound at all times or not—is untenable.
Why? Because impermanence is the non-existence of sound due to the cessation of what has arisen.
This being the case, there is no distinction between the locus and that which is located therein due to contradiction;
furthermore, because of the opposition between permanence and impermanence,
permanence and impermanence as two attributes of a single substratum (dharmin) are mutually exclusive.
This is not possible.
Regarding that which was stated concerning a single subject (*dharmī*)—
namely, "because permanence exists within impermanence, it is indeed permanent"— this is not tenable.
Therefore, it has been stated that this refers to an object not currently present. //36//
NyS 5.1.37: "The 'balancing of the effect' (kāryasama) occurs because effort has multiple effects."
"Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort.
That which acquires its own existence immediately after effort is indeed something that comes into being after having not existed,
just like an effect such as a jar.
And it is understood that "impermanent" means having come into being, one ceases to exist.
This being the case, the refutation is stated on the grounds that "the effects of effort are manifold":
for instance, the acquisition of their own nature immediately following effort is observed in the case of jars and other such things.
And manifestation is the removal of obstructions for those things that are obstructed.
Therefore, there is no distinction as to whether the sound acquires its own nature immediately after effort or whether it is manifested;
this counter-argument based on the non-distinction of the effect is "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*). //37//
The answer to this is:
NyS 5.1.38: "If there were a difference in the effect, effort would not be the cause, because the causes for non-perception are present."
If there were a difference between the effect [of production] and [the cause], then since the causes of non-perception would be possible, effort would not be the cause for the manifestation of sound.

Where manifestation occurs immediately after effort, there an obstruction as a cause of non-perception is logically possible; and through the removal of that obstruction, the manifestation—characterized by perception—occurs of the object existing immediately after the effort.
... [of that which occurs immediately after effort] ...

however, no cause for the non-perception of sound is established, such that the manifestation of sound—characterized by its perception—would occur through the removal of that [cause] immediately after effort.
Therefore, sound is produced; it is not manifested. //38//
If it is argued that the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), then because of its inconclusiveness, it would fail to establish [the thesis].
And if non-establishment follows from inconclusiveness—then the same fault applies even to the refutation (*pratiṣedha*). (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.39)
The negation is also inconclusive;
because it negates some things while not negating others, it is inconclusive and thus not a proof.
Alternatively, on the position that sound is impermanent, there is no specific reason [to distinguish] between its production immediately after effort and its manifestation.
Even in the case of the position that [sound] is eternal, there is no specific reason [to prefer one view], as the manifestation occurs immediately after effort rather than its production;
thus, this absence of a specific reason is equal for both positions, and consequently, both are inconclusive. //39//
In all cases, it is thus.

In all the reasons for negation, beginning with those based on similarity (*sādharmya*), wherever no distinction is observed, an equal consequence (*sama*) applies to both sides of the argument. //40//
In the counter-refutation of a refutation, there is a fault identical to the fault in the original refutation.

This same fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*), which occurs even in the case of the negation, remains equally applicable even in the case of the negation of that negation. First, there is the initial position (*pakṣa*) of the proponent of the proof (*sādhanavādin*), who establishes: "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort."
The second position is that of the opponent who states the refutation: "Because the effect is manifold due to effort, this is 'balancing the effect' (*kāryasama*).
This is called the "refutation" (*pratiṣedha*).
The third position is that even in this refutation, the fault is the same; this is called "contradiction" (*vipratiṣedha*).
In that refutation of the refutation as well, the same fault applies; namely, the inconclusiveness of the fourth position. //41//
NyS 5.1.42: Having accepted that the refutation is faulty, to then apply the same consequence of faultiness to the counter-refutation is "admission of the opponent's position" (matānujñā).

The fifth position is as follows: having accepted the second position—the negation—as being faulty, and without having remedied it, when the proponent of the refutation (the dūṣaṇavādī) applies the same fault of "inconclusiveness" (anaikāntikatva) to the third position—the negation of the negation (pratiṣedhavipratiṣedha)—then the charge of "accepting the opponent's view" (matānujñā) is incurred. //42//

NyS 5.1.43: When the reason is stated in the conclusion of an argument supported by proof while depending on the characteristics of one's own position, the same fault applies because one accepts the faults of the opponent's position.

In the case of the proponent's position (*sthāpanā*), the fault—"because the effects of effort are manifold"—constitutes a characteristic flaw of the proponent's own position (*svapakṣa*). Why? Because it arises from within his own position.

Thus, while overlooking this flaw that characterizes his own position and failing to extricate it, he—having admitted it—attributes the same applicable flaw to the opponent's position (*parapakṣa*) by asserting, "the same fault applies even to the refutation."

Thus, he points out the reason that the refutation is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). In that case, when there is both the attribution of a fault that is applicable with respect to the definition of one's own position (*svapakṣa*) and the statement of a reason, by this the fault of the opponent’s position (*parapakṣa*) becomes admitted. How so?

Without having removed the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) that was stated [by the opponent] in the passage beginning with "because of the multiplicity of things produced by another's effort," he says: "The same fault applies even to the refutation.
Thus, for one who, having accepted that the proof (sthāpanā) is faulty, imputes an equal fault to the refutation as well, the fault becomes equal because of his acceptance of the opponent's position.
...because of accepting the opponent's position while raising a consequence (*prasañjayataḥ*).

Just as, for example, when one accepts that the opponent's refutation is faulty and then raises the same consequence of fault even in the counter-refutation (*pratiṣedhavipratiṣedhe*), it results in the admission of the opponent's view (*matānujñā*);
likewise, when one accepts that the [proponent's] proof (*sthāpanā*) is faulty and then raises the same fault even in the refutation, it results in the admission of the opponent's view.
This indeed is the sixth position.

Among them, the first, third, and fifth positions belong to those who argue for establishment by means of a reason; the second, fourth, and sixth positions belong to those who argue for negation by means of a reason.
When their validity or invalidity is being examined, since there is no difference in meaning between the fourth and sixth [alternatives], the fault of tautology (punarukta) follows.

Regarding the fourth alternative, it is stated that the opponent shares the same fault: "In the case of a counter-refutation, the fault is like the fault in the original refutation. Regarding the sixth as well, it is stated that they share the same fault: "Because one accepts the fault in the opponent's position, the fault is the same. Thus, in both cases, the sharing of the same fault is asserted.
There is no difference in meaning whatsoever;
for the consequence of the fault of redundancy applies equally to both the third and the fifth [positions],
since even in the case of the third position, equality is admitted on the grounds that "the same fault exists even in the case of a negation."
Even in the fifth position, it is accepted that "in the case of a counter-refutation, the same fault arises," and no specific difference in meaning is stated. Therefore,
since there is no difference in meaning between the fifth and sixth positions, the fault of redundancy follows.

In the sixfold debate (*ṣaṭpakṣī*), both [the proponent and the opponent] fail to establish their positions: in the third and fourth [turns], there is the admission of the opponent's view; in the first and second, there is an absence of a distinguishing reason (*viśeṣahetu*).
When does the sixfold debate occur?
When [the argument] proceeds thus, "The same fault applies even in the case of a negation," then there is a failure to establish either of the two positions.

However, when the third position is joined by the statement, "If there were a difference in the effect, effort would not be its cause, because the grounds for non-perception are present," [then the argument holds].
If the third position is tenable,

then because of the statement of a specific reason— namely, "the sound acquires its own nature immediately after effort, it is not a manifestation"— the first position is established, and thus the "sixfold debate" (ṣaṭpakṣī) does not proceed. //43//
Thus ends the first Āhnika of the fifth Adhyāya in the Nyāyabhāṣya of the venerable Vātsyāyana.
[Now begins] the second Āhnika of the fifth Adhyāya of the Nyāyadarśana.
It was stated briefly that there is a multiplicity of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) due to the various conceptualizations regarding misconception and non-comprehension;
that [multiplicity] must now be analyzed.

Indeed, the points of defeat—objects of loss and bases for transgression—are generally dependent upon the members of the syllogism, such as the proposition (*pratijñā*), and they apply to both the proponent of truth and the proponent of untruth.
Generally... they converge [upon these].
Their classification is as follows:

*Nyāyasūtra* 5.2.1: loss of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*), shifting the proposition (*pratijñāntara*), contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*), abandoning the proposition (*pratijñāsannyāsa*), and providing a different reason (*hetvantara*).

The points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) are: shifting the subject (*arthāntara*), the meaningless (*nirarthaka*), the unintelligible (*avijñātārtha*), the irrelevant (*apārthaka*), the mistimed (*aprāptakāla*), the deficient (*nyūna*), the redundant (*adhika*), the repetitive (*punarukta*), failure to restate (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), lack of understanding (*ajñāna*), lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), admission of one's own position (*matānujñā*), neglecting to censure when it is required (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*), censuring when it is not required (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), deviating from an accepted tenet (*apasiddhānta*), and fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
These [fallacies] are divided into twenty-two types and are characterized as follows:
*Nyāyasūtra* 5.2.2: "The abandonment of one's own proposition (*pratijñāhāni*) occurs when one admits the property of the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) into one's own example (*svadṛṣṭānta*)."

*Pratijñāhāni* (abandonment of the proposition) occurs when, while an opponent has countered with a property contrary to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), one concedes that the property of the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭāntadharma*) applies to one's own example (*svadṛṣṭānta*).

An illustration: When it has been stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses, like a pot," another person objects: "Perceptibility is observed in the universal (*sāmānya*), which is eternal;
why then is sound not likewise [eternal]? When thus countered, [the original proponent] says this: [and thereby abandons his proposition].
When [the opponent] has thus countered, he says:
"If the universal (*sāmānya*) perceived by the senses were eternal, then let it be that the jar is eternal.
Indeed, by thus attributing eternity to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) of the proponent, he abandons his very thesis (*pakṣa*) up to its conclusion.
It is said that by abandoning the thesis (pakṣa), one abandons the proposition (pratijñā), because the thesis is the locus of the proposition. //2//
NyS 5.2.3: When the meaning of the proposition has been refuted, the statement of another purpose based on a modification of the property is "shifting the proposition" (pratijñāntara).

When the proposition "sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses, like a pot" has been stated, there is a refutation of this by means of a counter-example, which constitutes a deviation of the reason— namely, that "the universal (sāmānya) is perceptible by the senses and yet eternal.
And when there is such a refutation of the proposed meaning, [it is called *pratijñāsaṃnyāsa*].

Regarding the phrase "due to the difference in properties" (*dharmavikalpāt*): when there is a similarity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*), there is a distinction in their properties. [For instance,] the universal (*sāmānya*) is perceptible by the senses and all-pervading (*sarvagata*), whereas a jar is perceptible by the senses but not all-pervading.
The "specification of that purpose" (*tadarthanirdeśa*) is for the sake of establishing the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*).
How so? Just as a jar is indeed not all-pervading, so too is sound not all-pervading; and just like a jar, it is likewise impermanent.
In that case, "sound is impermanent" is the first thesis, and "it is not omnipresent" is the second thesis; this is a change of thesis (*pratijñāntara*).
How then can it be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)?
A further proposition is not the proof of the original proposition;
rather, the reason and the example are the proof of the proposition.
Therefore, this employment of what is not a proof is useless.
Futility is a point of defeat. //3//
