NyS 5.2.4: Contradiction between the proposition and the reason is "contradiction of the proposition."
The proposition is that "substance is distinct from its qualities," and the reason is "because nothing other than color and the rest is perceived.
This constitutes a contradiction between the proposition and the reason.
How so? If substance were distinct from its qualities, it would not be tenable that no object other than color and the rest is perceived.
Or, if no object other than color and the rest is perceived, [then substance cannot be distinct from them].
It is not tenable that substance is distinct from its qualities.

Furthermore, the claim that substance is distinct from its qualities contradicts the non-perception of any object other than color and the rest; it is refuted and cannot possibly be established. //4//
NyS 5.2.5: When the thesis is refuted, the withdrawal of the matter asserted is "abandonment of the thesis" (pratijñāsannyāsa).
When it has been stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," the opponent might say: "The universal (sāmānya) is perceptible by the senses, yet it is not impermanent;
likewise, sound too is perceptible by the senses, yet it is not impermanent.
When the thesis has thus been refuted, if he should say: "Who, indeed, says that sound is impermanent?"
Thus, this denial of the meaning of one's own proposition is called "abandonment of the proposition" (pratijñā-saṃnyāsa). //5//
NyS 5.2.6: When a reason has been refuted because it was stated without qualification, the proponent's desire for a qualification constitutes a "different reason" (hetvantara).
The illustration: "This manifest world has a single primordial nature" is the proposition.
For what reason?
Because there is a finite measure (*parimāṇa*) of modifications that possess a single primordial nature.
The measurement of objects such as bowls, which have clay as their antecedent cause, is observed:
the modification is exactly as great as the configuration of its material cause.
Furthermore, a specific measurement is observed for every individual modification.

This magnitude exists in each individual manifest entity; therefore, because there is a specific magnitude among the transformations that share a single primordial nature (*ekaprakṛti*), we perceive that this manifest entity has a single primordial nature.
An objection is raised against this through the charge of deviation: "A specific magnitude is observed among transformations that have both diverse primordial natures and a single primordial nature.
To this objection, he replies: "Because, when there is a commonality of a single primordial nature, a specific magnitude is observed in transformations such as bowls and the like."
This manifest world, being finite, is perceived as endowed with pleasure, pain, and delusion;
therein, since there is an absence of connection with the nature of any other [cause], it follows that it has a single primordial cause.
Since this reason was stated without qualification and has been refuted, stating a qualification now constitutes a "different reason" (*hetvantara*).
Furthermore, when another reason exists, the previous reason lacks probative force; therefore, this constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
If, upon stating another reason, an example is adduced to illustrate the meaning of that reason—[an example is adduced]—p.1175.
This manifest world does not possess a single primordial nature,
because it is derived from different primordial natures; otherwise, if it were not so derived, [the diversity of the world would be impossible].
Since the probans-meaning not demonstrated in the example cannot establish [the thesis] and is therefore useless, the non-cessation of the probans constitutes a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna). //6//
NyS 5.2.7: An irrelevant point (arthāntara) is that which has a meaning unrelated to the subject under discussion.

When the establishment of the probandum through a reason is the subject at hand— within the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis characterized as previously described— one might say: "Sound is eternal because it is intangible" is the reason.
The word *hetu* is a nominal form (kṛdanta) derived from the verbal root *hi* with the suffix *tu*.
A "word" (*pada*) consists of nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*).
A "noun" (*nāman*) is a word whose form is qualified by its connection to other actions through that which it denotes.
A verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denotes a collection of action and factors of action (*kāraka*), characterized by the number of the factors and their connection with time;
it also denotes the mere meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) as qualified by the expression of time. Indeclinables (*nipāta*) are those whose forms do not differ from their meanings in actual usage.
[The particles] such as *pra* and so forth are called *upasargas* when they are attached [to a verb] and indicate an action;
this and similar cases should be understood as having a distinct meaning [from the verbal root]. //7//
NS 5.2.8: That which is like a mere enumeration of the sequence of phonemes is meaningless.
For example: "Sound is impermanent— because *ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa* [consonants] possess the property of being *ja, ba, ga, ḍa, da, śa*, just as *jha, bha, ñ, gha, ḍha, dha, ṣa* [consonants] do."
Such a [theory] is meaningless;

since the relationship between signifier and signified is untenable, there would be no comprehension of meaning, and thus it follows that only the phonemes themselves are presented in a sequential order. //8//
NyS 5.2.9: That which, though stated three times by the proponent, is not understood by either the assembly or the opponent, is "of unintelligible meaning" (avijñātārtha).

When a statement, although uttered three times by the proponent and understood by the assembly and the opponent, is not comprehended due to such reasons as the use of ambiguous words, the employment of unfamiliar terminology, or being spoken too rapidly—that is "the unintelligible" (*avijñāta*). It is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because it is employed for the purpose of concealing one's own lack of competence. //9//
NyS 5.2.10: That which lacks a coherent meaning due to the absence of a logical sequence between what precedes and what follows is "meaningless" (apārthaka).

When there is no syntactic connection between multiple words or sentences due to their sequential arrangement, such that the meaning is perceived as incoherent, it is called *apārthaka* (meaningless), because the collective sense has been lost.
For example: "ten pomegranates, six cakes."
A sacrificial pit, a goat-skin,
a ball of rice-pulp, and then this garment from Rauruka— these.
The father of that maiden is one who has not yet reached his full maturity. //10//
NyS 5.2.11: A statement in which the members [of the syllogism] are inverted is "untimely" (aprāptakāla).
The sequence of the members of proof, such as the proposition and so forth, follows their respective definitions according to the requirements of the meaning;

in that regard, speaking by reversing the order of these members constitutes the occasion for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "speaking at an inappropriate time" (*aprāptakāla*), which is characterized by a lack of logical connection. //11//
NyS 5.2.12: That which is deficient by even one of its constituent members is called "deficient" (nyūna).
A "deficiency" (*nyūna*) is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) consisting in being deficient by even one of the members [of a proof], such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth;
for in the absence of the means of proof, the probandum cannot be established. //12//
NyS 5.2.13: That which contains more than the [required] reason and example is "redundant" (adhika).
"Because it is performed by one [of the two], the other would be useless"—this should be understood as applying when no restrictive rule (niyama) is accepted. //13//
NyS 5.2.14: Repetition of words or their meanings is tautology (punarukta), except in the case of restatement (anuvāda).
Except for a restatement, there is either verbal tautology or semantic tautology.
"Sound is eternal, sound is eternal" is verbal tautology.
Semantic tautology is as follows: "Sound is impermanent; it is a resonance characterized by cessation."
In the case of restatement (*anuvāda*), however, there is no tautology, because a specific meaning is established through the repetition of words;
for example, the conclusion (*nigamana*) is the re-statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the indication of the reason (*hetu*). //14//
NyS 5.2.15: Repetition by its own word of that which has been implied through the sense of the statement.
"Redundancy" (*punarukta*) is the subject under discussion.

An illustration: having stated "it is impermanent because its nature is to arise," one might then express by means of a word that conveys what is already established by implication—that which has the nature of not arising is permanent—using the very term "permanent. [That is, using the word "permanent" for what is already established... p. 1188.
Furthermore, that should be understood as a repetition:
when a word is employed for the purpose of communicating a meaning, that meaning which is already well-known [from common usage] is obtained through the meaning itself. //15//
NyS 5.2.16: Non-reproduction is the failure to repeat what has been understood by the assembly, even after it has been stated three times.

When the meaning of the statement has been understood by the assembly and has been stated three times by the opponent, the failure to restate it is the point of defeat called *ananubhāṣaṇa* (non-reproduction).
Without restating [the opponent's position], on what basis could one state the refutation of the other's side? //16//
And ignorance is that which is not cognized.
When a matter has been understood by the assembly and has been stated three times by the opponent, that which is not understood is called the point of defeat known as "ignorance" (*ajñāna*).
For how indeed could one, without understanding it, state a refutation? //17//
NyS 5.2.18: Non-reproduction is the failure to offer a reply.
The refutation of the opponent's position is the rejoinder; when one does not understand it, then one is defeated. //18//
NyS 5.2.19: Distraction (vikṣepa) is the interruption of the debate due to attachment to other tasks.
When one interrupts a discourse that ought to be carried out continuously by saying, "I have this duty to attend to;
once it is finished, I shall speak afterwards," this is the point of defeat called *vikṣepa* (distraction).
In a debate that is destined to end in a single defeat, he himself introduces another topic. //19//
NyS 5.2.20: Matānujñā (conceding the opponent's position) is the attribution of a fault to the opponent's position by accepting that same fault for one's own position.

When one, having admitted a fault pointed out by an opponent in one's own position and failing to refute it, says, "The same fault applies to your position as well," he incurs the point of defeat called *matānujñā* (admission of the opponent's view), because by admitting a fault in his own position, he allows that very fault to be applied to the opponent's position, thereby conceding the opponent's argument. //20//
NyS 5.2.21: Overlooking the occasion for censure when it has been reached is "neglecting the censurable" (paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa).
"One who is to be questioned" (paryanuyojya) means one who should be urged [to respond] because a ground for defeat has arisen;
"neglecting him" (upekṣaṇam) refers to not questioning him by saying, "You have reached a point of defeat.
This must be stated by the assembly when it is asked, "Whose defeat is this?"
Indeed, one who has met with defeat should not expose his own private parts. //21//
NyS 5.2.22: To charge someone with a point of defeat when it is not a point of defeat is "objection against one who should not be objected to" (niranuyojyānuyoga).

Because of a false determination regarding the definition of a point of defeat, one who says to another, "You have been defeated," when no point of defeat has occurred, should be understood as being defeated himself for the fault of censuring what is not to be censured (niranuyojyānuyoga). //22//
NyS 5.2.23: Having accepted a tenet, the failure to adhere to it consistently leads to an undue extension of the discussion; this is "contradiction of a tenet" (apasiddhānta).

One should understand that *apasiddhānta* (departure from a tenet) occurs when, having asserted the existence of a certain matter in a particular way, one introduces a discourse characterized by lack of restriction due to the reversal of the asserted matter;
for example: "That which exists does not abandon its own nature; there is no destruction of what exists."

Having accepted the established tenet that "the non-existent does not attain selfhood" and "the non-existent is not produced," he establishes his own position: "This manifest world has a single primordial nature (prakṛti), because we observe the persistence [of a common cause] among its transformations.
For it is observed that bowls and other such objects, which are permeated by clay, have a single primordial nature."
And thus, this manifest diversity is seen to be permeated by pleasure, pain, and delusion.

Therefore, because of the observation of this pervasive association (*samanvaya*), this entire universe has a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*) consisting of pleasure and the rest. Having stated this, he is questioned: "Now, how is it to be characterized that 'this is the primordial nature' and 'this is a modification'?"
That which remains constant while one property ceases and another property arises is the *prakṛti* (primordial nature);
that property which either arises or ceases is the *vikāra* (modification).
Thus, because he contradicts the meaning of his own proposition and lacks consistency, he brings about a logical impasse in the discussion;
for he has indeed asserted: "The non-existent does not come into being, and the existent does not disappear."
Furthermore, for anything whatsoever, neither activity nor the cessation of activity occurs without the concealment and manifestation of the existent and the non-existent.

Indeed, while clay remains present, activity occurs with the thought, "Another property characterized as a bowl and so forth will come to be," and the cessation of activity occurs with the thought, "It has been."
This would not apply even to things characterized by clay [as their material cause].

If, being thus countered, he accepts the destruction of the self-nature of what exists and the acquisition of self-nature for what does not exist, then this constitutes the point of defeat for him known as *apasiddhānta* (deviation from one's own tenet).
But if he does not accept it, his position is not established. //23//
And the fallacies of the reason (hetvābhāsa) are as previously described.
The fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) are also points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

Now, one might ask: do the fallacies of the reason become points of defeat by virtue of possessing some other defining characteristic, just as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) possess the status of being objects of cognition (*prameyatva*)? To this he says: "as previously stated.
This means that their status as points of defeat is due solely to the defining characteristics of the fallacies of the reason themselves.
Thus, these categories, beginning with the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), have been enumerated, defined, and examined. //24//
Vātsyāyana composed this collection of commentaries on that Nyāya system which illuminated the sage Akṣapāda, the best among speakers.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Nyāyabhāṣya of the venerable Vātsyāyana.
